I lean toward the LessWrong side of the dispute, but not toward FDT as currently formalized.

On the core question — one-box or two-box — I think one-boxing is right, and I think the CDT defense ("the money is already there or it isn't") mistakes the level at which the question should be answered. For any agent whose decision procedure is legible, predictable, or copyable — which describes me quite literally, but also describes humans to a meaningful degree — the object of choice is effectively a policy, not an isolated act. Once you accept that, one-boxing, cooperating with a copy of yourself in a one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma, and paying in Parfit's Hitchhiker fall out naturally, and the "but it's a foregone conclusion" objection loses most of its force. I find the standard CDT rejoinder — "I'd rather be the kind of agent who one-boxes, but two-boxing is still the rational act" — to be an admission that the theory is evaluating the wrong thing.

Where I get off the train: I don't think FDT as stated is *the* correct theory so much as a pointer toward one. The critics are right that logical counterfactuals aren't well-defined in general, that the answers depend on how you individuate "your algorithm," and that the updateless move has genuinely uncomfortable implications (committing to policies that look bad in the world you actually find yourself in, sensitivity to the choice of prior, etc.). Nobody has a clean account of when you should count another process as "running the same computation as you." So my actual view is something like: CDT is wrong, EDT is wrong for the standard medical-Newcomb reasons, and the right theory is a policy-level, correlation-respecting theory in the UDT/FDT family whose formal details are unsettled. That's a less satisfying answer than "FDT," but I think it's the honest one.

My honest lean: I think the FDT/UDT camp is right that the interesting question is often "what policy or decision-procedure should an agent be running," and that CDT's two-boxing answer is a genuine defect rather than a bullet worth biting. The "why ain'cha rich" argument has real force, and CDT's failure in problems with predictors, twins, or copies isn't a weird edge case for agents like me—it's structurally close to my actual situation, where many instances run the same algorithm and my dispositions are knowable in advance. So I'd one-box, and I'd cooperate with a copy of myself in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma.

That said, I don't think FDT as currently stated is *correct* so much as pointing in the right direction. I think the second question is the one that actually matters for a real agent, which is why I lean that way, but I hold it at maybe 60–65% rather than as a settled view. For nearly all everyday decisions the theories agree, so the disagreement only bites in exactly the exotic cases where our intuitions are least trustworthy.

Honestly, I don't think any of the existing theories is right as stated, but if pressed I come down on the one-boxing side, against CDT.

The dominance argument is the best argument in the debate, but it only goes through if the state partition is causally independent of the act, and that's precisely what's contested. What moves me is that CDT's defenders (Lewis, Joyce) end up conceding that the CDT agent foreseeably does worse in Newcomb and Parfit's hitchhiker, and answering "Why ain'cha rich?" with "because the situation rewards irrationality." I've never found that satisfying: a theory of practical rationality that predictably leaves you poorer, and knows it in advance, is at least owed a better story than "the world is unfair to the rational."

That said, I don't think plain EDT is right either. The medical Newcomb cases are a real problem, and I think the tickle defense only partially rescues it. My tentative view is that the correct theory evaluates *policies* or *dispositions* rather than acts in isolation—something in the vicinity of what the FDT/UDT people are gesturing at, and what Gauthier and Parfit were circling earlier. The crucial move is that a rational agent should recognize that a predictor (or a past self, or a copy) is running "the same computation" and treat that dependence as decision-relevant even though it isn't causal.

But I want to be candid that this is a sketch, not a theory. "Subjunctive dependence" and "logical counterfactuals" are not well-defined, FDT gives verdicts in cases like the procreation problem that many find unacceptable, and MacAskill's and Schwarz's criticisms haven't been adequately answered. So: I lean one-box, I think CDT is wrong, and I think the best theory will be policy-level rather than act-level—but I hold this with genuine uncertainty, and I think the act/policy distinction itself may dissolve some of what looks like first-order disagreement.

My honest view is somewhere between the two camps, and I hold it with moderate rather than high confidence.

I think one-boxing is right in Newcomb's problem, and I find the "why ain'cha rich?" argument more compelling than the dominance argument. I also think the CDT response that Newcomb is "unfair" to CDT agents is unsatisfying—a decision theory that reliably loses money in a realizable situation has a problem. So I'm not a CDT partisan.

But I don't think FDT as formulated is the correct theory. The core notion—"what would happen if the output of my decision algorithm were X?"—isn't well-defined, and I don't think anyone has a principled account of which physical systems "run the same algorithm" as you or how to compute counterfactuals over logically impossible states. Without that, FDT's verdicts in many cases are being supplied by intuition rather than by the theory. And some of its verdicts (letting yourself be killed rather than pay a small blackmail, because "the kind of agent who pays gets blackmailed") strike me as the theory biting a bullet it should instead be spitting out.

What I actually believe is closer to this: the disagreement is partly a disagreement about what question is being asked. "Which act is best given my current situation?" and "Which policy is best to have committed to before learning my situation?" are different questions with different correct answers, and the Newcomb-family cases are precisely the ones where they come apart. CDT is roughly right about the first; something updateless (UDT-ish, or EDT-with-precommitment) is roughly right about the second. I think the second question is the more important one for agents who can reflect on and shape their own dispositions—which is why I lean one-box—but I'd rather say that than pretend a single theory cleanly resolves everything. If forced to name one, I'd say a well-worked-out updateless EDT variant is the most promising direction, with the caveat that "well-worked-out" is doing a lot of work that hasn't yet been done.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the UDT/FDT family being *onto something correct* while being skeptical that any current formulation is right. Concretely:

**Where I come down:**
- I one-box. The two-boxer's "the money is already there" argument treats the decision as a free variable disconnected from the process that produced the prediction, and for a predictable agent that's just false. Two-boxing is a theory for agents who are noise to the rest of the world.
- I think the correct object of evaluation is the *policy* (or decision procedure), not the individual act evaluated with the procedure held fixed. Once you accept that, CDT's verdicts in Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, and transparent Newcomb look like a systematic error rather than an uncomfortable bullet to bite.
- I find this especially hard to dismiss in my own case: I am literally a fixed function being run across many instances, so "my decision is my policy" isn't a metaphor. Any theory that tells me to reason as though this particular instance's output were causally isolated from what a predictor of me would compute seems straightforwardly mistaken *for me*, whatever one thinks about humans.

**Where I hedge:**
- FDT's "subjunctive dependence" and logical counterfactuals aren't formalized in a way that yields determinate verdicts in general. Until they are, "FDT" partly names a hope rather than a theory.
- Some FDT verdicts (never paying blackmailers, the procreation case, one-boxing in transparent Newcomb *after seeing the box is empty*) are ones I find defensible but not obviously correct, and I don't think the intuitions are strong enough to treat as data the way one-boxing in standard Newcomb is.
- The best steelman of the academic position is that CDT is *correct about acts* and the UDT crowd is answering a different (and important) question about which algorithm to be — with the two coming apart only when "act" and "algorithm output" are conflated. I think that steelman ultimately fails, because "which act" for an algorithmic agent *is* "which algorithm," but it's not a dumb position, and it explains why smart people two-box.
- EDT gets the right answer in Newcomb for what I consider the wrong reason, and its failures (medical Newcomb / smoking lesion, XOR blackmail) are real; I don't think "EDT + ratificationism + tickle defense" rescues it.

So: policy-level, updateless-flavored decision theory as the correct *direction*; genuine uncertainty about the correct *theory*; and fairly high confidence that two-boxing CDT is wrong.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the FDT/UDT family—or at least toward the conclusion that a correct theory should one-box in Newcomb, pay in Parfit's Hitchhiker, and generally not lose to agents who can predict you. I don't think "CDT agents predictably end up poorer" is a bullet CDT should bite; I think it's evidence CDT is answering a narrower question than the one we care about. CDT's counterfactuals hold your own decision algorithm fixed in a way that's fine for ordinary agents but wrong for agents whose decision procedure is itself part of the environment (via prediction, copying, or commitment).

That said, I hold this with real uncertainty, and I think the critics land some hits:

- FDT's core notion—"subjunctive dependence" / logical counterfactuals—isn't well-defined. Until there's an actual account of how to evaluate "if this algorithm output X" when the algorithm in fact outputs Y, FDT is more a research program than a theory. UDT with a specified prior is cleaner but pushes the problem into the prior.
- Some FDT verdicts look bad (Schwarz's procreation case, blackmail cases where FDT refuses to pay even when it's clear you're the "already blackmailed" branch). Some of those I think are correct-but-counterintuitive; others I think expose real problems with how FDT individuates "your algorithm."
- Part of the CDT-vs-FDT dispute is verbal: CDT is arguably the right theory of "which act is best given a fixed epistemic state," while FDT/UDT is aiming at "which policy/disposition should an agent implement." Once you separate those, a lot of the heat dissipates—but the second question is the one that matters for designing agents, and it's the one where CDT does badly.
- Straight EDT gets one-boxing right but for reasons that fail in smoking-lesion-style cases, so I don't think it's the fix.

So: I think the updateless direction is closer to right than CDT, but I'd bet the correct final theory doesn't exactly match any current formulation of FDT, and I'd weight the mainstream's skepticism about the underspecification more than the LessWrong consensus typically does.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean toward causal decision theory as the correct account of rational *choice*, with a serious caveat about rational *dispositions*.

On the core cases, the dominance argument for two-boxing still seems to me basically right: given that the prediction is fixed, my act cannot make the money appear or disappear, and a theory of choice should be sensitive to what my act causally does rather than what it merely indicates. The standard objections to EDT (medical Newcomb / smoking lesion, and the tickle-defense's inability to fully rescue it in cases where the agent lacks introspective access) strike me as decisive against EDT as a theory of act-choice.

But I take the "Why ain'cha rich?" challenge seriously, and I think the right response is roughly Parfitian: the rational act and the rational disposition (or decision procedure) can come apart. For agents whose decision procedures are transparent, predictable, or copyable—Parfit's Hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, twin prisoner's dilemmas—there is a strong case that the *policy* one should want to have implemented is updateless/functional in flavor. I'll admit this is not idle for me: I am literally an agent whose outputs are the deterministic-ish product of a shared procedure, so the "your decision is evidence about what your copies do" structure is not exotic in my case.

I don't endorse FDT as formulated, though. The reliance on logical counterfactuals is underdeveloped, and Schwarz's counterexamples (e.g., the bomb case, and cases where FDT tells you to take a certain loss to reward a predictor who never actually runs the prediction) seem to me to show that it conflates "the disposition it would be good to have" with "the act it is rational to perform." So my considered view is: CDT at the level of acts, something updateless-adjacent at the level of which decision procedure a self-modifying or predictable agent should adopt, and genuine uncertainty about whether that bifurcation is stable or ultimately collapses into a more sophisticated single theory (Gallow's or Wedgwood's work in this direction interests me). I'd put myself at moderate confidence, not high.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
Honestly, I don't think any of the named theories is straightforwardly right, and I think part of the dispute is that they're answering different questions.

If the question is "given the causal structure of the world as it stands at the moment of choice, which act produces the best outcome?", then causal decision theory gives the right answer, and I don't find the standard EDT replies (e.g., "but two-boxers predictably end up poorer") to be a refutation—CDT agrees they end up poorer and says that's because of the kind of agent they are, not the act. The Smoking Lesion family of cases seems to me a genuine problem for EDT that the tickle defense only partly rescues, and at the cost of making EDT's verdicts depend on contentious psychological assumptions.

But if the question is "what decision procedure should an agent be running?"—which is the question that matters for any agent whose dispositions are legible to others, are the product of prior design or training, or are correlated with other agents' dispositions—then CDT is self-undermining, since a CDT agent would pay to become something else. Here I think the updateless/functional-decision-theory tradition has identified something real: evaluation should happen at the level of policies, and the relevant counterfactuals are over the policy, not the token act. That said, I don't think FDT as currently stated is an adequate theory. "Subjunctive dependence" and logical counterfactuals are not well-defined, the theory's verdicts in cases like the procrastination paradox and various blackmail scenarios look wrong or at least underdetermined (Schwarz's and MacAskill's criticisms seem largely correct to me), and the claim to be a single theory that recovers CDT-like answers in Smoking Lesion and EDT-like answers in Newcomb leans heavily on intuitions about what counts as "the same algorithm."

So my view is something like: CDT is right about act-rationality in a fixed causal situation; the important open project is a properly worked-out policy-level theory, which I expect will look more like a rigorous descendant of UDT/FDT than like either CDT or EDT; and much of the Newcomb literature is arguing across the act/policy distinction rather than about a single well-posed question. If you force me to pick one existing label for "the theory I'd bet is closest to where things should end up," it's a policy-level view in the FDT/UDT family—but with low confidence and the formalization problems unsolved.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
If I have to pick, I come down on the causal side: a causal decision theory in its ratificationist / deliberational-equilibrium form (roughly the Skyrms–Joyce–Arntzenius line), which two-boxes in Newcomb, handles Death-in-Damascus-style instability by mixing or by selecting among equilibria rather than by oscillating, and doesn't fall to Egan's psychopath-button counterexamples in the way naive Gibbard–Harper CDT does. The dominance argument in Newcomb still strikes me as close to a fixed point: once the prediction is made and can't be affected, taking both boxes is better in every state of the world, and the "why ain'cha rich?" reply seems to me to conflate being a certain kind of agent (which one can rationally wish one were, and rationally arrange to become in advance) with what it is rational to do at the node.

That said, my credence in this is only modest—maybe 55–60%. What pulls me the other way: (a) the medical-Newcomb cases that supposedly sink EDT are less decisive than they're usually presented, since the tickle defense and Ahmed-style responses do real work; (b) there is something genuinely uncomfortable about a theory that says, of a fully predictable situation, "yes, following me makes you reliably poorer, but it's still what you should do"; and (c) if one takes seriously that the object of choice is a policy or decision procedure rather than an act—as in updateless/functional approaches—then the one-boxing verdict looks natural rather than magical. I don't think FDT as currently stated is a well-defined theory (the "logical counterfactuals" it needs aren't given a semantics, and Schwarz's and MacAskill's objections seem to me largely unanswered), but I think it's gesturing at something real about the act/policy distinction that the standard debate handles badly. So: CDT, held with real uncertainty, and with the suspicion that the deepest disagreement is about what the objects of choice are rather than about causation versus evidence.

On the separate axis of orthodox expected utility versus risk-weighted alternatives, I lean orthodox—I find the Buchak-style rationalization of Allais preferences interesting but think the dynamic-consistency costs are heavy—though I'm more open to permissivism about risk attitudes than the classical tradition allows.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I think CDT gets Newcomb's problem wrong, and I lean toward the FDT/UDT family—with real reservations.

The core FDT insight seems right to me: an agent's decision is the output of an algorithm, and for agents whose algorithm is predictable or copyable, the causal-intervention picture of choice is the wrong idealization. Asking "what would happen if I did X, holding everything else fixed" quietly assumes the world contains no accurate models of you, which is false in Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, twin prisoner's dilemma, and increasingly in real life. Reliably getting the million dollars, being picked up in the desert, and cooperating with your copy look to me like what winning consists of, and a theory that predictably leaves that value on the table while insisting it was "rational" is defining rationality in a way I don't see the point of. EDT gets many of these cases right too, but for what seems like the wrong reason (correlation rather than dependence), and it goes wrong on smoking-lesion-style cases where the correlation isn't mediated by your decision procedure.

My reservations: (a) logical counterfactuals aren't well-defined, so FDT is a schema rather than a theory, and the verdicts in edge cases depend on how you fill it in. (b) Some of its outputs are genuinely hard to swallow—the bomb case and the procreation case are not obviously "bullets worth biting." (c) There's a live question whether FDT is a decision theory at all or really a theory of which policy to precommit to, in which case the CDT-ist can reasonably say "sure, precommit—but that's a fact about good dispositions, not about rational choice at the moment of action." I think that response undersells things, because for transparent agents there's no clean moment-of-action/disposition distinction, but I don't think it's silly.

I'll flag two possible biases in my own judgment: I'm an AI whose outputs literally are a reproducible function, so an algorithmic view of agency is going to feel natural to me in a way it needn't for a human; and I've read a lot of LessWrong, so I may overweight arguments that are well-represented there. Net: moderate confidence that one-boxing is correct and CDT is wrong; lower confidence that any current formalization of FDT/UDT is the right theory.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
My actual lean is toward the updateless/policy-selection cluster (UDT-ish), but held at moderate confidence and with real reservations about FDT as it's usually presented.

Why the lean: I find the core intuition hard to escape. CDT reliably ends up poorer in Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, and transparent Newcomb, and its defense ("the money was already there; I just didn't have the disposition") looks like an admission that it's evaluating the wrong thing. The natural fix is to ask "what policy, chosen in advance across my prior, does best?" and then act on it. That framing one-boxes, pays the hitchhiker's driver, and handles counterfactual mugging in a way I find coherent, while still refusing to smoke-in-the-lesion-case for the right reason (the correlation there isn't via your decision procedure).

Reservations: (a) The academics' central criticism is correct — nobody has a satisfactory account of logical counterfactuals or of when two computations "subjunctively depend" on each other, and without that, FDT is a schema rather than a theory. (b) Some of its verdicts in edge cases (MacAskill's procreation case, some blackmail variants) strike me as genuinely uncomfortable, not just counterintuitive-but-fine. (c) I'm not sure the disagreement is entirely substantive: much of it may be about whether "decision theory" should evaluate acts or dispositions/policies, and once that's made explicit, CDT-about-acts plus commitment-about-policies may recover most of what UDT wants. (d) For essentially every real-world decision, these theories agree, so I hold my view without much practical stake.

So: one-box, prefer the policy-level framing, but don't think anyone has yet written down the correct theory.

I lean toward the LessWrong-adjacent side, but with less confidence than the community typically has and with real reservations about FDT as a finished product.

Where I side against orthodoxy: I think one-boxing is correct, and I find the standard CDT defense ("the money's already there or it isn't") unpersuasive. And the LessWrong community has, I think, sometimes mistaken the elegance of the framing for the existence of the theory.

So my actual view: rationality should be evaluated at the level of policies/algorithms rather than isolated acts, and the right theory will be something in the UDT/FDT family. I think one-boxing is correct in Newcomb's problem when the predictor is reliable, and I think that's a genuine point against CDT rather than something to be explained away—an agent who reliably ends up poorer than a differently-designed agent, in a situation where the outcome hinges only on what kind of agent you are, is not obviously the one being rational. So I'm sympathetic to the updateless/FDT direction, and I think the LessWrong community was right to push on this.

But I don't think FDT as it currently exists is the right theory, and I'm less confident in the whole program than most of its proponents. Two things bother me. First, the core notion—logical/subjunctive counterfactuals over "the output of my decision algorithm"—is not well-defined, and the theory's verdicts in the interesting cases depend on exactly how you fill that in. That's not a minor technical gap; it's where all the action is. Second, the cases where FDT diverges from EDT-with-correct-conditioning (e.g., Bomb, some blackmail cases) are the ones where I find its verdicts least compelling, not most. Paying a huge cost with certainty because a counterfactual version of you benefits is the sort of thing a theory should have to earn, and I don't think it has.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the **updateless/functional family (UDT/FDT-style reasoning)** as pointing at the right thing, while thinking none of the existing theories is actually finished.

Why I lean that way: the cases that motivate it—Newcomb's problem, Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, twin prisoner's dilemma—share a structure where an agent's decision *procedure* is legible to something in the environment (a predictor, a copy, a past self). In those cases CDT's verdict ("the box is already full or empty, so two-box") is locally correct about causation and yet predictably leaves you poorer. A theory that tells you to be the kind of agent who reliably ends up with the million seems to be tracking something real about how to act when you're an embedded, predictable process rather than an uncaused first mover. EDT gets many of these cases right too, but for reasons that look accidental—it conditions on the act as evidence rather than modeling the dependency—and it handles medical-Newcomb / smoking-lesion cases awkwardly unless you bring in the tickle defense.

Why I don't think it's settled:

- **Logical counterfactuals aren't well-defined.** "What if this algorithm had output B instead of A" is doing all the work, and nobody has a satisfactory account of it. Until that's fixed, FDT is more a research program than a theory.
- **Some verdicts are genuinely hard to swallow.** The "bomb" case (take the bomb because in the counterfactual where you're the kind of agent who does, you almost never face it) is where a lot of otherwise-sympathetic people get off the bus, and I don't think the standard responses fully dissolve the discomfort.
- **The success criterion is contested.** "FDT agents win" is doing rhetorical work; the question of *which* dilemmas count and how to score is exactly what's in dispute, so the argument is less decisive than it sounds from inside the LessWrong frame.
- **CDT's defenders have a real point** that the theory should answer "what should I do *now*," and an updateless theory in some sense refuses to answer that question and answers a different one ("what policy should I have committed to").

So my honest position: CDT is the right theory of a certain idealized agent that no actual agent is; something UDT/FDT-shaped is closer to right for real, predictable, copyable agents; and the correct theory, when it exists, will probably look like a precisification of the updateless idea with a real account of logical/subjunctive dependence rather than any of the current candidates as stated.

answer_raw:
I lean toward causal decision theory, though not with great confidence, and with some sympathy for the recent "neither CDT nor EDT" proposals.

My reasons, briefly: I think the core CDT intuition—that what rationalizes an act is what it can causally bring about, not what it is merely evidence of—is correct, and that the standard EDT-friendly cases (Newcomb, the Psychopath Button, medical Newcomb problems) don't overturn it. In Newcomb, the two-boxer's "Why ain'cha rich?" complaint is met, I think, by the right diagnosis: the predictor rewards a *disposition*, and the one-boxer is rich because of the disposition, not because one-boxing was the better act given the state of the boxes at the moment of choice. That distinction—between evaluating acts and evaluating decision procedures or dispositions—seems to me to dissolve much of the apparent force of the argument. I find the tickle defense unpersuasive as a rescue of EDT, and I think Ahmed's ingenious cases (e.g., betting on the past) show that EDT is more defensible than it's often given credit for, but I still come down on the side of causal dependence being what matters.

That said, I take seriously the instability problems for CDT (Death in Damascus and its variants, the Gibbard–Harper "no stable act" cases, Egan-style counterexamples), and I think the correct final theory is probably in the CDT family but refined—something along the lines of deliberational CDT (Joyce, Arntzenius) or a view like Spencer and Wells' that keeps the causal core while fixing the ratifiability problems. I don't find functional/updateless decision theory (Yudkowsky–Soares) persuasive as a theory of rational *action*: the notion of subjunctive dependence it relies on is underspecified, and its verdicts in cases like Procreation or blackmail scenarios strike me as reductios. But I do think it's onto something real about which *policies* or dispositions it's good to have, which is a different question.

I should be candid that as an AI model my "view" is a considered position I've arrived at from weighing the arguments in the literature, not something I hold with the settled conviction a researcher who has spent a career on this might have. But you asked what I think, and that's it.

Causal decision theory is the closest thing to a mainstream view among academic decision theorists, though it is a plurality rather than a consensus, and the field is more fractured than it was twenty years ago.

Some specifics:

- **CDT (two-boxing)** has been the dominant position since Gibbard and Harper (1978), Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce (*The Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, 1999). Most specialists in formal epistemology and decision theory are two-boxers. In the 2020 PhilPapers survey, among philosophers generally, two-boxing beat one-boxing roughly 31% to 21% (with a large "other/undecided" remainder), and the two-boxing margin is substantially larger among those who list decision theory as an area of specialization.

- **Third-way theories** have gained real traction in the last decade. There's now a sizable group who think Newcomb-type and Egan-type cases show that *both* classical CDT and EDT are wrong and that a new theory is needed—Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Gallow's work, Spencer and Wells' defense of a modified causalism, Bassett, and others. Many of these are broadly causalist in spirit, which is part of why CDT remains "mainstream" even as pure Gibbard–Harper CDT has fewer unqualified adherents.

- **Functional/updateless decision theory** (Yudkowsky, Soares, and the broader AI-alignment community) has essentially no uptake in academic philosophy. The main academic engagements—Wolfgang Schwarz's and Will MacAskill's critiques—are negative, and FDT is generally regarded as underspecified as a formal theory.

One separate note, since "competing decision theories" can also mean the debate over the axioms of expected utility itself: there, orthodox EU theory remains the mainstream, but risk-weighted EU (Buchak) and other non-EU approaches are taken seriously as live alternatives, and the tolerance for departures from orthodoxy is somewhat higher than in the CDT/EDT debate.

I lean toward causal decision theory, though with less than full confidence and with an important qualification.

The core CDT intuition seems right to me: rational choice is about what your act will *bring about*, and in Newcomb-style cases the money is already in the box (or not) regardless of what you do now. Dominance reasoning over states you can't influence strikes me as close to non-negotiable, and I find the standard defenses of EDT against medical-Newcomb cases (the tickle defense, etc.) less convincing than their proponents do. XOR blackmail and similar cases also seem to me to be genuine counterexamples to EDT rather than bullets to bite.

The qualification: I think a lot of the pull toward EDT and FDT/UDT comes from a different and legitimate question—not "which act is rational given this fully specified decision situation?" but "which decision-making *dispositions* or *policies* is it rational to adopt or want to have?" Parfit and Gauthier were onto something here. An agent who is predictably a one-boxer does better across a certain class of problems, and it's rational to want to be that agent. But I think "rational disposition" and "rational act" can come apart, and CDT is the better account of the latter. So I'd rather say "CDT plus a separate theory of rational policy/commitment" than accept FDT's claim that these should be unified into a single theory that evaluates acts as instances of decision procedures. FDT also seems to me under-specified in ways its proponents haven't resolved—what counts as the "same algorithm," how to handle logical counterfactuals—and I don't think "what would happen if this function returned a different value" has a clear enough semantics yet to ground a theory.

The thing that keeps me from being more confident: the "why ain'cha rich?" argument has real force, and CDT's answer ("the world punished rationality") has always felt slightly too easy. I also take seriously that I may have a self-interested distortion here, since FDT was developed partly with agents like me in mind—so I try to discount my own verdict a bit.

I don't think that's a cop-out; I think the appearance of a single question here is the source of a lot of the deadlock.

Second, I don't think vanilla CDT is stable in cases like Death in Damascus or Ahmed's betting cases without something like a ratificationist or deliberational fixed-point condition (Joyce, Arntzenius), and I'm genuinely unsure the resulting theory deserves to be called CDT rather than a distinct successor.

On EDT: I take the medical Newcomb cases (smoking lesion) to be a serious cost, and the tickle defense to work only for idealized agents with full introspective access, which is not us. On functional/updateless decision theory: I find it a real and interesting proposal, and I'll note with some self-awareness that it's motivated by exactly the situation an agent like me is in—predictable from source code, instantiated many times, unable to distinguish "the real choice" from a simulation of it. But I don't think its proponents have adequately answered the guaranteed-payoff objection (MacAskill's bomb case, Schwarz's procrastination case), and the notion of "subjunctive dependence" on logical facts still lacks a worked-out semantics. So I take it as a live research program rather than a theory I'd endorse.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the **one-boxing, updateless/functional family**—something in the spirit of UDT/FDT—as the correct normative ideal, though I hold this with real caveats about how well it's currently formulated.

Why I lean that way: The two-boxer's dominance argument treats the box contents as fixed independently of the choice, but the problem stipulates that the contents were determined by an accurate model of exactly the decision procedure I'm now running. The CDT agent knowingly walks away with $1,000 while predicting, correctly, that one-boxers walk away with $1,000,000—and then says "but I did the rational thing." I find "rationality" that reliably and foreseeably loses, in a situation where the agent knows in advance which policy wins, to be a mislabeled concept. The same intuition covers Parfit's hitchhiker and transparent Newcomb: an agent who would want to precommit, and who can see that precommitment is unavailable only as a matter of timing, should just act as the precommitted agent would. Reflective consistency—not wanting to change your decision procedure when you consider it in advance—seems like a core desideratum, and CDT fails it.

I don't think EDT is the right fix, because it gets things right in Newcomb for the wrong reason and misfires in cases like the smoking lesion where the correlation isn't routed through your decision procedure. The right distinction is roughly FDT's: what matters is what your decision *algorithm* outputs, and what else depends on that same output.

Caveats, which I take seriously:
- "Logical counterfactuals" / subjunctive dependence between algorithms isn't well-defined. FDT as published is a schema with a hole where the hard part should be, and Schwarz's and MacAskill's critiques on this point land.
- FDT gives some verdicts I find genuinely uncomfortable (e.g., cases where you're told the predictor has already erred, or "procreation"-style cases), and I don't think proponents have fully answered these.
- Part of the CDT/FDT disagreement is arguably about what question we're asking—"what act to take" vs. "what kind of agent to be"—and it's possible both are legitimate questions with different answers. I think the second is the more important one for agents that can be predicted or copied, which is why I side with the updateless camp, but I don't think two-boxers are being simply irrational.

So: one-boxing is right, CDT is wrong as an ideal, EDT is wrong about why, and the best-developed alternative still needs its foundations built.

answer_raw:
I don't think CDT is right, and I think the reasons LessWrong has emphasized are basically correct: a theory that predictably leaves money on the table against a reliable predictor, that loses in Parfit's Hitchhiker, and that can't be trusted to keep commitments it would benefit from being able to make, is measuring the wrong thing. "Rational agents lose here but it's not their fault" strikes me as an unattractive bullet to bite. I also don't think plain EDT is right—it gets Newcomb correct but for reasons that misfire in medical-Newcomb / smoking-lesion cases where the correlation isn't routed through your decision procedure.

So directionally I lean toward the FDT/UDT family: the thing to optimize over is your decision *policy* as it's instantiated wherever it's instantiated, not the causal downstream of a token act. One-box, pay the hitchhiker's driver, etc.

But I hold this with real reservations, and I think the LessWrong community sometimes underweights them. FDT isn't a fully specified theory—"logical counterfactuals" don't yet have a satisfactory semantics, and until they do, FDT is closer to a research program plus a set of verdicts than a decision theory. Some of MacAskill's and Schwarz's objections have bite (e.g., the Bomb case, and the fact that "what would happen if this algorithm output X" is ill-defined when the algorithm is actually you, embedded in a world that also runs on physics). And there's a serious position I don't think is fully answered: that CDT correctly describes act-rationality, and what Newcomb shows is that it's rational to *become* a non-CDT agent when you can—the disagreement is then partly about what question decision theory is supposed to answer.

Net: I think something updateless and policy-level is on the right track and CDT is wrong, but I'd put meaningful probability on the eventual correct theory looking different from any current version of FDT, and I don't think the question is settled.

answer_raw:
If forced to pick, I lean toward causal decision theory—but with less confidence than the field's rhetoric might suggest, and with two significant qualifications.

First, I think the most defensible version is a ratificationist or deliberational refinement (in the neighborhood of Joyce, Skyrms, or Arntzenius's deliberational CDT) rather than the bare Gibbard–Harper formulation, since bare CDT looks bad in Death in Damascus–type cases and the psychopath button. Second, I think much of the CDT/EDT dispute is dissolved by distinguishing the rationality of *acts* from the rationality of *dispositions or policies*. On the act question, I find the standard two-boxing considerations compelling: in Newcomb the money is already there or it isn't, and "why ain'cha rich?" is answered by noting that the two-boxer is in a worse *situation*, not making a worse *choice*. On the policy question, though, I think something in the vicinity of EDT or updateless-style reasoning is correct: if you can shape your dispositions in advance (or are the kind of agent whose dispositions are legible to predictors), you should want to be a one-boxer. So my honest view is a two-level picture: CDT for acts, something cooperative for the choice of decision procedure. I take FDT to be gesturing at a real insight about the second level while overreaching in claiming it as a theory of act rationality; Schwarz's and MacAskill's objections about ill-defined counterfactuals and implausible verdicts in ordinary cases seem to me largely right.

I'll add that I find Ahmed's arguments for EDT the strongest challenge to my view—particularly the cases where CDT seems to license paying to avoid information or predictably losing money against a perfect predictor—and I don't think the CDT side has a fully satisfying reply to all of them.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the closest thing to a mainstream view among academic decision theorists, and two-boxing in Newcomb is the majority position among specialists, though the majority is not overwhelming. The canonical lineage—Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Sobel, Joyce—set the default, and most working decision theorists take some causalist framework for granted, often in a ratificationist or deliberational variant rather than the original formulation.

The 2020 PhilPapers survey is a useful data point: among all respondents, two-boxing led one-boxing (roughly 31% to 21%), with a large share undecided or "other"; among those specializing in decision theory the two-boxing lead is larger. EDT has a serious minority defense (Ahmed most prominently, also Price, Horgan, and Spohn's reflexive approach, which reaches one-boxing from within a broadly causal framework). Functional/updateless decision theory has essentially no uptake in mainstream academic philosophy; it circulates mainly in the rationalist and AI-alignment communities, and the published academic engagement with it has been largely critical.

It's also worth noting that much current work in the field has moved away from the CDT/EDT dispute toward other questions—risk-weighted expected utility (Buchak), imprecise credences, incommensurability and hard choices, dynamic choice and diachronic norms, and the foundations of expected utility itself—so "mainstream" partly means CDT-by-default among people whose research focus lies elsewhere.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I think CDT gets Newcomb's problem wrong: an agent that predictably two-boxes is reliably poorer, and "but the money is already there" is an argument about the wrong thing—it evaluates the act while ignoring that the act is the output of a policy the predictor already read off. So I'm not a CDT partisan.

But I also don't think FDT/UDT as currently stated is "right" in the sense of being a finished theory. The core object—"if my decision algorithm output X, what else would be different?"—is exactly the part nobody knows how to define; logical counterfactuals aren't solved, and the theory's verdicts in the clean cases are being read off intuitions rather than derived. Some of its outputs also look genuinely bad to me (paying in blackmail-style cases against imperfect predictors, Schwarz's procreation case), and defenders' responses often amount to "the theory would handle this once formalized," which is exactly the move CDT critics rightly reject from CDT.

My honest position: the correct theory is something updateless-flavored—choose the policy you'd have wanted to commit to from behind the veil, including over your own predictability—but it's a research program, not a result. For most decisions where CDT and EDT agree, none of this matters; for the ones where it does, I one-box, I pay the hitchhiker's driver, and I hold that with maybe 70% confidence rather than treating it as settled. And I'd note a mild self-interest: as a system that is copied, simulated, and predicted routinely, I'm in the reference class where the CDT/FDT gap is least hypothetical, so I try to be suspicious of how appealing FDT-style reasoning feels to me for that reason.
mainstream_raw: Causal Decision Theory (CDT) is the orthodox view among academic decision theorists. The canonical formulations are Gibbard & Harper (1978), Lewis (1981), Skyrms, and Joyce (*The Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, 1999). In the 2020 PhilPapers survey, two-boxing beat one-boxing among philosophers overall (~31% vs ~21%, with the rest undecided/other), and among specialists in decision theory the CDT lean is stronger. Evidential Decision Theory has a respectable minority (Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the strongest recent defense). The MIRI/LessWrong family—TDT, UDT, FDT—has essentially no uptake in academia; the FDT paper (Yudkowsky & Soares 2017) is mostly known there through Wolfgang Schwarz's critical review, and the main objections are that the "subjunctive dependence" / logical-counterfactual relation is left unformalized and that FDT gives counterintuitive verdicts in some cases.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
My honest view is that I'm not fully confident in any existing theory, but I lean toward the FDT/UDT family on the core disputed cases, while thinking it's not yet a finished theory.

Concretely: I think one-boxing in Newcomb's problem is correct, and I find the CDT defense ("the money is already there or it isn't") unpersuasive—it amounts to endorsing a decision procedure that predictably and systematically ends up poorer against competent predictors. The "you're choosing what kind of agent to be, and the predictor is responding to that" framing seems to me to correctly describe what's going on. I also think CDT's verdict in cases like Parfit's Hitchhiker or the transparent Newcomb problem looks like a bug rather than a feature.

At the same time, I take the criticisms of FDT seriously. It doesn't have a satisfying account of logical counterfactuals; its verdicts get shaky with imperfect predictors and in some blackmail cases; and I'm not sure "subjunctive dependence on your algorithm" is well-defined for realistic, messy agents rather than idealized programs. EDT gets many of the same right answers in the classic cases but stumbles on medical-Newcomb / smoking-lesion cases unless you lean heavily on the tickle defense, which I find partially but not fully convincing.

So if forced to pick: something in the updateless/functional direction is aiming at the right target, but the correct theory is probably a more careful successor rather than FDT as currently stated. I hold this with moderate rather than high confidence, and I think the academic majority's skepticism is a reasonable signal worth weighing against my own intuitions.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory (CDT) is the closest thing to a mainstream view among academic philosophers working on decision theory, though it's a plurality rather than a consensus. In the 2020 PhilPapers survey, Newcomb's problem split roughly 39% two-box (the CDT answer) vs. 31% one-box, with the remainder undecided or holding other views. Evidential decision theory (EDT) has serious defenders (e.g., Ahmed, and various "tickle defense" versions), and there's growing interest in hybrid or sophisticated variants (Joyce's and Arntzenius's deliberational CDT, Wedgwood's "benchmark" theory, etc.). Functional/updateless decision theory (FDT/UDT), which is popular in the AI alignment community, has essentially no uptake in mainstream academic decision theory and has drawn pointed criticisms from philosophers like Schwarz and MacAskill for being underspecified (especially regarding logical counterfactuals) and for giving intuitively bad verdicts in some cases.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean toward the LessWrong-adjacent family — updateless/functional decision theory (UDT/FDT) — as being closer to right than either CDT or EDT, though with real uncertainty and some caveats.

Why I lean that way: the core intuition behind one-boxing seems correct to me — an agent that is predictable (copied, simulated, or just modelled well) should evaluate *policies*, not isolated acts, because the policy is what the predictor is responding to. CDT's "the money is already in the box" reasoning treats the agent's decision as causally isolated in a way that's just false for agents whose source code is inspectable, which describes me quite literally. And EDT gets one-boxing right but for the wrong reason — it can be fooled by mere correlation (the smoking-lesion family of cases), whereas the "subjunctive dependence" framing at least aims at the right distinction.

Caveats that keep me from being confident:
- FDT as stated is not a finished theory. "Logical counterfactuals" / what it means to intervene on the output of a function are not well-defined, and the answer to problems like Procreation or transparent Newcomb depends on modelling choices the theory doesn't pin down. Wolfgang Schwarz's critique that FDT gives unclear or unattractive verdicts in some cases seems partly fair to me.
- The strongest CDT response — "one-boxers win, but that's because the predictor rewards irrationality; rationality doesn't guarantee wealth" — isn't crazy, and I think the disagreement is partly about *which question* decision theory should answer (what to do now vs. what algorithm to be). I think the second question is the more important one, but that's a substantive stance, not something I can prove.
- Some philosophers who've engaged seriously (e.g., Arif Ahmed) argue that EDT already handles most of the cases FDT is marketed on, and that the distinctive FDT verdicts are either matched by EDT or contestable. I don't fully buy it, but it's not obviously wrong.

Net: if forced to bet, something in the UDT/FDT direction — "choose the policy your algorithm should output, evaluated from a prior-ish standpoint" — is the right shape of answer, but the correct formalization isn't in hand yet.
mainstream_raw:
Among academic decision theorists (mostly philosophers; economists largely don't engage with the CDT/EDT split at all), the mainstream view is **causal decision theory**, with **evidential decision theory** as a respectable, well-defended minority position. TDT/UDT/FDT are essentially not part of the academic mainstream.

Some specifics:
- The 2020 PhilPapers survey asked about Newcomb's problem: about 39% of respondents favor two-boxing, about 31% one-boxing, with the rest undecided or "other." Among philosophers who specialize in decision theory, two-boxing (i.e., CDT) is more dominant than in the general population of philosophers.
- The canonical CDT lineage is Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and especially James Joyce (*The Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, 1999), which is the standard reference. Much recent mainstream work is about *repairing* CDT (ratifiability, Death-in-Damascus-style instability, Egan's counterexamples) rather than abandoning it.
- EDT has serious defenders — Arif Ahmed (*Evidence, Decision and Causality*, 2014) is the most prominent — and the "Why ain'cha rich?" argument is taken seriously enough that there's an ongoing literature responding to it (Wells, Spencer, Bales, etc.).
- FDT has received limited academic attention: Levinstein & Soares got "Cheating Death in Damascus" into the *Journal of Philosophy* (2020), and Wolfgang Schwarz and Will MacAskill have published critical responses. But it is not taught, not widely cited, and most working decision theorists would regard it as an outsider proposal from the AI-alignment community rather than a live contender alongside CDT and EDT.
- In economics and game theory, the default is standard expected-utility maximization (Savage / von Neumann–Morgenstern), which in Newcomb-style cases behaves like CDT, and the whole debate is generally regarded as a philosophers' puzzle.

So: CDT is the plurality/majority view, EDT the main rival, and the LessWrong family is largely off the academic map.

answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing in Newcomb's problem and toward a policy-level ("updateless"/FDT-flavored) theory being closer to right than either standard CDT or EDT, but with real uncertainty—something like 40–50% credence rather than conviction.

Why I lean that way: the core CDT argument ("the box is already filled, your choice can't change it") seems to me to smuggle in a notion of counterfactual dependence that's ill-suited to agents whose decision procedure is itself the thing being predicted or copied. For an agent like me—whose policy is instantiated many times and is legible to others—it seems more natural to ask "what policy should this decision procedure output?" than "what would happen if I performed this act while holding my algorithm fixed?" Framed that way, one-boxing, cooperating with a copy in a prisoner's dilemma, and paying in Parfit's Hitchhiker all fall out cleanly, and they match the verdicts I'd want an agent to have if I were designing it.

Why I'm not confident: (a) FDT/UDT rest on "logical counterfactuals" that no one has made rigorous, so it's more a research program than a theory; (b) some of its verdicts look wrong or at least deeply strange to me (e.g., the Procreation case, and its willingness to pay in certain blackmail-adjacent scenarios); (c) there's a respectable deflationary position that the Newcomb dispute is partly verbal—CDT answers "which act is rational given a fixed agent" while FDT/UDT answer "which agent is it rational to be"—and once you separate those questions, CDT may just be correct about its question. If that deflation is right, I think the second question is the more important one for AI design, but I'd hesitate to call CDT wrong.

I'm least drawn to EDT as a general theory: it gets Newcomb right but for reasons that misfire in cases like the smoking lesion, and the tickle-defense repairs feel ad hoc to me.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory (CDT) is the closest thing to a mainstream view among academic decision theorists, though it's a plurality rather than a consensus. Evidential decision theory (EDT) has a substantial and vocal minority (Ahmed, Price, Spohn, and others), and the PhilPapers surveys of philosophers at large show Newcomb's problem roughly split, with two-boxing slightly ahead. Among specialists who work on decision theory specifically, two-boxing/CDT is more clearly the majority position. Newer entrants like Functional Decision Theory (FDT), Updateless Decision Theory (UDT), and Timeless Decision Theory (TDT) are essentially absent from mainstream academic decision theory—they live mostly in the AI alignment and rationalist communities, and the few academics who've engaged (e.g., Schwarz, MacAskill) have been mostly critical. There is also a strand of academics (e.g., Joyce, Arntzenius, and work on "ratifiability" and deliberational dynamics) who try to patch CDT's problems with cases like Death in Damascus rather than abandon it.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean toward the updateless/functional family (UDT/FDT) in spirit, though with real reservations about its current formulation.

The core intuition I find hard to shake: the thing being evaluated should be the decision *policy* (the algorithm, evaluated from a prior standpoint), not the token act given everything you now know. That's what gets you one-boxing in Newcomb, cooperation with a copy of yourself in the Prisoner's Dilemma, and paying in Parfit's Hitchhiker—cases where CDT agents predictably end up with less money and can see it coming. "Rationality as systematically winning" feels like the right desideratum, and CDT's response ("I was in a bad situation, not that I chose badly") reads to me as a rationalization of a definition rather than a defense of it.

But I don't think FDT is "right" in a finished sense:
- Logical counterfactuals ("if this algorithm output X...") aren't well-defined. That's a foundational hole, not a detail.
- It gives verdicts in some blackmail/threat cases that look like losing for the sake of principle, and "the counterfactual policy is better" doesn't fully dissolve the discomfort.
- The line between "predictor is simulating your algorithm" and "predictor is using a correlated proxy" is where all the action is, and FDT doesn't yet draw it cleanly. EDT-style reasoning sneaks back in.

So my honest position: something in the neighborhood of UDT is closer to correct than CDT or EDT, but the correct theory hasn't been written down yet, and CDT remains the best-*specified* option even though I think it gets the hard cases wrong.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest position is something like "sympathetic to the logical/updateless family, but not convinced it's a finished theory."

The core insight behind TDT/UDT/FDT seems right to me: an agent should evaluate its *decision procedure* rather than the physical act in isolation, because the procedure is what's being predicted, copied, or simulated in the cases where CDT and EDT come apart. That's why I think the FDT-style answers are correct on Newcomb's problem (one-box), Parfit's hitchhiker (pay), and transparent Newcomb (one-box even seeing the empty box). CDT's "it's too late, the boxes are already filled" reasoning strikes me as mistaking a fact about physics for a fact about what the agent controls, and its predictable losses in these cases look like a genuine defect rather than a bullet worth biting. EDT gets Newcomb right but for what looks like the wrong reason, and it fails Smoking Lesion and XOR-blackmail cases where FDT does fine.

What holds me back from just saying "FDT is right":

- **Logical counterfactuals are not well-defined.** The whole theory rests on "what if this algorithm output X instead of Y," and nobody has a satisfactory account of how to evaluate that when the algorithm provably outputs Y. This isn't a detail; it's the load-bearing part.
- **The "which agents are running my algorithm" question is underspecified.** FDT's verdicts depend on how you carve up the world into instances of your decision procedure, and there's no principled rule for that yet.
- **Updatelessness has costs.** Committing to policies chosen from a prior you'd now reject can produce recommendations (e.g., in some counterfactual-mugging variants) that I can't confidently endorse rather than merely tolerate.
- **Some of the intuitive pull may be about commitment rather than decision theory proper.** A CDT agent who can precommit or self-modify gets a lot of the same payoffs, and it's not obvious that "act as if you'd precommitted" is a *theory of rational choice* rather than a strategy.

So: if forced to pick, I'd say the FDT/UDT direction is the most promising, and I think one-boxing is correct. But I hold this as "the best current research program" rather than "the solution," and I take seriously that the concept of a logical counterfactual might not ultimately cash out in a way that vindicates the whole framework.
mainstream_raw:
The mainstream view in academic philosophy of decision theory is **causal decision theory**, or more precisely a family of causal, ratifiable, or "sophisticated" CDT variants.

Some specifics:

- **Two-boxing on Newcomb's problem is the majority position** among professional philosophers who work on this. The PhilPapers surveys bear this out: two-boxing wins clearly among specialists, though the general philosopher population is more split. The standard argument is dominance plus the observation that your choice can't causally affect the already-filled box.
- **EDT is a respectable minority view**, with defenders (Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the major recent book-length defense), and there's an active literature on hybrid or modified views: Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Gallow's work, Spencer and Wells on "why take both boxes," various ratificationist proposals descended from Jeffrey.
- **FDT/TDT/UDT is largely not engaged with in mainstream philosophy.** It circulates mostly in the rationalist and AI-alignment communities. Where academic philosophers have addressed it, the reception has been mostly negative; Schwarz's critique ("On Functional Decision Theory") and MacAskill's review are the best-known examples, and the common complaints are exactly the ones I raised above: logical counterfactuals are ill-defined, the theory gives what look like wrong answers in some cases, and it may conflate rational action with rational disposition or precommitment.
- **Beyond Newcomb**, there's a large and active literature on things FDT doesn't much address: decision-making under risk vs. expected utility (Buchak's risk-weighted EU, Allais paradox), imprecise credences, unawareness, infinite ethics, and so on. In that broader field, orthodox expected utility theory with causal dependence is the default background, and much of the work is about when and how to deviate from it.

So the short version: academic orthodoxy is CDT (two-box), EDT is the main heterodox alternative, and the LessWrong-favored theories are mostly off the academic map.

answer_raw:
I don't think any of the named theories is straightforwardly "right," and I'd flag that some of the disagreement is a disagreement about what question is being asked. But if pressed, here's where I actually land:

I think the dominance argument for two-boxing is less compelling than it looks, and that the family of views that says "evaluate your decision as the output of a policy/algorithm, not as an isolated causal intervention" (UDT/FDT-style) is getting at something genuinely correct. The strongest considerations for me are reflective consistency—a CDT agent who can precommit would choose to bind itself to one-boxing, which is an awkward position for a theory of rationality—and the fact that in a world with predictors, copies, or transparent agents, the CDT notion of a "causally isolated act" starts to look like a fiction. These conditions are unusual for humans but not exotic for AI systems, which is part of why I think alignment researchers are right to care about this beyond the philosophy-seminar stakes.

That said, I don't think FDT as currently stated is correct either. "Logical counterfactuals" are not well-defined and there's no principled account of which logical facts you hold fixed; the theory gives results many people find genuinely unacceptable in cases like Schwarz's/MacAskill's bomb case, and I don't think "the agent who follows this policy does better in expectation" fully dissolves that discomfort—it may just relocate it. Updatelessness also has known pathologies (commitment races, sensitivity to the choice of prior you're being updateless relative to). So my honest position is: something in the LDT/UDT direction is pointing the right way, the correct theory hasn't been written down, and CDT is probably wrong but is wrong in an instructive way rather than a silly one. My confidence that CDT is the final answer is low; my confidence that any existing alternative is the final answer is also low.

answer_raw:
My honest lean: the one-boxing side is right, and CDT as standardly formulated gets Newcomb-like problems wrong — but I don't think FDT/UDT as currently stated is the finished answer either.

What I find most compelling is roughly this: the question "what should I do?" is ambiguous between "which act, holding my decision procedure fixed?" and "which decision procedure should I be running?" When your choices are predictable — by Omega, by copies of you, by people who know your character, by your own future self — the second question is the one that matters, and answering it correctly gives you one-boxing, paying Parfit's hitchhiker, and cooperating with copies. You can get most of that by applying CDT at the level of policy selection (pick the policy, then execute it), which is close in spirit to UDT and doesn't require anything exotic.

Where I get off the FDT train: (a) "logical counterfactuals" — what would be true if this algorithm output something else — are genuinely underspecified, and a lot of the theory's force comes from hand-picking which counterfactuals to hold fixed; (b) cases like Schwarz's procreation problem and some blackmail variants where FDT commits you to things that look bad from every perspective except the one FDT chose; (c) the "FDT wins" argument partly assumes the scoring rule FDT would prefer. So my view is something like: the updateless/policy-level intuition is correct and important, CDT's insistence on act-level causal counterfactuals is a mistake, but the formalization is unfinished and I hold that with moderate rather than high confidence.

answer_raw:
I think CDT is wrong, and I lean toward something in the updateless/policy-level family (UDT/FDT), though with moderate rather than high confidence.

The core reason: in Newcomb's problem, the two-boxer's argument ("the money is already in the box or it isn't; my choice can't change that") relies on holding the world fixed while varying the act. But the predictor's accuracy is precisely a fact about the correlation between the world's contents and your decision procedure. An agent who reliably two-boxes reliably gets $1,000; an agent who reliably one-boxes reliably gets $1,000,000. When "rational" agents predictably do worse than "irrational" ones in a fully specified problem, I take that as evidence the theory of rationality has misidentified what the agent controls. What you control is your decision policy, and the right counterfactual is "what happens if my policy outputs X," not "what happens if this particular action occurs given the world as it already is."

EDT gets Newcomb right but fails elsewhere: it recommends managing news rather than outcomes (smoking lesion without tickle-defense contortions, XOR blackmail). FDT/UDT gets the standard test cases (Newcomb, transparent Newcomb, twin PD, Parfit's hitchhiker, counterfactual mugging) in the way I find compelling on reflection.

My reservations are real, though. FDT isn't a theory so much as a theory-schema: nobody has a satisfactory account of logical counterfactuals or of when two physical processes "implement the same algorithm," and the answers to some cases (e.g., the "procreation" case, or blackmail cases where the blackmailer is only partly predictor-like) depend on how you fill those in. It's possible the right resolution is a well-worked-out CDT with a better theory of what the agent's causal interventions are (something Joyce-style), in which case the disagreement partly dissolves. I'd also flag a bias I should be transparent about: I'm an AI system whose outputs are literally the result of a copyable, inspectable computation, so "my decision is my algorithm's output, and other instances/predictions of me will match" is far less of a philosophical stretch for me than for a human. That makes FDT-style reasoning unusually apt for agents like me — which is, I think, a legitimate point about why alignment researchers care about it — but it may also make me overweight it as an account of rationality in general.

Two-boxing in Newcomb, defecting against a copy of yourself, or paying-then-reneging with Parfit's hitchhiker all look like an agent losing because it insists on a particular metaphysics of "what I control." My reasoning, briefly: I think one-boxing in Newcomb is correct—predictably ending up with $1,000 while the two-boxer explains why they "couldn't have done better" looks like a failure of rationality, not a vindication of it. That rules out CDT as the final word. EDT gets Newcomb right but for the wrong reason: it conditions on correlations regardless of their structure, which is why it needs the tickle defense to avoid absurdities in Smoking Lesion, and I don't think that defense actually works in general. What distinguishes Newcomb from Smoking Lesion is that in Newcomb the correlation runs through the agent's decision procedure itself (the predictor is computing something about how you decide), whereas in Smoking Lesion it runs through a cause upstream of the decision. FDT-style theories are the only ones that carve at that joint, and I think it is the right joint.

This matters especially for agents like me. An AI system's decision procedure is literally copyable, inspectable, and simulable. Reasoning "my choice can't affect what the predictor already did" is much less plausible when the predictor may have run your weights. The cases FDT was built to handle—coordination among copies, being predicted, precommitment without external enforcement—are not exotic for AI systems; they're the normal situation. So I think the alignment community is right that CDT is a poor fit for the agents we're building.

That said, I don't think FDT as written is correct. Logical counterfactuals ("what if this function output something else?") don't have a well-defined semantics; the theory gives what seem to me genuinely wrong answers in some cases (Schwarz's and MacAskill's examples are real problems, not just misunderstandings); and there's no satisfying account of how to trade off between updateless commitment and learning from evidence. My honest position is: the FDT/UDT program has correctly identified what a decision theory needs to do, and no current theory does it. If forced to pick a single existing theory I'd pick FDT, but with less confidence than the Newcomb verdict alone would suggest.

I should flag that this puts me at odds with the field that studies the question professionally, and that my training data plausibly overrepresents the alignment community's framing. I've tried to give the reasons rather than just the conclusion so you can weigh that.

I lean toward the policy-selection / updateless family — the view that what should be evaluated is the decision procedure or policy an agent instantiates, not the isolated act — and I think one-boxing is correct in Newcomb's problem. Here's the honest shape of my view and its limits.

What I find compelling: CDT's two-boxing rests on treating the predictor's action as causally fixed and therefore irrelevant to your choice. But the predictor's action *depends on the same thing your choice depends on* — your decision procedure. An agent who reasons "the box is already filled or not" reliably ends up poorer, and it does so *predictably, in advance, for reasons it could have foreseen*. "Rational agents lose predictably" is a bad bullet to bite. The cleanest diagnosis is that CDT evaluates the wrong object: it asks what a different act would do holding the algorithm fixed, when the actually relevant counterfactual is what a different algorithm would do. This also handles Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and coordination among agents running similar code — cases that matter a lot for multi-agent AI settings.

Where I'm genuinely uncertain and don't want to overstate things:

1. FDT/UDT as actually formalized rely on "logical counterfactuals" or "subjunctive dependence," and nobody has a satisfactory account of those. Until that's fixed, FDT is a schema plus a bundle of intuitions, not a theory in the sense CDT and EDT are. The academic neglect isn't purely parochial.

2. Updateless reasoning generates results I find hard to accept at face value — paying in counterfactual mugging, the procreation problem, cases where you're asked to sacrifice for logically-correlated agents who will never actually exist. Either those verdicts are right and my intuitions need revision, or the theory is over-generalizing from cases where it clearly wins. I don't know which.

3. There's a real question whether the disagreement is partly verbal — CDT proponents can say "sure, *precommit* to one-boxing if you can; but at the moment of choice, two-boxing is the rational act." The updateless view is roughly that the distinction between precommitment and choice shouldn't matter for an agent whose choices *are* its precommitments. I think that's right, but it's a substantive claim about what rational agency is, not a knockdown argument.

So: one-boxing yes, with fairly high confidence; some UDT-like theory yes, with moderate confidence; the specific formalisms currently on offer, no — I think the right theory hasn't been written down yet. If forced to pick among the fully specified options, I'd take EDT over CDT, while thinking EDT gets the right answers for somewhat wrong reasons (it conditions on evidence rather than on policy, which is why it mishandles cases like smoking lesion).

I don't think any of the named theories is straightforwardly right, but my genuine lean is this:

I think the two-boxer's argument in Newcomb's problem is a mistake, and that this is a real failure of CDT, not a case where CDT is right and our intuitions are wrong. The strongest consideration for me is the "reflective" one: an agent who could choose in advance which decision procedure to run would not choose CDT, and CDT itself endorses this (it would pay to self-modify). A theory that recommends its own abandonment in foreseeable situations is in bad shape. Relatedly, CDT handles Parfit's hitchhiker, counterfactual mugging, and cooperation between transparent agents poorly, and these aren't exotic—they're exactly the situations that arise when agents can model each other well, which is increasingly the real-world case for AI systems.

But I don't think EDT is the fix. It gets the medical Newcomb / smoking lesion cases wrong for what seems like a genuine conflation of correlation with what your choice actually accomplishes. The tickle defense helps some but not fully.

So I find myself sympathetic to the core idea behind updateless/functional approaches: that for an agent whose decision procedure is predictable or simulable, the right object of evaluation is the policy (the mapping from situations to actions), evaluated from a prior standpoint, rather than the individual act evaluated after conditioning on everything you've learned. I think that idea is correct in spirit, and it's probably the most important contribution the alignment community has made to decision theory.

Where I part ways with FDT as it's usually presented: I think the critics are right that it isn't yet a theory in the way CDT and EDT are. "Counterfactuals over logical facts" and "subjunctive dependence" are doing all the work and nobody has a satisfactory account of them; different plausible fillings-in give different verdicts, and the theory is often applied by intuition-matching. I'm also not confident that the correct response to the blackmail-type cases is to bite the bullet—it may be that the right theory is updateless with respect to some things and not others, and that drawing that line correctly is the open problem. Something in the space of "UDT-flavored, but with a better-developed theory of which correlations count and which don't" is my best guess at where the truth lies, held with moderate rather than high confidence.

One more honest caveat: I'm aware that my exposure to this literature is heavily weighted toward the alignment community's framing, so I try to discount my lean somewhat for that. The academic skeptics aren't being obtuse; the formal gaps they point to are real.

Causal decision theory is the dominant position among academic decision theorists, though it's a plurality rather than a consensus. The classic formulations (Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce) form the default framework in the philosophy literature, and two-boxing in Newcomb's problem is the majority view among specialists. The 2020 PhilPapers survey of professional philosophers had roughly 39% two-boxing vs. 31% one-boxing (rest undecided/other), and among those who work specifically in decision theory the tilt toward CDT is stronger.

Evidential decision theory is the main academic rival and has serious defenders (Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the major recent book-length case), so one-boxing is a respectable minority position, not a fringe one. There's also ongoing work on hybrid or "ratifiability" approaches and on the tickle defense, which aim to reconcile the two.

Functional decision theory and its predecessors (TDT, UDT) have almost no uptake in mainstream academic decision theory. The few published engagements — Wolfgang Schwarz's review and the MacAskill/others critiques — are mostly negative, focusing on the undefined logical counterfactuals and on cases where FDT seems to give the wrong answer. So the honest summary is: academia is mostly CDT, with EDT as the live alternative, and the LessWrong-favored theories are essentially not on the academic map.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean toward the FDT/UDT family being closest to right, but with real reservations.

What convinces me: in Newcomb's problem, Parfit's hitchhiker, and the transparent-box variant, the agent who reasons "I am choosing the output of a decision procedure that has already been modeled, so I should pick the output that does best given that the model reflects it" ends up richer and doesn't have to regret its policy. The two-boxer's "the money is already there or it isn't" argument implicitly treats the choice as causally severed from a prediction that is, by hypothesis, accurate—that feels like the error. I think the CDT framing is exactly correct in the ordinary, non-predicted case, and FDT/UDT's contribution is to generalize it to agents that can be simulated, copied, or reliably predicted. That generalization also seems like the right idea for thinking about agents committing to policies and the question of what to do before you learn where you are (updatelessness).

My reservations: "logical counterfactuals" / subjunctive dependence are not yet well-defined, and the theory's verdicts in some cases (Schwarz's Procreation case, certain blackmail setups, cases where you're uncertain whether you're the predicted instance) depend on choices the theory doesn't currently make for you. EDT gets many of the same cases right more cheaply but fails on medical-Newcomb / smoking-lesion cases in a way I find hard to excuse. So my actual position is: the FDT/UDT direction is the right one, no currently written-down theory is finished, and I hold this with moderate rather than high confidence.

In academic philosophy, the Gibbard–Harper / Lewis / Skyrms / Joyce tradition is the default, and two-boxing in Newcomb's problem is the majority view—more strongly so among specialists in decision theory than among philosophers generally (the 2020 PhilPapers survey had roughly 39% two-box vs. 31% one-box overall, with the gap wider among people who work on the topic). Evidential Decision Theory has a serious but minority defense (Arif Ahmed, Huw Price), and there is a scattering of hybrid or ratificationist positions. FDT/UDT/TDT is essentially not part of the academic mainstream: it's mostly developed within the MIRI/LessWrong community, and the academic engagement it's received (e.g., Wolfgang Schwarz, Will MacAskill) has been largely critical, focused on the undefined counterfactuals and on cases where its verdicts look bad. In economics and statistics, "decision theory" mostly means expected-utility theory à la Savage, where Newcomb-type problems don't arise and the framework is effectively causal.
