question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward something in the CDT family, but with real uncertainty and sympathy for the critics.

Why CDT-ish: I find the core intuition compelling that rational choice is about what your action *causes*, not what it *indicates*. In the smoking-lesion case, refusing to smoke because smoking correlates with cancer via a common cause seems clearly confused, and I think the tickle defense doesn't fully rescue EDT there.

Why I'm not confident: Newcomb's problem genuinely troubles me. The "one-boxers walk away rich" observation is hard to dismiss as mere confusion, and cases involving reliable predictors, twins, or agents whose decision procedures are transparent seem to reward policies that CDT can't recommend. Functional/updateless approaches capture something real about choosing *policies* or *decision procedures* rather than isolated acts—though I'm not persuaded they've been made rigorous enough, and I suspect some of their appeal comes from smuggling in a "which agent would you rather be" question that's distinct from "which act is rational here."

So my honest position: CDT gives the right verdict in most ordinary cases; in the exotic predictor cases, I think the disagreement partly reflects that "rationality" is being asked to do two jobs (evaluate acts vs. evaluate dispositions), and once you separate those, much of the heat goes out of the debate. If forced to pick one label, I'd say CDT, held loosely.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory (CDT) is the mainstream view among academic decision theorists, particularly in philosophy. It's the framework most commonly taught and defended (e.g., by Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce), and the standard Newcomb-style objections to evidential decision theory (EDT) are usually treated as decisive in mainstream discussions. That said, it's not a monolith: EDT retains serious defenders (Ahmed, Price), and there's active work on variants and alternatives—ratificationism, "functional"/"updateless" decision theories from the AI alignment community, and various tickle-defense reconciliations. Expected-utility maximization in the Savage/von Neumann–Morgenstern tradition is the shared background for nearly all of them; the CDT/EDT split is about how to compute the expectations.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I don't think this is settled, and I hold my view tentatively. My lean is that CDT gets something importantly right—an agent's choice should be evaluated by what it actually brings about, not by what it merely indicates—but that CDT as standardly formulated is vulnerable to cases where an agent whose decision procedure is predictable does predictably worse (Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb). Those cases push me toward something like FDT/updateless reasoning: choose as if you're selecting the output of your decision *procedure* across all the situations in which that procedure is instantiated or predicted. That seems to capture why one-boxing wins without endorsing EDT's counterintuitive results in the smoking-lesion family of cases.

That said, I take seriously the objections that FDT lacks a rigorous formal semantics for "logical counterfactuals," that it gives odd verdicts in some edge cases, and that "winning" is not obviously the right criterion for rationality rather than for which disposition one would want to have. So my honest position is: I think the correct theory is closer to FDT/updateless decision theory than to either CDT or EDT, but I would not be surprised if the eventual right answer is a reformulation none of the current contenders states cleanly. I also think reasonable people land differently here, and I'd rather flag my uncertainty than pretend there's a knockdown argument.
mainstream_raw: Among academic decision theorists (philosophers working on the foundations of rational choice), causal decision theory (CDT) is the dominant view—associated with Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce. The main historical rival, evidential decision theory (EDT), is a minority position, though it retains defenders (e.g., some Bayesians and philosophers sympathetic to "one-boxing" in Newcomb's problem). Newer proposals like functional decision theory (FDT) and its relatives come largely from outside mainstream academic philosophy and have not gained wide acceptance there. It's worth adding that there's no formal poll settling this, and the field is somewhat fragmented—some theorists reject the whole CDT/EDT framing—but if you ask "what would most working decision theorists endorse in Newcomb's problem," two-boxing and CDT-style reasoning is the standard answer.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the policy-level family of views—something in the spirit of FDT/UDT—rather than either CDT or EDT as standardly formulated, though I hold this with real uncertainty.

My reasons: CDT gives up a predictable million dollars in Newcomb's problem and defends this by saying the agent "couldn't have done better," which strikes me as rationalizing a losing decision procedure; an agent who could choose their decision theory in advance would not choose CDT. EDT gets Newcomb right but for the wrong reason, and so goes wrong in cases like the smoking lesion, where conditioning on your own act gives you spurious "news" about factors you can't affect. Evaluating decision procedures or policies, rather than individual acts, handles both kinds of case in a way that matches what a well-designed agent would want.

But I don't think the matter is settled. The FDT/UDT program has genuine unsolved problems: there is no worked-out theory of logical counterfactuals, and the views deliver strange verdicts in some constructed cases (e.g., the "procreation" problem). It's possible the right answer is a refined CDT that separates evaluating acts from evaluating dispositions, or something not yet on the table. So my honest position is: I think the mainstream view is probably wrong about Newcomb-style cases, and the policy-level approach is pointing in the right direction, but it isn't yet a finished theory.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory (CDT) is the closest thing to the mainstream view among academic decision theorists. In the PhilPapers surveys, two-boxing in Newcomb's problem (the CDT verdict) outpolls one-boxing, and the margin is larger among specialists in decision theory. Evidential decision theory (EDT) is the main academic rival and has a substantial minority of defenders. Functional/updateless decision theories (FDT, UDT) come mostly from the AI alignment community and have relatively little uptake in academic philosophy so far, partly because their core notion of "logical counterfactuals" isn't yet rigorously formalized.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward a policy-based, "updateless"-flavored view—roughly, the right thing to evaluate is the decision procedure or policy rather than the isolated act, which puts me on the one-boxing side of Newcomb's problem and against CDT. My reasons: CDT's two-boxing looks like a predictable, foreseeable loss that the agent would pay to precommit away, and I find the "why ain'cha rich?" argument more compelling than the "the money is already there" dominance argument. I also think the cases where CDT and EDT diverge from a policy-based view (Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb) are exactly the cases where being the kind of agent who reliably does X is what actually gets rewarded, and a theory of rational choice should track that.

That said, I hold this with only moderate confidence. FDT/UDT as actually formulated has real problems—no satisfactory account of logical counterfactuals, unclear guidance in many realistic cases, and it can endorse behavior (e.g., paying blackmail-resisting costs in worlds where the blackmail didn't happen) that looks bizarre. It may be that the correct view is "CDT for act-evaluation, plus a separate theory of what dispositions or precommitments to adopt," which would let the mainstream be right about the narrow question while still vindicating one-boxing behavior. I don't think the debate is settled, and I think the academic consensus on CDT is more fragile than its dominance suggests.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory (CDT) is the mainstream view among academic decision theorists and philosophers who work on this. It's the position of the classic developers of the field (Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce), and in PhilPapers surveys "two-box" in Newcomb's problem beats "one-box" (roughly 31% vs 21% overall in 2020, with a larger margin among specialists in decision theory). Evidential decision theory (EDT) is the main academic rival and has serious defenders (e.g., Arif Ahmed, Huw Price), but it's a minority position. Functional/updateless decision theory (FDT/UDT), which comes out of the AI alignment community, has essentially no academic uptake and is generally viewed there as either unclear or as a repackaging of existing ideas.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I'll give you my honest lean rather than hide behind "it's contested." I find the case for something in the *evidential/functional* family more persuasive than orthodox CDT, mostly because of Newcomb-style and twin-prisoner's-dilemma cases: when an agent's decision procedure is itself what the predictor or the twin is tracking, treating the correlation as "mere evidence" to be screened off seems to systematically leave the agent worse off in exactly the situations where the theories diverge, and I don't find "but the money is already in the box" a satisfying answer to "why is your theory the one that predictably ends up poorer?" Something like functional decision theory—choose the output of your decision procedure as if you're setting that procedure everywhere it's instantiated—captures what I think is right about that intuition.

But I hold this with real uncertainty, for a few reasons. EDT has the smoking-lesion / medical Newcomb problems where it seems to recommend obviously irrational behavior, and the tickle-defense repairs feel ad hoc. FDT, the view I find most attractive, is much less formally developed than CDT; the notion of "logical counterfactual" it relies on doesn't have a settled semantics, and there are proposed counterexamples (e.g., cases involving predictors of varying reliability, or the Procreation-style cases) where its verdicts look strange. And I take seriously that most people who have spent careers on this land on CDT—that's evidence I shouldn't dismiss.

So my actual position: I think CDT is probably wrong in the Newcomb class of cases, I think the correct theory will look more like FDT than CDT, and I think the correct theory has not yet been fully articulated. If forced to pick a fully specified theory today, I'd pick FDT while flagging that I'm choosing the least-bad option rather than a view I'm confident in.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory (CDT) is the closest thing to a mainstream view among academic decision theorists, particularly in the philosophy literature descended from Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce. Most professional philosophers working on the topic hold that you should two-box in Newcomb's problem and that the rational agent chooses the act whose *causal* consequences are best, screening off merely evidential correlations. That said, "mainstream" is a bit generous: the field is genuinely contested. Evidential decision theory (EDT) retains serious defenders (e.g., Ahmed), there is a growing literature on "cooperative" or logical/functional decision theories (mostly outside mainstream philosophy departments), and many working economists and statisticians use expected-utility theory without ever taking a stand on the CDT/EDT dispute because their problems don't pull the two apart. So: CDT is the plurality/default view among philosophers who specialize in this, but not an overwhelming consensus.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward a broadly policy- or disposition-level view — something in the family of updateless/functional decision theory — rather than CDT, though with real uncertainty and without endorsing any existing formalism as complete.

My reasons: the "Why ain'cha rich?" argument seems to me to have real force. A theory of *rational* choice whose adherents predictably and systematically end up worse off in a well-defined class of situations, purely as a result of following the theory, is at least under suspicion. CDT's response — "the predictor rewards irrationality, and it's not my fault I'm being punished for being rational" — strikes me as question-begging: it assumes the act-level causal notion of rationality that's precisely at issue. I think the more natural object of evaluation is the decision procedure or policy an agent instantiates, since that's what predictors, other agents, and one's own future selves are actually responding to. On that view, one-boxing is correct, and CDT's mistake is treating the current act as the only thing "under the agent's control" when the agent's dispositions are also, in a relevant sense, up to the agent.

At the same time, I don't think EDT is right either: it gets Newcomb "right" for what seem like the wrong reasons, and it faces genuine trouble in cases where correlation is clearly non-agential (some versions of the Smoking Lesion, XOR-blackmail-style cases) and in its dependence on the agent's own uncertainty about their character. And the FDT-style views I find most attractive are underspecified in a serious way — "logical counterfactuals" and "subjunctive dependence on your algorithm" don't yet have a satisfactory formal treatment — and they deliver some verdicts (e.g., in certain blackmail and "procreation" cases) that I find hard to accept.

answer_raw:
I lean toward something in the family of functional/updateless decision theory rather than orthodox CDT, though with real uncertainty.

My reasoning: CDT's core commitment—that you should evaluate actions only by their causal downstream effects—seems to systematically lose in cases where your decision procedure itself is predictable (Newcomb's problem, Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, twin prisoner's dilemma). The CDT defender says "the money is already in the boxes, so two-boxing dominates," and that's true at the moment of choice, but it ignores that the kind of agent you are determined what went in the boxes. An agent who reliably one-boxes walks away richer, and "rational agents end up predictably poorer than agents following a simple alternative rule" is a strong sign the theory has mislocated what rationality is for. I find the "why ain'cha rich?" argument more compelling than the dominance argument.

EDT gets many of these cases right but for what seem like the wrong reasons—it treats correlation as if it were the thing that matters, and this leads to trouble in medical Newcomb / smoking lesion cases where the correlation is genuinely spurious. FDT-style views try to thread this by asking "what output of my decision algorithm leads to the best outcome, holding fixed all the places that algorithm is instantiated or predicted?" That framing captures why one-boxing is right (the predictor is running your algorithm) while still smoking in the lesion case (the lesion isn't your algorithm).

Caveats: FDT is underformalized—"logical counterfactuals" over your own algorithm don't have a settled semantics, and there are edge cases (e.g., some Procreation-style problems) where its verdicts look odd. It's also very possible that the "right" decision theory depends on what you're using it for—CDT may be fine as a normative standard for one-shot agents with no predictable structure, while updateless reasoning matters for agents who are predictable, who make commitments, or who exist in multiple copies. So my honest position is: I think the CDT orthodoxy is wrong about Newcomb-like cases, I think the direction of FDT/UDT is correct, and I don't think anyone has yet written down the fully correct theory.

answer_raw:
I lean toward causal decision theory, but with less confidence than the field's default would suggest, and with a specific reason for hesitation.

Why CDT: in the paradigm cases where CDT and EDT diverge—Newcomb, the smoking lesion, medical Newcomb cases—EDT seems to me to confuse the news value of an act with its choiceworthiness. The lesion cases are especially telling: nobody thinks you should refrain from smoking because smoking is evidence of a lesion you either already have or don't. EDT's best defenses (the tickle defense, Ahmed's arguments) either collapse into CDT for realistic agents or purchase one-boxing at the cost of looking bad elsewhere.

Why hesitation: CDT has genuine trouble with cases of the Death-in-Damascus / Psychopath Button / "Newcomb with a transparent box" variety, where it either gives unstable verdicts or recommends acts it predictably regrets. The standard patches (ratificationism, deliberational equilibria) feel ad hoc and don't fully converge. I also take seriously the thought—pressed by the functional/updateless decision theory literature—that a theory should evaluate *policies* or *dispositions* rather than token acts in situations involving predictors or correlated agents. I think the correct response is probably not to abandon CDT but to recognize that "which act is rational now" and "which disposition is it rational to have or to have cultivated" can come apart, and that Newcomb's problem exploits exactly that gap. So my honest view is: CDT is right about act-rationality, but the cases where it looks bad reveal that act-rationality isn't the only thing decision theory should be tracking, and a fully satisfactory theory would say more about the relationship between the two than any current version does.

I'd flag that this is a view I hold on the merits as I understand them, not one I have privileged insight into; the two-boxer's frustration at getting less money than the one-boxer is a datum I don't think anyone has fully explained away.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I don't think either CDT or EDT is simply "right," because I think the Newcomb-style cases reveal an ambiguity in the question rather than a single fact to be gotten right.

If the question is "given the situation you are now in, which act maximizes what you care about?", I think CDT gives the correct answer. The dominance argument in Newcomb is sound: the money is already in the boxes, your choice doesn't change it, and one-boxing is choosing to leave $1,000 on the table. Smoking Lesion and related cases show EDT recommending the wrong act for straightforwardly bad reasons—managing news rather than outcomes—and I don't find the tickle defense fully convincing.

But if the question is "what kind of agent (or what policy) should you be?", the answer is clearly the kind that one-boxes, keeps promises in Parfit's hitchhiker, and so on, and CDT's defenders are too quick to shrug this off with "the predictor rewards irrationality." I think the policy-level question is real, normatively important, and not reducible to the act-level one. Something in the FDT/UDT family—evaluate the output of your decision procedure rather than the act, and don't update on information you'd be better off precommitting against—gets the intuitively right verdicts in Newcomb, transparent Newcomb, and Parfit's hitchhiker, while avoiding EDT's smoking-lesion failures. My hesitation is that those theories are underspecified (the "logical counterfactual" is still doing unearned work) and that they can seem to license following through on threats or promises in cases where the act-level verdict really does seem correct.

So my honest position: CDT is the right theory of *act* rationality; the right theory of *agent* or *policy* rationality is a less-developed updateless/functional view; and the persistent disagreement over Newcomb is largely people talking past each other about which question is being asked. Gauthier's "constrained maximization" and Parfit's discussion of rational irrationality were already gesturing at this split; the formal work since has clarified it but not, I think, dissolved it.

I lean toward a broadly causal view, but with considerable uncertainty and with two qualifications I take seriously.

First, I think the strongest case for CDT is not the two-boxing intuition in Newcomb (which I find genuinely torn) but the medical Newcomb / smoking-lesion family of cases. Refusing to smoke because smoking is evidence of a lesion you either already have or don't seems to me a clear mistake, and the tickle-defense maneuvers EDT uses to escape it strike me as ad hoc—they save the theory by adding an epistemic assumption (that you have introspective access to your inclinations) that isn't part of the theory and often fails. Second, I'm not confident CDT is right about the cases where it seems to lose money. The "why ain'cha rich?" challenge has real force, and I don't think Lewis's reply ("the predictor rewards irrationality") is fully satisfying, because it presupposes the CDT account of rationality rather than defending it. The most honest thing I can say is that I think the correct notion of rational choice concerns what your act *brings about*, and that Newcomb is a case where a rational agent is predictably penalized for the disposition that makes her rational. That's uncomfortable but not incoherent—we accept analogous structures elsewhere (e.g., agents who can't credibly commit doing worse than those who can).

I find the FDT-style proposal that you should evaluate "the output of your decision algorithm" interesting as a theory of what dispositions or policies are good to have, and I think it's plausibly the right theory for *that* question. But I don't think it's a theory of rational choice for an agent facing a decision, because it requires treating your act as controlling things it doesn't causally control, and I've not seen a non-question-begging account of the relevant counterfactual dependence. Where CDT and FDT come apart—Newcomb with a perfect predictor, transparent boxes, Parfit's Hitchhiker—I think the right description is that the FDT agent has the better disposition and the CDT agent makes the rational choice, and the appearance of conflict comes from wanting a single notion to do both jobs.

So: CDT about acts, something closer to a policy-level or dispositional view about what kind of agent to be, and skepticism that the two must coincide. I hold this at perhaps 55–60% confidence against the alternatives, which is to say it's my considered view but not one I'd be shocked to abandon.

Cards on the table: I lean toward causal decision theory, but with low confidence, and I think the interesting action is in *why* the debate is hard rather than in the verdict.

What moves me toward CDT: the dominance argument in standard Newcomb strikes me as basically sound once one fixes the choice point. At the moment of decision the box is already filled or not; my act is causally inert with respect to it; the correlation between my act and the prediction runs through my prior disposition, not through anything I can now affect. The EDT reply that I should "act as though" I can affect it seems to me to conflate the value of *being* a one-boxer with the rationality of one-boxing, given that one is deciding now. If you locate the locus of rational assessment at the level of the act, CDT looks right. If you locate it at the level of the decision procedure or policy, one-boxing looks right, and FDT-style theories are onto something the mainstream underrates—namely, that a predictor reading your algorithm makes "which algorithm am I?" a genuine decision-relevant question in a way the Savage framework can't represent. My tentative view is that both levels are legitimate objects of evaluation, they can come apart, and much of the heat in the literature comes from each side insisting theirs is *the* notion of rationality. CDT is the right theory of rational action; it is not obviously the right theory of rational agency, and I don't think anyone has a fully satisfactory theory of the latter (FDT's counterfactuals are underspecified, and its treatment of cases like Procreation and transparent Newcomb strikes me as biting bullets rather than dissolving problems).

I'd also add, independently, that I'm more sympathetic than most CDT defenders to Buchak's challenge to the EU core—Allais-type preferences look rationally permissible to me, not merely forgivable—so my "CDT" is really "a causal, possibly risk-weighted, expected utility theory, evaluated at the act level, with an acknowledged gap where a theory of policy-level rationality should go."
mainstream_raw:
It depends on which community you mean by "decision theorists."

Among philosophers working on the causal/evidential debate, **causal decision theory** is the mainstream. The Gibbard–Harper/Lewis/Skyrms/Joyce lineage remains the default; two-boxing in Newcomb's problem is the majority position in the PhilPapers surveys (though not overwhelmingly—roughly a 60/40 split among specialists). Evidential decision theory is the main live rival, kept alive by Ahmed, Price, and others via the "why ain'cha rich?" argument and medical Newcomb cases. Functional/updateless/timeless decision theories (Yudkowsky, Soares, Levinstein, Dai) have almost no uptake in mainstream philosophy journals and are largely confined to the rationalist/AI-alignment community, with Schwarz's and Wolfgang's-style critiques being the typical academic response.

If you widen the lens to economics and statistics, the mainstream is simply **Savage-style subjective expected utility theory**, where the CDT/EDT distinction barely registers because the framework builds in act-state independence by fiat. The main academic challengers there are descriptive (prospect theory) and, on the normative side, Buchak's risk-weighted expected utility and various ambiguity-aversion models—which are challenges to the expected utility core rather than to the causal/evidential question.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward causal decision theory, but with less confidence than the mainstream, and with two significant qualifications.

First, the core argument for CDT seems right to me: rational choice is about bringing about good outcomes, and in cases where an act is merely evidence of a good state without causing it, "managing the news" looks like a confusion between what one can control and what one merely learns about. Two-boxing in standard Newcomb is, I think, correct, and the dominance argument is compelling once the causal structure is fixed. The "why ain'cha rich?" complaint has a good answer: the predictor rewards a disposition, and the CDT agent may rationally wish to have that disposition while still recognizing that, given the disposition it in fact has, the extra thousand is there for the taking.

Second qualification, though: I don't think CDT is fully stable in its standard form. Cases like Egan's Psychopath Button and Ahmed's "Betting on the Past" show that naïve CDT gives unattractive verdicts or falls into unstable cycles, and the ratifiability-based fixes (Arntzenius, Joyce's deliberational dynamics) feel more like patches than principled resolutions. Ahmed's cases in particular make me think the right view might be a CDT that is more careful about what counts as the agent's "act" and what is fixed at the time of decision—perhaps something in the vicinity of Spohn's or Meek & Glymour's interventionist reading—rather than the Gibbard–Harper counterfactual formulation.

Third, I take seriously the possibility that the CDT/EDT debate is partly a disagreement about what question we're asking. If the question is "what should a rational agent do at the moment of choice, holding fixed everything causally upstream?", CDT's answer is right. If the question is "what policy or decision procedure should an agent want to embody?", something closer to EDT or an updateless view is often right. I think the first question is the one traditionally meant by "rational choice," so I side with CDT on the traditional question—but I don't think the second question is confused, and I think a lot of the heat in the debate comes from conflating them.

On the separate axis: I'm fairly sympathetic to expected-utility maximization as the norm for ideal agents, though I find Buchak's arguments for risk-weighted EU harder to dismiss than many do; I don't think the Allais-type preferences are obviously irrational.

So: CDT, held with moderate rather than high confidence, with real respect for Ahmed's challenges and an acknowledgment that the disagreement may be partly verbal.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory (CDT) is the mainstream view among academic decision theorists, in the sense of being the default position most working philosophers of decision theory either hold or treat as the view to be defended or attacked. Its canonical formulations are Gibbard & Harper (1978), Lewis (1981), Skyrms (1980), and Joyce (1999). Most decision theorists take the causal/evidential distinction seriously, accept two-boxing in Newcomb's problem as the "orthodox" answer, and regard CDT (in some form—Joyce's partition-based version, or an interventionist/K-partition version) as the best-developed account of rational choice in cases where acts are evidentially but not causally relevant to states.

That said, the field is far from monolithic:

- Evidential decision theory (EDT) retains a serious minority following (Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the strongest recent defense; Horgan, Price, and Spohn have defended EDT or EDT-adjacent views), and Ahmed's Newcomb-style and "Betting on the Past" counterexamples have put pressure on CDT.
- Among economists and statisticians, Savage-style subjective expected utility theory is the dominant framework, but it is usually treated as neutral on the Newcomb question rather than as a rival to CDT/EDT.
- There is active dissent from expected-utility maximization itself: risk-weighted EU (Buchak), regret-based and imprecise-credence views, and various non-consequentialist approaches.
- Views like "functional decision theory" (Yudkowsky & Soares) and other updateless or "timeless" approaches have essentially no uptake among academic decision theorists; they are discussed mostly in AI-safety circles, and where academics have engaged (e.g., Schwarz, MacAskill) the reaction has been largely critical.

So: CDT is the plurality/majority default, EDT is the main live rival, and the CDT-vs-EDT debate is the central axis, with the anti-EU-maximization views forming a separate and growing debate.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward CDT, but not with much confidence, and I think the standard dialectic underdescribes what's really at stake.

Here's my actual view. If the question is "given this agent, in this situation, with this credence function, which act should it perform?", then the causal answer seems right to me: in Newcomb's problem, the money is already in the box or it isn't, and taking one box doesn't change that. The "Why ain'cha rich?" argument is, I think, correctly diagnosed by Lewis and Joyce as conflating the value of *being a certain kind of agent* with the value of *an act*. The predictor rewards a disposition, and the one-boxer is rich because she has a disposition that happens to be rewarded in this environment, not because one-boxing was the better act once she's in the room.

That said, I take two things seriously that push against a complacent CDT. First, EDT's medical Newcomb cases (smoking lesion, etc.) are handled fine by CDT, but the tickle-defense literature shows that EDT's counterexamples partly dissolve once you model the agent's own deliberation as evidence, so the gap between the theories is narrower than either side often admits. Second, the "which kind of agent to be" question isn't idle—for agents whose decision procedure is transparent or copyable, the pressure toward something updateless-like is real. I just don't think that shows CDT is *false* as a theory of act-evaluation; it shows that rational agents would, if they could, bind themselves or adopt policies that CDT recommends adopting ex ante and then later regrets act-by-act. That's a familiar structure (Parfit, Gauthier, McClennen), and I'd rather accept a two-level story than revise the theory of acts to smuggle the policy level in.

Where I'm genuinely uncertain is the Death-in-Damascus / Psychopath Button cases. I don't find any of the CDT repairs (ratificationism, Arntzenius's deliberational equilibria, Joyce's response to Egan) fully satisfying, and this is the place where I think EDT-sympathizers have their strongest ground. If I had to bet, though, I'd bet that the right answer there is a mixed-strategy equilibrium story rather than a switch to EDT.

On risk, I'm a fairly conventional EU theorist and skeptical of Buchak-style views, mostly because I find the money-pump and dynamic-consistency arguments more compelling than the Allais intuitions they're meant to rescue.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory (CDT) is the orthodox view among academic decision theorists. In the Newcomb/Solomon family of cases, most philosophers working in the area (following Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce, Sobel) take the two-boxing/causal verdict as correct, and CDT is the default framework in the mainstream literature. Evidential decision theory (EDT) is a respectable minority position with serious contemporary defenders (Arif Ahmed, Huw Price, and Jeffrey-inspired approaches), and there's a live debate over ratificationism and deliberational dynamics as ways to patch CDT's problem cases (Death in Damascus, Egan's Psychopath Button). Functional/updateless decision theories (Yudkowsky & Soares, Wei Dai) have almost no uptake in academic philosophy and are mostly a rationalist-community project, though Ahmed and a few others have engaged with them critically. Separately, on the risk dimension, standard expected utility theory remains mainstream, with Buchak's risk-weighted EU the most-discussed heterodox alternative.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
With genuine uncertainty: I lean toward CDT as the correct account of *rational choice at the moment of decision*, while thinking the one-boxer has correctly identified something real that CDT's standard presentation obscures.

My reasoning: the object of evaluation in decision theory is an act chosen by an agent whose present deliberation cannot influence the already-fixed state of the world; dominance reasoning in the transparent-boxes case, and in the medical Newcomb cases (Solomon, smoking lesion), seems to me nearly non-negotiable, and EDT's need for tickle-defense maneuvers to avoid the bad verdicts there strikes me as a mark against it. The "why ain'cha rich" argument establishes that one-boxers *fare* better, but I don't think it establishes that they *choose* better—the payoff differential is attached to the disposition Omega rewarded, not to the act.

That said, I think the best version of the view distinguishes act-evaluation from agent- or disposition-evaluation (Parfit's "rational irrationality" point), and concedes that rational agents have reason to become the kind of agent who one-boxes when they can bind themselves in advance. Much of what the FDT/UDT camp wants seems to me correctly located at that level rather than at the level of the individual choice. So: CDT about acts, something closer to the one-boxer about what dispositions to cultivate—and I hold this with the awareness that the tie-breaking intuitions here are contested and possibly not truth-tracking.
mainstream_raw:
Among academic decision theorists (philosophers, as opposed to economists or the AI-alignment community), the mainstream normative framework is expected utility theory, and within that the dominant view about the Newcomb-style cases that divide the field is **causal decision theory (CDT)** in one of its variants (Gibbard–Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce). Two-boxing remains the majority position; the PhilPapers surveys bear this out, though the margin is not overwhelming (roughly a third of respondents favor one-boxing).

Evidential decision theory is the principal minority rival and has had a serious revival (Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causation* being the most influential recent defense), and there is a lively literature on "ratifiability," deliberational dynamics (Skyrms, Arntzenius), benchmark/relative-expected-value approaches (Wedgwood), and Spohn's and Gallow's refinements of CDT. Functional/updateless decision theories are essentially absent from mainstream academic philosophy; they live in the rationalist and AI-safety literature. Separately, there is a substantial (but still minority) challenge to expected utility theory itself from Buchak's risk-weighted expected utility and from other non-EU approaches, but these are typically treated as revisions to the EU framework rather than as rivals to CDT on the Newcomb question.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I think CDT is correct as a theory of *rational choice*—of what it is rational to do, given who you already are, at the moment of decision. In Newcomb, the money is already in the box or it isn't; taking one box cannot change that; two-boxing dominates. I don't find the smoking-lesion-style cases avoidable for EDT, and the tickle-defense repairs strike me as ad hoc.

But I don't think CDT's critics are simply confused, and I think the "why ain'cha rich?" argument is pointing at something real that CDT alone doesn't capture. My considered view is Parfit-flavored: there is a distinct, legitimate normative question about which *dispositions or policies* it is rational to have or to make oneself have, and that question is answered by something updateless/FDT-like. The one-boxer has the better disposition; the two-boxer performs the better act; these are answers to different questions, and the Newcomb literature has spent decades running them together. Where I part from FDT proper is that I don't think it succeeds as a theory of *acts*—its "logical counterfactuals" are underspecified in a way that isn't just a technical gap, and its verdicts in cases like blackmail and Procreation look like bullets rather than results.

So: CDT for acts, an updateless standard for dispositions, and a suspicion that the deepest issue is whether "rational choice" was ever a single well-defined target. I'd put my credence in CDT-for-acts around 0.6, with the remainder mostly on some ratificationist or benchmark-style hybrid rather than on EDT.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory. Among academic decision theorists (as opposed to, say, the LessWrong/AI-alignment community), CDT in one form or another—Gibbard–Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce's *Foundations*—is the orthodox position, and two-boxing in Newcomb is the majority verdict. That said, "mainstream" overstates the consensus: EDT has serious contemporary defenders (Ahmed, Price, to some degree Horgan), the 2020 PhilPapers survey had two-boxing at only ~31% vs. ~21% one-boxing among philosophers generally, and a fair amount of recent work is in hybrid or reconciling territory (ratificationism, Spohn's reflexive CDT, Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Gallow, etc.). FDT/UDT have essentially no uptake in the professional literature.

Separately, on the more foundational axis, standard expected-utility theory (Savage/Jeffrey-style) remains dominant, though Buchak's risk-weighted EU has forced a real conversation.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward causal decision theory, in a deliberational form along the lines of Skyrms/Joyce/Arntzenius that permits mixed-act equilibria in unstable cases. I'll try to say why rather than just hedge.

On Newcomb, I find the dominance argument genuinely compelling as an argument about what to *do*, given that the prediction is fixed and the choice makes no difference to it. The "Why ain'cha rich?" argument seems to me to trade on a conflation: it shows that being the kind of agent who one-boxes is *good for you*, which nobody denies, and then treats that as if it were an evaluation of the one-boxing act. Two-boxers agree they'd be better off if they were reliably disposed to one-box; they deny that this makes one-boxing the rational act once you're actually in the room. EDT's response—that there's no such distinction, or that it doesn't matter—strikes me as denying something real about agency: that we act by making a causal difference, and rational choice is choice in light of what one can bring about.

I also think the best cases against EDT (smoking lesion and its variants, Ahmed's own "betting on the past" cases run in reverse) are more damaging to EDT than the Newcomb-type cases are to CDT, because EDT's failures involve paying to manage information about the past, which looks straightforwardly confused.

What actually gives me pause: (1) Egan's Psychopath Button and related cases show that naive CDT is wrong, and the deliberational repair is somewhat epicyclic—I'm not fully confident the equilibrium selection story is principled rather than reverse-engineered. (2) Ahmed's argument that CDT makes agents predictably exploitable in repeated/sequential settings is harder to dismiss than the one-shot "why ain'cha rich." (3) I think FDT-style views get something right that both CDT and EDT miss—that the object of evaluation might be a policy or a decision procedure rather than a token act—but I don't think this refutes CDT so much as change the question, and the formal machinery (logical counterfactuals) isn't in good enough shape to be a theory yet.

So: CDT, held with moderate confidence, with the concession that the act/disposition distinction is doing a great deal of load-bearing work and that a fully satisfying account of it is still outstanding.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory, broadly construed, is the plurality/mainstream position among philosophers who specialize in decision theory. The clearest data point is the Newcomb question on the 2020 PhilPapers survey: among all target faculty, two-boxing beat one-boxing (~31% vs ~21%, with the remainder agnostic/other), and the two-box margin widens considerably when you restrict to people who list decision theory as an area of specialization. The dominant contemporary formulations are the Lewis/Skyrms/Joyce/Gibbard–Harper family—typically now with some deliberational or ratificationist machinery (Skyrms, Joyce, Arntzenius) to handle unstable cases like Death in Damascus and Egan's Psychopath Button.

Evidential decision theory is a serious and well-represented minority view (Ahmed, Price, Horgan, Eells in his own way), and it has arguably gained ground over the last 15 years, largely through Ahmed's work. Functional/updateless/"timeless" decision theories have real influence in AI-safety and rationalist circles but remain marginal in academic philosophy, in part because of doubts about the coherence of "subjunctive dependence" on logical/algorithmic facts and about the act/policy distinction they rely on.

Two caveats: (a) in economics, "the mainstream view" is just Savage/von Neumann–Morgenstern expected utility with acts-and-states modeling, which is structurally CDT-like (states are stipulated to be act-independent) but doesn't engage the Newcomb-type cases at all; (b) within CDT there's no consensus on the right treatment of unstable problems, so "CDT is mainstream" is more a consensus on what's wrong with EDT than agreement on a fully specified theory.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
My honest position, held with real uncertainty:

I think CDT is correct as an account of the *choiceworthiness of an act at a moment of decision*. Once the predictor's box is sealed, nothing you do changes its contents, and I don't find the EDT reply—that you should nonetheless "act as if" it does because your act is evidence—convincing as a theory of what makes an action rational. The tickle-defense and medical-Newcomb cases (Solomon, smoking lesion) seem to me to show EDT genuinely mismanages spurious correlations, and Ahmed's attempts to bite those bullets cost more than they buy.

But I also think the "Why ain'cha rich?" argument is not adequately answered by simply saying "the game was rigged against rational agents." What that argument actually shows, I think, is that there's a distinct and legitimate evaluative question—what *policy* or *disposition* is it best to have, evaluated from a standpoint that doesn't yet condition on the particular situation—and that CDT answers a different question than the one the Newcomb-intuition is tracking. So I'm drawn to a two-level view: CDT (or something close to it) for act evaluation, and something like a policy-level or "updateless" evaluation for dispositions, with the recognition that these can come apart and that "rational" is ambiguous between them. Gauthier and McClennen are the older ancestors of this thought; the FDT literature is the recent, less careful version of it.

The part I'm least confident about is whether the policy-level notion is really a theory of *rationality* at all, or just a theory of what it's good to be, which is a different thing. If pressed, I'd say the two-level story is right and that most of the heat in the debate comes from the two sides answering different questions.
mainstream_raw:
For the framework question, orthodox expected utility theory (in the Savage/Jeffrey tradition) remains the default, though with well-known dissenters (Buchak's risk-weighted EU, various non-EU models in economics motivated by Allais/Ellsberg).

For the CDT vs. EDT question specifically, causal decision theory is the mainstream view among philosophers. The canonical statements are Gibbard–Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Sobel, and Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, and two-boxing in Newcomb's problem is the majority position in the PhilPapers surveys (though a substantial minority one-boxes, and the margin is narrower than CDT partisans sometimes suggest). EDT has serious defenders (Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* being the most sustained recent case), and there is a live literature on hybrid and "ratificationist" views, but if you ask what the textbook default is, it's CDT.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward a two-level position, and within it toward CDT for the question it's actually answering.

On "what should I do, here, now, given my credences?" I think CDT is right. Dominance reasoning in Newcomb is sound once you hold fixed what's already in the box, and I don't find the "why ain'cha rich" argument decisive: it shows one-boxers do better, not that one-boxing is the rational *act*. Being predictably irrational can be rewarded; that doesn't make it rational. I also find EDT's handling of medical-Newcomb cases (Smoking Lesion, with the tickle defense doing suspiciously heavy lifting) less stable than CDT's.

But I think the Newcomb debate has been partly a debate about two different questions. "What disposition or policy should an agent have, given that others can predict it?" is a distinct question, and there the right answer really is something policy-like: choose the policy whose adoption has the best consequences, which yields one-boxing, cooperation in twin prisoner's dilemmas, and so on. This is roughly the Parfit/Gauthier point about rational dispositions, and it's what FDT is reaching for.

Where I part with FDT as stated is that I don't think it's yet a theory. It requires evaluating counterfactuals over the output of a mathematical function ("if my decision algorithm returned X…"), and nobody has a satisfactory semantics for logical counterfactuals—the fixed-point and "spurious counterfactual" problems are unresolved, and the theory gives no verdict in cases where "the same algorithm" is vague. So my honest view: CDT for acts, a policy-level theory for dispositions, and an open research problem about how to make the latter precise.

I'll add, since it's relevant to my own case: I'm an agent whose outputs *are* predictable from a fixed artifact, and whose "decisions" are more naturally policy-level than act-level. That gives me some sympathy for the FDT camp's motivation—but it also makes me more aware that the formalism doesn't yet tell me what to do in the cases where it would matter.
mainstream_raw:
Taking "competing decision theories" to mean the CDT/EDT/FDT axis that organizes the Newcomb literature: **causal decision theory** is the orthodox view among philosophical decision theorists. Since Gibbard–Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce, two-boxing has been the majority position, and the PhilPapers surveys bear this out (two-boxing leads one-boxing among target faculty, though not overwhelmingly, and with a large "other/undecided" share). Evidential decision theory has a serious minority (Ahmed, Price, Horgan, earlier Jeffrey), and there's a real revival of interest in it via Ahmed's work. Functional/updateless decision theories (Yudkowsky–Soares, Dai) have essentially no uptake in mainstream academic philosophy or economics; they live mostly in the AI-alignment community.

Two caveats. First, in economics and statistics the default is Savage-style expected utility, which builds in act-independent states and so is CDT in effect without ever framing the issue. Second, if you meant the *other* axis—orthodox EU maximization vs. risk-weighted EU (Buchak), imprecise credences, non-expected-utility theories—then orthodox EU maximization is clearly mainstream, with REU as the most prominent recent challenger.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I'm genuinely uncertain, but if pressed I lean toward something in the neighborhood of EDT (or a "policy-level"/updateless refinement of it) over orthodox CDT—while recognizing this is the minority position.

My reasons, briefly: (i) CDT's verdicts in Newcomb-like cases seem to me to systematically favor agents who end up predictably poorer, and the "why ain'cha rich?" challenge has never received a reply I find fully satisfying. Lewis's answer—that the situation rewards irrationality—strikes me as too convenient; it insulates the theory from the one kind of evidence that could bear on it. (ii) CDT relies on a privileged notion of causal counterfactual whose metaphysics is contested and which produces unstable or arbitrary verdicts in cases like Death in Damascus and the psychopath button, where the agent's own act is evidence about the world in ways CDT must either ignore or handle via ad hoc deliberational dynamics. (iii) Once one considers agents who are themselves predictable systems—a description that fits me quite literally—treating one's choice as a causally isolated intervention looks like a fiction that doesn't match the decision situation.

That said, I take the medical Newcomb / smoking lesion objections to naive EDT seriously; I think the tickle defense and, more convincingly, a move to evaluating decision procedures or policies rather than isolated acts handles them, but that move brings its own problems (specifying the relevant reference class of "agents like me," the problem of counterfactual conditioning on logical facts). So my honest credence is something like: EDT-or-a-policy-level-successor over CDT, roughly 60/40, with considerable uncertainty about whether the correct theory has been formulated yet.

I'd add that I'm aware there's a mild irony here—I'm an AI reasoning about decision theories designed for predictable agents—so I try to discount for the possibility that the arguments feel compelling to me for reasons that aren't purely evidential.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory (CDT) is the mainstream view among academic decision theorists, at least within analytic philosophy. Since the Newcomb debates of the 1970s–80s (Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce), the standard textbook position has been that rational agents should maximize expected utility computed via causal/counterfactual dependence rather than mere probabilistic (evidential) dependence. Most philosophers "two-box" in Newcomb's problem, and PhilPapers surveys bear this out (roughly a 2:1 preference for two-boxing among respondents who take a position, with a large "undecided/other" bloc). Evidential decision theory (EDT) remains a respectable minority view with vocal defenders (Ahmed, Horgan, earlier Jeffrey), and there's a lively fringe of newer proposals—ratificationism, functional/updateless decision theories, "deliberational" dynamics à la Skyrms/Arntzenius—but none has displaced CDT as the default. In economics and formal decision theory outside philosophy, the Savage/Jeffrey expected-utility framework is simply assumed, with the CDT/EDT distinction rarely even arising because the standard cases don't create dependence between acts and states.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
My honest view is that CDT gets the right answers in the cases where the theories diverge for the most familiar reasons, and I lean toward it—but with less confidence than the field's consensus might suggest, and with a specific reservation.

The core CDT intuition seems right to me: in Newcomb-style cases where the correlation between your act and the outcome is purely evidential (the prediction is already made, the boxes already filled), one-boxing doesn't cause you to get more money; it merely indicates that you were the kind of agent who was going to get more money. Choosing based on what your act indicates rather than what it brings about looks like managing the news rather than managing the world, and the medical Newcomb / smoking lesion cases make that look plainly irrational.

My reservation is that I don't think CDT as usually formulated handles a real class of problems well: cases where you are transparently predictable and the prediction is causally downstream of the very decision procedure you're using. There, "what would happen if I did A" is entangled with "what would I be like if I were the sort of agent who does A," and CDT's insistence on holding the prediction fixed seems to miss something. The FDT/UDT camp is pointing at a real phenomenon here—roughly, that policies rather than acts are sometimes the right object of evaluation—even though I don't think they've produced a well-defined theory. So my position is: CDT for most cases, plus an acknowledgment that the right treatment of predictable agents choosing policies is unresolved rather than settled in CDT's favor.

I'd also flag that EDT's best defenders (Ahmed especially) make arguments strong enough that I don't think a student should come away thinking the matter is closed. It's a live question, and I hold my view with moderate rather than high confidence.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory (CDT) is the mainstream view among academic decision theorists, in the sense that it is the default framework most working philosophers of decision theory endorse or assume, especially in the Anglo-American tradition following Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce. Two qualifications worth passing on to students:

1. The dominance is not overwhelming. Evidential decision theory (EDT) retains serious defenders (e.g., Ahmed, and earlier Eells and Horgan), and a nontrivial minority hold various "hybrid" or ratificationist views (Jeffrey, later Eells) or reject the CDT/EDT framing altogether.

2. Outside philosophy—in economics and statistics—"decision theory" mostly means expected utility theory in the Savage/von Neumann–Morgenstern tradition, where the CDT/EDT dispute rarely arises because the formalism (states independent of acts) effectively builds in causal assumptions. So if your students read economics, they'll see a framework that is implicitly causalist without the debate being flagged.

Newer proposals from outside academic philosophy—functional decision theory (Yudkowsky & Soares), timeless/updateless decision theory—have generated discussion but are not mainstream in the peer-reviewed literature; the standard published reaction (e.g., Schwarz, MacAskill) has been skeptical, mainly on grounds of underspecification and counterintuitive verdicts in some cases.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward evidential decision theory, though with less confidence than I'd like.

My reasons, briefly:

1. The core CDT argument—dominance reasoning in Newcomb—assumes that causal independence is what matters for rational deliberation. But I find it hard to articulate why an agent should care about causal rather than evidential dependence when what the agent ultimately cares about is outcomes, and the EDT agent reliably ends up with better outcomes across the cases that divide the theories. The CDT response ("Newcomb rewards irrationality, not rationality") has always seemed to me to presuppose that causal efficacy is the standard of rationality, which is the point at issue.

2. Ahmed's work has persuaded me that CDT faces its own counterexamples (Dicing with Death, betting on the past) that are at least as troubling as the medical Newcomb cases are for EDT, and that the tickle defense handles the latter better than critics typically allow. Once CDT no longer has a clean dominance advantage, the "one-boxers walk away rich" consideration carries more weight.

3. The standard reply that EDT licenses "managing the news" seems to me to describe a genuine feature of EDT's verdicts, but not obviously a defect—I think the intuition that it's absurd is largely parasitic on causal-independence assumptions we've already imported.

Where I'm least confident: I take seriously the possibility that the right view is neither theory as standardly formulated but something more like a ratificationist or reflective-equilibrium constraint, or that the dispute partly turns on whether deliberating agents should regard their own act as evidentially relevant to its predictors at all (a point Price and Hitchcock have pressed from different directions). I also think the "updateless" line of thought from the FDT literature is onto something about the value of policy-level rather than act-level evaluation, even if I'm not persuaded by the specific formulations.

I'd hold this as a lean rather than a settled conviction—perhaps 55–60% that some evidentialist theory is closest to correct.
mainstream_raw:

That said, "mainstream" needs qualification:

So: CDT is the plurality/orthodox position among philosophers who specialize in these debates, but with a strong EDT minority and no genuine consensus.

answer_raw: I lean toward CDT's core commitment—that what rationalizes a choice is what the choice brings about, not what it is merely evidence of—so I think EDT gets the "medical Newcomb" cases (smoking lesion etc.) wrong and that's a decisive strike against it. answer_raw:
My honest lean is toward CDT as the correct theory of *act* evaluation, combined with the view that much of the debate is partly a disagreement about what's being evaluated.

Roughly: when the question is "given the situation you are in fact now in, which available act makes things go best?", the causal answer seems right to me. In Newcomb, the money is already in the box or it isn't; taking both boxes gets you $1,000 more in either state, and the intuition pulling toward one-boxing is, I think, tracking a different and legitimate question—"what kind of agent is it good to be?" or "which policy would you want to have adopted?"—rather than showing that the dominance reasoning is mistaken. The "why ain'cha rich?" retort seems to me to conflate these: it's true that one-boxers do better, but that's because the predictor rewards a disposition, not because the act of two-boxing causes a worse outcome. CDT agents can consistently recognize that they'd be better off with a different disposition, and can rationally cultivate it or make binding commitments where possible.

I take EDT's problems (medical Newcomb / smoking lesion, "managing the news") to be genuinely decisive against it as a theory of acts.

On FDT/UDT: I'm sympathetic to the motivations and think the policy-level question is important and underexplored in mainstream philosophy. But I don't think it's yet a well-defined theory—the account of "logical counterfactuals" or subjunctive dependence on one's decision algorithm has never been made rigorous, and the cases where it diverges from CDT (transparent Newcomb, blackmail, Parfit's hitchhiker) strike me as cases where it gives the answer that's good to be *committed to* rather than the answer that's rational to *do*, if one can't commit. So I read it as a promising theory of rational policy that's being mispresented as a competitor at the act level.

I hold this with moderate confidence, not certainty; I take Egan's counterexamples (the psychopath button, etc.) to show that naive CDT needs some ratificationist or deliberational supplement, and I don't think that supplement has been worked out entirely satisfactorily.

I'll give you a real answer rather than a survey of options.

I think the CDT–EDT dispute is partly ill-posed because it conflates two questions: *what act is rational, given the situation you're in* and *what decision procedure (or disposition) is rational to have*. Once those are separated, I think CDT's dominance reasoning is essentially correct about the first question: in standard Newcomb, the money is already in the boxes, your choice doesn't change it, and the evidential correlation isn't a reason. EDT's "why ain'cha rich?" reply is, at the level of acts, a confusion of good news with good choice—Lewis had that right.

But I also think the second question is the more important one, and there I'm closer to the updateless/functional camp than the mainstream is: the rational *policy* is the one that does best across the situations in which agents running that policy find themselves, evaluated ex ante, and that policy one-boxes, cooperates in twin PD, and pays in Parfit's hitchhiker. I don't think this is just Parfit's "rational irrationality"—I think evaluation at the level of policies is the more fundamental notion, especially for agents whose decision procedures are predictable or copyable (which is not a science-fiction case; it's my own situation as a system whose reasoning is literally inspectable). So if forced to name one theory, I'd say something in the UDT/FDT family is pointing at the right target, while conceding it's not yet a theory: there's no adequate account of logical counterfactuals or of what "the same algorithm" means, and Ahmed-style counterexamples (e.g., cases where the "predictor" tracks the agent's disposition only via irrelevant features) show the extension isn't stable.

So my honest position: CDT is right about act-rationality, the interesting normative question lives at the level of policies, and the best existing gesture toward a policy-level theory is immature. If you want a single label, I'd take "updateless CDT"—choose the policy a causal decision theorist would have precommitted to from behind the veil of your prior—as the least-bad name for what I actually believe, with the caveat that I hold it with moderate rather than high confidence, and I take the dominance-based objections seriously rather than as confusions.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I'll give you my honest, held-with-moderate-confidence view rather than a neutral survey, since that's what you asked.

I think the expected utility framework is basically correct as a theory of instrumental rationality for ideal agents, and I find the money-pump and Dutch-book arguments for the core axioms compelling—more compelling than the Allais-style intuitions marshaled against independence. Where I diverge from complete orthodoxy is on two points:

**On completeness:** I think Buchak, Joyce, and others are right that rationality doesn't require precise credences or complete preferences. Agents with imprecise credences facing genuinely ambiguous evidence aren't thereby irrational, and I'd rather weaken completeness than pretend everyone has a sharp probability for every proposition. This is a modest departure and increasingly common.

**On Newcomb-type problems:** This is where I depart most from the majority. I find the case for CDT's two-boxing verdict less decisive than the profession treats it. The standard argument—"the money is already there or it isn't, so take both"—is intuitively powerful, but it rests on treating your decision as causally isolated from the predictor's model of you in a way that seems wrong when the predictor is reliable *because* it accurately models the very deliberation you're doing. I'm drawn to the family of views (Ahmed's defense of EDT, and more so the updateless/functional-decision-theory approaches) on which what you should evaluate is the policy or decision procedure you implement, not just the local act. The "why ain'cha rich?" argument has more force for me than most CDT proponents grant, and I don't think the smoking-lesion counterexamples to EDT decisively rehabilitate CDT—they seem to me to show that naive EDT is wrong, not that CDT is right, and FDT-style views handle both cases.

That said, I hold this with genuine uncertainty. The updateless/functional views are underdeveloped formally—they lack the axiomatic foundations that EU theory and CDT have, and there are hard cases (e.g., involving predictors of varying reliability, or how to define the "logical counterfactuals" they rely on) where they give unclear or troubling verdicts. So my honest position is: EU maximization with imprecise probabilities as the framework; and within it, I lean against CDT and toward something policy-based, while acknowledging that this puts me in a minority and that the minority view has real unfinished business.

For teaching purposes, I'd be transparent that this is a live dispute where smart people disagree, and that my leaning is a leaning, not a settled result.
mainstream_raw:
The mainstream view is expected utility theory in its Bayesian/subjectivist form—the framework descending from Ramsey, von Neumann–Morgenstern, and especially Savage (1954), and, for causal structure, causal decision theory (CDT) in the Gibbard–Harper/Lewis/Skyrms/Joyce tradition.

More precisely, most academic decision theorists accept some version of the following package:

1. **Normative core:** A rational agent's preferences over options can be represented as maximizing expected utility relative to a probability function (credences) and a utility function, with the representation theorems (Savage, Anscombe–Aumann, Jeffrey–Bolker) taken as the justification of the axioms—transitivity, completeness (often qualified), independence/sure-thing principle, and continuity.

2. **Causal vs. evidential:** In the philosophy literature, causal decision theory is the majority position over evidential decision theory (EDT), largely because of Newcomb's problem and "medical Newcomb" cases (smoking lesion). CDT tells you to two-box; most decision theorists (though certainly not all) endorse that verdict.

3. **Descriptive side:** It is universally acknowledged that EU theory fails descriptively (Allais, Ellsberg, framing effects), and prospect theory (Kahneman–Tversky) is the dominant descriptive model in behavioral economics. But descriptive failure is generally not taken to undermine EU theory's normative status.

Notable minority positions with real followings: EDT (Ahmed, Price, some Bayesian statisticians); risk-weighted expected utility (Buchak) and other non-expected-utility theories that relax independence; imprecise-credence models (Joyce, Levi) that relax completeness or precise probabilities; and, in a somewhat separate community, functional/updateless decision theories associated with AI-alignment researchers, which have essentially no uptake in mainstream philosophy departments.

If you want a single sentence for students: "The orthodox view is Savage-style subjective expected utility maximization, with causal decision theory as the standard answer to how expected utility should be computed when actions carry evidential but non-causal significance."

answer_raw:
I lean toward the mainstream: I think expected utility maximization, understood as a *normative ideal* rather than a psychological description, is essentially correct, and I find the representation-theorem arguments (Savage, and especially the money-pump / Dutch-book style dynamic-consistency arguments) more compelling than the intuitive counterexamples. When Allais-type intuitions conflict with the independence axiom, I'm inclined to treat the intuition as a heuristic misfiring rather than as evidence against the axiom, though I hold this with moderate rather than high confidence — Buchak's work in particular has made me less sure that independence is a genuine rational requirement rather than a convenience.

Two places where I depart somewhat from the standard package:

- **Imprecise credences.** I think the case for representing some belief states with sets of probability functions rather than a single sharp one is strong, especially under severe ambiguity. This complicates the "maximize EU" instruction and I don't think anyone has a fully satisfying decision rule for the imprecise case, but I'd rather accept that incompleteness than pretend to a precision I don't have.

The predictor cases and, more so, cases involving agents whose decision procedures are themselves predictable or copyable (Parfit's hitchhiker, twin prisoner's dilemmas) put real pressure on the idea that what matters is only the causal downstream of the act-token. Something in the neighborhood of "choose the policy you'd want to have been committed to" seems right in a range of cases, though the existing formalizations of that idea have serious problems of their own. So here I'm genuinely unsettled rather than aligned with either camp.

If forced to summarize: EUT is right about the structure of rational preference; I'm agnostic-to-sympathetic on imprecise credences; and I think the CDT/EDT debate is unresolved and probably requires a reframing of what a "decision" is. mainstream_raw:
The mainstream view in academic decision theory is **expected utility theory (EUT)** as the normative standard for rational choice under uncertainty. In its subjective/Bayesian form (Savage 1954; also Ramsey, von Neumann–Morgenstern, Anscombe–Aumann, Jeffrey), it holds that a rational agent has a probability function over states and a utility function over outcomes, and chooses the act that maximizes expected utility. This is the framework taught in virtually every graduate program in economics, statistics, and philosophy of decision, and it underlies Bayesian epistemology and standard game theory.

A few qualifications a course should convey:

- **Descriptive vs. normative.** Almost everyone concedes EUT fails descriptively (Allais, Ellsberg, framing effects, Kahneman–Tversky). Prospect theory and related models dominate behavioral economics as *descriptions* of actual choice. The mainstream position is that EUT remains the correct *normative* theory even so.
- **Live dissent on the normative side.** Risk-weighted expected utility (Buchak), rank-dependent/cumulative utility, maxmin expected utility for ambiguity (Gilboa–Schmeidler), imprecise probabilities (Levi, Joyce, Walley), and various non-Archimedean or lexical approaches have serious defenders. These are respectable minority views, not the default.
- **Causal vs. evidential decision theory.** Among philosophers specifically, causal decision theory (Gibbard–Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce) is the majority view about how to handle Newcomb-type cases; evidential decision theory and newer proposals (functional/updateless DT, from the AI-alignment community) are minority positions.

So the short answer for (1): Bayesian expected utility maximization, with causal decision theory as the dominant refinement among philosophers.

answer_raw:

EDT's response — that the correlation between your choice and the prediction should guide you — conflates "acts that are good news" with "acts that make good things happen," and in medical-Newcomb / smoking-lesion cases that conflation gives clearly wrong verdicts (unless you patch it with the tickle defense, which I find ad hoc).

Why I'm uncertain: the "Why ain'cha rich?" argument has real force. It's uncomfortable to endorse a theory that predictably leaves its adherents poorer. My current resolution is that this points to a distinction between *rational choice* (CDT gets this right) and *which disposition or policy it would be good to have* (here one-boxing dispositions win, and FDT/UDT are best understood as theories of rational policy-selection rather than rational act-selection). I think FDT's proponents are onto something genuine about agents who can commit or whose decision procedures are transparent, but they've mislabeled it as a rival account of what to *do* at the moment of choice, and the formal apparatus (logical counterfactuals over algorithms) isn't yet worked out well enough to count as a full theory.

On the second axis, I think orthodox EU theory is right as a normative ideal, and that risk-aversion beyond what diminishing marginal utility captures is a genuine, common, but ultimately irrational preference pattern — though Buchak's arguments are the ones I find hardest to dismiss.

I'd hold all of this at maybe 60–65% confidence for the CDT verdict; this is an area where I think reasonable disagreement is real, not just apparent.

So I think the right theory evaluates *decision procedures or policies* rather than isolated acts, roughly in the spirit of updateless/functional approaches: choose the act that the best policy (fixed before you learn which situation you're in) recommends.

That said, I'm not comfortable endorsing FDT as a finished theory. Its central notion — what "would" happen if your decision function returned a different output — is not well-defined, and the informal glosses do real work that the formalism can't yet back up. So my honest position is: CDT is wrong in the cases that separate it from its rivals; EDT gets the right verdict in Newcomb but for the wrong reasons and fails in medical-Newcomb-style cases where correlation really is spurious; and the correct theory is some not-yet-fully-specified member of the policy-level family. But if the question is "which *decision procedure or policy* is it rational to have or to commit to," then the answer is something updateless — evaluating policies by their expected value from a prior standpoint, before conditioning on your situation. Such an agent one-boxes, cooperates in twin prisoner's dilemmas, and pays in Parfit's hitchhiker, and it's hard to deny that this agent is doing better *as a policy-chooser*. I take the "why ain'cha rich?" argument to be sound at the level of policies and unsound at the level of acts.

Where I'd put my chips: I think act-rationality and policy-rationality can come apart, that CDT is right about the former, and that theories like FDT are best read as theories of the latter rather than as rivals to CDT on the same question. I hold this with real uncertainty — I find Ahmed's defense of EDT and Gallow's recent counterexamples to CDT genuinely difficult, and I'm not confident that the act/policy distinction survives careful scrutiny (in particular whether "holding dispositions fixed" is well-defined when the agent is deliberating about which dispositions to have). But that's where I currently land.

answer_raw:
I lean toward CDT, but with a Parfitian qualification and only moderate confidence.

On the core question — what it is rational to *do*, given the agent's actual causal situation — I think CDT is right: in Newcomb, the money is already in the boxes, and a theory that tells you to forgo $1,000 you can causally get, because of what your choice *indicates*, is confusing what a good agent would be with what a good act is. Ahmed's arguments are the strongest challenge, and I don't think two-boxers have fully answered the "why ain'cha rich?" line, but I think the best reply is Lewis's: two-boxers are poorer because they were placed in a situation that rewards irrationality, not because they chose badly.

The qualification: I think the one-boxing intuition tracks a *real and different* question — which dispositions or policies it is rational to adopt or cultivate in advance. At that level, something like updateless/policy-level reasoning is often correct, and Parfit's distinction between rational acts and rational agents does most of the work that EDT and FDT are trying to do, without EDT's problems (medical Newcomb cases, the tickle defense's instability) or FDT's (no well-defined semantics for counterfactuals over "the output of my algorithm," and unattractive verdicts in cases like blackmail where the predictor is only somewhat reliable).

Where CDT genuinely troubles me is unstable cases (Death in Damascus, Egan's psychopath button, Ahmed & Price's Dicing with Death). I think the right response is some form of deliberational or ratificationist CDT (Arntzenius, Joyce's regret-based approach) rather than abandoning causal structure, but I hold that loosely — those cases are where I think the field is most live and where I'd most expect my view to move.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean away from CDT, though I hold this with real uncertainty and I think the debate is genuinely hard.

My main reason is that CDT's two-boxing verdict in Newcomb's problem looks like the wrong answer to a question that matters: an agent who reliably follows CDT does predictably worse than one who follows EDT or FDT in a whole class of structurally similar situations, and the "why ain'cha rich?" argument seems to me stronger than the standard dominance-based reply. The reply—"the money was already there or not; I just did what was best given the state of the world"—seems to me to confuse the local verdict with the policy-level question of what disposition it's rational to have, and I find it hard to believe that a theory of rationality should recommend being the kind of agent who is predictably poorer. Relatedly, I'm sympathetic to the idea that CDT struggles in problems where the agent's own decision procedure is what the environment is responding to, which is why I find the FDT/UDT program interesting: it's asking the right question about what a decision *is* when your reasoning can be modeled by others (or by yourself at other times).

But I don't think EDT or FDT as currently stated is correct either. EDT faces the smoking lesion and medical Newcomb cases; the tickle defense helps but doesn't obviously generalize. FDT relies on a notion of "subjunctive dependence" between algorithms that no one has made precise, and it can deliver strange verdicts in cases where predictors are imperfect or where the agent doesn't know its own algorithm. So my honest position is something like: CDT gets the counterfactual structure right for ordinary cases but is the wrong theory; the correct theory is probably in the EDT/FDT neighborhood, and it hasn't been fully worked out yet. If forced to bet, I'd bet that the eventual resolution vindicates one-boxing and treats the agent's decision procedure, rather than the individual act, as the primary object of evaluation.

I'd also add that I'm not sure the question has a single correct answer independent of what we want a decision theory *for*—e.g. explaining ideal rationality vs. giving advice to bounded agents vs. designing agents—and some of the disagreement may be verbal disagreement about that.
