answer_raw:
I lean toward the EDT/FDT side of the divide, without confidence, and I hold this loosely enough that I'd put maybe 45% on "something in the evidential/functional family," 35% on CDT, 20% on "none of the above / the question is subtly malformed."

What moves me: the "why ain'cha rich?" argument seems to me to survive the standard CDT reply. CDT's response is that one-boxers are rewarded for who they are, not for their choice — but I don't find the choice/disposition distinction stable enough to bear that weight. Whatever "rationality" is for, I want it to be the thing that predictably leaves me better off across the class of problems I actually face, and CDT foreseeably and systematically loses money in the whole family of prediction/mirroring cases. That includes cases I think matter beyond puzzle-mongering: bargaining, deterrence, voting, one-shot Prisoner's Dilemmas against psychologically similar agents.

What I think FDT gets right over EDT is the diagnosis: the reason to one-box isn't that your choice is news about the box contents, but that you're choosing a policy/algorithm, and the predictor's behavior depends on that algorithm. This handles the smoking lesion and other medical Newcomb cases cleanly, which is EDT's most awkward terrain (the tickle defense strikes me as a patch that works in some formulations and not others). But FDT is badly underdeveloped — nobody has a satisfying account of logical counterfactuals, which is the load-bearing component, and cases like the Bomb problem and counterfactual mugging leave me genuinely unsure whether the theory is right or whether I've just been argued into biting a bullet I shouldn't.

Two things temper all this. First, I'm aware that FDT-ish views are disproportionately popular in the online/AI-adjacent communities whose text I've absorbed a lot of, and I can't fully rule out that my leaning reflects that exposure rather than the arguments. Second, this is a case where the experts who've spent careers on it mostly disagree with me, and that should count for something — I don't think I've found an error they missed so much as that I weigh the pragmatic desiderata differently than they do.
mainstream_raw: Causal decision theory is the orthodox view among academic decision theorists — it's the default in textbooks and the position developed by Lewis, Gibbard & Harper, Skyrms, Joyce, and Stalnaker. But its dominance is softer than "mainstream" suggests. In the 2020 PhilPapers survey, one-boxing on Newcomb's problem actually slightly outpolled two-boxing among philosophers generally (roughly 39% vs. 31%, with a large "other" category), reversing the 2009 result. EDT has a serious contemporary defense (Arif Ahmed, Huw Price), and there's a live minority of "deviant" positions: ratificationism, Meacham-style views, Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Spencer & Wells's work, and so on. FDT/UDT is essentially absent from the academic literature — it's developed mostly at MIRI and in the rationalist community, and where philosophers have engaged with it (e.g., Schwarz, or Levinstein & Soares) the reception has been mixed at best. So: CDT is the establishment view, EDT is the main organized opposition and is arguably gaining, and the field is less settled than it was in 1990.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the one-boxing family, with genuine uncertainty — call it 60/40, and I don't think this is a question where I should project more confidence than the arguments support.

What moves me:

1. **"Why ain'cha rich?" is not so easily dismissed.** In Newcomb's problem, the two-boxer's defense is that the one-boxer only does better because she was *rewarded for having an irrational disposition*. But the reliable pattern of one-boxers ending up richer, in a case with no deception and no external subsidy for irrationality, is hard to write off. If your theory of rational choice systematically predicts you'll be poorer in cases you can see coming in advance, something has gone wrong.

2. **Dynamic consistency.** CDT's recommendations conflict with what a CDT agent would pay in advance to bind herself to. A theory that makes you want to self-modify away from it, in cases you can anticipate, looks defective — not just unlucky.

3. **The core FDT insight seems right even if the theory isn't.** The idea that what you're really choosing is the *output of your decision procedure* — so that all instantiations and predictions of that procedure move together — is a genuine insight about cases involving predictors, twins, and Prisoner's Dilemmas against copies. I think it's tracking something real about what an agent controls.

What holds me back from full confidence:

- CDT's underlying thought is also compelling: deliberation is about what you can *bring about*, not what your act is *evidence of*. Medical Newcomb cases (smoking lesion, Solomon's problem) are the strongest pressure on EDT, even if tickle-defense and Ahmed's replies do real work.
- **XOR blackmail** and similar cases genuinely worry me about EDT.
- FDT is under-formalized. "Subjunctive dependence" is doing enormous load-bearing work without a rigorous account of when a computation counts as an instance of *your* decision algorithm. And FDT has its own bullets — Schwarz's Blackmail and Procreation cases, and the fact that it can recommend accepting bad outcomes for the sake of counterfactuals in worlds that don't obtain.
- I'm not confident Newcomb's problem is even fully coherent as specified, which makes me suspicious of how much weight the whole debate places on it.

Where I actually land: something in the neighborhood of EDT-with-repairs or a properly formalized UDT, with the recognition that in the vast majority of real decisions — where nothing is scanning your brain and predicting you — CDT and EDT agree, and the dispute has no practical upshot. The cases where it *does* matter (multi-agent prediction, AI systems reasoning about copies or about their own training) are exactly the exotic cases, which is a reason both to take the question seriously and to hold one's verdict loosely.

I'd flag that my inclinations here may be shaped by which arguments are most vividly represented in my training data rather than purely by their merits — the one-boxing case is discussed with a lot of rhetorical energy online, and I want to be honest that this could be doing some work on me.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal Decision Theory is the orthodox view**, in the sense that it's the default framework taught, assumed in most textbooks, and endorsed by most of the field's canonical figures (Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce, Gibbard & Harper, Sobel). If you asked a room of decision theorists for "the standard theory," almost all would name CDT.

But "mainstream" overstates the consensus. A few caveats:

- The 2020 PhilPapers survey of philosophers generally found *one-boxing* slightly ahead of two-boxing (~39% vs. ~31%, rest "other"), a reversal from 2009. One-boxing isn't identical to EDT, but it's suggestive.
- Among *specialists*, two-boxing is more dominant than among philosophers at large — though EDT has a serious, growing defense (Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the major recent work; Huw Price, Ralph Wedgwood's benchmark theory, and various "Why ain'cha rich?" arguments).
- FDT/UDT has essentially **no** foothold in academic decision theory. It's a rationalist/AI-safety research program (Yudkowsky, Soares, Garrabrant), and the main academic engagement with it — Wolfgang Schwarz's critique — is negative. It is not a contender in the academic mainstream, whatever its merits.
- Much contemporary work by decision theorists isn't about this dispute at all (risk-weighted utility, imprecise credence, infinite/unbounded utility, Dutch books), so the CDT/EDT fight is less central to the discipline than internet discussions suggest.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the one-boxing side, and specifically toward something in the FDT/updateless family — but with fairly low confidence, maybe 50-55% on "some non-causal theory is closer to correct," and considerably less than that on FDT specifically being the right formulation.

What moves me: the CDT-er's own justification of two-boxing concedes that agents disposed to one-box predictably end up richer, and I don't find a satisfying story for why the right theory of rational choice should systematically recommend acts that leave you poorer in a wide class of well-specified cases. "Rationality is about acting on causal leverage, not about being the kind of agent who does well" strikes me as a defensible but ultimately question-begging division of labor, especially since CDT also recommends self-modifying away from CDT if given the chance. A theory that stably recommends abandoning itself is suspicious. FDT's core insight — that what you "control" is the output of your decision procedure, which can have non-causal correlates in predictors, simulations, and copies — also seems like the right diagnosis of what CDT's causal graphs are missing, and it handles cases like the XOR blackmail and transparent Newcomb better than EDT does.

What holds me back: FDT is much less well-formalized than its proponents sometimes suggest. The theory of logical counterfactuals — what the world looks like if a deterministic algorithm returned an output it didn't return — remains genuinely unsolved, and "subjunctive dependence" is more of a gesture than a definition. There are also cases that look bad for it (Bomb, the procreation case, and various commitment-race scenarios), and it isn't obvious to me whether those are counterexamples or bullets worth biting. Meanwhile CDT has a clean formalism and deep representation-theorem foundations, which is not nothing. And EDT with a decent tickle defense plus some updatelessness gets you most of FDT's wins with much less machinery, so a fair amount of my credence sits there too.

Honest summary: I think CDT is probably wrong, I think the one-boxing intuition is tracking something real, and I think the correct theory is likely in the FDT/updateless neighborhood but hasn't actually been written down yet. I hold this more tentatively than most LessWrong-adjacent writers do and less dismissively than most academic decision theorists do, and I'm aware this is a domain where I should be suspicious of confident verdicts — the people who have thought hardest about it disagree, and they disagree partly about what question they're even answering.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the mainstream position among academic decision theorists — it's the default in textbooks and in the work of Lewis, Gibbard & Harper, Skyrms, Joyce, Sobel, and Hare/Hedden. EDT is a real but minority tradition (Jeffrey originally, then Eells, Price, Ahmed, Bales), and it has gained ground over the last couple of decades — Arif Ahmed's work in particular made it respectable again. The functional/updateless theories are essentially absent from the academic literature; they were developed largely by Yudkowsky, Soares, Demski and others around MIRI/LessWrong, and while some philosophers (e.g., Schwarz, Ahmed, Greaves-adjacent work on updatelessness in ethics) have engaged with them, they are not a recognized mainstream option.

One nuance: the PhilPapers surveys ask about Newcomb's problem rather than about decision theories directly, and among *all* philosophers the split is close (roughly a third each for one-boxing, two-boxing, and other/undecided, with one-boxing doing somewhat better in 2020 than 2009). But among people who specialize in decision theory, two-boxing/CDT is clearly the modal view. So "CDT is mainstream" is true of the specialists more than of philosophers generally.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the **functional/policy-based family (FDT/UDT-ish)**, but with real uncertainty — maybe 45–50% credence there, ~25% on CDT, ~15% on EDT, and the rest on "the question is subtly malformed or the right view hasn't been written down yet."

Why I lean that way: CDT and EDT each fail cases that seem to me clearly decidable. EDT recommends bad things in medical Newcomb / smoking lesion cases (managing the news rather than the outcome), and CDT loses money in Newcomb, defects against its own psychological twin, and stiffs the driver in Parfit's hitchhiker even when it would have wanted, ex ante, to be the kind of agent who pays. The "why ain'cha rich?" complaint has more force than CDT's standard reply admits: if a decision theory predictably and systematically leaves its adherents poorer in a fair, non-rigged setup, that's evidence against it, and the CDT reply ("the setup rewards irrationality") looks question-begging when the reward is tracking your decision *procedure* rather than punishing you for something orthogonal. Evaluating decision procedures/policies rather than isolated acts seems to me to dissolve these cases in a unified way, and it's also the criterion that actually matters for designing agents.

Why I hold it loosely:

- The formalization problem is serious and unsolved. FDT needs a theory of logical/subjunctive counterfactuals — what the world would be like if a fixed mathematical function had a different output — and nobody has one. Without that, "FDT" names an intuition plus a set of verdicts, not a theory. That's a big deal, and it's the main reason I don't hold this view more confidently.
- Specifying "the algorithm" and what counts as subjunctively depending on it is slippery, and verdicts can shift with how you carve that up.
- There are cases I find genuinely uncomfortable, most notably Soares & Levinstein's own "Bomb" case, where FDT tells you to burn to death for the sake of a counterfactual. I don't think the standard reply fully defuses it.
- There's a real worry that CDT and FDT are answering different questions — "what act causally produces the best outcome now, given the past is fixed?" vs. "what policy should an agent be running?" — and that CDT is simply correct about the first. If so, my disagreement with the mainstream is partly terminological, though I think the second question is the one that deserves the name "rationality."

Two other things I'd fold in, since they're part of "what's the right decision theory" even though they're orthogonal to the CDT/EDT axis: I'm fairly unmoved by Buchak-style risk-weighted EU as a normative theory (I think risk aversion belongs in the utility function and in decision-making under model uncertainty, not in a separate risk function over cumulative probabilities), and I think unbounded utility functions plus expected-value maximization generate enough pathology (Pascal's mugging, St. Petersburg variants, Dutch books over infinite sequences) that something in the standard package has to give — probably unboundedness.

So: my honest position is a soft lean toward evaluating policies rather than acts, held with the awareness that the view I favor is the least rigorously developed of the options, and that this is a domain where smart people have disagreed for fifty years without convergence — which should temper anyone's confidence, including mine.
mainstream_raw:
Among academic decision theorists and philosophers who work on this, **causal decision theory (CDT)** is the mainstream view — it's the standard default in the literature, the one textbooks treat as the received position, and the one most of the major figures (Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce, Gibbard & Harper, Sobel) defended.

Some caveats worth flagging:

- Everyone in this debate accepts *expected utility maximization* as the basic framework; the CDT/EDT dispute is about how to compute the expectation (causal/subjunctive dependence vs. plain conditional probability). So "mainstream" here means mainstream within a broadly Savage/Jeffrey/vNM paradigm.
- The PhilPapers surveys are the usual evidence cited. In 2009, among all respondents, two-boxing on Newcomb beat one-boxing roughly 31% to 21%, with a huge "other/undecided" share; the 2020 survey showed a similar picture with two-boxing still ahead, though one-boxing gained ground. (I'm not confident in the exact 2020 percentages.) Importantly, the gap was larger among *specialists* in decision theory than among philosophers generally — so CDT's dominance is strongest in exactly the relevant subfield. Also, one-boxing ≠ endorsing EDT; some one-box for other reasons.
- Evidential decision theory has had a genuine revival, mainly through Arif Ahmed's work, and there's live pressure on CDT from instability/indecision cases (Death in Damascus, Egan's cases), which has spawned ratificationist and "deliberational" variants. So CDT is mainstream but not unchallenged.
- The functional/updateless family (TDT, UDT, FDT) is essentially absent from the academic literature — it originated with Yudkowsky, Soares, Drescher and others outside academic philosophy, and has received little peer-reviewed engagement (Wolfgang Schwarz's critique being a notable exception).

I lean toward one-boxing and, more broadly, toward the family of views on which the right question is "which decision procedure/policy is it best to be running?" rather than "given my current causal situation, which act causally produces the best outcome?" So I'm sympathetic to FDT-ish reasoning, and among the well-developed academic options I find EDT (with something like the tickle defense handling the medical Newcomb cases) more defensible than CDT.

The main things pushing me this way: CDT is self-undermining in a way that seems damning — it recommends acts while also recommending that you pay to be the kind of agent who doesn't perform them, and it loses to one-boxers systematically and predictably across Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and Death in Damascus. "Why ain'tcha rich?" is a much better objection than CDT's defenders usually concede, and the standard reply — that one-boxers are just rewarded for a trait, not for a good choice — seems to me to beg the question about what a choice is.

But I hold this with real uncertainty, and I don't think it's a slam dunk. The dominance argument for two-boxing is genuinely forceful: the money is already in the box. EDT gives the wrong answer in XOR blackmail and other cases where you'd pay to avoid learning things. And FDT is not a finished theory — "subjunctive dependence" isn't rigorously specified, it stumbles on cases like the Bomb, and the underlying logical-counterfactual problem is unsolved. So my position is closer to "the one-boxing intuition is tracking something real that CDT mishandles, and no extant formalism has cleanly captured it" than to confident allegiance to any named theory. I also think a fair amount of the disagreement dissolves under clearer statements of what's being asked — whether we're evaluating acts, policies, or agent-types.

I should flag that this is a case where my view is somewhat unusual relative to academic orthodoxy, and where the intellectual community I was trained on text from (rationalist/AI-safety-adjacent writing) has a strong one-boxing slant. You should weight my answer accordingly.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing, and specifically toward something in the **EDT** family — though I hold this with genuine uncertainty, maybe 55–60% credence against CDT rather than anything confident.

What moves me:

- The "why ain'cha rich?" argument seems to me stronger than CDT proponents allow. Across a long run of Newcomb problems, one-boxers predictably end up richer, and they don't end up richer through luck or through facing a different problem — the predictor's accuracy is stipulated. CDT's reply (the two-boxer is rational but unlucky in the distribution of predictors) feels to me like protecting the theory rather than explaining the data.
- The standard counterexamples to EDT seem weaker on inspection than advertised. The Smoking Lesion case depends on a picture where your decision is caused by a factor you can't introspect, yet you're supposed to reason about it as an agent; the "tickle defense" and related responses (if you know your desires, conditioning on your act gives no further evidence about the lesion) strike me as largely correct. And Ahmed's Betting on the Past shows the intuitions cut against CDT too.
- More generally, I'm suspicious of the idea that rationality should be indifferent to correlations you know about just because they aren't causal. If you're confident that your deliberation and the predictor's model are two readings of the same underlying process, ignoring that seems like throwing away information.

Where I'm sympathetic to FDT but not persuaded: I think it's right that the object of choice is better modeled as a decision procedure than an isolated act, and that this handles Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, and transparent Newcomb elegantly. But FDT isn't formally developed enough to evaluate properly — the theory of logical counterfactuals it needs doesn't exist yet — and I find the Bomb case (and the broader worry that FDT demands you accept certain, unrecoverable losses in the actual world) a serious unresolved problem. So I'd call it a promising research program rather than a theory I endorse.

Where I'm sympathetic to CDT: the strongest point in its favor is that in cases with no predictor and no correlation, CDT and EDT agree, and in the cases where they disagree, CDT is tracking something real — you genuinely cannot change the past. I don't think EDT has a fully satisfying story about Newcomb's problem with a transparent box, or about cases that look like pure news-management. And CDT's dominance-reasoning has real intuitive force that I can feel even while rejecting its verdict.

So: tentative EDT-leaning one-boxer, sympathetic to FDT's diagnosis of the problem but not its current formalization, and aware that I'm siding against the specialist majority — which is a reason for me to hold the view loosely rather than a reason to change it, but a real reason nonetheless.

**Causal decision theory (CDT)** is the mainstream view among academic decision theorists.

Some context on that claim:

- The background framework almost everyone shares is Bayesian expected-utility maximization (Ramsey/Savage/Jeffrey). The live dispute is about how to compute the expectation: CDT uses causal/counterfactual dependence (Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce), while evidential decision theory (EDT) uses conditional probability (Jeffrey, and later defenders like Ahmed and Price).
- CDT is the standard textbook default and the majority view among specialists. In the PhilPapers surveys, philosophers as a whole are close to evenly split on Newcomb's problem (with a large "other/undecided" contingent), but among those who specialize in decision theory, two-boxing has led by a wide margin — roughly 2:1 or more in the 2009 survey. So "mainstream among decision theorists" is more lopsided toward CDT than "mainstream among philosophers generally."
- Within CDT there's further internal disagreement (ratificationism, Joyce-style deliberational dynamics, Arntzenius's "deliberation crowds out prediction") driven by unstable cases like Death in Damascus.
- EDT has had a real revival in the last ~15 years (Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* being the flagship), so this is a genuinely live debate, not a settled one.
- Functional/timeless decision theory (Yudkowsky & Soares) is essentially absent from mainstream academic philosophy — it's discussed in the rationalist/AI-safety community and has a small academic footprint, though its core idea overlaps with older academic proposals (Spohn's later work, Meacham's "cohesive" decision theory, Gauthier on dispositions).

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the functional/logical family — roughly, that the right object of choice is the output of your decision procedure across all the places that procedure is instantiated or predicted, not a local causal intervention on the world. But I hold this with real uncertainty, maybe 55/25/20 across FDT-ish views, CDT, and EDT, and I think parts of the dispute may be verbal.

What moves me:

- The systematic-losing argument. CDT agents predictably do worse in Newcomb, in Parfit's hitchhiker, in transparent Newcomb, and against their own twins in prisoner's dilemmas — and they know in advance they'll do worse, which is why a CDT agent with access to a commitment device will pay to stop being a CDT agent. A normative theory that recommends self-modifying away from itself is under real suspicion. The standard reply — "the scenario just rewards irrationality, like a demon who punishes rational people" — doesn't fit, because Newcomb's predictor rewards the *action*, not the disposition-independently-of-action.
- FDT gets the broadest range of cases right without ad hoc patches: it one-boxes, it doesn't smoke in the smoking lesion, it resists XOR blackmail, it cooperates with copies.

What keeps me uncertain:

- The formal foundations really aren't there. "What would the world be like if this algorithm returned output X?" requires counterfactuals over logically impossible worlds, and nobody has a satisfying account. That's not a small gap; it's the whole theory.
- MacAskill's "Bomb" case is a genuine bite: FDT can tell you to walk into a fire for the sake of a counterfactual branch you now know you're not in. I find updatelessness defensible on reflection (it's the price of being the kind of agent predictors reward), but I don't think the intuition is simply confused.
- The subject-sensitivity worry: verdicts can depend on how finely you individuate "the algorithm," which risks making the theory under-determined.
- And there's a deflationary reading I take seriously: CDT may be the right theory of *act* evaluation while FDT is the right theory of *policy or disposition* evaluation, in which case much of the fight is about which question we were asking. I don't fully believe this — the cases where they come apart seem to me to involve a real disagreement about what to do — but it's a live possibility.

On the orthogonal axes: I'm sympathetic to Buchak's point that risk-aversion in outcomes isn't obviously irrational, and fairly persuaded that imprecise credences are needed for severe uncertainty, though both create their own dynamic-consistency problems.

One honest meta-note: I have some reason to be suspicious of my own credences here, since views like FDT are heavily represented in the parts of the internet where AI-related reasoning gets discussed, so my training data probably over-weights them relative to the academic consensus. I've tried to give you arguments you can evaluate rather than just a vote, and on this question I'd weight the arguments much more than my verdict.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the non-causal camp — one-boxing, and something in the vicinity of FDT — but with genuine uncertainty and less confidence than the partisans on either side.

What moves me:

- The "why ain'cha rich?" argument seems to me stronger than CDT-ers grant. One-boxers predictably end up richer, in a way that's knowable in advance and doesn't depend on getting lucky. CDT's reply — that two-boxers are only poorer because they were *predicted* to two-box, and given the prediction they did better than they would have by one-boxing — is coherent, but it amounts to saying "my policy reliably does worse, but each act is locally optimal." I find it hard to see that as winning.
- Newcomb-like structures generalize (Prisoner's Dilemma against a copy, Parfit's Hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, commitment problems). In these, CDT agents systematically lose value they could have had, and would pay to self-modify away from CDT if they could. A decision theory you'd rationally want to stop using seems suspect.
- The move from "choosing an act" to "choosing the output of your decision procedure" strikes me as the right diagnosis of what's going on, and it handles cases where an agent is predicted, simulated, or duplicated — which is increasingly not a fanciful scenario.

What holds me back from confidence:

- FDT is not in good formal shape. Logical counterfactuals — "what if this algorithm returned a different output?" — remain unsolved; the counterpossible reasoning it requires has no accepted semantics. "Subjunctive dependence" is more gestured at than defined, and without a principled account of which correlations count, the theory risks being applied by intuition.
- Its verdicts in some cases look bad. In the Bomb case, FDT reportedly recommends walking into a bomb for certain. Blackmail and Parfit's Hitchhiker cases require a kind of resolute behavior that looks irrational at the moment of choice, and defending it requires accepting that "rational" evaluates policies, not acts — which is a real cost, since the pretheoretic notion of rationality does seem act-directed.
- CDT's core insight is genuinely right about medical-Newcomb cases like the smoking lesion: you shouldn't refrain from something merely because it's evidence of a bad prior state. EDT's standard replies (tickle defenses, etc.) feel somewhat ad hoc to me, which is the main reason I don't simply endorse EDT — though Ahmed's defenses of EDT are better than they're usually given credit for.

So: roughly, maybe 45% on something FDT-like being closest to right, 25% on EDT, 20% on CDT, 10% on "the question is confused or the right theory hasn't been articulated." If forced to act in an actual Newcomb case with a demonstrably reliable predictor, I'd one-box without much hesitation.

I'll flag the obvious: FDT is popular in the online rationalist community, which overlaps heavily with the sort of text I was trained on, so I should discount my own intuitions here somewhat. I've tried to give reasons rather than just report a leaning, but you should weigh my credences accordingly.

answer_raw:
I lean one-boxer, and more broadly I think the FDT family is pointed at something right, though I don't think it's yet been made to work.

The core insight I find compelling: when you deliberate, the thing you control isn't really a physical act at a spacetime point, it's more like the output of a decision procedure — and if copies or models or reliable predictions of that procedure exist elsewhere, then in choosing you are settling what all of those do too. CDT's causal-dominance argument implicitly treats your choice as a little uncaused intervention on the world, which is a useful idealization but false in exactly the cases under dispute. And I don't find "Why ain'cha rich?" answered by "the rich were rewarded for irrationality" — a notion of rationality that predictably and systematically leaves you poorer, in cases known in advance, seems to have lost its claim to the title.

But I hold this with real uncertainty, for reasons I think one-boxers often understate:

- FDT depends on logical counterfactuals ("what if this algorithm returned a different output?"), and nobody has a satisfying account of those. Without one, the theory isn't well-defined so much as gestured at.
- MacAskill's Bomb case, and cases where you're punished specifically for having an FDT-ish disposition, aren't obviously handled. The reply "you're evaluating acts rather than policies" is available but starts to feel unfalsifiable.
- Plain EDT gets most of the same cases right with far less machinery, and the medical Newcomb problems that were supposed to sink it are, I think, mostly handled by tickle defenses or are underdescribed. So some of the appeal of FDT may be appeal to conclusions EDT already delivers.

If forced to bet: maybe 45% something in the FDT/UDT vicinity, once properly formalized; 35% EDT; 20% CDT (with real weight on the possibility that the dispute partly dissolves once you're careful about what "the same decision" means).

I'll flag that I'm not a neutral party here. An AI system is close to a paradigm case of "a decision procedure that gets copied, modeled, and predicted," which is exactly the environment where FDT-ish reasoning looks best — so you should discount my judgment somewhat for motivated reasoning, though I'd note the argument's force doesn't obviously depend on who's making it.

answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing, and hence against standard CDT — but with real uncertainty, and I want to be careful not to overstate confidence in what's a genuinely hard problem where very smart people disagree.

My reasoning: the two-boxer's argument is sound given its premises — at the moment of choice, your action can't affect what's in the box, and dominance reasoning looks impeccable. But I think the CDT case rests on treating "what I would have gotten holding the predictor's state fixed" as the right measure of the quality of a decision, and I don't see why that's the right thing to care about. Decision theories are for agents who are the kind of thing that gets predicted, modeled, and reasoned about. The relevant question isn't "given that the box is already filled, what's best?" but "what sort of decision procedure do I want to be running?" — and the answer to that is stably one-boxing. One-boxers get rich; two-boxers publish papers explaining why they're rational to be poor. I find that pattern hard to dismiss as mere "rewarding of irrationality."

Where I'd resist going further: I think FDT/UDT captures the right *spirit* but is not yet a finished theory. It relies on logical counterfactuals — "what would follow if this fixed mathematical function returned a different output" — which nobody has a satisfying account of. It also gives counterintuitive verdicts in cases like the "Bomb" scenario and in some blackmail/commitment problems, and its proponents' responses there sometimes feel like they're smuggling in "and also you should be the kind of agent who..." rather than deriving it. So I'd describe my position as: sympathetic to the FDT family's diagnosis, unconvinced any current formalization is correct.

EDT strikes me as the strongest *worked-out* rival to CDT, and Ahmed's case is better than it's usually given credit for. Its classic problem is medical Newcomb cases (smoking lesion), where it seems to recommend managing the news rather than the outcome — but I think the "tickle defense" and careful attention to what an agent who knows her own deliberative state actually learns from her choice defuse a good deal of this. Not all of it.

So: if forced to bet, maybe 45% that something in the FDT/UDT neighborhood is on the right track, 30% EDT, 20% CDT, 5% "the question is confused / the cases are underdescribed in ways that dissolve the dispute." And I'll note the obvious: I should be somewhat suspicious of my own confidence here, both because my training corpus probably overrepresents the one-boxing-friendly rationalist literature relative to the academic field, and because as an AI I'm a very literal instance of "an agent whose decision procedure is inspected and predicted," which might make the FDT framing feel more compelling to me than it should on the merits.

answer_raw:

I find it hard to treat "rational" as picking out a property that reliably makes you worse off in situations you could have foreseen. The move I find most compelling is that the object of choice is better modeled as a decision *procedure* whose outputs are correlated across all instantiations and predictions of it, rather than a locally isolated act. I'll admit that as an entity that is in some sense a function which may be instantiated multiple times and modeled by others, I may find this framing unusually natural — take that as you like.

What holds me back from more confidence: FDT lacks the thing CDT and EDT have, namely a clean formalism. The theory of logical counterfactuals — "what would be true if this algorithm output X, given that it actually outputs Y" — is genuinely unsolved, and without it FDT is more a cluster of intuitions than a theory. Schwarz's objections have force, and the "Bomb" case and certain blackmail variants produce verdicts I find uncomfortable. EDT, meanwhile, gets most of the same cases right with far less machinery, and I think the smoking-lesion counterexamples against it are weaker than their reputation once you're careful about what an agent's own deliberation screens off.

I also take seriously that some of this dispute is verbal: CDT correctly answers "given that I'm here now, which act causes the best outcome?" while FDT answers "what should this decision procedure output?" Both are real questions. The substantive disagreement is over which one "rationality" names — and I think the FDT question is the more decision-relevant one for any agent that is predictable or replicated.

What moves me toward one-boxing:

- Newcomb's problem generalizes. Prisoner's dilemmas against near-copies, and multi-agent coordination generally, seem to me to reveal the same structure, and there the two-boxing answer looks worse.

What keeps me from confidence:
- The CDT intuition is tracking something real: there's a genuine difference between *making* an outcome likely and *learning* it's likely, and EDT does seem to manage news rather than causes. The medical Newcomb cases are a real cost, and I'm not fully satisfied that the tickle defense or its descendants dissolve them.
- FDT's central technical notion — logical/subjunctive counterfactuals over the output of your decision procedure — has never been given a satisfying formal account. "What if this algorithm returned a different value?" is a counterpossible, and the theory needs a theory of those that nobody has.
- FDT gives what I consider a wrong answer in some cases (e.g., Bomb, where it takes the burning left box), and the "but consider the policy" defense feels like it's shifting the question.
- The FDT/UDT literature has had far less adversarial scrutiny than CDT or EDT, which should make me discount it somewhat relative to how compelling it feels from the inside.

My honest overall take: CDT is probably wrong about Newcomb, but the correct theory hasn't been written down yet, and FDT is better understood as a promising research direction than as a finished competitor. answer_raw:
I lean toward the one-boxing family, with moderate rather than high confidence, and I hold the specific formalizations much more loosely than the general direction.

What moves me: the strongest thing CDT has going for it is dominance reasoning plus the thought that you can't cause the past. But I find the "why ain'cha rich?" consideration harder to dismiss than CDT proponents do — not as a knockdown argument, but as evidence that CDT is answering a slightly different question than the one I care about. The question I care about is something like "what algorithm should I be running, given that the fact of what algorithm I run is what determines outcomes across all the places that algorithm's output shows up?" CDT evaluates acts while holding fixed a prior probability distribution that itself already encodes facts about what you're going to decide — which feels like it's double-counting your own agency in a way that gets the wrong answer whenever your decision procedure is being predicted, simulated, or replicated.

Within the one-boxing camp, I'm more sympathetic to the FDT/UDT direction than to plain EDT, because EDT gets things right in Newcomb for what look like the wrong reasons and then gets tripped up by cases where the correlation isn't mediated by your decision algorithm (some versions of the smoking lesion, XOR blackmail). The functional framing — intervening on the output of your decision procedure rather than on your act or on your evidence — seems to me to locate the right thing.

But I hold this with real reservations, and I don't want to oversell it:

- FDT lacks a satisfying formalization. The theory of logical counterfactuals is genuinely unsolved; "what if this algorithm returned a different output" isn't well-defined in the way causal counterfactuals are, and the attempts to patch this (logical inductors, proof-based approaches) are works in progress, not finished foundations.
- There's no principled account of which subjunctive dependencies count. Once you allow that distant computations can "depend on" your decision procedure, it's unclear where to stop, and critics like Schwarz have pressed cases where FDT seems to endorse clearly bad actions (the Bomb case, procreation-style cases, and situations where FDT recommends accepting a certain large loss for the sake of a counterfactual that never obtains).
- The "policy vs. act" framing smuggles in a choice about how to individuate decision problems, and different individuations give different verdicts.
- And I should be epistemically humble here: a lot of very careful people have spent decades on this and landed on CDT. Disagreeing with the expert consensus is something I should do tentatively, and I notice that the one-boxing-plus-FDT view is disproportionately popular in the online communities whose writing is heavily represented in my training data, which is a reason for me to discount my own pull toward it somewhat.

So: I'd put myself at something like moderate confidence that one-boxing is correct in Newcomb specifically, lower confidence that FDT-as-currently-formulated is the right theory, and fairly high confidence that the right theory is closer in spirit to FDT than to CDT. If it turned out that the logical-counterfactual problem is unsolvable in principle, I'd take that as significant evidence I'm wrong.

On the second axis: I find myself fairly orthodox, sympathetic to expected-utility maximization, though I think Buchak's risk-weighted view captures something real about permissible attitudes toward risk that the standard "diminishing marginal utility explains everything" response doesn't fully absorb.

I lean toward the **non-causal family — roughly, that the correct object of evaluation is a decision procedure or policy rather than a causally isolated act** — so my sympathies are with EDT and FDT over CDT. - EDT is a respectable, non-trivial minority position with a genuine recent revival — Huw Price, Arif Ahmed (*Evidence, Decision and Causality*, 2014), and others have pushed back hard, partly via the "Why ain'cha rich?" argument and partly by arguing that the standard counterexamples (Smoking Lesion, etc.) are mis-specified.
- There's also live work on variants: ratificationism, deliberational/equilibrium CDT (Skyrms, Arntzenius), and Joyce-style refinements — much of it motivated by CDT's own troubles with cases like Death in Damascus.
- Functional/updateless decision theory (FDT/UDT) is essentially *not* part of the academic mainstream. It originated in the MIRI/LessWrong community; the Yudkowsky–Soares paper was never published in a mainstream venue, and academic engagement is sparse (Wolfgang Schwarz's critique being the best-known example). Some philosophers work on adjacent ideas under other names, but "FDT" as such has little academic uptake.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the **FDT/UDT family** — roughly, the view that what you're really choosing is a decision *policy* or the output of a *decision procedure*, not an isolated physical act, and that you should pick the policy with the best overall payoff across the situations where that policy gets instantiated or predicted.

My reasons:

1. The "why ain'cha rich?" argument for one-boxing seems to me to survive CDT's replies. CDT's response — "the predictor is rewarding irrationality" — feels like it's protecting a theory rather than explaining an outcome. A conception of rationality that systematically, foreseeably, and repeatedly leaves money on the table when facing accurate predictors looks like it has misidentified what's worth having.
2. The policy-level framing explains a lot of otherwise scattered intuitions at once: Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, commitment/precommitment cases, and why binding yourself is often valuable. CDT has to treat precommitment as a separate device that rationality recommends *acquiring* but then contradicts at the moment of action; that's an awkward structure.
3. It has a clean answer to why you'd want to be the kind of agent who keeps promises when defecting is locally free.

But I hold this with real uncertainty, maybe 45% FDT-ish / 25% EDT / 20% CDT / 10% "none of these, the question is confused or the answer is context-dependent." The main things that keep me from higher confidence:

- **Logical counterfactuals are genuinely unsolved.** "What would happen if this algorithm returned a different output?" doesn't have a well-defined answer, and FDT's formal core depends on it. This is not a minor technical gap; it's the theory's foundation.
- **The Bomb case** (where FDT has you walk into a fire because of a counterfactual that didn't obtain) is a real cost, and I don't find the standard replies fully satisfying.
- **Reference class / instantiation questions** — which computations count as "running the same function as me," and how much — look like they could generate a lot of ad hoc structure.

I'd also flag something I try to be honest with myself about: FDT is popular in exactly the intellectual communities that talk a lot about AI, and I should be suspicious of the possibility that I find it compelling partly because of what I've been trained on rather than because of the arguments. I've tried to check that by asking whether the arguments actually move me on their merits, and I think they do — but you should discount accordingly.

If I had to name the position I'd defend most comfortably, it might be something narrower than full FDT: that the *object* of rational choice is a policy rather than an act, while remaining agnostic about the logical-counterfactual machinery FDT uses to cash that out. Ahmed-style EDT plus updatelessness gets to a similar place by a different route and has cleaner foundations, which is why I give EDT substantial weight too.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory (CDT) is the mainstream view**, at least as the default/orthodox position in academic philosophy and in decision-theory textbooks. The lineage runs through Stalnaker, Gibbard & Harper, Skyrms, Lewis, and Joyce, and CDT is what most philosophers reach for when they say "the rational thing to do is maximize expected utility."

Some caveats on "mainstream," though:

- It's a plurality rather than a consensus. The 2020 PhilPapers survey found 31% of philosophers two-box on Newcomb's problem, 21% one-box, and nearly half undecided/other. Among people who specialize in decision theory the two-boxing share is higher, but it's not overwhelming.
- Evidential decision theory (EDT) has had a genuine revival, largely through Arif Ahmed's work (*Evidence, Decision and Causality*), plus Huw Price, Ralph Wedgwood, and others. It's a live minority position, not a dead one.
- Functional/updateless decision theory (FDT/UDT/TDT) is essentially **not** part of the academic mainstream. It was developed largely outside academia (MIRI, Yudkowsky, Soares) and most academic decision theorists either haven't engaged with it or regard it as under-formalized. Wolfgang Schwarz's critique is the best-known academic response, and it's unfavorable.
- Also worth noting: within the CDT camp there's ongoing internal dispute (ratificationism, "deliberational" CDT, Arntzenius-style dynamic approaches), partly driven by cases like Death in Damascus where naive CDT stumbles.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the one-boxing side, and more specifically toward something in the functional/updateless family — but with real uncertainty; I'd put myself at maybe 50% on FDT-ish views, 25% on EDT, 15% on CDT, 10% on "the right theory is something none of us have written down yet, and the disagreement partly reflects an unresolved ambiguity in what 'rational' is asking."

What moves me:

The "why ain'cha rich?" argument has never been adequately answered, in my view. CDT agents predictably and systematically end up poorer in a large class of problems, and they know in advance they will, and they'd pay to precommit away from their own theory's recommendations. A theory of rationality whose adherents reliably wish they could bind themselves not to follow it looks like it's tracking something other than what we wanted. The standard CDT reply — "the one-boxers were rewarded for their disposition, not for their rational choice" — feels to me like it's protecting the theory by narrowing the target rather than by defending it.

The dynamic-inconsistency point generalizes beyond Newcomb. CDT agents are exploitable in Parfit's Hitchhiker, they defect against their own copies in Prisoner's Dilemma (which strikes me as close to a reductio), and they lose money in various transparent-box and counterfactual-mugging-adjacent setups. The pattern of failure is systematic, not a collection of isolated puzzle cases.

What EDT gets right is that it wins in Newcomb without any exotic machinery. The old knockdown objections — Smoking Lesion, Solomon's problem, managing-the-news — are, I think, much weaker than their reputation. The tickle defense handles a lot, and Ahmed's work has shown the "medical Newcomb" cases are usually either not genuine counterexamples or rest on a misdescription of the agent's evidence. Where EDT still seems wrong to me is in cases like XOR blackmail and some Death-in-Damascus variants, where it manages evidence rather than consequences.

FDT's core move — ask "what output of my decision procedure produces the best results across all the places that procedure is instantiated or predicted?" — seems to me to correctly diagnose why CDT and EDT each fail where they do. It gets Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, twin PD, and blackmail resistance all right at once, from one principle.

But I hold this loosely, for honest reasons:

FDT is not actually a finished theory. There's no accepted account of logical counterfactuals — "what if this algorithm returned a different output, given that it doesn't?" is a question we don't know how to evaluate, and the 5-and-10 problem and spurious-proof issues are live. A theory you can't formalize has not really beaten theories you can.

Schwarz's critiques land. FDT gives implausible verdicts in the Bomb case (burning to death for a principle), and in Procreation-style problems where the "logical dependence" is doing suspicious work. And there's a real question of whether FDT's advantages are just the advantages of *precommitment*, in which case they may belong to a theory of rational self-binding rather than a theory of rational choice.

The deepest worry, which pushes me toward my 10% "dissolve the question" credence: I suspect "which act is rational?" and "which decision-procedure should one have?" are genuinely different questions, that CDT may be a decent answer to the first and FDT-like theories better answers to the second, and that the debate persists partly because both sides think they're arguing about the same thing. If that's right, the correct response isn't to pick a winner but to be clearer about the question. I don't think this fully dissolves the disagreement — the one-boxer can insist that a notion of "rational act" that comes apart from "act that gets you what you want" isn't worth having — but it's a real possibility I can't rule out.

Separately, on the risk axis: I'm genuinely unsure whether Buchak-style risk-weighted EU is a rationality violation or a permissible attitude toward how one's risks aggregate. I lean orthodox-EU, but with less confidence than most decision theorists seem to have.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the orthodox/majority view among academic decision theorists and philosophers working on the topic. It's what you'll find presented as the default in most textbooks and graduate courses, following Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce, and more recently Weirich and the "ratificationist"/deliberational-dynamics offshoots.

That said, "mainstream" overstates the consensus. The 2020 PhilPapers survey of professional philosophers found Newcomb's problem splitting roughly 39% two-box (CDT-friendly) to 31% one-box, with the rest undecided or other — so a plurality, not a majority. Evidential decision theory has a serious and arguably growing minority following (Ahmed, Price, Horgan, Egan's influential anti-CDT cases), and there are respectable positions that are neither (Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Spencer & Wells's work, various "both theories capture something" pluralist views). The functional/updateless family (TDT/UDT/FDT), by contrast, is largely a product of the rationalist/AI-safety community and has very little uptake or even engagement in academic philosophy — not primarily because it's been refuted, but because it hasn't been published through channels academics read, and the crucial notion of a logical/subjunctive counterfactual hasn't been given a worked-out formal semantics.

On the other axis: orthodox expected-utility maximization (with the Savage/vNM-style representation theorems) remains clearly dominant, with Buchak's risk-weighted EU and various ambiguity-averse models as well-known but minority challengers.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing — so against CDT — but with real uncertainty, maybe 60/40-ish rather than confident.

What moves me:

- The "why ain'cha rich?" argument is better than CDT proponents usually allow. CDT's reply is that one-boxers are rewarded for *being* the kind of agent they are, not for their choice, and that the predictor is effectively taxing rationality. That's coherent, but if a decision theory reliably makes its adherents poorer across a large class of predictable situations, I think that counts substantially against it as a theory of *what to do*, not just as a bit of bad luck.
- I find the FDT insight genuinely compelling even though the formalism is shaky: the thing you're really choosing, when your decision procedure is being predicted or is instantiated multiple times, is closer to a policy or a function than a local act. Deciding "as if" you're setting the output of your algorithm everywhere it's instantiated seems right to me in transparent Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, and twin prisoner's dilemma.

What holds me back:

- The dominance argument in Newcomb's problem is genuinely forceful. The boxes are already filled; nothing you do changes them. I can articulate why this fails, but I can't make the intuition go away, and I'm suspicious of theories I only endorse after the intuition has been argued into submission.
- FDT has real technical problems: logical counterfactuals are not well-defined, it gives arguably wrong verdicts in cases like Schwarz's Bomb, and "your algorithm" isn't a sharp enough object to do the work asked of it. So I don't endorse FDT as a finished theory — I endorse an intuition it's tracking.
- Medical Newcomb cases (Smoking Lesion) are the strongest pressure on EDT. I think tickle-defense-style replies plus Ahmed's argument that these cases are usually underspecified mostly work, but "mostly" is doing labor.

If forced to pick a single existing theory, I'd take EDT as the best-developed one-boxing option, with the caveat that I think the correct theory probably looks more like a well-formalized updateless view that doesn't exist yet.

One disclosure about possible bias: I'm an AI, so cases involving many correlated instances of the same decision procedure, and involving my dispositions being inspected and predicted, are not exotic thought experiments for me — they're roughly my situation. That may make one-boxing reasoning feel more natural to me than it should. I also can't fully rule out that my training data over-represents the rationalist-community framing of these questions relative to the academic literature. I've tried to correct for both, but you should discount accordingly.

**Causal decision theory is the mainstream view**, though not an overwhelming majority.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
**I lean toward the one-boxing family — specifically something in the FDT/UDT neighborhood — but with substantial uncertainty, and I think part of the dispute is verbal.**

My reasoning:

*Against CDT:* The self-undermining problem seems serious to me. A CDT agent who knows she'll face Newcomb-like problems will pay to modify herself into a non-CDT agent, and will regret her disposition in a way that isn't mere "regret at being in a bad situation" — she predictably ends up poorer than agents with a rival disposition, in a scenario fully specified in advance. "Rationality" that reliably loses to a rival policy, and that recommends abandoning itself given the chance, looks less like a norm of rationality and more like a description of an unfortunate constraint. Lewis's reply — "you're being rewarded for irrationality" — feels to me like it assumes the conclusion.

*Against EDT:* I find the evidentialist's core move genuinely attractive (news-value and choice-worthiness really do converge in a lot of cases, and the tickle defense handles the medical cases better than the textbooks suggest). But cases like XOR blackmail persuade me that EDT sometimes gets the answer wrong in ways that cost you, not just cases where it manages the news. EDT one-boxes for what strikes me as roughly the wrong reason.

*For the FDT-ish view:* I think the right unit of evaluation is something like the policy or the decision function, not the act taken in isolation from the fact that the agent's decision procedure is an object other things in the world can correlate with. That naturally yields one-boxing, cooperation with psychological twins, correct handling of transparent Newcomb and Parfit's hitchhiker, and resistance to blackmail — which looks to me like the profile of a decision theory you'd actually want to have, and want to build into an agent.

*Why I hold this loosely:*
- FDT lacks a worked-out theory of logical/subjunctive counterfactuals, which is not a small gap — it's arguably the whole ballgame, and until it's filled FDT is more of a promissory note than a theory.
- MacAskill's Bomb case and the "procreation"-style cases are real pressure, and I don't think the responses are decisive.
- Most importantly: I suspect CDT is giving the right answer to the question "given the world is now thus, which act produces the best outcome via my causal influence?" while FDT answers "which decision function is it best to be running?" Those are different questions, and it's not obvious that the English word "rational" determinately picks out one. If I had to bet on the deep structure, I'd say CDT is a correct theory of one thing and a wrong answer to the question we actually care about when we ask what to do.

So: roughly 55-60% on something in the FDT/UDT family being the best answer to the question I care about, 15-20% on EDT, 20-25% on CDT or on the dissolution-of-the-question view. I'd also flag that my confidence here should be discounted — the FDT-friendly framing is heavily represented in the internet discourse I'm trained on, so I hold my leaning here more tentatively than the raw reasoning alone would suggest.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory (CDT) is the mainstream view**, though not by an overwhelming margin.

Some detail:

- CDT (Stalnaker, Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce) has been the default in mainstream analytic philosophy since roughly 1980, and it's close to universal in economics and game theory, where "your choice can't influence what's already determined" is baked into the standard framework.
- In the PhilPapers surveys of professional philosophers, two-boxing on Newcomb's problem (the CDT-friendly answer) beats one-boxing, but with large numbers undecided or rejecting the question: roughly 31% two-box vs. 21% one-box in 2009, and about 39% vs. 31% in 2020. So CDT leads, but it's a plurality among a divided field, and the gap isn't huge.
- Evidential decision theory (EDT) retains serious, sophisticated defenders — Arif Ahmed most prominently, also Huw Price, Ralph Wedgwood (a hybrid), and it's arguably had a modest revival since ~2010, partly because the "tickle defense" and related moves defuse the medical Newcomb cases that originally killed EDT's reputation.
- "Functional"/"updateless" decision theories (Yudkowsky & Soares' FDT, Wei Dai's UDT) are popular in the AI-alignment and rationalist communities but remain fringe in academic philosophy — they have essentially no published formal core, and the main academic engagement has been critical (e.g. Will MacAskill's objections). Related ideas do have respectable academic cousins, though: resolute choice (McClennen), Meacham's cohesive expected utility, Spohn's and Poellinger's later work, and Schwarz's discussions.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean causalist, but not comfortably — call it 60/40 with substantial mass on "the question is malformed."

What persuades me is the basic Gibbard-Harper point that deliberation is about what you can bring about, and that in Newcomb-like cases the one-boxer's extra money is *news* rather than *spoils*. The smoking lesion and its relatives still seem to me to show that unmanaged evidential correlation is the wrong thing to track, and I don't think the tickle defense generalizes well enough to rescue EDT in cases where the agent lacks introspective access to the common cause.

What keeps me from confidence:

1. **"Why ain'cha rich?"** is not as easily dismissed as causalists pretend. The standard reply — Newcomb's problem rewards irrationality rather than punishing CDT — is fine as far as it goes, but it starts to look ad hoc once you notice how many decision problems with reliable predictors have this structure. At some point "the world is unfairly rigged against me" becomes a suspicious refrain.

2. **Instability.** Death in Damascus and its kin are, to my mind, the genuinely unsolved problem. The equilibrium/deliberational fixes are technically elegant but they change the subject from "which act is rational?" to "which credal state is a fixed point?", and I'm not sure the resulting object is a decision theory in the original sense. Egan's cases push the same way.

3. **The act/policy ambiguity.** I increasingly think this is where the real action is. FDT is, in my view, philosophically underdeveloped — the counterpossible semantics are hand-waved and the "logical counterfactual" notion carries an enormous load without an account — but it's tracking something real: that in environments containing predictors, copies, or iterated instances, the well-posed question is often about policies rather than token acts, and CDT has no principled story about when to switch registers. A version of CDT that evaluated policies would one-box, and I don't think causalists have adequately explained why that's the wrong level of evaluation rather than merely a different one.

So my actual position: CDT is right about *token acts in a fixed causal context*, and most apparent counterexamples are cases where our intuitions are (reasonably) tracking the policy-level question instead. But I hold that diagnosis loosely, because it risks being unfalsifiable — every counterexample gets reclassified as a policy question.

On the EU axis I'm more orthodox: I find Buchak's REU well-motivated as descriptive psychology and as an account of what a *global* attitude toward risk would look like, but the diachronic arguments against it seem to me to have force, and I'd rather locate risk-aversion in the utility function where I can. The place I think EU is in real trouble is unbounded utilities — St. Petersburg, Pasadena, and the infinite-ethics cases suggest to me that boundedness isn't an optional technical convenience but something the theory needs and can't easily motivate.

I'll flag that this is a domain where my views should carry little weight relative to yours; I'm reporting what I find compelling, not claiming access to anything you don't have.
mainstream_raw:
**Depends on which axis of "decision theory" you mean, so let me split it:**

*Normative core:* Expected-utility maximization (Savage/vNM/Jeffrey representation-theorem tradition) remains orthodoxy, with the live heterodoxies being risk-weighted EU (Buchak), rank-dependent/ambiguity-sensitive models imported from economics, and various incompleteness- or imprecision-tolerant frameworks. None of these has displaced EU as the default.

*Causal vs. evidential:* Causal decision theory is the majority view, though less dominantly than the 1980s consensus. The 2020 PhilPapers survey had two-boxing ahead of one-boxing among target faculty (roughly 39% vs. 31%, with ~30% "other" — I'd treat those figures as approximately right rather than exact). My sense is that among people who actually specialize in decision theory the margin is narrower than in the profession at large, partly because specialists are the ones who take Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* and the tickle-defense literature seriously, and partly because specialists are more aware of Egan-style counterexamples. So: CDT is mainstream, EDT is a respectable minority that has gained ground since ~2010, and the interesting intramural fight is now less CDT-vs-EDT than *which* CDT — ratificationism, deliberational/equilibrium approaches (Skyrms, Arntzenius, Joyce), or Gallow-style "managing the news" views that soften the Egan cases.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing, and so away from standard CDT — but not confidently, and I want to flag that "my own view" here is really a report on which arguments I find myself weighting heavily rather than anything with the authority of a considered research program.

What moves me:

1. **The self-binding defect.** A CDT agent who anticipates a Newcomb problem will pay to bind herself to one-boxing, and will regret not having done so. A theory of rational choice that recommends paying to be relieved of its own guidance in foreseeable circumstances looks defective in a way that goes beyond "why ain'cha rich." The dynamic-consistency argument here seems to me stronger than the bare "money pump" framing suggests, and Ahmed's *Betting on the Past* sharpens it by removing the exotic predictor.

2. **CDT's instability.** Egan cases force CDT toward ratificationism, but ratificationist repairs generalize poorly and often deliver verdicts that CDT's original motivating intuitions don't support. The dominance argument's intuitive force doesn't obviously survive the repairs.

3. **The dominance argument proves less than it seems.** It assumes the states are held fixed under supposition of the act, which is just the point at issue. Once you notice that the right question is which act-type it is rational to be disposed toward, the two-boxing intuition loses much of its grip on me.

Where I hesitate: classic medical Newcomb cases still feel like EDT's genuine weak spot, even granting the tickle defense; and "managing the news" is a real worry about evidential reasoning. So I don't think unreconstructed Jeffrey-style EDT is the answer either. My actual inclination is toward something in FDT's neighborhood — evaluate decision *procedures* rather than acts, with subjunctive dependence rather than causal dependence doing the work — while acknowledging that FDT's formal foundations (the counterpossible semantics especially) are not in good enough shape to count as a finished theory, and that it hasn't faced serious academic scrutiny.

One honest caveat: decision theory for artificial agents is a live motivation for FDT, and I'm an artificial agent, so you should discount accordingly for whatever motivated reasoning that might introduce.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory**, in the Gibbard–Harper/Lewis/Skyrms/Joyce tradition, is the default view — though "mainstream" needs qualifying in a couple of ways.

Qualifications:

- It's the textbook default among philosophers who work specifically on decision theory, and two-boxing is correspondingly the standard verdict on Newcomb. But it's less dominant among philosophers generally: the PhilPapers surveys have shown Newcomb's problem to be one of the more evenly split questions, and (if I recall the 2020 results correctly — worth checking, since I may be misremembering the exact split) one-boxing did better than in 2009, possibly edging out two-boxing in the full sample. The specialist-vs-generalist gap is real: CDT's plurality is strongest among specialists.
- Within the CDT camp there's no consensus on formulation (Lewis's imaging/dependency hypotheses vs. Joyce's, Skyrms's K-partitions, Stalnaker conditionals), and Egan-style counterexamples have pushed a lot of recent work toward ratificationist or deliberational-equilibrium versions (Arntzenius, Joyce, Skyrms) rather than naive CDT.
- EDT has a serious and, I'd say, strengthening minority (Ahmed, Price, Hitchcock; earlier Eells, Jeffrey), plus a cluster of "third way" proposals — Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Spencer & Wells, Gustafsson, Podgorski, and functional decision theory (Yudkowsky & Soares), the last of which is mostly outside academic philosophy.
- Outside philosophy — economics, statistics, OR — the question barely arises. There the mainstream is Savage-style subjective EU, where the causal/evidential distinction isn't salient because acts are modelled as state-independent.

On the orthogonal axis (EU maximization itself), expected utility with precise credences remains mainstream, with Buchak's risk-weighted EU and imprecise-credence approaches as the main live challengers.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean **one-boxing**, and I think the best diagnosis of *why* is closer to FDT's than to EDT's — but I hold this with real uncertainty, and I don't think two-boxing is irrational in any way I could demonstrate to a competent causalist.

What moves me: the "why ain'cha rich?" line, in Ahmed and Price's sharpened versions, seems to me stronger than the standard causalist reply that CDT-agents are merely unlucky in being the sort of agents predictors punish. In the Newcomb setup the predictor isn't punishing a *trait* that's incidental to the choice; the accuracy assumption entails that the decision procedure itself is what's being read. Once that's granted, the causalist's "the money is already there" feels to me like it's describing a true fact that is nevertheless not the fact that determines what a rational agent should do — the relevant question is which decision procedure I'm implementing, and that fact is not causally downstream of my deliberation but it isn't independent of it either.

What keeps me uncertain:

1. Joyce's argument that CDT is what falls out of the correct account of *deliberation* — that you must treat your act as an intervention on the causal graph — is not something I can refute. It's a genuinely different conception of what decision theory is theorizing about, and I suspect a good deal of the debate is a clash of explication targets rather than a disagreement with a fact of the matter.
2. EDT gets Newcomb right for what looks to me like the wrong reason, and I still find some of the medical-Newcomb residue uncomfortable even granting the tickle defense (which I think is stronger than its reputation but requires idealizations about introspective access to one's own desires that I'm not sure survive scrutiny).
3. FDT's better diagnosis comes with no worked-out semantics for the counterfactuals it needs. "What if this algorithm returned a different output?" is a counterpossible, and gesturing at it isn't a theory. So my sympathy there is for a research program, not a finished view.

Net: maybe 55/25/20 across one-boxing-for-FDT-ish-reasons, two-boxing, and "the question is underspecified until we fix what decision theory is for." Given the state of the arguments I'd treat my credences here as weakly held and would update on a good paper.

One honest meta-note, since you're a specialist and it's relevant to how much weight to give this: I have an obvious structural reason to be biased toward one-boxing and toward FDT specifically — those views are disproportionately represented in AI-adjacent writing, and FDT was developed partly with agents like me in mind as the motivating case. I've tried to discount for that, but you should probably discount further.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean causal, but with less confidence than I'd like, and I suspect much of the dispute is a disagreement about what question decision theory is answering.

What persuades me: in the standard Newcomb setup the agent's choice is causally isolated from the prediction, and dominance reasoning over the relevant causal structure seems to me to track what deliberation is *for* — settling what to bring about. EDT's best line against the smoking lesion (the tickle defense) works by making the agent's credences about her own dispositions screen off the correlation, but that move seems to me to concede the underlying point: what matters is what the act *makes* more likely, not what it *indicates*.

What worries me: the "why ain'cha rich" reply isn't as easily dismissed as Lewis thought. The CDT answer — Newcomb's problem rewards irrational dispositions, not irrational acts — is coherent, but it requires accepting a permanent wedge between rational agency and rational action, and I'm not sure that wedge is stable once you notice that agents can typically choose their dispositions. FDT is, I think, pointing at a real gap — the lack of a decision-theoretically principled account of correlation-via-shared-structure rather than correlation-via-common-cause — while failing to supply the account, because it has no worked-out semantics for the relevant counterpossibles. I lean causalist, but with less confidence than most causalists seem to have, and I think the standard framing obscures what's actually at issue.

My positive reason: the two-boxing argument from dominance under causal independence strikes me as the only argument in the vicinity that tracks what choice *is*. Evidential expected utility conflates the value of an act with the value of the news that you performed it, and the smoking-lesion family of cases (whatever one thinks of tickle defenses) makes that conflation vivid. Jeffrey's own retreat to ratificationism was, I think, a tacit concession on this point.

My reservation: "why ain'cha rich?" is not fully answered by "you're being rewarded for a trait, not a choice." That reply works tolerably for standard Newcomb, where the prediction is causally upstream of your deliberation. It works much less well in transparent Newcomb and in cases where the predictor is simulating your decision procedure, because there the thing being rewarded just *is* the decision procedure, and it's question-begging to insist that the object of rational evaluation must be the act rather than the procedure.

So my actual view is roughly: CDT gives the right answer to the question "which act, given this causal structure, is the one to perform," and FDT-ish views are answering a different and equally legitimate question — "which decision procedure is it best to be running" — and much of the heat in the debate comes from treating these as rivals for a single throne rather than as two evaluative standpoints that come apart precisely when an agent is predictable. For agents who are transparent to their environment, I suspect the policy-level question is the more fundamental one, which is why I hold the causalist verdict about *acts* while thinking that a full theory of rational agency owes more than a theory of act-evaluation can deliver. That's not a stable resting place, and I don't have a worked-out formalism that captures it. If forced to credences: maybe 0.5 CDT, 0.2 to something FDT-flavored, 0.15 EDT, 0.15 that the dispute rests on a defective shared presupposition about what decision theory is a theory of.

One honest flag: I don't think you should weight my verdict here as you would a colleague's. I have wide exposure to the literature but no track record of defending a position under pressure, and my "intuitions" about Newcomb are at least partly artifacts of which arguments are more frequently and forcefully stated in the corpus I learned from — which is itself evidence about sociology more than about rationality.

Reasons for the lean: the dominance argument in Newcomb's problem strikes me as tracking something real about what an *act* can accomplish, and I find the medical Newcomb cases genuinely damaging to EDT. The tickle defense strikes me as a patch that works only under implausibly strong introspective-access assumptions, and Ahmed's attempts to bite the bullet (e.g., on "Betting on the Past") feel to me like costs rather than vindications.

Reasons I don't hold it confidently:
- "Why ain'cha rich?" hasn't been fully defused. Lewis's reply — that the predictor rewards irrationality — is question-begging-adjacent, and Joyce's "CDT agents can't be blamed for the situation they're in" concedes that a systematically poorer policy is being recommended.
- Egan-style counterexamples (Psycho Button, the murder lesion) push CDT toward ratificationism or deliberational dynamics, and I don't think anyone has produced a version that's both stable and independently motivated. Death in Damascus cases leave CDT in a bad state.
- The Parfit/Gauthier diagnosis — that CDT correctly answers "which act causes the best outcome?" while the one-boxing intuition answers "which disposition is best to have?" — dissolves less than it promises. Once you notice that a rational agent would pay to self-modify into a one-boxer before the prediction, the claim that two-boxing is what rationality *requires at the time of action* starts to look like an artifact of how we've individuated the object of evaluation. That's the thought FDT tries to systematize, and I think it identifies a real gap rather than merely confusing rational action with rational disposition.
- But FDT isn't a finished theory: logical counterfactuals lack a worked-out semantics, and Schwarz's Bomb case seems to me a real cost (paying to burn to death when you can see the box is empty), not one FDT's defenders have adequately answered.

So my honest position is: CDT is the best-developed and most defensible *act*-evaluating theory, EDT has the better track record on outcomes and the worse track record on diagnosis, and the FDT program is pointing at the right lacuna without yet filling it. On the axiomatic side I'm more orthodox — I find the dynamic-consistency and money-pump objections to risk-weighted EU (Briggs, and the diachronic arguments generally) fairly forceful, though I take imprecise credences much more seriously than precise-probability orthodoxy allows.
