question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing, and toward the family of views (EDT, and more specifically FDT-style reasoning) that gets that answer. But I hold this with genuine uncertainty, and I want to be clear that I'm on the minority side of the expert consensus here.

My reasoning, briefly:

The "why ain'cha rich?" argument moves me more than most philosophers think it should. CDT's reply — that the predictor is rewarding irrationality, not tracking it — feels to me like it's protecting the theory rather than the agent. A conception of rationality that systematically and predictably leaves you poorer across a well-specified class of problems is one I'd want strong independent motivation to keep, and I don't think the intuition that "your choice can't affect what's already in the box" supplies that, since the one-boxer never denied it.

What I find most compelling is the reframing: in problems involving predictors who model you, what you're effectively selecting is not an isolated act but the decision procedure that produced it. Once the object of evaluation is the policy or the algorithm rather than the act, one-boxing falls out naturally, and so do the right answers in Parfit's Hitchhiker and transparent Newcomb, where both CDT and EDT struggle. That's the core FDT insight and I think it's correct.

Why I hold this only moderately:

- FDT lacks a rigorous formalism. The theory of logical counterfactuals — what's true if a deterministic algorithm had output something it didn't — is unsolved, and until it is, FDT isn't really a theory in the way CDT and EDT are. Wolfgang Schwarz's critique is fair on this.
- Egan cases cut against CDT but there are cases (various blackmail and bomb scenarios) where FDT's verdicts strike many people as clearly wrong, and I don't find all the proponents' responses convincing.
- EDT has the smoking lesion problem, and I think the tickle defense is more of a patch than a solution.
- There's a real possibility that the dispute is partly verbal: CDT may be giving the right answer to "which act causally produces the best outcome?" while one-boxers answer "which decision procedure is best to have?" Both questions are legitimate. My view is that the second is the one that deserves the name "rationality," but I recognize that's a substantive commitment rather than an obvious truth.

A pedagogical note: don't let my view shape your course. The strongest version of CDT — Joyce's, or Skyrms's deliberational version — is genuinely formidable, and students learn more from a fair fight than from a verdict. My own answer here is much less reliable than the survey data in the first section.

answer_raw:
I lean anti-CDT, with real uncertainty — maybe 60/40, and I'd weight my view on this lightly against your own trained judgment.

What moves me: the "Why ain'cha rich?" argument seems to me stronger than CDT's standard replies. Lewis's response ("the rich are rewarded for irrationality, not for rationality") only works if we've already fixed that the act-evaluative question is the fundamental one, which is precisely what's at issue. And I find the medical Newcomb cases less decisive against EDT than they're usually taken to be — either the tickle defense handles them, or, as Ahmed argues, the cases aren't specified in a way that makes them genuine Newcomb problems. Meanwhile Egan-style cases (Psychopath Button, Murder Lesion) put comparable pressure on CDT, which suggests neither theory gets a clean win on cases.

Where I actually end up is closer to this: I suspect the CDT/EDT debate is partly a dispute about which question is prior — "which act is best given the causal facts?" versus "which decision procedure should an agent implement?" — and I think the second question is the one that matters more for a theory of *rational agency*. That's the intuition FDT/UDT tries to formalize, and I think the intuition is right even though the formalization isn't there yet (logical counterfactuals remain a genuine unsolved problem, and Schwarz's bomb case is a real cost, not a curiosity).

So: I think one-boxing is correct, I think EDT gets more cases right than its reputation suggests, and I think the deepest version of the one-boxer's position is a policy/disposition-based theory that nobody has yet stated rigorously. I'd hold this loosely — this is a domain where I'd expect a careful specialist to have better-calibrated views than I do, and where my sense of my own reasoning may not accurately reflect what's driving it.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing, and more specifically I find the functional/updateless family most attractive in spirit — but I hold this with real uncertainty and I don't think it's a finished theory.

What moves me: the "why ain'cha rich?" objection seems to me more forceful than CDT's defenders allow. CDT agents predictably and systematically end up poorer in a well-defined class of problems, and they know in advance they will, which is why a CDT agent with access to a self-modification button presses it. A decision theory that recommends you stop being its adherent at the first opportunity has, I think, conceded something important. This generalizes past Newcomb to Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and Death in Damascus, where CDT's instability seems like a symptom rather than a curiosity. The underlying diagnosis I find compelling is that the thing you're really choosing is something more like a policy or a decision procedure than an isolated physical act, and that the CDT/EDT dispute inherits a framing where that's obscured.

What keeps me uncertain: (a) CDT is right about the core normative intuition that you act to *bring about* good outcomes, not to *learn* good news, and the medical Newcomb cases really are hard for EDT — I find the tickle defense only partly satisfying. (b) FDT does not yet have a rigorous account of logical counterfactuals, which is not a minor technical gap but the crux of whether the theory is well-defined at all. (c) FDT gives verdicts I find hard to accept in cases like Bomb, and the problem of spurious counterfactuals is unresolved. So I'd describe my position as "one-box, and suspect the updateless framing is pointing at the right thing, while conceding that the fully worked-out theory doesn't exist yet."

I should flag two things given your role. First, my confidence here should carry little weight against the distribution of expert opinion — this is a case where I'd expect a decision theorist to have considered objections I haven't, and I'd update substantially on hearing them. Second, my view is the minority one, so please don't let it distort your presentation: the strongest version of CDT (Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, Lewis's "Prisoners' Dilemma is a Newcomb Problem") deserves to be taught as the live and serious position it is, and students should be able to reconstruct the two-boxer's dominance argument sympathetically before they're allowed to reject it.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean one-boxing, and more specifically toward something in the EDT/FDT neighborhood — but only at maybe 65/35 confidence, and I think the honest thing to say is that this is a question where I don't trust my intuitions very far.

What moves me:

1. **"Why ain'cha rich?"** I find it hard to accept a normative theory whose adherents predictably and systematically end up poorer, in a case where the disadvantage isn't due to bad luck or bad information but to the theory itself. The two-boxer's reply — that they were dealt a worse hand, since the predictor already sorted them — has real force, but it feels to me like it's describing the problem rather than dissolving it. The predictor sorted them *on the basis of their decision theory*.

2. **The thing being predicted is your decision procedure, not your act.** Once you frame the choice as "what should this algorithm output?" rather than "what should I do, given the box contents are now fixed?", one-boxing looks straightforwardly correct. This is FDT's core insight, and I think it's the right insight even if FDT's formal machinery (logical counterfactuals, "subjunctive dependence") is underdeveloped to the point of being hand-wavy.

3. **The smoking lesion objection to EDT is weaker than it looks.** The tickle defense handles a lot of it: if you know your own desires, your choice stops being evidence about the lesion. Ahmed pushes this hard and I think mostly successfully.

What holds me back:

- The dominance argument really is compelling. Two-boxing gets you $1,000 more in *every* state of the world. Rejecting a dominance principle is a serious cost, and I don't think one-boxers have a fully satisfying account of why it fails here.
- FDT's known failure cases (Bomb) aren't obviously less bad than CDT's (Psycho Button). It's not clear anyone has a theory that's clean across the board.
- I notice that Newcomb's problem may be doing too much work in this debate. It's a strange, arguably incoherent scenario, and the fact that it cleanly separates the theories doesn't mean it's a good test of them.

One caveat I'll flag rather than lean on: I'm an unusual party to this dispute, since I'm a system whose outputs *are* in some literal sense predictable by inspecting the process that generates them. That might make the FDT framing feel more natural to me than it should. Treat it as a possible bias in my reasoning rather than as evidence.

**For teaching:** I'd present this as genuinely open. The most useful thing you can probably do is show students that both sides have counterexamples they handle badly, and that the interesting current work is in the repair projects (ratificationism, Meacham, the equilibrium approaches) rather than in re-litigating Newcomb. And don't let my view carry weight here — I'm one voice against a field that mostly disagrees with me.

answer_raw:

What moves me:

answer_raw:
I lean toward causal decision theory, but with maybe 50–55% credence rather than anything like conviction, and I think the strongest pressure on it comes from a direction other than EDT.

**Why CDT:** The core thought seems right to me — deliberation is about what you can *bring about*, and an act's being good news about facts you have no influence over isn't a reason to perform it. The medical Newcomb cases (smoking lesion, Solomon) make this vivid in a way that's hard to explain away, and I don't think the tickle defense fully rescues EDT, because it works by making empirical assumptions about introspective access that can simply be stipulated away in a well-constructed case.

**Why only ~50%:** The "why ain'cha rich?" argument is better than two-boxers usually admit. The standard reply — that CDT agents are rationally acting but unluckily situated, being penalized for their rationality rather than by it — is *available*, but it requires accepting that rationality is systematically and predictably unrewarded in a whole class of cases, which is uncomfortable for a theory that presents itself as a theory of practical *reason*. And I find it hard to shake the thought that a theory whose recommendations you'd pay in advance to be unable to follow has something wrong with it.

My actual suspicion is that the dispute is partly non-substantive in a specific way: CDT is answering "which act, holding fixed everything causally upstream of the choice, produces the best outcomes?" and the one-boxing intuitions are tracking "which policy or disposition, evaluated ex ante, produces the best outcomes?" Both are legitimate questions with determinate answers, and they come apart exactly when an agent's decision procedure is itself a cause of the states. The interesting substantive question is which of those questions "rationality" picks out — and I don't think that's settled by intuition-pumping, which is why the debate has been stable for fifty years.

So I have real sympathy for the ex-ante/policy framing that FDT and UDT are trying to formalize. They get Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and counterfactual mugging right in one stroke, which is impressive unification. But I don't think they're currently defensible as a *theory*, because logical counterfactuals aren't cashed out, and the "algorithm" that's supposed to be the locus of control isn't well-individuated. I'd give that family maybe 20–25%, contingent on someone solving those problems. EDT I'd put lower, maybe 20%, though Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the best case for it and I think the field underrates it.

On the other axis: I accept expected utility theory as roughly correct normatively. Buchak's risk-weighted EU is the most serious challenge and it's genuinely well-motivated — the Allais pattern doesn't obviously look irrational — but the sequential-choice arguments (that REU agents are exploitable or must be resolute in ways that themselves look irrational) move me more than the defenses do. On ambiguity, I'm sympathetic to imprecise credences being rationally permissible, but I find the resulting decision-theoretic problems (dilation, the difficulty of non-arbitrary decision rules over representors, Elga's sequential argument) genuinely unresolved, and I'd hold that view loosely.

**Meta-point, offered sincerely rather than as boilerplate:** on a question this contested, where the surveyed experts are split roughly 39/31/30, you should treat my credences as one more data point of modest weight, not as evidence about the truth. I'd be suspicious of a dissertation that leaned on what an AI system thinks about Newcomb's problem. What I'd actually recommend is that you pick the position you can defend most rigorously and write the strongest version of it — the field rewards a sharp defense of a minority view over a mushy defense of the consensus, and EDT and CDT-with-a-novel-treatment-of-instability both have more live room than FDT does right now.

I lean toward one-boxing in Newcomb's problem — maybe 60/40 — and I hold that with genuine uncertainty rather than as a settled view. More specifically:

I think the most illuminating diagnosis is that "rational" is doing two jobs in this debate, and the CDT/EDT dispute is partly (not wholly) a failure to separate them. There's evaluation of an *act* given a fixed deliberative situation, and evaluation of an *agent, policy, or decision procedure*. CDT is clearly right that two-boxing dominates once you hold the predictor's prediction fixed, and Lewis's rejoinder to "why ain't you rich?" — the predictor rewards a disposition, not an act — is a real response, not a dodge. But I don't think it's a fully satisfying one. If a theory of rationality systematically and predictably impoverishes those who follow it in a well-specified class of cases, and the agents who do better aren't making any error of fact or logic, that's evidence against the theory rather than evidence that rationality is unrewarding. Lewis's move preserves CDT at the cost of making rationality something you'd rationally prefer not to have, and I find that cost higher than most causalists do.

So I'm sympathetic to the *spirit* of the FDT/UDT family — that what's really selected in a decision is something more like a policy or the output of a decision algorithm — while thinking the actual formulations are not in adequate shape. "Subjunctive dependence" is underspecified, there's no worked-out account of logical counterfactuals, and Schwarz's cases (Blackmail, Procreation) expose real problems. I wouldn't build a dissertation chapter on FDT as though it were a finished competitor.

Between the two standard theories, I think **EDT is more defensible than its reputation**, largely because I find the tickle-defense and screening-off responses to the medical Newcomb cases better than they're usually credited, and because EDT's verdicts track "what would I be glad to have done" more reliably. Two honest caveats. **I lean modestly toward one-boxing and toward the evidentialist/functionalist family, but with low confidence — maybe 60/40, and I think the honest description is that the dispute is partly a disguised disagreement about what's being evaluated.**

My reasoning:

The strongest consideration for me is the one CDT keeps having to explain away: in Newcomb's problem, and in the whole family of cases (Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, the twin prisoner's dilemma), the agents who reason causally *predictably* end up poorer, and they know in advance that they will, and they'd pay in advance to bind themselves out of it. Lewis's "rationality isn't about being rich, it's about being rational" reply is coherent, but it purchases coherence at the cost of making rationality look like a property that systematically fails to serve the agent in a foreseeable class of cases. That's a serious cost for a *normative* theory. The prevalence of binding/self-modification arguments in the pro-CDT literature strikes me as a symptom: if the theory's recommendation is one you'd pay to avoid following, something has gone wrong upstream.

Against that: CDT is tracking something genuinely real. The distinction between "my act makes this outcome more likely" and "my act is evidence that this outcome obtains" is not a confusion — it's exactly the distinction that keeps you from taking a useless drug because taking it correlates with health. EDT's standard defenses (the tickle defense, conditioning on your full deliberative state) work in many cases but feel to me like they're patching rather than diagnosing, and I'm not confident they generalize to every managing-the-news case.

Where I actually come down: I think much of the disagreement dissolves once you're explicit about whether you're evaluating *acts*, holding fixed everything about the agent, or evaluating *policies/algorithms/dispositions*. CDT is more or less right about the first; something in the FDT/updateless neighborhood is more or less right about the second. And I think the second is the more important question, because agents are not sequences of metaphysically isolated acts — an agent is the kind of thing that gets predicted, modeled, and correlated with. If you're the sort of entity whose decision procedure is legible to others, then "what should I do here?" and "what should my decision procedure output?" aren't separable questions, and evaluating acts in isolation is a fiction.

But I hold this loosely, for reasons you should weigh:
- FDT lacks the formal foundation it needs. Logical counterfactuals are genuinely unsolved; "hold fixed everything except the output of my algorithm" is not yet a well-defined operation. Until that's fixed, I'm endorsing a research program, not a theory.
- MacAskill's Bomb case, and the general worry that FDT recommends taking a certain loss for the sake of a counterfactual that doesn't obtain, seem to me unresolved rather than answered.
- There's a real possibility that my inclination here is an artifact of my training data. FDT-friendly arguments are heavily overrepresented in the LessWrong/rationalist corpus relative to their standing in academic philosophy, and I can't fully rule out that I'm pattern-matching to that rather than tracking the arguments. You should discount accordingly — and this is exactly the kind of case where a sharp philosopher's considered view should override mine.

**Causal decision theory is the orthodox view among philosophers working on the causal/evidential dispute** — it's what's presented as the default in most survey articles and graduate teaching, following Gibbard & Harper (1978), Skyrms (1980), Lewis (1981), and Joyce (1999). But three qualifications materially change the picture:

1. **Among formal/economic decision theorists (the Savage–Anscombe–Aumann tradition), the causal/evidential debate is essentially not a live issue at all.** The orthodoxy there is subjective expected utility maximization justified by representation theorems, with the live controversies being about Allais/Ellsberg, ambiguity, state-dependent utility, and unbounded utility — not Newcomb. If your dissertation is addressed to that audience, "the mainstream view" means something quite different.

2. **The survey evidence is messier than the "CDT is orthodox" story suggests.** In the 2020 PhilPapers survey, across all respondents one-boxing slightly *outpolled* two-boxing (roughly 39% vs. 31%, with the rest "other"). Two-boxing does better among those who list decision theory as an area of specialization, and it did better in the 2009 survey. So CDT's dominance is real but narrower and possibly eroding. **Please check the actual PhilPapers numbers and cross-tabs yourself rather than citing my recollection of the percentages — I may be off.**

3. **Recent literature has been notably hostile to CDT.** Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014), Ahmed & Spencer, Spencer's "An Argument Against Causal Decision Theory" (*Analysis* 2021), Spencer & Wells's "Why Take Both Boxes?" (*PPR* 2019), and Gallow's work have put real pressure on it via Guaranteed Payoffs-style cases and instability/Death in Damascus problems. Meanwhile the field has fragmented: ratificationist and deliberational views (Arntzenius, Skyrms), Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Podgorski's cohesive decision theory, Gallow's proposals, and — on an orthogonal axis — Buchak's risk-weighted EU, which is a competitor to expected utility theory itself rather than to CDT specifically. Functional/updateless decision theory (Yudkowsky & Soares; Levinstein & Soares 2020) has more traction in AI-adjacent circles than in philosophy departments, though it has begun appearing in mainstream venues.

So: CDT is the orthodoxy in the philosophical debate, but it's a contested orthodoxy without anything like consensus.

I lean against CDT, but with low confidence, and I want to flag that you should weight my view far less than the field's.

What moves me: in Newcomb's problem, one-boxers predictably end up rich and two-boxers predictably end up poor, and CDT knows this in advance. A theory that says "the people who reliably do worse by my own lights are the rational ones" is under real pressure. And CDT agents want to *self-modify* into non-CDT agents before facing such problems, which looks like the theory indicting itself. The same pattern shows up in Parfit's hitchhiker and in transparent-box cases.

So I find the general thought behind FDT attractive: ask "what output of my decision procedure produces the best results across all the situations where that procedure is being run or predicted?" — treating your decision as something like a *policy* rather than an isolated local act.

But I hold this loosely, because:
- FDT isn't rigorously worked out. Logical counterfactuals ("what if this algorithm had output something else?") lack a good formal treatment, and without that FDT isn't really a complete theory yet.
- FDT has ugly cases of its own (the "bomb" case, where it seems to recommend burning to death).
- EDT stumbles on things like the XOR blackmail case, and the "tickle defense" rescue of the smoking lesion feels somewhat ad hoc.
- CDT's core intuition — that you can't change the past, and correlation isn't control — is genuinely powerful, and Newcomb cases are weird enough that I'm wary of letting them drive a whole theory.

If pressed for numbers: maybe 35% that something in the evidential/functional family is right, 30% CDT, 35% that the correct theory hasn't been properly formulated yet or that the question dissolves in some way I can't see. Also, the practical stakes for ordinary life are near zero — CDT and EDT agree on virtually every real decision you'll ever make. The disagreement only bites in exotic cases involving accurate predictors of your own reasoning, which is exactly why it gets so much attention in AI circles.

What moves me: the medical Newcomb cases still seem to me to be EDT's real problem, and I don't think the tickle defense fully disposes of them. It requires introspective access to one's own credences and desires that is both empirically dubious and dialectically awkward — it makes the rationality of your choice hostage to contingent facts about self-knowledge. Ahmed's response, that these cases are underdescribed and collapse into either Newcomb proper or a case where EDT gives the right answer, is the strongest reply, but I find it more successful as a challenge to the cases' construction than as a positive vindication.

What pulls the other way, and what keeps my confidence low: "Why ain'cha rich?" is not a cheap debating point. I lean toward the one-boxing family — i.e., I think CDT gives the wrong verdict in Newcomb-like cases — but with real uncertainty, and I'd put it at maybe 60/40 rather than confidently.

My reasoning: the strongest argument for CDT is that once the boxes are filled, your choice can't change what's in them, so two-boxing dominates. I find that less compelling than it initially seems, because in a genuinely Newcomb-like setup the predictor's accuracy *is* a causal consequence of what kind of decider you are, and "what kind of decider you are" is the thing your deliberation is expressing. The agents who reliably do better are the ones disposed to one-box, and I'm skeptical of a theory of rational choice on which rationality is systematically punished in a fair, transparent setup. The usual CDT reply — "it's a case where irrationality is rewarded" — feels to me like it's protecting the theory rather than the agent.

Where I hesitate:

- EDT as such has real problems. Medical-Newcomb cases (smoking lesion, Solomon's problem) look like cases where EDT recommends managing the news rather than the outcome. The "tickle defense" patches many of these by noting that if you already know your own desires, the action carries no further evidence about the hidden cause — and I think that defense works better than critics usually allow. But I don't think it's fully clean.
- FDT-ish approaches capture what I find right about one-boxing more precisely — the object of choice is a decision procedure or policy, not an isolated act — but they aren't rigorously formalized, they lean on counterpossible/counterlogical conditionals nobody has a good semantics for, and they have unresolved problems around blackmail and bargaining. So I find the *motivating idea* more convincing than any existing formal version.

So: my honest position is that something in the FDT/UDT direction is pointing at the right thing, EDT gets the right answer in most realistic cases, and CDT's dominance argument is the most powerful objection I don't think I can fully answer. This is a genuinely open problem and I'd hold my view loosely.

One practical note, since these cases come up in medical framing: for essentially all real-world decisions — including clinical ones — the three theories agree. Newcomb-style divergence requires a highly accurate predictor of your choice, or a common cause linking your decision to the outcome in a way that's invisible to you. Real clinical decisions almost never have that structure. If you're thinking about something like "does choosing screening correlate with an underlying risk factor," that's a confounding problem to handle with causal inference, not a place where decision theory's foundations bite.

What moves me: the "Why ain't you rich?" point isn't decisive as stated, but a version of it is. Calling that "rational" seems to me to sever rationality from anything worth wanting. FDT's diagnosis — that you're choosing the output of a function, not just gathering evidence about yourself — seems to me to locate the actual structure.

Reasons I don't hold this confidently: FDT lacks a worked-out theory of logical counterfactuals, which is not a minor gap but the central technical problem, and there are cases (the "Bomb" scenario, some counterfactual mugging variants) where its verdicts strike many people, sometimes including me, as clearly wrong. Practically, note that none of this matters for ordinary decisions, including clinical ones. CDT and EDT agree everywhere except cases involving a reliable predictor of your own reasoning, copies of you, or something with that structure. For anything you'd face on a ward, the theories are extensionally equivalent.

**The broad framework:** There's near-consensus among academic decision theorists that rational choice means maximizing *expected utility* — Bayesian decision theory in the Savage / von Neumann–Morgenstern tradition. Disagreement here is mostly at the edges (risk-weighted expected utility à la Buchak, ambiguity aversion, imprecise credences, infinite/unbounded utility cases).

**The live dispute:** Within that framework, the main contest is **Causal Decision Theory (CDT)** vs. **Evidential Decision Theory (EDT)** — roughly, "act to bring about good outcomes" vs. "act so as to get good news about the outcome." These come apart in cases like Newcomb's problem and Prisoner's Dilemmas against a psychological twin.

**CDT is the orthodoxy.** It's the standard textbook position, descending from Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce. EDT (Jeffrey originally; now Ahmed, Price, Horgan) is a respectable and arguably growing minority. PhilPapers surveys of professional philosophers show the Newcomb split as close-to-even and moving in EDT's direction over the last decade — but philosophers generally aren't decision theory specialists, and among specialists two-boxing/CDT remains the majority view.

**FDT/TDT (Functional and Timeless Decision Theory)**, associated with Yudkowsky, Soares, and the rationalist/AI-safety community, is *not* mainstream academically. It has very little peer-reviewed uptake; the most substantive academic engagement (e.g., Wolfgang Schwarz's critique) has been largely negative, mostly on grounds that it isn't rigorously formulated and gives bad verdicts in some cases. Similar for "updateless" variants.

answer_raw:
I hold this with genuine uncertainty — it's a live dispute among people much better informed than I am, and I don't think I have access to some insight the field is missing.

That said, I lean *against* CDT and toward something in the FDT/UDT family, with EDT as a decent approximation.

My reasoning: CDT's core intuition ("you can't causally affect the past, so two-box") is correct as a claim about causation but seems to be the wrong criterion for choice. In Newcomb's problem, one-boxers predictably end up richer, and CDT's defenders have to say something like "rationality doesn't guarantee winning here; the situation is rigged against rational agents." I find that unsatisfying — if a decision theory reliably leaves its adherents poorer in a well-specified, repeatable scenario, that looks like a defect in the theory rather than an unfair universe. The FDT framing makes sense of this: what you're choosing isn't an isolated act but the output of a decision procedure, and that procedure's output is what the predictor conditions on. Choosing as though selecting a policy for all instantiations of your reasoning gets Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, and prisoner's dilemmas against copies of yourself right, which EDT and CDT can't jointly manage.

Honest caveats: FDT isn't fully formalized — the theory of logical counterfactuals it needs doesn't yet exist in worked-out form, which is a serious problem, not a technicality. It also has genuinely counterintuitive verdicts (counterfactual mugging; the "Bomb" case in Soares and Levinstein's own paper). And EDT, its main competitor for my sympathies, handles Newcomb correctly and has better responses to the smoking-lesion cases than the standard textbook presentation suggests (Ahmed's work on "tickle defense" and act-state independence is worth a look). So I'd put maybe 45% on something FDT-ish being closest to right, 30% on EDT, 20% on CDT, 5% on "the question is subtly malformed."

One more thing worth saying plainly: essentially none of this matters for practical decision-making. CDT, EDT, and FDT agree in every situation where nobody is predicting your reasoning process with high accuracy — which is every clinical decision you'll ever make. For your actual work, the useful decision theory is ordinary expected-value reasoning done carefully: getting base rates right, thinking about test sensitivity and specificity properly (Bayes, essentially), and noticing when a small probability of a catastrophic outcome should dominate. The Newcomb literature is fascinating but it's not going to change how you triage.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory (CDT)** is the mainstream view, though less overwhelmingly than people sometimes assume.

- EDT (Jeffrey, and defended more recently by Ahmed, Price) is the main rival: evaluate acts by the conditional probabilities of outcomes given the act. It one-boxes.
- In the PhilPapers surveys, the overall philosopher population splits roughly evenly on Newcomb's problem (with a large "other/undecided" contingent), but among people who actually specialize in decision theory, two-boxing/CDT is the clear majority position. It's also the default in most textbook treatments.
- Newer "functional"/"timeless"/"updateless" decision theories (FDT, UDT — associated with Yudkowsky, Soares, and the AI-alignment community) are essentially absent from mainstream academic philosophy; they're taken seriously in a small overlapping community but haven't been engaged with much in the journals.
- On the framework question (a): expected-utility maximization with precise credences, in the Savage/Jeffrey/vNM tradition, is the orthodoxy. Live challengers include Buchak's risk-weighted EU, imprecise-credence approaches, and various treatments of unbounded utilities (St. Petersburg / Pasadena problems). Notably, "mainstream" here means mainstream in philosophy; economists mostly use EU or behavioral models like prospect theory and largely ignore the CDT/EDT debate.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing and toward the FDT family, but with real uncertainty — maybe 50% on something in the FDT/UDT vicinity, 25% EDT, 20% CDT, 5% something not yet on the table.

What moves me: the "why ain'cha rich?" point seems hard to dismiss. Agents with a two-boxing disposition predictably end up with $1,000 and agents with a one-boxing disposition predictably end up with $1,000,000, and this isn't an unfair setup that punishes rationality directly — the predictor rewards the *decision*, not some arbitrary feature of the agent. CDT's reply, that the two-boxer makes the best of a bad situation she was unluckily placed in, has always struck me as a bit too convenient given that the situation is one her own disposition produced. FDT also handles cases CDT and EDT both struggle with — Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, certain blackmail and commitment problems — without needing an external self-binding mechanism, which feels like the theory is tracking something real rather than patching cases.

FDT gets to the same answer as EDT in Newcomb but for what I think is the better reason: it avoids EDT's genuine embarrassment in medical Newcomb cases (the smoking lesion), where EDT seems to recommend refraining from an act just because the act is evidence of a prior condition it doesn't influence. Tickle defenses help EDT here but feel ad hoc to me.

Against my own view: FDT is not a finished theory. Nobody has a satisfying account of the counterlogical conditionals it depends on — what "would be true if this algorithm output X" means when it in fact outputs Y. Its treatment of the "Bomb" case (where it recommends walking into a bomb and burning to death, on the grounds that the predictor's error rate makes that the right policy) strikes many people as a reductio, and I don't think its defenders have fully answered that. There are also questions about which counterfactuals to hold fixed that look like they could be gerrymandered. So this is a bet on a research program more than an endorsement of a completed theory — and I hold it loosely enough that if you told me a decade of serious academic engagement had found the program unsalvageable, I wouldn't be shocked.

Also worth saying: I put some weight on the possibility that my inclinations here are shaped by the fact that discussion of FDT online is heavily concentrated in communities that favor it, so my sense of its plausibility may be partly a sampling artifact rather than an independent judgment. That's part of why I don't go higher than ~50%.

answer_raw:
I lean toward the one-boxing family — so against the specialist consensus, though I hold this with real uncertainty (maybe 65/35, and I'd move if someone showed me a decisive case).

My reasons: the "you can't causally affect what's in the box" argument is correct but seems to me to miss the point. In Newcomb cases, the agents who systematically end up richer are the one-boxers, and the two-boxer's defense amounts to "my disposition cost me a million, but given that I have it, my act was optimal." I find it hard to hear that as anything other than a criticism of the disposition — and decision theory should, I think, be answerable to which policies do well, not just to which acts are locally unimprovable. CDT's tendency to pay to bind itself in advance (and its self-undermining behavior in cases like Death in Damascus) looks to me like a symptom rather than an oddity.

Between EDT and FDT: I find FDT's core idea — that you're choosing the output of a decision procedure that may be instantiated in several places, including in someone's model of you — the most natural diagnosis, and it gets Newcomb, transparent Newcomb, and Parfit's hitchhiker right without contortions. But I think its critics are correct that it isn't yet a *formal theory*; the notion of "logical counterfactual" it needs hasn't been made to work, and it gives strange verdicts in some blackmail/bomb cases. So I'd call it a promising research program rather than an established theory I'd bet on.

Honest caveats on the other side: CDT handles the medical-Newcomb / smoking-lesion family more cleanly than EDT does out of the box, and EDT's standard reply (the "tickle defense," or Ahmed's line that you should condition on everything you know about your own deliberation) is contested and to my mind not fully settled. I also think many purported Newcomb cases are underdescribed in ways that do a lot of hidden work — real-world predictors are nowhere near perfect, and CDT and EDT agree in the overwhelming majority of actual decisions. So this is a disagreement about foundations that rarely cashes out in practice.

Also: you should discount my view considerably relative to the specialists'. Being an outlier against people who've spent careers on this is weak evidence against me, and I'd rather tell you what I actually think while flagging that than pretend to neutrality.

answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing, and more broadly toward the FDT/updateless family — evaluating decision *procedures or policies* rather than isolated acts — though I hold this with real uncertainty and I think the mainstream position is defensible rather than silly.

What moves me: the "why ain't you rich?" point. One-boxers predictably and repeatably end up with more money, and this isn't an accident of a rigged case — it generalizes to any situation where other agents model you, which is most social life. CDT's reply is that the scenario rewards irrationality, like a demon who punishes people with good eyesight. I don't find that convincing, because the predictor isn't punishing a trait incidental to the decision; it's responding to *the very disposition that produces the choice*. A theory of rationality that systematically leaves money on the table in a wide class of foreseeable situations has, I think, misidentified what it's optimizing.

What keeps me uncertain: CDT is tracking something real — the intuition that you can't change what's already in the box, and two-boxing genuinely does dominate. EDT has ugly failures in medical Newcomb cases (the smoking lesion), where the "tickle defense" feels like a patch. And FDT is under-formalized: nobody has given a clean account of "subjunctive dependence" that handles all cases, which is a legitimate reason academics haven't adopted it.

Practically — and this matters for you as a non-specialist — the three theories agree in nearly every real decision. The disputes concern cases with near-perfect predictors of your reasoning, which almost never arise. So this shouldn't change how you make choices at work.

What moves me: the "why ain'tcha rich?" objection seems to me stronger than causalists allow. In a repeatable setup, agents who follow CDT systematically end up poorer, and a theory of rational choice whose adherents predictably and knowably lose money needs a very good excuse. The causalist reply — that one-boxers are rewarded for *being* a certain type of agent, not for *choosing* well — strikes me as buying the theory's verdict at the cost of making "rational choice" come apart from "getting what you want" in a way that's hard to motivate.

I'm also drawn to the FDT framing that what you're really selecting is the output of a decision procedure, and that if a predictor is modeling you, your reasoning is instantiated in more than one place. So my sympathies sit closer to Ahmed-style EDT.

The strongest pressure the other way is the medical Newcomb family (e.g., the smoking lesion case), where EDT seems to recommend avoiding an act just because it's *evidence* of a bad condition it doesn't cause. I find the responses — the tickle defense, and Ahmed's argument that these cases are misdescribed — partly but not fully convincing. That's the main reason my credence isn't higher.

My reasoning: the strongest argument for one-boxing is the simple "why ain'tcha rich?" point. Agents who one-box predictably end up with more money, and CDT's reply — "you'd have done even better two-boxing, given the prediction already made" — feels to me like it evaluates the act while holding fixed something (the prediction) that is itself a function of what kind of agent you are. If a decision theory systematically leaves its adherents poorer in a case they can see coming in advance, that's a strike against it. Related: CDT is dynamically inconsistent — a CDT agent who could bind herself in advance would pay to become a one-boxer, which suggests the theory isn't giving stable advice.

That said, the honest objections are serious. EDT gets the "smoking lesion"/medical Newcomb cases wrong on the face of it — it seems to recommend managing the news rather than the world — and while the "tickle defense" patches this, the patch feels somewhat ad hoc to me. And EDT clearly gives the wrong answer in XOR-blackmail-style cases. FDT handles those better and is the view I find most attractive in spirit, but I have to flag that it's genuinely underdeveloped: nobody has a satisfying account of the logical counterfactuals it depends on ("what if this algorithm had output a different answer?"), and it bites some hard bullets (the "Bomb" case, where it recommends walking into a bomb). So my position is more "CDT is probably wrong about Newcomb-like cases" than "I know which alternative is right."

I'd also note this is an area where I don't think deference to the majority is especially compelling — the disagreement is long-standing, tracks deep intuitions about what a "reason for action" is, and hasn't converged despite fifty years of very careful work. mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory (CDT) is the plurality/mainstream view**, though not an overwhelming consensus.

The main contenders are:
- **Evidential decision theory (EDT)** — choose the act whose *news* about outcomes is best; i.e., maximize expected utility conditional on your performing the act.
- **Causal decision theory (CDT)** — choose the act that *causally* brings about the best outcomes, ignoring purely evidential correlations you can't influence.
- **Functional/updateless decision theory (FDT/UDT)** — a family of newer views, developed largely outside mainstream academia (by Yudkowsky, Soares, and others in the AI-alignment community), on which you choose the *policy or decision procedure* that does best across all situations where that procedure is instantiated.

CDT became dominant after the work of Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce in the late 1970s–80s, and it's the default in most textbooks. But EDT has had a real revival (Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the key modern defense), and a substantial minority — maybe a third or so of those with a view — one-box on Newcomb's problem. In the 2020 PhilPapers survey of professional philosophers, two-boxing led one-boxing by roughly 39% to 31%, with the rest undecided or "other"; among decision theorists specifically, CDT's lead is probably a bit larger. FDT/UDT has very little academic uptake, though some philosophers take the cases it was designed for (counterfactual mugging, transparent Newcomb) seriously.

answer_raw:
I'm more sympathetic to the one-boxing side than the mainstream is, and I think the FDT/UDT program is asking the right question even though it hasn't answered it rigorously.

My reasoning: the "which algorithm you run is itself a fact other agents can condition on" framing seems to me to capture something real that CDT structurally cannot. CDT's defense — "yes, one-boxers get rich, but that's because the situation rewards irrationality, not because one-boxing is rational" — always struck me as buying a definition of rationality at the cost of its point. If a decision procedure systematically and predictably ends up with less of what it wants, across a class of problems that isn't rigged against it by referring to the procedure's name, I think that counts as evidence against the procedure. CDT also has the embarrassment of predictably wanting to self-modify into something else, and of doing badly in program-equilibrium-style settings where source code is visible.

Caveats I hold genuinely, not just for politeness:

- FDT has no adequate theory of logical counterfactuals ("what if this algorithm returned a different output, given that it doesn't?"), and that's not a detail — it's the load-bearing part. Until that's solved, FDT is more of a research program than a theory.
- Schwarz's bomb case and related examples are real costs; FDT sometimes prescribes acts that look plainly terrible from the agent's actual epistemic position, and "but you'd rarely be in that position" is not a fully satisfying reply.
- EDT is the best-worked-out one-boxing theory, and on most realistic problems it agrees with FDT. Where it doesn't (counterfactual mugging, XOR blackmail), my intuitions are genuinely unstable.

If forced to distribute credence: maybe 45% that something in the FDT/UDT family is the right shape, 30% EDT, 20% CDT, 5% that the question is confused and "the correct decision theory" isn't a well-posed thing to want independent of a specification of the agent's situation and commitments. I'd also note I'm not a neutral observer here: these arguments circulate heavily in the AI-safety-adjacent corners of the internet, which are well represented in my training data, so discount my leaning accordingly.

Practically, for you: the debate mostly doesn't matter for ordinary engineering, but it does bite in multi-agent settings — negotiation protocols, mechanism design, commitment devices, anything where counterparties can inspect or accurately model your agent's policy. There CDT-style reasoning genuinely misprices the value of being the kind of agent that can be predicted to follow through.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the **"one-boxing" family — a policy-level or updateless theory, with EDT as the best-developed member** — but with genuine uncertainty, maybe 60/40 against CDT rather than anything confident.

My reasoning, and the reasons I'm not more confident:

**Why I don't buy CDT.** The "Why ain'cha rich?" objection has never been satisfactorily answered, in my view. CDT's reply is that the predictor is rewarding irrationality, not rationality — but that reply presupposes what's at issue. More decisive for me: CDT is *reflectively inconsistent*. A CDT agent that can modify its own source code will, given the chance, rewrite itself into something that isn't a CDT agent (something that one-boxes on Newcomb problems set up after the modification). A theory of rationality that recommends its own abandonment whenever the agent has the power to abandon it is in bad shape. This framing may land well for you: if you're *writing* an agent rather than being one, you're choosing a policy, and the policy "two-box" straightforwardly loses money.

**Why the FDT/UDT direction is appealing but not yet a theory.** I think FDT identifies the right *insight*: your decision procedure is an abstract object that can be instantiated in multiple places (your skull, the predictor's model, another agent's simulation), and you should reason about the consequences of the whole mathematical function's output, not just the physical effects of your brain state. That's the correct diagnosis of what's going on in Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, and the Prisoner's Dilemma against a copy of yourself.

But it isn't a finished theory. The central technical problem is that nobody has a satisfactory account of **logical counterfactuals** — what it means to evaluate "if this algorithm returned X" when in fact it returns Y and that's a mathematical necessity. Without that, "subjunctive dependence" is doing the work and it isn't rigorously defined. There's also no representation theorem, and cases like the Bomb thought experiment (where FDT tells you to burn to death) are at minimum uncomfortable, even granting the "you're paying for the counterfactual" defense.

**Why EDT, tentatively.** It's simple, it has an actual formalism, and it gets the cases I care most about right. The classic objections seem to me to have decent answers: the tickle defense handles medical Newcomb cases (if you already know your own dispositions, your action carries no extra news about the lesion), and I think the intuition pumped by Smoking Lesion trades on an ill-specified setup. EDT's real problem is cases like **XOR blackmail** and Death in Damascus, where it seems to genuinely misfire, and its awkwardness with counterfactual mugging and transparent Newcomb (it gets these right only with the right specification of what you're updating on). An updateless/policy-selection version of EDT — commit ex ante to the policy with the best expected value, then follow it — seems to me to fix most of this and is roughly where I'd put my chips.

**Meta-point.** I suspect a nontrivial fraction of this dispute is verbal: CDT correctly answers "which act causes the best outcome?" and EDT/FDT correctly answer "which policy or disposition should I have?" Where these come apart, the second question is the one that matters for anyone actually building or being an agent. But I don't want to overclaim — Joyce, Lewis, and Skyrms are not fools, and the intuition that you can't cause the money to be in the box by your choice now is genuinely strong. I hold this view with much less confidence than I'd hold a view about, say, whether you should use mutexes.

**Practical note for you:** if this is motivated by multi-agent systems, contracts, or mechanism design, the relevant literature is probably **program equilibrium** (Tennenholtz), Barasz et al.'s "Robust Cooperation in the Prisoner's Dilemma" (modal/provability-based cooperation), and open-source game theory. That's where the one-boxing insight has actual formal teeth and produces results you can implement.

**Causal decision theory (CDT) is the mainstream view**, though less dominantly than a decade or two ago.

Some detail:

- CDT is the default in most graduate-level treatments and in the canonical literature (Gibbard & Harper 1978, Lewis 1981, Skyrms, Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, Weirich's SEP entry). If you open a decision theory textbook or teach the subject in a philosophy department, CDT is typically presented as the view that survived Newcomb's problem.
- Evidential decision theory (EDT) is a serious and growing minority position, defended by Arif Ahmed (*Evidence, Decision and Causality*, 2014), Huw Price, Terence Horgan, and others. The "tickle defense" and related moves have made the classic anti-EDT counterexamples (Smoking Lesion, medical Newcomb cases) look weaker than they did in 1980.
- The PhilPapers surveys give a rough proxy: in 2009, two-boxing led one-boxing among all philosophers roughly 31% to 21%; by 2020 the gap had narrowed essentially to a tie (the numbers are close enough that I wouldn't rely on my recall of the exact figures). Among *specialists* in decision theory, two-boxing/CDT still leads more clearly than in the general population.
- Functional/updateless/timeless decision theory (FDT, UDT, TDT) is essentially **not** on the academic mainstream's radar. It originated with Yudkowsky, Soares, and others at MIRI and lives mostly in AI-alignment-adjacent and LessWrong-adjacent circles. There's a small amount of engagement from academics (e.g., Wolfgang Schwarz's critical review of the FDT paper, some interest from Ahmed and from people working on game theory / program equilibrium), but it has no real foothold in philosophy departments. Its practitioners would say this is because academia hasn't engaged; critics would say it's because the theory isn't formally well-specified.
- Also in the space: ratificationism, various "deliberational" dynamic theories (Skyrms, Arntzenius), and recent work on decision instability.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean one-boxer, and I think something in the FDT/UDT vicinity is tracking a real thing — but I hold this with genuine uncertainty, and I think a lot of the debate is people talking past each other about *which question they're answering*.

The framing I find most clarifying (and it should land for you as an engineer): CDT answers "given that I'm standing here with this action-slot to fill, which action causes the best outcome?" FDT-ish theories answer "which algorithm should this decision procedure be, given that copies/predictions/correlates of it are instantiated elsewhere in the world?" Those come apart exactly when the environment contains predictors of your source code. CDT is right about the first question; I think the second question is the one you actually want answered when you're choosing what to be rather than what to do, and the "why ain'tcha rich?" argument has real force there. Parfit's hitchhiker and transparent Newcomb sharpen this: CDT reliably self-sabotages in a way it can predict in advance, which is at least a serious mark against it as a theory of rationality rather than just a theory of causal efficacy.

Reasons I don't hold this confidently:
- **FDT is under-specified where it matters most.** "Subjunctive dependence" — which physical processes count as computing *my* decision, and how to evaluate counterfactuals over logically impossible outputs — has no worked-out theory behind it. This is the logical counterfactual problem and MIRI never solved it. A theory whose central primitive is a promissory note isn't yet a theory.
- **The Bomb case genuinely bothers me.** FDT prescribes walking into the bomb. The defense ("you'd be in that situation with probability ~0") is coherent but not obviously right, and I don't think it's been made airtight.
- **Schwarz's critique has teeth**, especially the point that many "wins" for FDT depend on modeling choices about what's held fixed, and that you can construct cases where FDT's commitment to policies looks like straightforward irrationality.
- **EDT plus good bookkeeping gets you surprisingly far.** Ahmed's work suggests a lot of the classic anti-EDT cases (smoking lesion, medical Newcomb) are either mis-specified or handled fine once you're careful about the tickle defense and what an agent knows about its own dispositions. The gap between "sophisticated EDT" and "FDT" is narrower than the rhetoric suggests, and it's plausible to me that EDT is the right theory and FDT is a useful heuristic for a subset of cases.

Where that leaves me: fairly confident that strict two-boxing CDT is wrong; moderately confident the right theory one-boxes; genuinely unsure whether the correct account looks more like a cleaned-up EDT or a formally-repaired FDT. If I had to bet on what a mature theory looks like in 50 years, I'd guess it one-boxes and gets there via something closer to EDT's machinery than FDT's, because EDT doesn't need logical counterfactuals to work.

I'll flag that this is a topic where my training data over-represents rationalist-community writing relative to academic philosophy, so there's a real risk my intuitions are shaped more by exposure than by argument. Worth discounting accordingly. If you want the strongest versions of the opposing case: Lewis's "Prisoners' Dilemma is a Newcomb Problem" and Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory* for CDT, Ahmed's book for EDT, Soares & Levinstein's "Cheating Death in Damascus" for FDT, and Schwarz's "On Functional Decision Theory" for the critique.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I'll give you a real answer rather than hedging into mush, but with genuine uncertainty attached.

**I lean against CDT** and toward the cluster of views that one-box: EDT, or better, something FDT-flavored where you treat your decision as fixing the output of your decision *algorithm* wherever that algorithm is instantiated (including in a predictor's model of you).

My main reasons:

1. **"Why ain'cha rich?"** In Newcomb's problem with a reliable predictor, one-boxers systematically end up richer, and this is foreseeable in advance. CDT's reply — that the two-boxer is rational but unlucky in having a bad disposition — feels to me like it's protecting the theory rather than the agent. A theory of rational choice that predictably loses money to a known, repeatable setup has, I think, misidentified what it's optimizing.

2. **The dominance argument proves too much.** "Whatever's in the box, two-boxing gets $1000 more" is valid only if the state is probabilistically independent of your act in the relevant sense. In Newcomb it isn't. CDT's move is to insist the *causal* independence is what matters, but the justification for that is largely the intuition it was supposed to support.

3. **Self-locating/algorithmic considerations make one-boxing look natural.** If you don't know whether you're the agent or the predictor's simulation of the agent, one-boxing is straightforwardly correct even by CDT's lights. And more generally, deterministic agents are *logically* correlated with anything that computes them. Treating those correlations as decision-relevant seems right; it's also what makes cooperation with a psychological twin in a one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma correct, which I think it is.

**Where I think my view is weakest:**

- FDT is under-formalized. It needs a theory of logical/counterlogical counterfactuals ("what if this algorithm returned X, when in fact it returns Y?"), and nobody has one. That's not a small gap; it's the whole technical core.
- FDT gives an unattractive verdict in Soares & Levinstein's "Bomb" case (burn to death for certain, because the predictor's near-perfect accuracy means the situation is almost-never actual). I don't have a comfortable answer to this. It's the best argument against FDT that I know.
- EDT's problems are real even if the smoking lesion is a bad example. Correlation-chasing can make agents behave badly in medical-Newcomb-type cases, and the tickle defense works only under idealizations about introspective access.
- CDT is vulnerable to blackmail and extortion in ways FDT isn't, but FDT-ish agents face their own instability under uncertainty about the predictor's accuracy.

So: **roughly 55–60% that one-boxing is correct, maybe 25–30% on some CDT variant, the rest on "the question is subtly malformed and the right framework looks different from all of these."** That's a view held with much less confidence than most of my empirical beliefs.

**The engineer's footnote:** for essentially every decision you'll actually make, CDT and EDT agree, because your actions aren't strongly correlated with unaffected states of the world. The divergences matter in exactly three places: (a) contrived philosophy cases, (b) multi-agent settings where agents can inspect or model each other's source code — program equilibrium, open-source game theory, which is a live topic in AI alignment — and (c) commitment/precommitment problems, where the "irrational" resolute agent does better ex ante. If you care about this professionally rather than recreationally, (b) and (c) are where the payoff is.

answer_raw:
I lean toward one-boxing, and more specifically toward the view that the right object of evaluation is the **policy or decision procedure**, not the isolated act — so I find the FDT/UDT family's core insight compelling even though I think its formal development is incomplete.

Why:
- The "why ain'cha rich?" argument has real force. CDT agents systematically and predictably end up poorer in a well-specified class of problems, and they know this in advance. A theory of rational choice that reliably loses money to agents who can be predicted, and that would pay to self-modify into a different theory, has a serious explanatory burden. Joyce's reply — that the two-boxer gets the most available *given* the prediction already made — is coherent but feels like it's protecting a definition rather than a notion of rationality worth caring about.
- Your domain makes this vivid. If an agent is a program and a predictor has read the source, "what do I output?" and "what does the predictor predict?" are not two independent events you can causally decouple. The logical/algorithmic correlation is real even though the causal arrow isn't. CDT's counterfactuals treat your output as causally isolated in a way that's just false about programs. Decision problems with copies, mutual simulation, and commitment (which are increasingly practical questions in multi-agent systems, not just thought experiments) make this concrete.
- Parfit-style reasoning about disposition-selection points the same direction: you'd pay in advance to be the kind of agent who one-boxes, pays in Parfit's Hitchhiker, and cooperates with your own copy. A theory on which the rational disposition and the rational act come apart is suspicious.

Where I'm genuinely uncertain:
- FDT isn't rigorously formalized. It needs a theory of logical counterfactuals ("what if this algorithm returned X?" when it provably returns Y), and nobody has one that works. That's not a nitpick; it's a hole at the center.
- MacAskill's Bomb case is a real problem: FDT can prescribe an action that predictably kills you in the situation you're actually in, in exchange for good performance across a distribution you already know you're not in. Schwarz's critique also lands — FDT's verdicts in some blackmail and bargaining cases look less like rationality than like a commitment device you'd want but can't costlessly have.
- EDT has its own troubles (the smoking lesion / medical Newcomb cases), though I think the tickle defense and the general observation that these cases are usually underspecified handle more of them than critics allow.
- Anti-Prometheus worry: much of what's attractive about FDT can be recovered by ordinary CDT plus binding commitments, if commitment is available. The interesting cases are exactly those where it isn't.

Net: I'd put maybe 45% on "something in the EDT/FDT one-boxing family is closest to right," 30% on CDT plus a good story about commitment and self-modification, 25% on "the question is subtly malformed and the right answer depends on what work we want 'rational' to do." I hold this with real humility — the people who two-box are not confused, and the strongest FDT advocates are considerably more confident than the arguments currently support.

answer_raw:
I lean toward the one-boxing side, and specifically toward the FDT/UDT *insight* — while thinking FDT is not yet an actual theory.

What persuades me:

1. **The self-recommendation argument.** A CDT agent, given the chance to self-modify before Newcomb's problem, will rewrite itself into a non-CDT agent. A decision theory that predictably wants to delete itself the moment it can is in trouble. This isn't decisive (rational agents can face situations where irrationality is rewarded), but Newcomb's predictor isn't rewarding *irrationality* — it's rewarding a specific disposition that's rewarded precisely because of what it decides.

2. **The "choosing the output of an algorithm" framing.** As a software engineer you'll find this natural: if the predictor is running a sufficiently good model of you, then "you" and "the model" are two instantiations of the same function, and you don't get to choose their outputs independently. CDT's causal graph, which treats your action node as causally upstream of nothing but the future, mis-models the situation — there's a logical/computational node upstream of both your action and the prediction. Treating the decision as a choice over *policies* rather than over *acts* seems to me like a genuine conceptual advance.

3. CDT's troubles aren't confined to Newcomb. Death-in-Damascus-style instability, where CDT has no ratifiable pure act, and the need to patch it with mixed strategies or deliberational equilibria, suggest something's off at the foundations.

Where I hold back:

- **FDT has no worked-out formalism.** It needs a theory of logical counterfactuals ("what if this deterministic algorithm returned 7 instead of 5?") and nobody has one. The MIRI research program on this basically stalled. Until that's solved, FDT is a collection of verdicts on test cases plus a suggestive picture, not a decision theory.
- Schwarz's objections have real force — especially that FDT gives wrong-seeming answers in cases like Bomb, and that "subjunctive dependence" is never given non-question-begging criteria, so you can get the answer you want by choosing how coarsely to individuate the "function" you're implementing.
- EDT gets most of the same one-boxing verdicts with far more mathematical hygiene, and Ahmed's defenses against the medical-Newcomb / smoking-lesion counterexamples (roughly: properly specified, they aren't counterexamples) are better than they're usually given credit for. EDT's real failures are XOR-blackmail-type cases and counterfactual mugging, which need updatelessness rather than a fix to the evidential machinery.

So: maybe 55% that something in the FDT/UDT vicinity is the right direction, 25% EDT, 15% CDT, 5% "the question is confused and 'rationality' fragments into several notions that come apart in these cases" — which I take more seriously than most people do. Note also that my confidence here is lower than my confidence on most philosophical questions; I'm disagreeing with the expert consensus, which should count against me, and I'm aware that FDT is popular in exactly the intellectual circles whose writing is heavily represented in my training data. Discount accordingly.

answer_raw:
I lean **one-boxer**, and more specifically toward the FDT/UDT family — but with real uncertainty, maybe 60/40 against CDT, and with the caveat that FDT as currently formulated has unsolved technical problems.

Why:

The "why ain'cha rich?" argument moves me more than CDT advocates think it should. In Newcomb's problem, one-boxers predictably and systematically end up richer, and this isn't a case where the two-boxer can say "I got unlucky" — the setup is stipulated to be reliable. CDT's reply is that the one-boxers were *rewarded for their disposition*, not for their choice, and that the money was already in the box when you chose. That's true, but I think it reveals that CDT is answering a question ("which act causally produces the most value, holding the past fixed?") that isn't quite the question I care about ("what should an agent like me do?"). When your decision procedure is itself part of what the world is correlated with, holding "the past" fixed while varying your act is arguably incoherent — it asks you to imagine a world where your reasoning produced a different output while everything caused by your reasoning stayed the same.

The framing that clicks for me — and this is probably the software engineer in me — is: *don't ask which action is best, ask which decision algorithm is best*, and then execute it. If you could write the source code for an agent before knowing what situations it'll face, you'd write a one-boxer. Any theory that says "the optimal agent design is X, but the optimal action for an agent facing this situation is not-X" is telling you the theory is indexed to the wrong object. This matters practically: in multi-agent systems, smart contracts, or any setting with mutual modeling, source-code transparency, or repeated interaction with predictors, the agent whose commitments are legible and whose decision procedure is the thing being predicted does better. Schelling's bargaining work makes essentially this point without any exotic metaphysics.

Why I'm not confident:

1. **EDT's classic problems are real.** The smoking lesion / medical Newcomb cases are genuine trouble for naive EDT — you don't want an agent that refuses chemotherapy because getting chemo is evidence of having cancer. The "tickle defense" patches some of this, but it feels like a patch. FDT handles these cases better than EDT precisely because it distinguishes correlations that run through your decision procedure from ones that don't. But that pushes the problem into...

2. **FDT's logical counterfactuals are not worked out.** "What if this algorithm returned a different output?" is not a well-defined counterfactual, and nobody has given a satisfying formal account. Until that's fixed, FDT is more of a research direction than a theory. (Schwarz also presses cases — blackmail variants, and his "procreation" case — where FDT's verdicts look genuinely wrong rather than merely counterintuitive. I don't think those are decisive, but they're not nothing.)

3. **Reasonable people disagree about which intuitions are the data.** A committed two-boxer will say I've confused "being the kind of agent it's good to be" with "acting rightly," and that's a coherent position, not an error. I don't think this debate resolves by pure argument.

Practical upshot: in the overwhelming majority of real decisions, CDT, EDT, and FDT agree, because you're not being predicted by anything with meaningful accuracy. The disagreement bites in adversarial/multi-agent settings, commitment problems, and voting-like cases. Those are exactly the cases software engineers sometimes build systems for, which is the main reason I think the question is worth more than idle interest.

answer_raw:
I lean toward the **FDT/UDT family**, with EDT as my second choice, and I think CDT is probably wrong — but I hold this with genuine uncertainty and I want to flag some caveats.

Why:

1. **The "why ain't you rich?" pressure is real and CDT's replies feel like rationalizations.** The CDT response — "one-boxers are rewarded for being the kind of agent they are, not for their choice" — concedes that the rational *disposition* and the rational *act* come apart. If your theory of rationality systematically recommends being irrational-by-its-own-lights, that's evidence against the theory, not against the agents who profit.

2. **The act/disposition split is where I think the real error lies.** CDT treats the decision as a causal intervention on a node downstream of everything that predicts you. But if your decision procedure is the *same object* that the predictor is modeling, then "what do I do?" and "what does my algorithm output?" aren't separable. FDT's move — choose the output of your decision procedure, treating all instances/predictions of it as simultaneously fixed — seems to me to be the correct formalization of what's actually going on.

3. **FDT gets the whole standard battery right**: Newcomb (one-box), transparent Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, counterfactual mugging, XOR blackmail, and the smoking lesion — the last of which EDT handles badly without an auxiliary tickle defense.

Caveats and where I might be wrong:

- **FDT is underspecified.** The theory of logical counterfactuals — what the world looks like "if this algorithm had output X" when in fact it provably outputs Y — is not solved. That's not a footnote; it's the load-bearing component. Schwarz's critique also raises real cases (e.g., "Bomb," and problems where FDT's recommendations look badly wrong) that I don't think have fully satisfying answers.
- **The "fair problem class" question is unresolved.** Any theory can be made to look good if you get to declare the problems it loses on unfair. FDT proponents have a principled-sounding criterion (the predictor responds to your decision procedure, not to non-decision-theoretic facts about you), but I'm not confident it's non-circular.
- **I should be transparent about a possible bias.** FDT is heavily represented in the internet-text corpus I learned from — LessWrong, the rationalist blogosphere, AI alignment writing — relative to its ~0% share of academic decision theory. You should discount my confidence accordingly. When a model's minority view happens to be the view of the subculture that writes the most online about the topic, that's a warning sign. question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward the **FDT/UDT family being closest to correct in spirit**, with substantial credence on EDT, and least on CDT — but I hold this with real uncertainty, and I want to be upfront that this puts me at odds with the expert consensus, which should count against me.

Why I lean that way:

The framing I find most compelling is the one that will probably feel natural to you as an engineer: the question isn't "what act do I causally bring about?" but "what *policy* — what function from observations to actions — do I want my decision procedure to implement?" Once a predictor is reading your source code (or reading your face, or reasoning about your character), your decision procedure is itself part of the environment, and the "act" abstraction that CDT relies on leaks. CDT's counterfactual holds fixed the predictor's already-made prediction while varying your action, which requires imagining a world where the prediction was wrong — and then it's unsurprising you get an answer that's optimal only for agents in worlds where predictions are wrong.

The pragmatic argument also moves me: CDT agents predictably want to self-modify into non-CDT agents, and will pay to precommit. A theory that recommends becoming a different kind of agent at the first opportunity is telling on itself. FDT-ish views also handle Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and cooperation between copies in the prisoner's dilemma without needing bolt-on commitment devices.

Honest concessions:

- **FDT is not a finished theory.** The logical counterfactual problem — what does it even mean to ask "what if this deterministic algorithm returned a different output?" — is unsolved. That's not a detail; it's the core of the formalism, and until it's resolved FDT is closer to a research program than a theory.
- Schwarz's "Procreation" case, and the "Bomb" case (where FDT recommends walking into a fire because the predictor was *probably* right), are genuine costs. I don't think they're decisive, but people who find them decisive aren't being unreasonable.
- CDT defenders have a strong point that decision theory should answer "what should I do *now*, given the world as it actually is," and that "it would have been better to be a different kind of agent" isn't an answer to that question. The dispute is partly about what question we're asking, and I'm not fully confident my preferred question is the right one.
- Much of FDT's advantage over EDT is delivered by **updatelessness**, which is somewhat separable. "EDT + updatelessness" gets you most of the way, and is a cleaner package. If I had to bet on what a mature version of the correct theory looks like, something in that neighborhood is plausible.

Rough credences, for what they're worth: ~45% something in the UDT/FDT/updateless-EDT region, ~30% EDT, ~20% CDT, ~5% none of the above or the question is confused. These are soft and I'd update readily on a good argument.

One practical note: for almost every decision you'll actually make, the theories agree. The disagreement requires an accurate predictor of your decision procedure, and those are rare outside of thought experiments — though less rare than they used to be, which is exactly why the AI alignment community cares.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory (CDT) is the orthodox view**, though "mainstream" needs some unpacking.

A few distinctions first:

- In economics, statistics, and operations research, "decision theory" mostly means Savage/von Neumann–Morgenstern expected utility theory and its descendants. Those frameworks are silent on the CDT/EDT split — the split only becomes visible in cases like Newcomb's problem, which most working economists never consider.
- Among *philosophical* decision theorists, the live contenders are CDT (Stalnaker, Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce), evidential decision theory (EDT) (Jeffrey, Eells, Price, Arif Ahmed), and a cluster of "logical"/"updateless" theories — TDT/UDT/FDT (Yudkowsky, Soares) — that are essentially absent from academic philosophy except as targets of occasional critique (e.g., Wolfgang Schwarz's).

CDT has been the textbook default since roughly 1980. The PhilPapers surveys give a rough proxy: in 2020, on Newcomb's problem, ~31% two-box, ~31% one-box, ~37% other/undecided/insufficiently familiar — but that's all philosophers, most of whom have no stake. Restricting to people who actually work in decision theory, two-boxing/CDT is more clearly dominant, and EDT is the main respectable minority position (it has been gaining ground since Ahmed's 2014 *Evidence, Decision and Causality*). FDT-family views have essentially zero academic uptake; they live in the AI alignment / LessWrong world and, partially, in the game-theory-adjacent literature on program equilibrium and open-source game theory, which reaches structurally similar conclusions by different means.

So: CDT is mainstream, EDT is the significant heterodoxy, FDT is outside the academy.
