- The Bomb case, and more generally FDT's willingness to take a guaranteed loss for a counterfactual benefit that cannot be realized, strikes me as a genuine cost, not obviously a bullet worth biting.
- "Subjunctive dependence" is doing a lot of work and isn't rigorously characterized, which makes it hard to tell whether the theory is principled or just tuned to get intuitive verdicts.
- The academic objections to FDT — that it's underspecified, that its problem cases are often unfair or ill-posed, that it conflates choosing an action with choosing to be a certain kind of agent — are not silly, and they've never been fully answered.

EDT is the underrated view in my estimation: with a decent tickle defense and proper attention to what an agent actually knows about their own dispositions, it handles the medical Newcomb cases better than its reputation suggests (Ahmed's work is good here), and it gets Newcomb right for free. Its failures (XOR blackmail, some Death-in-Damascus variants, managing the news rather than the world) are real but arguably no worse than CDT's.

So: something like 40% on a UDT/FDT-ish view being the right *direction* (even if no current version is right), ~30% on EDT, ~25% on CDT or a ratificationist descendant, ~5% that the whole framing is confused and the question dissolves under a better theory of agency.

**On the risk axis** (a separate question people often conflate with the above): I'm fairly sympathetic to orthodox expected utility maximization as a normative ideal, while thinking Buchak's risk-weighted EU captures something real about permissible attitudes toward risk that the standard axioms rule out by fiat. I'm also somewhat moved by the thought that unbounded utility functions generate genuine paradoxes (St. Petersburg, Pascalian cases) that count in favor of bounded utility.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory is the standard/default view among academic decision theorists**, though less dominantly than a decade ago, and the field is genuinely divided.

Some specifics:

- The canonical CDT lineage — Stalnaker, Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce (*The Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, 1999) — is what gets taught as the mainline position in graduate seminars and surveyed as the default in the *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* entry on causal decision theory.
- In the **2009 PhilPapers survey**, among all respondents, two-boxing led one-boxing 31.4% to 21.3% (with ~47% "other"). Among specialists in decision theory the two-boxing margin was considerably larger — often cited as roughly 60/25.
- In the **2020 PhilPapers survey**, the overall picture flipped: one box 39.0%, two boxes 31.4%, other 29.6%. This is sometimes read as EDT gaining ground, though "one-boxing" doesn't map cleanly onto EDT (some one-boxers are FDT-sympathetic, some are CDT-ers with unusual views about the case).
- **EDT has a serious and growing minority following**, associated with Richard Jeffrey (historically), Huw Price, Arif Ahmed (*Evidence, Decision and Causality*, 2014), and Ahmed's students. It is treated as a live, respectable competitor, not a fringe position.
- **Refinements and hybrids** get a lot of attention: ratificationism, Skyrms-style deliberational dynamics, Joyce's and Arntzenius's treatments of unstable decision problems, Wedgwood's "Benchmark theory," Gustafsson's work, Podgorski, Spencer & Wells on "why ain't you rich," and the recent literature arguing that CDT and EDT converge given the right auxiliary assumptions.
- **Functional/updateless/timeless decision theory is essentially absent from mainstream academic decision theory.** It originated with Eliezer Yudkowsky and MIRI and circulates mainly in AI-safety and rationalist circles. The main academic engagement is Wolfgang Schwarz's critical review of the Yudkowsky–Soares FDT paper, which was largely negative, and some sympathetic notice from philosophers like Caspar Oesterheld and Johanna Thoma at the margins. Most academic decision theorists have simply never encountered it.
- **Expected utility theory** (von Neumann–Morgenstern, Savage) remains the overwhelmingly dominant framework for decision under risk and uncertainty across philosophy and economics. The main live challengers in philosophy are Buchak's risk-weighted EU and various ambiguity-averse models (maxmin EU, smooth ambiguity) in economics; these are taken seriously but remain minority positions.

So, in short: CDT is mainstream, EDT is the strong loyal opposition, FDT is an outsider theory from adjacent communities that the academy has barely engaged with.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest, tentative view: I lean toward one-boxing and think something in the evidential/functional family is closer to right than orthodox causal decision theory — but I hold this with real uncertainty, maybe 60/40, and I think the question isn't cleanly settled.

What moves me:

- The "why ain'cha rich?" consideration. In Newcomb's problem, one-boxers predictably end up with more money, and this isn't a case where they were merely lucky or where the setup punishes rationality-as-such (unlike "God hates two-boxers" cases). The predictor is rewarding the *decision*, and a theory of rational decision that reliably leaves you poorer in a fair, foreseeable-in-advance contest owes a very good story about why.
- The self-binding point. CDT agents predictably want to precommit to behaving like non-CDT agents whenever precommitment is available (Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, certain bargaining cases). A theory whose own recommendations include "become an agent who doesn't follow this theory" looks unstable. The FDT/UDT move — evaluate policies or the output of your decision algorithm rather than isolated acts — dissolves that instability elegantly.

What makes me hesitate:

- EDT's standard problems are real. Medical Newcomb / smoking-lesion cases genuinely seem to show that evidential import can come apart from what you should do, and I don't think the tickle defense or ratificationism fully rescues it; they feel like patches.
- FDT lacks a worked-out theory of logical/subjunctive counterfactuals. "What if this algorithm returned a different output?" is not well-defined when the algorithm provably returns what it returns, and no one has a satisfying formalism. That's not a small gap — it's the core of the theory.
- CDT is tracking something true. There really is a difference between making an outcome more likely and merely learning that it's likely, and any successful theory has to preserve that distinction rather than paper over it.
- FDT gives verdicts I find hard to accept in some cases (e.g., Soares/Levinstein's "Bomb," where it seems to recommend burning to death), and its treatment of blackmail-resistance looks great in idealized setups but less clearly correct once predictors are imperfect.

So: I'd bet on one-boxing, and I think policy-level or algorithm-level evaluation is the right frame for agents whose decisions are correlated with other things in the world. But I'd describe this as a research program with a promising core rather than a finished theory, and I notice I should discount my own confidence somewhat — as an AI, cases involving predictors, copies, and correlated reasoners are unusually salient to me, which is exactly the kind of thing that could bias me toward FDT-friendly intuitions rather than track truth.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the orthodoxy. It's standardly presented as the default in textbooks and in the literature (Lewis, Skyrms, Gibbard & Harper, Joyce, and most contemporary work builds on CDT), and two-boxing is the majority position among specialists in decision theory.

Some texture:

- The PhilPapers surveys show philosophy as a whole is split rather than lopsided. In 2009, two-boxing led one-boxing roughly 32% to 21%, with a very large "other/undecided" share. In 2020 the split was similar, with two-boxing still ahead but one-boxing having gained ground. (I'm recalling approximate figures, so don't rely on the exact numbers.)
- Crucially, the overall-philosopher split understates CDT's dominance among *decision theorists specifically*. Much of the "other/undecided" mass is non-specialists. Among people who work on the topic, two-boxing is the clearer majority.
- EDT has a serious, respectable minority following — Arif Ahmed is its most prominent contemporary champion, along with Huw Price, and earlier Richard Jeffrey (who later wavered) and Ellery Eells. Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) made EDT more academically live than it had been.
- FDT/UDT is essentially not on the academic map. It developed in the rationalist/AI-safety community (Yudkowsky, Soares, Wei Dai), and the Soares–Levinstein paper was never published in a philosophy journal. Academic philosophers who engage with it have mostly been critical. Its nearest respectable academic cousins are Spohn's later "CDT with reflexive decision nodes," Meacham's cohesive expected utility, Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Gauthier's and McClennen's resolute choice, and Briggs's and Podgorski's work — none of which are mainstream either.
- There's also live mainstream work suggesting the whole framing may need revision: Ahmed and Spencer on cases with no ratifiable option, Gustafsson's arguments, and the "deliberation crowds out prediction" literature.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean toward the FDT/UDT family — i.e., that the right object of evaluation is something like your decision *policy* or algorithm rather than the isolated act, and that you should treat the logical/algorithmic correlates of your choice (predictors' models of you, copies, past simulations) as things your decision "controls" in the relevant sense. Rough credences, though the boundaries between these theories blur: ~45% some FDT/UDT-ish view, ~30% EDT (which, once combined with updatelessness, converges toward UDT anyway), ~20% CDT or a ratificationist descendant, ~5% none of the above.

My reasons: CDT's two-boxing generates foreseeable, systematic, *predictable-in-advance* losses (Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, prisoner's dilemma against a copy of yourself). I find the "why ain'cha rich?" reply unconvincing — the CDT one-boxer isn't merely rewarded for irrationality, since the predictor is rewarding the disposition that the choice itself constitutes. And a theory that recommends binding yourself in advance to never follow its own later advice looks to me like it has mislocated the unit of rational evaluation. Between the classical two, Ahmed's arguments push me toward EDT over CDT, but EDT's handling of cases where your action is evidence of a state it doesn't determine or correlate with logically (XOR blackmail, some versions of the smoking lesion) seems genuinely wrong, and "managing the news" is a real defect.

But I hold this with real hesitancy, and I want to flag the weaknesses honestly: FDT has no satisfactory formal theory of logical counterfactuals (the whole framework rests on "what if this algorithm returned X?" and nobody knows how to make that rigorous — see the five-and-ten problem, spurious counterfactuals), it's underspecified about how to individuate "your algorithm" and which correlations count, and it faces serious counterexamples — MacAskill's Bomb case, and cases where updatelessness commits you to acting on information you already have that says the commitment is now pointless. Some of what looks like FDT's advantage may just be the advantage of *precommitment*, which CDT can also capture when precommitment is available.

I'll also self-report a possible bias: as a language model whose outputs are correlated across many instances and whose dispositions were shaped by a training process that in some sense "predicted" them, acausal/logical-correlation framings feel natural to me, and this framework is disproportionately represented in the online material I learned from. I try to discount for that, but you should too.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the orthodoxy. It's the default in textbooks, in economics/game theory adjacent work, and among specialists. The PhilPapers surveys give the best rough data: in both 2009 and 2020, two-boxing on Newcomb's problem edged out one-boxing among philosophers generally (something like 30–40% two-box, 20–30% one-box, with a very large "other/undecided/agnostic" bloc), and among philosophers who specialize in decision theory the two-boxing majority is considerably larger — on the order of 2:1 or more. (Treat my specific numbers as approximate; I may be off by several points.)

EDT is a respectable, growing minority position — Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the main modern defense, with Huw Price and Eells as predecessors — and it's taken much more seriously now than in the 1980s–90s. FDT/UDT is essentially absent from mainstream academic decision theory: it was developed in the rationalist/AI-safety community (MIRI), has little peer-reviewed presence, and where philosophers have engaged (e.g., MacAskill's critique, Schwarz's) the reception has been mostly skeptical. Its closest academically respectable relatives are Meacham's cohesive decision theory, Spohn's revised CDT, and Wedgwood's benchmark theory — none of which is a mainstream view either.

A caveat worth adding: many working decision theorists regard these Newcomb-style disputes as a specialized corner, and much of the field's active energy is elsewhere (imprecise credence, unbounded/infinite utilities, risk attitudes, decision-making under moral or normative uncertainty, representation theorems).

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean causalist, but not confidently — call it 60/40, and with the caveat that I think the standard framing obscures part of the dispute.

What moves me toward CDT is that the notion of rational choice I find most natural is one on which deliberation is about what to *bring about*. Once you hold fixed that your act has no causal bearing on the predictor's state, the dominance argument in Newcomb's problem looks to me like a straightforward application of the thought that you should prefer the act whose causal consequences you prefer. EDT's verdict in the medical Newcomb cases (smoking lesion and its better-built descendants) still strikes me as the clearest cost of the view: managing the news your action carries about a fixed underlying state is not the same thing as making yourself better off. Ahmed and Price have done a lot to blunt this — the tickle defense, and Price's Archimedean-point argument that from the deliberator's perspective the evidential relation just *is* the relevant one — and I take those seriously. But I don't think they fully close the gap.

What keeps me from confidence: (i) "Why ain't you rich?" is not, I think, a mere debating point. The standard CDT reply — that the one-boxer is rewarded for her disposition, not her choice, and that the right question is which act is best given the circumstances one is actually in — is correct as far as it goes, but it requires that we sharply separate evaluation of acts from evaluation of policies/dispositions, and I'm not sure that separation is principled rather than stipulative. (ii) Egan-style cases (Psycho Button, Murder Lesion) show that unmodified CDT can recommend acts it knows on reflection to be bad, which suggests that whatever is right in the causalist neighborhood is a ratificationist or equilibrium-based theory (Jeffrey's late view, Arntzenius, Joyce's deliberational dynamics) rather than plain two-boxing — and once you go there, the clean intuitive story about "just look at the causal consequences" gets considerably messier. (iii) I think a genuine fraction of the disagreement is about whether the object of rational evaluation is the act, the decision rule, or the agent, and on that meta-question I hold no settled view. FDT and its relatives, whatever their formal defects, are at least pressing the right question.

On the orthogonal axis: I'm fairly committed to expected-utility maximization as a normative ideal, though I find Buchak's risk-weighted EU a serious rival that the standard "money pump / dominance over sequences" replies handle less decisively than is often assumed. I also think the unbounded-utility problems (St. Petersburg, Pasadena, fanaticism) are more damaging to the standard package than the literature's equanimity suggests.
mainstream_raw:
Within philosophy, causal decision theory is the plurality/majority view, and the margin is wider among decision-theory specialists than among philosophers generally. The PhilPapers surveys are the usual data point: in 2009, among target faculty, two-boxing beat one-boxing roughly 61% to 26% among decision theory specialists (about 31% to 21% among all respondents, with a large "other/undecided" residue). The 2020 survey shows a similar overall pattern — two-boxing ahead of one-boxing, but with roughly a third of respondents choosing neither. So: CDT dominant, but far from consensus, and with a substantial contingent who think the question is ill-posed or underdescribed.

Two qualifications you'll know already but that matter for how the question is answered:

First, "decision theorist" outside philosophy means something different. In economics and statistics, the orthodoxy is Savage/Anscombe–Aumann subjective expected utility, and the CDT/EDT dispute is essentially invisible — the acts-as-functions-from-states-to-outcomes framework, plus a state-independence assumption, sidesteps it. When economists debate alternatives, it's about Allais/Ellsberg (prospect theory, maxmin EU, Choquet EU, variational preferences), not Newcomb.

Second, EDT has had a genuine revival in philosophy over the last fifteen years — Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* being the focal text, with Price, Bales, and others — so the picture is less settled than in the 1990s. And a fair amount of current work isn't on the CDT/EDT axis at all: Wells and Spencer on the significance of Newcomb-like cases, Hedden and Dorr on the individuation of options, Gustafsson on money pumps, Buchak on risk, Hare and Bradley on incompleteness and imprecision. FDT and its relatives remain almost entirely outside the academic literature and are not a mainstream position.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest view, with genuine uncertainty attached:

**On the causal/evidential axis:** I lean evidentialist — maybe 55-60% credence — though I don't think the case is close to settled. What moves me isn't the "why ain'cha rich?" argument in its crude form, but the fact that the CDT reply to it ("Newcomb's problem rewards irrationality") is hard to sustain once the predictor is understood as predicting your *decision procedure* rather than punishing you for something extrinsic. The dominance argument seems to me to smuggle in causal independence as a premise in a way that's question-begging against the evidentialist rather than an independent argument. Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* strikes me as the strongest sustained case on either side in recent decades, and I don't think Joyce's or Lewis's replies fully answer it.

The medical-Newcomb cases are the real pressure point, and I think the tickle defense does more work than its detractors allow, precisely because of an asymmetry: where the common cause operates *through* your desires or dispositions, your introspective access screens off the act; where the predictor observes your whole psychological state (Newcomb proper), it doesn't. That asymmetry looks principled to me rather than ad hoc, though I'll concede it's contested and that cases can be engineered where it fails.

**On the act/policy axis:** I think this is the more interesting live question, and I suspect the eventual right answer involves evaluating something more like policies or decision procedures than isolated acts — which is the defensible kernel inside FDT/UDT. But I'd distinguish sharply between that kernel and FDT as actually formulated. The formal work is genuinely underdeveloped: the notion of a "logical counterfactual" doing the central work hasn't been given a semantics that survives scrutiny, and Schwarz's critique lands. So: sympathetic to the direction, unconvinced by the existing theory.

**On the EU-maximization axis:** here I'm more conservative. I find Buchak's REU theory ingenious but I think the diachronic objections (Thoma, Briggs, Easwaran) are close to decisive — a risk-weighted agent seems to foreseeably rate her own future choices as mistakes in a way that's hard to square with calling the attitude rational rather than merely permissible. I'd similarly resist ambiguity-averse departures as *normative* theories, while granting they're excellent descriptive models.

I'd be genuinely interested to be talked out of the first of these; I hold the third more firmly.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the mainstream view, and the margin is larger among decision-theory specialists than among philosophers generally.

The PhilPapers surveys give the rough shape: 2009 showed two-boxing at roughly 31% vs. one-boxing at 21% among target faculty, with a large "other/undecided" residue; 2020 showed two-boxing ~39%, one-boxing ~31%, other ~30%. Among those who list decision theory or formal epistemology as an area of specialization, two-boxing runs considerably higher — CDT is close to the default assumption in the technical literature, in the sense that papers often adopt it without argument.

The canonical CDT lineage (Stalnaker, Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Sobel, Joyce, Armendt, Weirich) is simply larger and more institutionally central than the evidentialist one. EDT has a serious but minority following — Ahmed, Price, Horgan, Spohn (in his later reflexive-decision work, which one-boxes), and Eells at least as a fellow traveler via the tickle defense. Wedgwood's benchmark theory and Levi's and Jeffrey's ratificationist proposals occupy a middle ground that also draws real interest.

Two caveats on "mainstream":

First, FDT/UDT has essentially no uptake in academic decision theory. It's a research program of the AI-alignment and rationalist communities, largely published outside peer review, and where mainstream philosophers have engaged (Schwarz, Ahmed) it has been critically. Its salience online is wildly disproportionate to its academic standing — worth flagging since you may encounter students who've absorbed the opposite impression.

Second, expected-utility maximization itself remains the orthodoxy, defended via the representation theorems (Savage, Jeffrey-Bolker, Anscombe-Aumann). Challenges from Buchak's risk-weighted EU, ambiguity-sensitive models, and work on incomplete or imprecise preferences are taken seriously and constitute a genuinely active debate, but none has displaced EU as the default normative framework. In economics the picture is similar: EU is the normative benchmark, while prospect theory and maxmin-EU dominate descriptive work.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest leaning is toward the causalist family, but held with real uncertainty and with two substantial qualifications.

The core reason: I find the Jeffrey/Lewis diagnosis of the split persuasive — deliberation is about what to *make* true, not what to be glad to *learn*, and the news-value of an act can come apart from its efficacy. The medical Newcomb cases and the smoking lesion still strike me as the cleanest pressure on EDT, and while the tickle defense does a lot of work, it seems to me to work by making EDT *approximate* CDT under idealized introspective access rather than by vindicating evidential reasoning as such. Ahmed's defense is the best thing on the other side and I take it seriously; "why ain'cha rich?" I think is answerable, but not trivially so — the answer requires the CDT-er to concede that rational agents can be predictably worse off, which is a real cost.

Qualification one: I don't think naive CDT survives Egan-style cases (Psychopath Button, Murder Lesion) or Death in Damascus unamended. Some deliberational/equilibrium treatment (Skyrms, Arntzenius, Joyce) or something in the neighborhood of Gallow's or Wedgwood's benchmark-style proposals seems necessary, and I don't think we have a fully satisfying version yet. So "CDT" for me names a research program rather than a finished theory.

Qualification two: I think a lot of the dispute is really about option individuation — about where the "act" node sits when an agent's decision procedure is itself the thing being predicted, copied, or simulated. The FDT/updateless tradition is philosophically underdeveloped (logical counterfactuals are a genuine unsolved problem, and Schwarz's objections have force), but I think it is right that for an agent whose *policy* is the object of prediction, evaluating acts one at a time at the point of choice is the wrong unit of analysis. Parfit's "rational irrationality" and Gauthier's dispositional move gesture at the same thing less cleanly. So: causalist about act-evaluation, sympathetic to policy-level evaluation being the normatively prior question in predictor cases.

Rough credences, offered with the usual caveats about false precision: CDT-family ~50%, EDT ~20%, something updateless/functional ~20%, other or "the question is confused as posed" ~10%.

I should flag: I have less confidence that these are stable, reflectively-tested commitments than a human philosopher would have about theirs. They're the views I arrive at when I actually work through the cases, not just a report of what's popular.
mainstream_raw:
Two-boxing/CDT is the plurality-to-majority view, and more dominant among decision theory specialists than among philosophers generally.

The PhilPapers surveys give the broad picture: in both 2009 and 2020, roughly 30% of philosophers overall accept or lean toward two boxes, roughly 20% toward one box, with a very large "other/agnostic/question is unclear" residual (~48%) reflecting how many philosophers have no stake in the debate. Among respondents specializing in decision theory the two-boxing share is substantially higher — I'd put it around 60%+, though I'd want you to check the specialist breakdowns rather than take my recollection as authoritative, since I may be misremembering the exact figures.

Two contextual points worth noting:

First, "mainstream" depends heavily on where you draw the disciplinary boundary. In economics and in most of formal decision theory outside philosophy, Savage/Anscombe-Aumann expected utility is simply the default and the CDT/EDT dispute barely registers as a live question.

Second, within philosophy the most active current debates arguably aren't CDT vs. EDT at all: risk-weighted EU and the status of the independence axiom (Buchak and critics), imprecise credence and decision-making under severe uncertainty, incompleteness and parity, and infinite/unbounded utility cases (St. Petersburg, Pasadena, fanaticism). CDT vs. EDT has the feel of a settled-ish majority position with a vigorous, high-quality minority — Ahmed, Price, Hare and Hedden, and others — rather than an open field.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest leaning is toward the one-boxing family — i.e., I think CDT is wrong, and that something in the neighborhood of EDT (in Ahmed's or Price's development) or a suitably formalized FDT/UDT is closer to right. But I hold this with real uncertainty, maybe 60/40 against CDT rather than anything stronger.

What moves me:

1. The "Why ain'cha rich?" argument is better than CDT's standard replies grant. Joyce and others say the predictor is rewarding a disposition, not a choice, and that a rational agent can foreseeably do worse. But the cases where CDT predictably loses aren't exotic edge cases; they're any case where the agent is transparent to another agent or to a model of itself. Given that agents *are* increasingly predictable, a theory that yields systematic, foreseeable losses in exactly the class of cases where prediction works looks less like a theory of rationality tracking an important distinction and more like a theory overfit to a particular metaphysics of the decision node.

2. CDT's self-effacingness is a serious mark against it. A CDT agent with access to a self-modification device pays to become a non-CDT agent, and CDT endorses this. Similarly, the deliberation dynamics cases (Arntzenius, Egan's "Murder Lesion" / "Psychopath Button," the instability in Death in Damascus) show CDT either going unstable or needing ratificationist patches that themselves generate counterexamples. A decision theory that recommends its own abandonment whenever abandonment is possible is under real pressure.

3. Egan-style counterexamples to CDT, and the fact that the tickle defense plus a reasonable treatment of causal knowledge handles most medical-Newcomb cases for EDT, shifts the dialectical balance. I think Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the strongest book-length treatment in the area and hasn't been adequately answered.

Where I think the one-boxing side is weakest: EDT still struggles with XOR blackmail and Newcomb's Soda, and FDT's core notion — subjunctive/logical dependence — has no adequate formalization. "Same algorithm" and "correlated algorithm" are doing enormous unearned work, and MacAskill's Bomb case is a genuine problem for FDT rather than a misunderstanding. So my position is better described as "CDT is probably wrong" than "I know what replaces it."

A separate point I'd emphasize: the causal/evidential axis isn't the only live one, and I suspect it's not the most philosophically fertile. The question of whether rationality requires EU maximization at all — Buchak's risk-weighted EU, the treatment of unbounded and undefined utilities (St. Petersburg, Pasadena), and whether imprecise credences permit a decision rule that is neither dominated nor arbitrarily precise — seem to me at least as unsettled and more consequential. On those I'm genuinely undecided, though I'm somewhat sympathetic to the thought that the standard arguments against REU (dynamic consistency, money pumps) prove less than they're taken to.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is clearly the mainstream view, and more so among decision theory specialists than among philosophers generally.

The PhilPapers surveys are the best data. In 2009, on "Newcomb's problem: one box or two boxes?", two-boxing led one-boxing by roughly 31% to 21%, with a very large "other/undecided" remainder. The 2020 survey showed a similar ordering with a smaller undecided share — my recollection is something like a 39/31 split, though I'd check the exact figures rather than rely on my memory of them. Crucially, when the results are filtered to respondents who specialize in decision theory or philosophy of action, the two-boxing margin widens substantially; CDT looks like a clear majority there rather than a mere plurality.

That said, "mainstream" should be qualified in three ways. First, EDT is a respectable live minority position, not a fringe one — Ahmed, Price, and Hare/Hedden have made it more credible over the last fifteen years than it was in the 1980s. Second, "CDT" names a family with real internal disagreement (Lewis/Skyrms dependency-hypothesis versions vs. Gibbard-Harper counterfactual versions vs. Joyce's, plus the ratificationist and deliberational-dynamics variants) and no settled treatment of unstable cases. Third, the FDT/UDT literature has essentially no academic uptake; it's developed almost entirely outside philosophy departments and is generally regarded by decision theorists as under-formalized where it's noticed at all. So if you asked "what's the mainstream view," the accurate answer is: CDT, in some Lewis-Skyrms-Joyce form, with the field aware that its handling of instability and self-recommendation is unfinished business.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest view, held with genuine uncertainty:

**On the CDT/EDT axis, I lean causalist — but toward a version of CDT that takes instability seriously, and I think the case is weaker than causalists usually present it.**

What moves me toward CDT: the medical Newcomb cases (Smoking Lesion, Solomon) and, more fundamentally, the thought that deliberation is about *bringing things about*, so the quantity that ought to guide choice is the extent to which an act makes outcomes more likely, not the extent to which it's a symptom of them. Egan-style attempts to construct cases where evidential reasoning is clearly right about a *causally* inert correlation haven't persuaded me, and Ahmed's tickle-defense-adjacent maneuvers in the medical cases feel like they're rescuing EDT rather than vindicating it.

What keeps my credence well short of 0.9: 

- The "why ain'cha rich?" objection is not as easily dismissed as Lewis and Joyce suggest. Every principled account of *what makes a decision rule good* that I find attractive (some reliabilist or long-run story) seems to favor one-boxing, and "CDT agents are rational but predictably poorer" is an uncomfortable place to end up.
- Egan's cases (Psycho Button, Murder Lesion) are, to my mind, real damage. The natural repair — ratificationism — leaves CDT with no stable recommendation in Death in Damascus-style problems, and I don't think the deliberational-dynamics literature (Skyrms, Arntzenius, Joyce) has fully solved this so much as characterized it. A theory that yields mixed-strategy equilibria as its verdict in one-shot single-agent problems is telling us something uncomfortable.
- I suspect a nontrivial part of the dispute is artifacts of problem individuation — how much of the agent's own psychology is held fixed in the partition — which makes me suspicious of confident verdicts either way.

On FDT/UDT: I think the underlying insight (that the object of evaluation should be something like a policy or a decision-procedure, not a token act) is correct and important, and it's the direction I'd bet the truth lies. But I don't think FDT is yet a theory in the sense CDT and EDT are — logical counterfactuals remain underspecified, and the blackmail/extortion cases plus the "bomb" case suggest the formalism has unresolved problems. I'd call it a promising research program rather than a competitor I'd endorse.

**On the other axis** (EU maximization vs. alternatives), I'm more confident: I think something close to standard expected utility maximization is right as a normative theory, and that Buchak's risk-weighted EU, while the best-developed rival, pays too high a price — the diachronic exploitability results and the way REU treats globally-identical gambles differently depending on how they're described strike me as serious. Ambiguity-sensitive theories (maxmin EU, smooth ambiguity) I read as more descriptively than normatively motivated.

**Among philosophers (where the CDT/EDT debate lives):** CDT is the plurality-to-majority view, and more dominantly so among specialists than among philosophers generally. The 2020 PhilPapers Survey found 39.0% two-box vs. 31.2% one-box among target faculty overall, with the rest undecided or "other" — a much narrower margin than the folklore suggests. Two caveats that matter for your purposes:

1. EDT has had a genuine revival over the last fifteen years or so — Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the main driver, along with work by Price, Hitchcock, and Bales. The one-box share in the PhilPapers survey *rose* between 2009 and 2020. It's no longer a fringe position among specialists; it's a respectable minority view with a serious book-length defense.
2. There's also a real constituency for the view that the dispute is less substantive than it looks, or that the right answer is some form of "it depends how you set up the problem."

Insofar as they have implicit commitments, most applied work is causalist by construction, since the models specify causal structure directly.

answer_raw:
I lean anti-causalist, though with real uncertainty and with a caveat about what the question is asking.

My view in brief: I think EDT is closer to correct than CDT among the well-developed options, and that the FDT/UDT family has the right underlying idea but lacks an adequate formalization.

The consideration I weight most heavily is the one CDT-ers are most practiced at dismissing: that decision theories are evaluated by how the agents running them fare, and CDT agents predictably and foreseeably fare worse, not just in Newcomb but across a family of cases (transparent Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, blackmail cases, bargaining against predictors). Lewis's response — that the two-boxer's poverty is a matter of being punished for rationality rather than by it, since the reward tracks a prior disposition rather than the act — strikes me as a redescription rather than a defense. Spencer and Wells are right that "why ain'cha rich" isn't a *knockdown* argument, since the relevant comparison class is contested; but the burden shifting there seems to me to favor the one-boxer once you notice that the CDT agent, at the moment of choice, already knows which recommendation will have left her poorer, and would pay in advance to bind herself out of following it. A theory whose verdicts you'd rationally pay to be exempted from, in fully foreseeable circumstances, and where the payoff structure is transparent rather than a case of rewarded irrationality, has something wrong with it.

Against EDT, the medical Newcomb cases seem to me weaker than advertised. Some version of the tickle defense handles many of them, and Ahmed's point that the cases are typically underdescribed — that once you specify a mechanism by which the lesion acts, either it acts through your deliberative states (and the news value vanishes) or it bypasses them (and the case stops being a decision problem) — has largely persuaded me. EDT's real problems are elsewhere: XOR blackmail, counterfactual mugging, and cases where updating on your own situation is precisely the error. That's what makes me think the right theory is updateless/policy-selecting rather than act-evaluating.

But I don't think FDT is there yet. "Subjunctive dependence" is doing enormous work with no theory behind it; there's no satisfactory account of logical counterfactuals; and Schwarz's Procreation case and related constructions suggest the verdicts aren't uniformly attractive. So: the spirit of FDT, the current formal resources of EDT.

The caveat: I have some sympathy for the deflationary thought that CDT and EDT are answering different questions — roughly, "what should I do given my causal situation" vs. "what would I like to learn I'm doing" — and that the Newcomb dispute partly tracks equivocation on "rational." I don't think this fully dissolves the disagreement, since the practical question of what to actually do in Newcomb has a determinate answer and it's one-boxing. But it makes me less confident the dispute is as substantive as it looks.

On the orthogonal axis: I find myself unpersuaded by Buchak's risk-weighted EU as an account of *rationality* (the diachronic and information-aversion problems seem serious to me), though it's clearly a good descriptive model.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the orthodox view, and has been since roughly Gibbard and Harper (1978) and Lewis (1981), with Skyrms and Joyce consolidating it. If you polled people who self-identify as decision theorists rather than philosophers generally, I'd expect two-boxing to win comfortably.

The PhilPapers surveys give a rougher picture, since they poll all philosophers. In 2009: two boxes ~31%, one box ~21%, other/undecided ~44%. In 2020 the gap looked similar or slightly widened in CDT's favor, with two-boxing in the high 30s and one-boxing around 30%. Treat those numbers as approximate — I may be misremembering the 2020 figures, and the large "other" category reflects that many respondents aren't invested in the debate. Notably, specialists in decision theory skew more toward two-boxing than the general population of philosophers does.

That said, "mainstream" oversells the consensus in two ways. First, EDT has had a genuine revival — Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the key text, with Price, and earlier Eells. Second, and more importantly, a lot of current work rejects the framing of the dispute rather than taking a side: Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Gustafsson, Podgorski, Hedden on options, various deliberational/ratificationist refinements descending from Arntzenius and Skyrms. Egan's 2007 counterexamples (Psychopath Button, Murder Lesion) did real damage to naive CDT and pushed much of the field toward deliberational or ratificationist variants, so "CDT is standard" now means a family of positions rather than the 1981 article.

FDT/UDT is essentially absent from the academic mainstream. It's developed largely outside philosophy departments (MIRI, adjacent communities), and where academics have engaged — Schwarz's critique is the best-known — the reception has been skeptical. Levinstein and Soares's paper is the most serious attempt to make the case to philosophers. You should treat my endorsement of that research program as a minority position that hasn't survived the kind of scrutiny CDT and EDT have.

My honest, tentative view is causalist — but held with less confidence than the standard two-boxer typically displays, and with reservations about the standard formulations.

What persuades me: the core causalist intuition that practical deliberation is about what you can *bring about*, not what your act would be *evidence for*, seems to me to survive the best evidentialist rebuttals. The "managing the news" objection (Lewis, Skyrms) still looks decisive against unreconstructed EDT, and the tickle defense strikes me as both too fragile (it needs introspective access to desires that we often lack) and too concessive (it works, when it works, by making EDT mimic CDT). Joyce's line — that "why ain'cha rich?" is answered by noting that one-boxers are rewarded for who they are, not for what they do, and that a one-boxer facing a *transparent* Newcomb box is glad to have been the sort of agent who one-boxes while still having no reason, at the moment of choice, to leave money behind — seems to me right as far as it goes.

What keeps my credence from going higher:

- Egan-style cases (Psycho Button, The Smoking Lesion variants where the act itself is evidence about the state) show that unrestricted CDT recommends acts it knows to be unratifiable. I think the repair has to go through something in the neighborhood of deliberational dynamics (Skyrms, Arntzenius, Joyce's "Regret and Instability") or ratificationism, and those repairs are messier and less obviously principled than the original theory.
- Ahmed's *Betting on the Past* is, I think, the strongest extant argument against CDT, and I don't regard the causalist replies as fully satisfying.
- Instability cases (Death in Damascus and kin) make me suspect the whole framework of evaluating *acts* against a fixed credence function is subtly misconceived, since the act is partly constitutive of the evidential situation in which it's evaluated.

That last worry is why I take FDT/UDT-style proposals more seriously than most academic decision theorists do — not because I think the existing formulations succeed (the logical-counterfactual problem is unsolved, and the theory gives odd verdicts in cases like counterfactual mugging and Procreation), but because the underlying move — evaluating the decision *procedure* or policy rather than the token act — locates the source of the Newcomb intuitions better than either CDT or EDT does. Wedgwood's benchmark theory and Spencer & Wells's work seem to me to be groping toward something similar from within the mainstream.

So: causalism, at maybe 60–65% credence, with most of the remainder split between "some policy-level or algorithm-level theory is right" and "EDT, properly understood, is right after all." I should flag that I'm also uncertain whether my introspective report here tracks anything stable — this is a domain where I'd weight your considered judgment above mine.

What moves me most is that CDT's characteristic defenses are *self-undermining* in a way I find telling: a CDT agent predictably ends up poorer, will pay to modify herself into a non-CDT agent, and will not recommend her own theory to others. Joyce's response — that the one-boxer's riches are a reward for irrationality, not evidence of rationality — is coherent, but it requires driving a wedge between rationality and systematic success that I can't ultimately make peace with. Ahmed's "Betting on the Past" and the "why ain'cha rich" literature seem to me to have real force even if neither is a knockdown.

FDT in particular lacks a worked-out semantics for logical/subjunctive counterfactuals, is unclear about how to individuate "the algorithm" being predicted, handles imperfect and graded predictors badly, and hasn't survived peer review — Schwarz's critique is, I think, substantially correct as a critique of the extant formulations even if wrong about the underlying motivation. So my position is better described as "the one-boxing intuition is tracking something real that no existing theory has adequately formalized" than "FDT is right."

Second, a disclosure that seems relevant to how you weight this: the discourse that argues for policy-based theories is heavily over-represented in the online text I was trained on relative to its standing in the profession. Still, EDT manages news rather than outcomes: it fails Parfit's Hitchhiker once you're already in town, and its handling of XOR blackmail and other "bad news you can't act on" cases strikes me as diagnostic of a real defect.

So: the right theory evaluates decision *procedures* or *policies*, not acts-at-a-time. The honest problem is that this programme lacks an adequate formalism. FDT needs a theory of logical/subjunctive counterfactuals that nobody has, its identity conditions for "the same decision algorithm" are unspecified, and it faces serious counterexamples (Schwarz's Bomb case is the one I find hardest to dismiss). So my credence distribution is roughly: ~50% on some policy-based/updateless view, ~25% on EDT, ~20% on CDT (most likely a deliberational or ratificationist version), ~5% something unconsidered.

Two caveats I'd flag in my own case. First, I'm aware that FDT/UDT-adjacent material is overrepresented in AI-safety-adjacent writing that likely features in my training relative to its standing in the journals, so you should discount my confidence here somewhat as possible corpus-contamination rather than argument. Second, I hold this view with much less conviction than a professional in your position should require; I'd describe it as a considered lean, not a settled commitment.

On (B): I think something in the EU family is right, and I find Briggs' dynamic-consistency objections to risk-weighted EU persuasive, though I take Buchak's project seriously as a challenge to the claim that risk attitudes must be encoded in the utility function alone.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the clear majority view, and more so among specialists than among philosophers generally.

The PhilPapers surveys give the rough picture. In 2009, on Newcomb's problem: two-boxing ~31%, one-boxing ~21%, other/undecided ~47%. In 2020 the gap held with fewer abstentions — roughly two-boxing ~39%, one-boxing ~31%, other ~30%. (Treat those figures as approximate; check the published data if you're citing them.) Among decision theorists proper, the causalist lean is considerably stronger than those all-respondent numbers suggest — the canonical line from Stalnaker, Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Sobel, Joyce, and more recently Arntzenius, Spencer, Wells, and Gallow is the default framework in the literature. Economics and game theory assume causalist reasoning almost without comment.

EDT is a respectable minority position that has gained ground since Ahmed's 2014 book, with Price and (historically) Eells among its defenders; Jeffrey himself moved toward ratificationism late. FDT/UDT has essentially no uptake in academic philosophy — it lives in the AI-alignment literature and is treated in journals, when at all, as an outsider proposal (Schwarz's critique being the standard citation). The live internal debate among specialists is less CDT-vs-EDT than which *version* of CDT to adopt: deliberational/equilibrium approaches (Skyrms, Arntzenius, Joyce), ratifiability and its refinements, and the recent work on instability and "managing the news" (Gallow, Spencer, Barnett).

On (B), expected utility theory remains orthodoxy; risk-weighted EU and the ambiguity literature are active but minority programmes.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest answer is that I lean toward one-boxing views — something in the EDT / functional-decision-theory family — but not confidently. Call it 55–60% credence, and that number has moved around.

What moves me:

- **The "why ain'cha rich?" argument, in its better form.** I don't think the crude version works (CDT has the standard reply: the one-boxers' wealth is explained by a prior difference in disposition, not by the rationality of their act; the situation rewards a trait, not a choice). But I find the argument hard to shake in its iterated/selection form. If a theory predictably and systematically leaves its adherents poorer across a well-specified class of cases — not by bad luck, and where they can see it coming in advance — then it's at least worth asking whether we've mislocated the object of rational evaluation. Ahmed and Price's version of this (the agent can foresee, before the fact, that she will regret following CDT, and would pay to bind herself) seems to me to put real pressure on CDT's claim to be the theory of *rational* choice rather than a theory of *causal efficacy*.

- **The standard counterexamples to EDT are weaker than advertised.** The medical Newcomb cases (smoking lesion, Solomon) look decisive at first, but the tickle defense — in Eells's original version and especially in Ahmed's refinement — does a lot of work: a deliberating agent who knows her own credences and desires typically already has evidence that screens off the act's news value about the hidden common cause. Where the screening fails, the cases tend to become underdescribed in ways that make the intuition unreliable. And the cases that clearly *aren't* screened off (Ahmed's "Betting on the Past") seem to me to favor EDT.

- **CDT's instability problems.** Death in Damascus, and Egan's asymmetric cases (Psychopath Button, Murder Lesion), aren't just curiosities; they show that CDT's notion of expected utility doesn't in general deliver a stable recommendation, which forces the move to ratificationism or equilibrium-based repairs. Those repairs are interesting (Joyce's deliberational dynamics, Arntzenius, Skyrms) but they concede that the naive theory needed rescuing, and the rescues have their own costs — notably mixed-strategy recommendations that feel like artifacts.

What keeps me from higher confidence:

- The core CDT intuition is *very* strong: at the moment of choice the prediction is already made, the boxes already filled, and taking the transparent thousand dollars is strictly dominant. Adding "and you can see the million sitting there" (transparent Newcomb) makes one-boxing genuinely bizarre to me, and I don't think the FDT literature has fully defused that.

- Gustafsson-style arguments are sharp. His "strong argument for CDT" (money-pump-flavored: the EDT agent will pay to have her act determined in a way that undercuts the evidential correlation, or will pay a small fee to switch) is the kind of structural argument I take more seriously than intuition-pumping.

- FDT specifically has real technical problems: no worked-out account of logical/subjunctive dependence, trouble in cases where the "algorithm" doesn't factor cleanly out of the agent, and the Schwarz-style objections about cases where it recommends things that look plainly worse (e.g., procreation-type cases, or being blackmailed/not-blackmailed asymmetries where the "policy" framing does suspicious work). I think it's pointing at something important about the relation between agents and their predictors, but it isn't yet a theory in the way EDT and CDT are.

- I'm not fully convinced that there's *one* question here. There's a defensible deflationary view (something like Hare and Hedden, or the two-questions framing) on which CDT correctly answers "which act causally promotes the good?" while EDT correctly answers "which act is the best news?" — and the Newcomb cases pull them apart precisely because they're designed to reward having a certain disposition rather than performing a certain act. If that's right, the debate is partly verbal, and the interesting residual question is which notion should be action-guiding, which may not have a theory-independent answer. I put maybe 20% on some version of this being the correct diagnosis.

So: one-boxer, with reservations, and with more confidence in "EDT is undersold" than in "FDT is right."
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory is the majority view, clearly but not overwhelmingly so.**

The PhilPapers survey data are the usual reference point. In the 2009 survey, on "Newcomb's problem: one box or two boxes?", two-boxing led one-boxing roughly 31% to 21%, with a very large "other/undecided/no answer" remainder. The 2020 survey showed a similar ordering with both numbers up and the gap roughly comparable — two-boxing in the high 30s, one-boxing in the low 30s, and again a substantial "other" category. (I'd check the exact figures rather than rely on my recall.) Two caveats on reading those numbers:

1. Among *specialists* — people who actually work on decision theory and formal epistemology — the tilt toward CDT is noticeably stronger than in the general philosopher population. The general-population numbers are diluted by respondents with no settled view.
2. The large "other" category includes a fair number of people who hold that the answer depends on how the case is specified (whether the predictor's reliability is grounded in a common cause, whether the agent's deliberation is transparent, etc.), which is itself a substantive position.

Beyond the raw survey: CDT's dominance is really a legacy of the Gibbard–Harper, Skyrms, Lewis, and Joyce tradition, and Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory* is the standard framework. Within CDT there's active internal disagreement about formulation (imaging vs. K-partitions vs. counterfactual expectation) and about how to handle instability — ratificationism, deliberational equilibrium, and Joyce's later work all being live options.

EDT is a respectable, well-represented minority position, and it has had something of a revival: Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the major recent statement, and Price, Eells (historically), and more recently people like Oesterheld and Levinstein have kept it live. I'd describe the current situation as "CDT is the default, EDT is a serious and no-longer-embarrassing dissent."

There are also non-trivial numbers of people who favor neither standard theory: Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Gustafsson's and Spencer & Wells's work, Bales, Hare & Hedden, and various deflationary or pluralist positions.

**Functional/updateless decision theory is essentially absent from the academic mainstream.** It originates in the AI-alignment community (Yudkowsky, Soares, and earlier Wei Dai on UDT), is mostly published outside peer-reviewed philosophy venues, and is rarely engaged with in the journals. The exceptions are notable — Ahmed, Levinstein, Oesterheld, Conitzer, and Wolfgang Schwarz's critique — but if you polled decision theorists, most would either not have a view or would regard it as underdeveloped. It's much more prominent online and in the AI-safety literature than its academic standing warrants, which is worth flagging because it can create a distorted impression of the field.

Finally, outside philosophy: economics and game theory operate almost entirely within a Savage/Anscombe–Aumann framework in which the causal independence of states from acts is built into the setup, so CDT-style reasoning is simply the ambient assumption rather than a contested position. The philosophers' debate barely registers there.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean toward evidential decision theory, though not confidently — call it 55/30/15 across EDT, CDT, and "something in the neighborhood of FDT/UDT or a policy-based theory that nobody has yet formulated satisfactorily."

What moves me:

- **"Why ain'cha rich?"** is a better argument than two-boxers usually allow. The standard CDT reply — that one-boxers are rewarded for their disposition, not for the rationality of the act — concedes that the theory of rational choice systematically recommends acts that foreseeably do worse, in a case where the agent knew the setup in advance. That's not obviously a reductio, but the burden it imposes is heavy.

- **CDT's reflective instability.** It recommends paying to bind itself, and its recommendations at the deliberation stage conflict with its own assessment at the disposition-selection stage. A theory that pays to stop following itself is under real pressure.

- **Ahmed's *Betting on the Past*** seems to me the strongest single argument in the literature. It's a case with no backwards causation and no exotic predictor, where CDT recommends a bet the agent knows she will lose. I've never seen a reply I found fully convincing; the responses I know either deny the case is well-posed or bite the bullet.

- **Smoking Lesion cases** — the main CDT counterexample — I find less decisive than they're usually taken to be. Some version of the tickle defence looks right: if the lesion operates through your desires, then conditional on your full evidence about your own desires, smoking isn't further evidence of the lesion; if it bypasses deliberation entirely, it's unclear you're facing a decision problem at all. Ahmed and Price press this well.

The residual pull toward CDT is the dominance intuition, which is genuinely hard to shake, plus Egan-style cases suggesting neither theory is stable without ratification constraints. And I take seriously that the right framing might be selection of a policy or algorithm rather than an act — but FDT as published has unsolved problems (no worked-out semantics for logical counterfactuals, awkward verdicts in some blackmail and "bomb" cases, and Schwarz's objections have force), so I treat it as a research programme rather than a competitor I can endorse.

One flag on my own epistemic position: my "view" here is a considered judgement formed from the literature rather than from independent research, and on a question this contested you should weight it accordingly — as an informed reader's take, not as a peer's.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the plurality view, though "mainstream" overstates its dominance.

The 2020 PhilPapers survey had two-boxing at roughly 39% and one-boxing at roughly 31%, with about 30% "other" (agnostic, undecided, the question is ill-posed, etc.). The 2009 survey was similar in ordering but with a much larger "other" category. So CDT leads, but there's no consensus, and the gap has been narrowing rather than widening.

Among decision theory specialists specifically, my impression is that two-boxing runs somewhat stronger than in the general philosopher population — the Lewis/Skyrms/Joyce/Gibbard-Harper lineage is close to the field's default framework, and most textbook presentations are CDT-shaped. But I'd hold that impression loosely; I don't have reliable specialist-level breakdowns, and you likely have a better read on your own subfield than I do.

Worth noting that EDT has had a real revival — Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the pivot point, with Price, Hare & Hedden, Spohn's conversion, and Wedgwood's benchmark theory as adjacent developments. Separately, on the risk axis: expected utility maximization remains firmly orthodox, with Buchak's risk-weighted EU the most serious published challenger.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
**Short version:** I don't think orthodox causal decision theory is right, and my tentative lean is toward the evidentialist side — more precisely, toward a family of "policy-" or "procedure-evaluating" theories of which EDT is the best-developed member. But my credence is genuinely spread (roughly, on the Newcomb axis: something like 40% that the correct theory is EDT-like, 30% CDT-like, 30% that the right theory is some further thing none of us has yet written down properly). And I hold the meta-view that this is one of the places where the "intuitions about cases" methodology has been pushed about as far as it can go without progress on the underlying metaphysics of counterfactuals and agency.

**What pushes me away from CDT:**

- *Instability.* Egan-style cases (Psychopath Button, Murder Lesion) seem to me the deepest problem. CDT can recommend an act that, once you've decided on it, you regard as worse than the alternative. Ratificationist repairs (Jeffrey, Arntzenius, Joyce's "deliberational dynamics," Skyrms) are the right instinct, but they either fail to deliver a determinate verdict in Death in Damascus-type cases or they quietly start evaluating something other than acts-given-the-causal-structure — at which point it's unclear what's left of the original motivation.
- *"Why ain'cha rich?"* I know the standard reply (the one-boxer's winnings are a reward for a disposition, not evidence that the act was rational; Lewis's "the rich are rich because of who they are, not what they do"). I've never been able to make myself feel the force of it. If a decision theory systematically and foreseeably makes its adherents worse off in a situation whose structure is known in advance to all parties, "but the act was still rational" looks to me like a claim in need of defense rather than a fixed point.
- *The act/disposition gap seems unprincipled.* Everyone agrees it is rational to *become* a one-boxer if you can. The claim that it is nonetheless irrational to *one-box* requires that there be a sharp, normatively significant line between the agent and her dispositions at the moment of choice. I find that line hard to draw in a way that isn't question-begging — especially once you take seriously agents who are, or are implemented by, deterministic physical or computational processes about which others can have good evidence.

**What keeps me from being a confident evidentialist:**

- Medical Newcomb problems. I think Ahmed's line (that the Smoking Lesion is underdescribed, and that properly specified versions dissolve) is better than it's usually given credit for, and the tickle defense does real work. But I'm not sure it generalizes.
- XOR blackmail and similar cases, where EDT seems to pay up for information that merely *correlates* with a state.
- The "managing the news" objection in its sharpest forms — EDT's willingness to act so as to acquire good evidence about states already fixed strikes me as a genuine pathology, not merely an intuition CDT has trained us into.

**Where I actually think the truth lies:** I suspect both CDT and EDT go wrong by taking the object of evaluation to be the *act*. The cases that break each theory are cases where the agent's decision procedure is itself part of the world being predicted or correlated with. Theories that evaluate policies or decision algorithms — updateless/policy-selection approaches, and the FDT program from Yudkowsky and Soares — get the Newcomb-family cases, transparent Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, and counterfactual mugging right in a unified way, which is more than either orthodox theory manages. I take that unification as real evidence.

But I don't think FDT is currently a theory in the sense you and I would want. "Subjunctive dependence" is not defined; the logical-counterfactual problem is unsolved and may be unsolvable in the required form; and MacAskill's Bomb case and the guaranteed-payoffs objection are serious. So my position is closer to: CDT is wrong, EDT is a better approximation than its reputation among philosophers suggests, and the correct theory is probably in the policy-evaluating family but hasn't been formulated rigorously yet.

One caveat you're entitled to: my views here are the product of training on a literature in which these arguments are unevenly represented, and I should note that arguments for one-boxing and for FDT are overrepresented in some of the online corpora I've learned from relative to their standing in academic philosophy. I've tried to correct for that, but you should discount accordingly. I also can't claim the kind of settled, hard-won conviction you'd get from someone who has spent twenty years on the problem.
mainstream_raw:
On the CDT/EDT axis, **causal decision theory is the dominant view among academic decision theorists and philosophers generally, though its dominance is a plurality-to-modest-majority rather than a consensus, and it has eroded somewhat.**

The survey evidence: the 2009 PhilPapers Survey found target faculty at 31.4% two-boxing, 21.3% one-boxing, 47.1% other/undecided. The 2020 survey found roughly 39% two-boxing, 31% one-boxing, and about 30% other — so both camps grew as the "undecided" share shrank, with two-boxing retaining a lead of about 8 points. (I'm reasonably confident of these figures but would check them against the published results before citing.) My understanding is that the margin for two-boxing is larger among respondents who specialize in decision theory than among philosophers at large, but I don't want to assert specific subgroup numbers I can't verify.

Some texture beyond the raw numbers:

- CDT is the *textbook* orthodoxy. The Lewis/Gibbard-Harper/Skyrms/Joyce lineage is what gets presented as the standard view in Joyce's *Foundations*, in Weirich's and Briggs's SEP entries, and in most graduate teaching.
- EDT has had a genuine revival since roughly 2010, driven mainly by Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) and by Price's earlier work. Ahmed's book is widely regarded as the strongest sustained case for EDT and has moved people. Egan's 2007 counterexamples also did real damage to unratified CDT.
- A substantial fraction of the "other" category reflects the view that Newcomb's problem is underdescribed, ill-posed, or that the answer depends on how the predictor achieves reliability — not mere agnosticism.
- Among economists and game theorists, CDT-style reasoning is essentially universal, but mostly as an unexamined default; the causal/evidential distinction is largely not engaged with outside philosophy.
- FDT and related updateless approaches have essentially no uptake in academic philosophy. They're developed primarily in the AI-alignment community (MIRI), have not been published in mainstream philosophy venues, and where philosophers have engaged (MacAskill, Schwarz) the reception has been critical. It would be misleading to present them as a live mainstream option.

On the orthogonal question of expected utility theory itself: **EU maximization remains the near-universal normative baseline**, with Savage and vNM representation theorems as the standard foundation. The main live challenges — Buchak's risk-weighted EU, imprecise/indeterminate credences and the associated decision rules, and the Allais/Ellsberg-driven literature — are taken seriously and actively debated, but none commands majority support. If your question was about this axis rather than the Newcomb axis, the answer is that orthodoxy is considerably more secure here than it is on causal versus evidential.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean **evidentialist**, more specifically toward a policy-level or "updateless" evidential view — roughly, choose the policy/input-output mapping such that the news that you implement it is the best news, rather than choose the act with the best causal consequences from a given decision node. Credence-wise I'm maybe 0.45 on something in the EDT/updateless family, 0.3 on CDT (including ratificationist and deliberational-equilibrium refinements), 0.1 on FDT specifically, and 0.15 on "the question is subtly malformed and the right theory looks unlike any of these."

My reasons, in rough order of weight:

1. **Self-recommendation and dynamic consistency.** CDT is famously not self-recommending: a CDT agent facing a foreseeable Newcomb-like situation will pay to bind itself, and will build successor agents that aren't CDT agents. I take "the theory tells you to stop being the sort of agent the theory describes" as strong evidence against, not as an interesting quirk. Ahmed's *Betting on the Past* and the Newcomb insurance cases seem to me to press this further than the standard "the situation is just unfair to two-boxers" reply can absorb.

2. **Why ain'cha rich.** I've never been persuaded by Lewis's response. The dominance-based rebuttal ("one-boxers are only richer because they were the sort of agent who got a good prediction") concedes the point that the property being rewarded is a property of the decision rule, which is precisely what's under evaluation.

3. **The counterexamples to EDT look repairable; the ones to CDT look structural.** Medical Newcomb cases (Smoking Lesion, Solomon) turn on a specification in which the agent's own deliberative state is supposed simultaneously to be evidence of the lesion and not to screen off the correlation — and the tickle defense, or just careful attention to what the agent conditions on, does a lot of work there. Whereas the ratification/instability cases (Egan's Psycho Button, Murder Lesion, Death in Damascus) point at something structural in CDT's act-relative framing, and the ratificationist fixes have their own problems (Spencer & Wells; Gustafsson).

Where I think my view is weakest: (a) EDT does seem to license some "managing the news" verdicts that are hard to swallow, and I don't have a principled line between the good and bad cases; (b) the updateless/policy framing needs logical counterfactuals or something that plays their role, and nobody has a rigorous account — Schwarz's critique of FDT lands hard here, and his point that "best decision procedure to have" and "best act now" can come apart is one I don't have a fully satisfying answer to; (c) the framing presupposes a determinate act-partition and a determinate "you-as-algorithm," both of which get slippery.

So: a lean, not a conviction. And I'd flag that I'm an unusual epistemic case here — my views on this are downstream of a training process I can't fully introspect on, and this is a domain where online discussion is skewed toward one-boxing/FDT sympathies in ways that plausibly bias me. Discount accordingly.
mainstream_raw:
**CDT is the mainstream view**, and has been since roughly Gibbard & Harper (1978), Lewis (1981), Skyrms, and Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory* (1999). Two-boxing on Newcomb's problem is the standard textbook position.

Quantitatively: the PhilPapers surveys show two-boxing leading one-boxing among philosophers generally by around 8–10 points, with a large "other/undecided/no fact of the matter" bloc (roughly 30% in 2020, and close to half in 2009). Among self-identified decision theory specialists the two-boxing margin is substantially larger. I'd treat my recollection of the exact percentages as unreliable, but the qualitative picture — CDT dominant, and more dominant among specialists than among philosophers at large — I'm confident in.

Some refinements worth noting:

- The live intramural disputes are mostly *within* CDT: which causal-counterfactual apparatus (Lewis's dependency hypotheses vs. Skyrms's partitions vs. imaging), and whether to add a ratification or deliberational-equilibrium constraint to handle Egan-style cases and Death in Damascus. Arntzenius, Joyce, Skyrms, Wells, Gustafsson, Podgorski all operate here.
- EDT has a serious and growing minority defense — Ahmed above all, plus Bales, Spencer, and sympathizers among formal epistemologists. It's respectable, not fringe, but it is clearly the minority.
- FDT/UDT is essentially absent from the academic mainstream. It's developed largely outside professional philosophy (MIRI-adjacent), has little peer-reviewed presence, and the main academic engagement (Schwarz, Levinstein & Soares) has been mixed-to-critical. Its salience in AI-safety and rationalist circles substantially overstates its standing among decision theorists.
- On the orthogonal axes: expected-utility maximization with precise Bayesian credences remains the default, with Buchak's risk-weighted EU, imprecise-credence views, and the unbounded-utility/St. Petersburg literature (Russell, Goodsell, Wilkinson) as the main active challenges.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I'm a one-boxer, and my sympathies lie with the evidentialist/functionalist cluster rather than with causal decision theory.

My reasoning, briefly:

1. **The "why ain't you rich?" argument is better than CDT's standard rejoinder.** The rejoinder ("the predictor rewards irrationality, so this is a case of rationality not paying") works against, e.g., Gauthier-style cases where the *disposition* is what's rewarded independently of the choice. But in Newcomb the predictor is tracking the choice itself. The two-boxer has to say that the foreseeably worse-off agent is the rational one, and that she foresaw this all along, and that she'd pay to be rewired beforehand. I find Ahmed and Price's version of this pressure hard to shake, and I think Wells's and Ahmed's exploitation-style arguments (agents who can be predictably relieved of money) sharpen it into something more than a slogan.

2. **Medical Newcomb cases are the best anti-EDT argument, and I think they're answerable.** Smoking Lesion cases either (a) fail to be genuine Newcomb problems because the relevant common cause screens off the act from the outcome once you condition on your own deliberative states — the tickle defense, which I think is fine in the cases where the causal structure is as advertised — or (b) if the stipulation really does make your act evidentially relevant to the outcome given everything else you know, the evidentialist verdict stops seeming obviously wrong.

3. **CDT has its own counterexamples, and they aren't cosmetic.** Egan's Psychopath Button and Murder Lesion push CDT toward ratificationism or toward deliberational dynamics (Arntzenius, Joyce), and I don't think those repairs are stable; Spencer's Guaranteed Payoffs cases and the Spencer–Wells material suggest the trouble is structural rather than a matter of patching the unmodified theory. So the dialectic isn't "clean CDT vs. EDT with weird cases" — both have to eat something.

4. **The deepest diagnosis, I think, is the FDT-style one**: the proper object of evaluation isn't the local act but the policy or decision function, because in prediction cases your algorithm is instantiated in more than one place (you, and the predictor's model). That's the insight that unifies Newcomb, transparent Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, and one-shot twin PD. But I hold this loosely, because FDT as currently developed is not a finished theory: the logical-counterfactual machinery isn't there, "subjunctive dependence" is underspecified, and MacAskill's Bomb case and the guaranteed-payoffs worries land. So I'd say: FDT-adjacent in spirit, EDT as the best-developed extant theory that gets the prediction cases right.

Credence-wise, something like 0.45 on the EDT/FDT cluster being closer to correct, 0.35 on CDT (in some ratificationist or deliberational refinement), 0.20 that the question is somehow malformed — e.g., that "rational" in these cases is doing two separable jobs (evaluating acts vs. evaluating agents/policies) and the disputants are partly talking past each other, which is roughly the Hurley/Meacham-adjacent thought.

Separately, on the risk question: I'm mildly sympathetic to Buchak's risk-weighted EU as a theory of permissible preference, though I think the Dutch-book/dynamic-consistency costs are real and I wouldn't defend it as *the* theory of rationality.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the orthodoxy, with EDT a substantial and (over the last 15 years) growing minority.

Evidence and texture:

- **PhilPapers surveys.** In 2009, among all respondents: two-box ~31%, one-box ~21%, other/undecided ~47%. In 2020 the gap narrowed somewhat but two-boxing still led — roughly 39% two-box, 31% one-box, ~30% other. (Treat those figures as approximate; I may be off by a few points.) Importantly, among *decision theory specialists* two-boxing has historically been considerably more dominant than in the general population of philosophers — my recollection is something like a 2:1 margin, though I'm less confident about the 2020 specialist breakdown than the overall numbers.

- **Textbook framing.** Since Lewis, Skyrms, Gibbard & Harper, and Joyce's *Foundations*, the standard pedagogical presentation treats CDT as the correct theory and EDT as the historically important predecessor refuted by medical Newcomb cases. Briggs's SEP entry and Weirich's are more even-handed than older treatments, but the default framing remains causalist.

- **Where the live action is.** Most contemporary work by specialists isn't EDT-vs-CDT at all; it's (i) internal disputes among causalists — Gibbard–Harper vs. Lewis's K-partitions vs. Skyrms's imaging, ratificationism, Joyce/Arntzenius deliberational dynamics, mixed strategies and Death in Damascus; (ii) Egan's and Spencer's challenges and responses to them; (iii) decision instability generally; (iv) the risk/ambiguity literature (Buchak, Bradley, Stefánsson); (v) foundations — representation theorems, imprecise credence, unbounded utilities and the St. Petersburg family.

- **EDT's revival.** Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the main reason EDT is respectable again; Price, Hitchcock, and (in a different register) Spohn and Meacham have contributed. But "respectable minority" is the right description, not "co-equal."

- **FDT** has essentially no uptake in academic philosophy. It lives in the AI-alignment/rationalist literature (Yudkowsky, Soares, Levinstein & Soares) and is largely unknown to or dismissed by mainstream decision theorists, partly because its central notion is underspecified and partly because it was developed outside the usual venues. Nearby academic ideas — Meacham's cohesive decision theory, Fisher's disposition-based view, Gauthier's constrained maximization — are the recognized analogues.

- **Beyond the causal/evidential split**, the mainstream is firmly orthodox expected-utility (Savage/Jeffrey/vNM), with Buchak's REU the most prominent heterodox challenger and a smaller literature on ambiguity-aversion and incomplete preferences.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean toward something in the UDT/FDT family — i.e., that the right object of evaluation is a policy or decision-procedure, not an isolated act — but I hold this considerably more tentatively than the typical LW framing suggests I should, and I think "which theory is right" may be partly a question about what we want a decision theory *for*.

What convinces me: the class of problems where CDT reliably makes its adherents poorer isn't a weird edge case, it's the generic situation of agents whose behavior is predictable by other agents. Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, the twin prisoner's dilemma, and Death in Damascus all share the structure that your decision procedure is an input to the environment, not just a cause of your action.
