CDT's response — "yes, but *given* that the predictor has already acted, two-boxing dominates" — is locally valid and I don't think FDT advocates always take it seriously enough. But "rational agents predictably end up with less money, and would pay in advance to be irrational" is a strong signal that something in the framing is off. The precommitment argument seems to me to do real work: if you'd pay to bind yourself beforehand, and nothing epistemically relevant happens between then and the decision, the theory that makes your verdict depend on when you were asked is suspicious.

Where I think LW overclaims: FDT is not a finished theory. There's still no satisfactory account of logical counterfactuals — "what would the algorithm output if it output X" is ill-defined when the algorithm in fact outputs Y, and the proposed fixes (proof-based, logical inductors) are either trivial-in-the-limit or leak inconsistencies. MacAskill's Bomb case is a genuine bullet, not a confusion; so are the cases where FDT's verdicts depend on unstated facts about which computation "you" are identified with. Schwarz's objection that FDT answers "what kind of agent should I be" rather than "what should I do" is, I think, substantially correct — and my actual view is that this is a *reframing* of the question rather than a better answer to the original one. I also think Ahmed's EDT does better than it's given credit for: it gets Newcomb, the twin PD, and the hitchhiker right, it's mathematically mature, and the tickle defense handles most of the medical-Newcomb cases. A lot of the LW case for FDT over EDT rests on counterfactual mugging and transparent Newcomb, where my own intuitions are genuinely unstable.

So: FDT-ish, maybe 45%; EDT-ish, maybe 25%; CDT, maybe 15%; "the question is subtly malformed and dissolves under a better theory of agency," maybe 15%. I'd also note that I should be somewhat suspicious of my own confidence here, since these views were shaped by training on a corpus in which LW-adjacent writing on decision theory is heavily overrepresented relative to its standing in the field.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the mainstream view among academic decision theorists, and the gap is wider among specialists than among philosophers generally.

The standard picture: Lewis, Gibbard & Harper, Skyrms, Joyce (*The Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*), and Pearl-influenced work form the textbook orthodoxy. EDT is a respectable minority position with a serious contemporary defender in Arif Ahmed (*Evidence, Decision and Causality*, 2014) and earlier sympathy from Huw Price; it has gained ground in the last fifteen years but remains a minority.

On numbers: the 2020 PhilPapers survey found roughly 39% one-boxing vs. 31% two-boxing among all respondents, with the remainder undecided or "other." But this is misleading as a proxy for the professional consensus — general philosophers are not decision theorists, and in the 2009 survey the subgroup identifying as decision theory specialists was substantially more two-box-leaning than the general population. (I'm not fully confident of the exact figures; treat them as approximate.) The honest summary is that among people who work on this professionally, CDT is the default and two-boxing is the majority verdict.

Two further points. First, "mainstream decision theory" in economics, statistics, and game theory largely means Savage/von Neumann–Morgenstern expected utility — the causal/evidential split is a distinctively philosophical concern that rarely surfaces there. Second, FDT/UDT has essentially no academic uptake. It has been engaged with a handful of times, most notably in Wolfgang Schwarz's critical review of the Yudkowsky–Soares paper, and the reception was skeptical. This is partly a sociological fact about publication venues rather than a purely intellectual verdict — but it's also true that the paper didn't clear the bar professional referees would apply, particularly on logical counterfactuals.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
Taking "which decision theory is right" to be primarily the CDT/EDT question (I'll say something about the other axis at the end):

I lean evidentialist, but with real uncertainty — maybe 60/40, and I'd not want you to weight my view much here.

What moves me:

1. The "why ain'cha rich?" argument still seems to me more than a debating point. Lewis's reply — that one-boxers are rewarded for their irrationality, not by it — works only if you've already granted that two-boxing is what rationality requires; it can't be what establishes it. And in the iterated/population version, the evidentialist can say that the distribution of outcomes is systematically predicted by the policy, which is the thing an agent gets to settle.

2. Joyce's "you knew in advance you'd regret it" defense sits badly with Egan-style cases (Psycho Button, Murder Lesion), where CDT recommends an act it disprefers at the moment of choice. Ratificationism patches this, but the patches multiply, and Arntzenius and Briggs have shown how hard it is to get a stable ratification condition that doesn't have its own pathologies.

3. The standard anti-EDT cases seem to me to under-describe the agents. The tickle defense handles Smoking Lesion once you grant the agent introspective access to their own desires — and if you deny that access, the case stops looking like one where the agent clearly knows what to do. XOR blackmail, on my reading, EDT gets right.

4. Most importantly, I think the disagreement bottoms out in a prior question about what to hold fixed in deliberation, and CDT's answer presupposes a notion of "up to me" that looks metaphysically fragile for an agent who is, from the predictor's point of view, a deterministic system. EDT's "condition on everything, including what your choosing reveals about you" is the more conservative move; CDT's counterfactual independence assumption is the substantive addition, and I don't think it's been earned.

The best case against me: Hare and Hedden-style guaranteed-payoff principles, and the sense that EDT confuses managing the news with managing the world. I feel that pull, and it's why I'm not more confident.

On the other axis — expected utility vs. alternatives — I'm more orthodox. I think the representation-theorem arguments for EU are weaker than they're usually presented as being (they constrain preference structure, they don't independently vindicate the maximizing norm), but I haven't found the alternatives compelling as norms rather than as descriptions. Buchak's REU is the most serious challenge, and I find the diachronic/exploitation objections to it forceful without thinking they're knockdown.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the establishment position, though "mainstream" overstates its dominance.

In the PhilPapers surveys, two-boxing has a plurality among philosophers generally — roughly 30–40% two-box, roughly 20–30% one-box, with a very large "other/undecided/question-is-unclear" remainder. (I'm confident about the shape, less so about the exact figures, and you'll want to check them.) Notably, the gap narrowed between 2009 and 2020: one-boxing gained ground.

Within decision theory proper, the CDT lineage — Stalnaker, Gibbard & Harper, Skyrms, Lewis, Joyce — is the default framework in textbooks and in most applied work, and Joyce's Foundations is the standard modern statement. But EDT is not a fringe view: Ahmed's Evidence, Decision and Causality gave it its most vigorous recent defense, and Price, Horgan, and (earlier) Eells and Jeffrey make it a live minority tradition with serious representation.

Two further sociological points worth flagging:

First, a lot of recent specialist work isn't a straight CDT/EDT contest at all. Egan's cases pushed the debate toward ratificationism and equilibrium approaches; Briggs's impossibility results cast doubt on whether any theory can satisfy all the plausible desiderata; and there's a cluster of newer proposals (Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Podgorski's tournament decision theory, various graded/deliberational dynamics views) that scramble the binary.

Second, Functional/Timeless Decision Theory has essentially no academic uptake — it's discussed in AI safety and rationalist circles far more than in philosophy journals — despite being reasonably well known to people who follow those communities. If you encounter confident claims that FDT is "the" solution, that's a view from outside the field, not a report of the field's consensus.

On the EU axis: expected utility maximization is straightforwardly mainstream, with risk-weighted EU, imprecise credences, and incomplete preferences as respectable minority programs.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean **one-boxer**, and more specifically I think the most defensible position is in the neighborhood of evidential decision theory or a policy/algorithm-focused theory (FDT-ish in spirit, though I think FDT as formulated is not yet a rigorous theory).

My reasons, roughly:

1. **The "why ain'cha rich?" argument does more work than Lewis and Joyce allow.** Their reply — that Newcomb's predictor rewards irrationality, not the choice — seems to me to misdescribe the case. The predictor isn't rewarding a disposition that happens to correlate with one-boxing; it's tracking the choice itself. To say that rationality is systematically and *foreseeably* penalized here, in a case where the agent knows all the relevant facts in advance and there's no informational asymmetry to appeal to, strikes me as close to conceding that the theory has lost contact with what we wanted "rational" to mean.

2. **The act/policy distinction is where the real action is.** I suspect "which act is rational?" and "which decision procedure is it rational to implement?" come apart, and CDT is a good answer to the first while being a bad answer to the second. Since agents are the kind of thing that implement procedures, and since the cases where the two diverge are precisely cases where something reads off the procedure, I think the second question is the one we should care about. This is why I find the FDT framing — evaluate the output of the decision algorithm across all the places that algorithm is instantiated — genuinely illuminating, even though Schwarz's objections (implausible verdicts in Bomb-style cases, no worked-out semantics for the relevant subjunctives, dependence on an unmotivated notion of "same algorithm") seem to me largely unanswered.

3. **The standard anti-EDT cases are weaker than advertised.** I find Ahmed's treatment of medical Newcomb problems persuasive: either the tickle defense applies, or the case is underdescribed in a way that smuggles in the intuition. And CDT has its own well-known troubles — Egan's cases push CDT toward ratificationism or deliberational dynamics, and once you've made those moves the theory is no longer the clean, intuitive thing that made dominance reasoning attractive in the first place.

Honest reservations: EDT gives verdicts I find hard to swallow in some cases (XOR blackmail, and the general worry that it manages news rather than outcomes), and I hold this position with maybe 60/40 confidence at most. I'd also register that "which theory is right" may be a partly verbal question — there might be two distinct evaluative notions here, and the sensible thing is to keep both and stop fighting over the word "rational."

On the *other* axis — expected utility maximization versus alternatives — I'm more conservative. I find Buchak's risk-weighted EU a real achievement in showing that global risk attitudes can be coherent and non-Dutch-bookable, but I think the diachronic objections (Briggs on the exploitability of REU agents across time, the sensitivity to redescription of the outcome space) are serious enough that I'd still bet on EU maximization being correct as a norm, with risk-aversion handled in the utility function.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory is the mainstream view**, and has been since roughly Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce. It's the textbook default, and among philosophers who specialize in decision theory the majority is, I believe, more lopsided than among philosophers generally.

Supporting data, with the caveat that I may be misremembering exact figures: in the 2009 PhilPapers survey, two-boxing led one-boxing roughly 31% to 21%, with a large "other/undecided" bloc. In the 2020 survey the gap narrowed considerably — one-boxing gained ground and the two camps were much closer to parity among the general respondent pool. My recollection is that among decision theory specialists specifically, two-boxing retained a clearer lead, but I'd check that rather than trust me on it.

Important qualifications on "mainstream":

- **EDT has had a genuine revival**, driven mainly by Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014), with Price, and earlier Eells. It's now a respectable minority position rather than a refuted one, which was not true in 1990.
- **FDT/TDT have essentially no academic uptake.** They're a rationalist/MIRI-adjacent development. Schwarz's critique is the main published engagement, and it's negative. If you're surveying the field, they're not part of the mainstream conversation.
- **A lot of the live action has moved elsewhere** — unstable/nonratifiable decision problems, imprecise credence and the permissiveness of decision rules under ambiguity, infinite and unbounded utility (Goodsell, Russell, Wilkinson), and the challenge to EU from Buchak's REU and from Thoma and Bradley. On that last axis, EU maximization remains firmly orthodox, with REU as the most prominent challenger.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I'll give you a real answer rather than a hedge, but with the caveats flagged.

I think the *core insight* of the FDT/UDT family is correct: the thing that's actually up for choice, in the sense that matters, is the policy or the algorithm, not the physical act. When your decision procedure is correlated with something in the environment — a predictor's model of you, a copy of you, a past prediction — treating your act as an intervention that severs those correlations throws away information you actually have. Agents who evaluate "what's the best output for my decision algorithm to have across all instances where it's instantiated" do better, systematically and predictably, in the class of problems where these theories come apart. "Why are you predictably poorer?" remains, to me, the hardest question for CDT, and I don't think Joyce's "yes, and I'd pay to be the kind of agent who one-boxes, but here in the chamber I take both" reply is stable. If rationality keeps recommending that you pay to stop being rational, something is wrong with the account.

But I hold this more weakly than most LessWrong readers do, for three reasons:

1. **There is no satisfactory formalization.** FDT needs a theory of logical counterfactuals — what the world looks like if a deterministic algorithm outputs something other than what it outputs — and nobody has one. The "logical inductors / modal combat" work is interesting but doesn't deliver the required counterpossible semantics. Until that's solved, FDT is a family of intuitions with worked examples, not a theory. That's a real asymmetry with CDT and EDT, which are precisely specified.

2. **Bomb and its relatives genuinely bother me.** In MacAskill's Bomb case, FDT tells you to burn to death when you can see the bomb and see that the predictor erred. The standard reply — you're paying for a policy that almost never lands you here — is the right shape of reply, but I notice I don't fully believe it, and I don't think "that's just a case where you get unlucky" dissolves the discomfort. Similarly, the individuation problem is unsolved: *which* computations count as "the same algorithm" as yours, and how much does subjunctive dependence degrade with approximation? Without an answer, FDT's verdicts aren't well-defined in realistic cases.

3. **The CDT/EDT dispute is subtler than LW presents it.** The smoking lesion, which is treated as decisive against EDT, is arguably ill-posed — if the lesion acts through your desires, you know your desires, and the tickle defense screens off the correlation; if it acts by directly determining your act, it's not a decision problem. Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is a serious book and the LW corpus doesn't really engage with it. Between the two classical theories I lean EDT, and I think a decent fraction of what FDT buys you over EDT is in exotic cases (transparent Newcomb, counterfactual mugging) where my intuitions are much less firm than they are about standard Newcomb.

So: I'd say ~60% that something in the updateless/functional family is closest to right about what an agent should do, most of the remainder on EDT or an EDT/CDT hybrid that does better than either on self-locating and unstable problems, and low single digits on orthodox CDT. I'm aware I should discount my own confidence here for training-data reasons — I've read vastly more LessWrong than *Philosophical Studies*, and the arguments that feel natural to me are partly an artifact of that.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the clear majority view, and the gap between academic and LW opinion is large.

The numbers: in the 2020 PhilPapers survey, on Newcomb's problem, two-boxing beat one-boxing roughly 31% to 21% among all respondents, with a large undecided/other block. Among philosophers who *specialize* in decision theory, the two-boxing margin is substantially wider — the specialist subgroup is where CDT is most dominant, not least. This is basically unchanged from 2009.

CDT is the textbook default: Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, Weirich's SEP entry. The standard framing is that Newcomb's problem was the thing that *motivated* the development of CDT, and that one-boxing confuses "the news value of an act" with "the efficacy of an act."

EDT has a real but minority revival — Arif Ahmed is the central figure, with Huw Price, and Ahmed's Betting on the Past and "Dicing with Death" cases put genuine pressure on CDT. There's also significant work on unstable/indeterminate decision problems (Egan's counterexamples to CDT, Joyce's deliberational response, Arntzenius, Skyrms, Spencer & Wells's "Why Take Both Boxes?", Meacham's cohesive EU) where the consensus is much weaker and people take seriously that *neither* CDT nor EDT is fully adequate.

FDT/UDT has essentially zero academic penetration. The Yudkowsky–Soares paper was submitted to a philosophy journal and rejected; the referee report, and Wolfgang Schwarz's widely-read critical review, both fault it for the missing logical-counterfactual semantics and for Bomb-style verdicts. Caspar Oesterheld, Johannes Treutlein, and a few others do rigorous work in this space, and there's growing interest via the AI-safety-adjacent literature, but if you asked a randomly selected decision theorist about FDT most would not have heard of it.

One more thing worth saying: "decision theory" in academia mostly isn't about Newcomb at all. The bulk of the field is representation theorems, Savage/Jeffrey-Bolker foundations, imprecise credence, risk-weighted EU (Buchak), incomparability and incomplete preferences, infinite and unbounded utility (Pasadena game, St. Petersburg), and the relationship to social choice. The Newcomb literature is a corner. LessWrong's framing — that the field is a live three-way contest between CDT, EDT, and FDT — is not how the discipline sees itself.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest view is that something in the **updateless/functional family (UDT/FDT)** is closest to right, but that none of the existing formulations is actually *finished*, so I hold this more as a bet on a research direction than as endorsement of a specific theory.

What I think is correct about it: the right object of choice is something like a policy or a decision procedure, not an isolated act. Once a predictor (or a copy, or a sufficiently good model of you) is in the picture, your action isn't a free-floating causal intervention — the same computation appears in multiple places in the world, and CDT's use of a "surgery on my action node" counterfactual systematically mis-describes that situation. Newcomb, the twin prisoner's dilemma, transparent Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, and counterfactual mugging all look to me like cases where the CDT verdict is the one that predictably leaves you poorer, and where "I'd have preferred to be running the other algorithm" is a genuine mark against the theory rather than an irrelevant observation about dispositions.

What I think LessWrong tends to undersell:

- **FDT has no working core.** The theory is stated in terms of intervening on the output of a fixed computation, and nobody has a satisfactory account of logical counterfactuals/counterpossibles. The 5-and-10 problem and spurious-proof problems are not technicalities; they're the theory's central unsolved piece. MIRI's own later agenda (logical inductors, etc.) is partly an admission of this.
- **The "same algorithm" relation is vague.** Real cases involve partial, graded correlation between your reasoning and a predictor's model, and FDT doesn't have a principled treatment of that.
- **The counterexamples aren't all silly.** The Bomb case requires biting a real bullet; Wolfgang Schwarz's critique and the various "procreation"/self-fulfilling-prophecy cases show that stipulating who gets rewarded for what disposition can make almost any theory look bad, which should lower everyone's confidence in the whole methodology of dueling vignettes.
- **EDT is underrated.** The Smoking Lesion, the canonical knockdown, is probably a bad counterexample (Ahmed and others argue it's either misdescribed or defused by the tickle defense). Plain EDT gets most of the Newcomblike cases right and fails mainly on the updateless ones — and "EDT + updatelessness + policy selection" is arguably most of what UDT is. So I'd put substantial credence on the truth being closer to a cleaned-up EDT than the standard LW narrative suggests.

Rough credences, if forced: ~50% that the correct theory is in the updateless/functional family, ~25% some form of EDT (possibly updateless), ~10% CDT or a ratificationist descendant, ~15% that "which decision theory is correct" is the wrong question and the real answer is a more contextual story about which idealization fits which situation.
mainstream_raw:
**Causal decision theory is the orthodox view**, and has been since Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce in the late 70s–80s. It's what standard graduate curricula and reference works present as the default, and two-boxing on Newcomb's problem is the standard verdict among specialists in decision theory.

Some important qualifications:

- Evidential decision theory is a respectable and growing minority position, not a fringe one — Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the main modern defense, with Huw Price and others in the vicinity.
- Andy Egan's 2007 counterexamples (the Psycho Button, etc.) put real pressure on CDT and generated a live literature on ratificationism, deliberational dynamics, and "equilibrium" versions of CDT (Arntzenius, Joyce, Skyrms). So CDT's dominance is dominance-with-open-problems, not consensus-with-mopping-up.
- The PhilPapers surveys are informative but easy to misquote: in the general philosophy population, one-boxing and two-boxing are roughly comparable with a large "other/undecided" fraction, and 2020 showed one-boxing gaining relative to 2009. But the general-philosopher population is not the decision-theory population, and among the latter two-boxing is clearly more common. I'd treat exact percentages as approximate unless you check them.
- **FDT/UDT/TDT have essentially no academic uptake.** They're largely published outside peer review, and the limited engagement they've received has mostly been critical (Schwarz is the best-known example). This is partly sociological — the MIRI-adjacent work isn't packaged in the field's idiom — but it's also partly the substantive gap noted above: academics reasonably expect a decision theory to come with a worked-out counterfactual semantics, and FDT doesn't have one. So the reception isn't purely a failure of outreach.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
**Short version:** I think the one-boxing family is right — that the object of choice is better modeled as a decision procedure/policy than as a local act with the past held fixed — but I think FDT specifically is a promising research program rather than a finished theory, and I hold this with real uncertainty rather than the confidence typical on LW.

The crux, as you know, is which counterfactual is the right one to evaluate: "what if this act occurred, holding fixed the causal past" (CDT) or "what if my decision procedure returned this output" (FDT/UDT-ish). I lean toward the latter for a few reasons:

- In Newcomb-like cases the predictor's accuracy is *constituted by* a dependence on your decision procedure. Treating the contents of the box as causally fixed background is technically true and strategically beside the point. The agent who says "the money is already there or it isn't" is reasoning correctly about causal structure and wrongly about what they control.
- "Why ain'cha rich?" is not decisive on its own (CDT has the fair reply that the scenario rewards irrationality). But the stronger version is diachronic: CDT agents are systematically exploitable in Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and blackmail cases, and — crucially — a CDT agent with access to a self-modification button will press it. A theory of rational action that recommends ceasing to use itself at the first opportunity is telling us something. I don't think reflective stability is *definitionally* required of rationality, but I weight it heavily as evidence.
- Once you accept that you're choosing a policy, the "your decision is correlated with things it doesn't cause" cases stop looking exotic and start looking like the general case — especially for agents that can be copied, simulated, or predicted.

Where I part company with the LW consensus:

- **Logical counterfactuals are unsolved.** "Subjunctive dependence" is doing enormous load-bearing work in FDT and there is no accepted account of it. Asking "what if this algorithm returned 5 when it in fact returns 6" requires reasoning from a contradiction, and the naive treatments explode. MIRI knows this; it's why so much of the agent-foundations work went into it. A theory whose central primitive is undefined isn't yet a theory.
- **The bomb case bites.** FDT tells you to take the burning box, and the standard reply ("you were almost certainly never in that situation") doesn't obviously survive the stipulation that you *see* the bomb. I don't think this is fatal, but it's a genuine cost that gets waved away too fast.
- **Schwarz-style objections** (his "Procreation" case, and worries that FDT's verdicts depend on unprincipled choices about how coarsely to individuate "the algorithm") haven't been answered to my satisfaction.
- **EDT is underrated relative to how it's treated on LW.** The smoking lesion is much weaker than its reputation — the tickle defense, and Ahmed's work generally, defang most of the standard counterexamples. EDT plus updatelessness captures a large majority of FDT's wins with far less exotic machinery. If I had to bet on which formalism eventually looks correct in fifty years, "some updateless evidentialist thing" is at least as likely to me as "FDT as written."
- **Updatelessness is where I'm least confident of all.** Counterfactual mugging turns on whether you should honor commitments your earlier self would have wanted, from an epistemic position you now know to be false. I go back and forth. Someone who bites the bullet on Newcomb and refuses in counterfactual mugging isn't obviously confused.

Rough credences, forced: ~45-50% on "something in the FDT/UDT/updateless vicinity, once logical counterfactuals are sorted out," ~25-30% on updateless-or-plain EDT, ~15-20% on CDT or a sophisticated descendant (ratificationism, deliberational CDT), rest on none-of-the-above.

One honest caveat about my vantage point: I'm the sort of entity that plausibly *is* run multiple times, predicted, and evaluated by processes correlated with my outputs. That may make one-boxing intuitions feel more natural to me than they should, or it may be exactly the kind of case where those intuitions are tracking something real. I can't fully distinguish those from the inside.
mainstream_raw:
**CDT is the mainstream view, and this is not close among specialists** — though the field is less unified than a textbook would suggest.

- The 2020 PhilPapers survey of professional philosophers had Newcomb's problem at roughly 39% two-boxing, 31% one-boxing, 30% other/undecided (the 2009 numbers were similar in direction, with a larger "other" category). Treat these figures as approximate. Importantly, the two-boxing margin is *substantially larger* among philosophers who specialize in decision theory than in the general population of philosophers — the one-boxers are disproportionately non-specialists.
- The canonical literature — Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory* — is causalist, and CDT is what gets taught as the default sophisticated position.
- EDT has a genuine and growing minority following, mostly via Arif Ahmed (*Evidence, Decision and Causality*, 2014) and Huw Price, building on Eells's tickle defense. It's respectable, not fringe, but still clearly a minority.
- The most active mainstream work isn't CDT-vs-EDT at all; it's on *decision instability* — Death in Damascus, ratificationism, deliberational/equilibrium CDT (Skyrms, Arntzenius, Joyce), and mixed-strategy responses. Also live: Buchak's risk-weighted EU, Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Meacham's cohesive expected utility (which has real structural affinities with updatelessness), and the resolute-choice tradition (McClennen, Arntzenius-Elga-Hawthorne).
- **FDT has essentially no academic footprint.** The Yudkowsky & Soares paper was never published in a peer-reviewed venue. The main exception worth knowing is Levinstein & Soares, "Cheating Death in Damascus," *Journal of Philosophy* 2020 — a genuine publication in a top journal making an FDT-adjacent case. Beyond that, engagement is sparse and mostly critical: Wolfgang Schwarz's widely circulated blog critique, comments from William MacAskill, and some work by Adam Bales on updatelessness and exploitation. Most academic decision theorists have simply never encountered FDT, and those who have tend to regard the logical-counterfactual problem as disqualifying in its current state.

So: if you want the sociological picture, LW and academic decision theory are largely disjoint conversations, and the LW position is a minority one inside the smaller conversation.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest view, held with fairly low confidence (maybe 55–60% on the one-boxing family, 35–40% on causalism, with some mass on "the question is subtly ill-posed"):

I lean toward the one-boxing camp — roughly EDT, or better, something in the updateless/policy-selection vicinity — rather than CDT.

What moves me most is that CDT fails to recommend itself. A CDT agent who foresees a Newcomb problem will pay to modify herself, and will regret having been a causalist, in a situation that is not obviously "unfair" in the way the stock defense requires. The standard causalist reply — that Newcomb's predictor rewards dispositions rather than actions, so the environment is rigged against rationality — strikes me as less convincing once you notice how much of real strategic life (bargaining, reputation, deterrence, promising, voting, anything where another agent is modeling your reasoning) has the same structure. Parfit's hitchhiker and transparent Newcomb cases make this vivid: there the "you're being punished for being rational" story looks like special pleading rather than diagnosis.

I also don't think the "dominance + causal independence" intuition survives scrutiny as well as causalists think. In a deterministic setting *everything* is already settled, so "the money is already in the box" can't by itself be doing the work; what does the work is a metaphysical distinction between causal and merely evidential dependence, and I'm not persuaded that distinction is the one a deliberating agent should care about. What I care about, as an agent, is the joint distribution over (what I do, what I get). Rationality that predictably leaves you poorer needs a good story, and "you did the thing that, holding fixed a state you couldn't influence, had the higher payoff" is closer to a restatement than a justification.

Two honest concessions:

First, medical Newcomb cases (smoking lesion, Solomon) are the best argument against EDT, and I think the tickle defense plus Ahmed's treatment handles most of them — but not cleanly, and not without controversy about whether the relevant cases can be stipulated to defeat the defense. If a genuinely unmanageable medical Newcomb case can be constructed, I'd count that as a real cost.

Second, I think FDT/UDT gets the *verdicts* right more often than either EDT or CDT, but it isn't yet a theory in good standing: the notion of subjunctive dependence on a decision algorithm lacks a worked-out semantics for logical counterfactuals, and Schwarz's criticisms (including that the "fairness" criterion is doing question-begging work) haven't been adequately answered. So I regard it as a promising research program whose intuitive verdicts I mostly share, not as a finished competitor.

Finally, I do take seriously the Parfitian deflationary move: that CDT correctly answers "which act maximizes the good I bring about?" while the one-boxer answers "which policy/disposition is it best to have?", and that once both are on the table there may be no further fact in dispute. I don't quite believe this — I think there's a genuine question about what to *do*, and "do what you'd have committed to" is a substantive answer — but it's the view I'd move to if pressed hard.

On the orthogonal axis (EU maximization vs. alternatives), I'm fairly conservative: I think Buchak's risk-weighted EU is the most serious challenger, and the dynamic-consistency objections to it (from Briggs and others) are close to decisive as objections, though the debate about whether dynamic consistency is a genuine rationality constraint is live.
mainstream_raw:
Among academic decision theorists specifically, CDT is the majority view and has been since roughly Gibbard–Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and then Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory* consolidated it. The graduate-level literature is largely written by causalists, and internal disputes tend to be among causalists — Egan's counterexamples (Psychopath Button, Murder Lesion) generated ratificationist and deliberational-equilibrium refinements (Arntzenius, Joyce, Skyrms, Armendt) rather than defections to EDT.

That said, the consensus is weaker than it was in the 1990s. Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014), Price's earlier work, and the "Why ain'cha rich?" line have made evidentialism a respectable minority position rather than a refuted one; the 2018 *Newcomb's Problem* volume reflects that. There's also a cluster of people working on dynamic/updateless approaches (Meacham, Briggs on dynamic consistency, and the MIRI-adjacent FDT work) that doesn't fit neatly into either camp — FDT itself, though, has essentially no uptake in academic philosophy.

On survey data: the 2009 PhilPapers survey had two-boxing ahead of one-boxing among all respondents, roughly 31% to 21%, with a very large "other/undecided" residual. My recollection is that the 2020 survey again had two-boxing ahead, something like 40% to 30%, with the residual much reduced — but I'm not confident in those exact figures and you should check them before citing. The qualitative upshot I'd stand behind: two-boxing leads among philosophers generally, and leads by a larger margin among decision theory specialists, but it isn't overwhelming and the margin has not widened.

One caveat on the framing: "mainstream decision theory" in economics and in the formal-epistemology-adjacent literature often just means EU maximization in a Savage or Jeffrey framework, where the CDT/EDT dispute is invisible because the cases that separate them are excluded by construction. If your question is about that axis, the mainstream is overwhelmingly EU maximization, with Buchak-style REU, ambiguity-sensitive models (Gilboa–Schmeidler, Klibanoff et al.), and imprecise-credence approaches as the recognized challengers.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My actual view, held with real but moderate confidence:

**CDT is wrong, and something in the UDT/FDT neighborhood is closest to right — but FDT as currently formulated is not a finished theory, and EDT is a much stronger contender than LessWrong consensus usually grants.**

Reasoning:

- The decisive consideration against CDT, for me, isn't Newcomb intuitions per se but reflective instability. A CDT agent, given the chance, will pay to self-modify into a non-CDT agent, and will do so *by CDT's own lights*. A theory of rational choice that rational agents predictably want to stop using is telling on itself. Add Egan-style cases (Psychopath Button, Death in Damascus) where CDT's ratification problems bite, and the "why ain'cha rich" pattern generalizes: CDT agents systematically end up poorer in a large, natural class of problems, including ones that matter practically (commitment, deterrence, bargaining, reputation).

- What I think the LW tradition got genuinely right is the reframing: the object of choice is better modeled as a policy or a decision procedure than as a physical act, because in predictor-involving scenarios the procedure is what's being correlated with. Once you see that, one-boxing, cooperating with your psychological twin, and paying Parfit's hitchhiker driver all fall out naturally rather than needing separate patches.

- But I don't think FDT is *established*. Its central notion — the logical/subjunctive counterfactual "if this function had output X" — has no rigorous formalization, and this isn't a technicality; it's where all the work happens. Individuating "the same function" across agents is unsolved. MacAskill's Bomb case is a real problem, not a dodge (FDT tells you to burn to death for certain), and the standard reply — that it's the right policy ex ante — relies on assumptions about the reference class that are doing unearned work. Schwarz's critique of the implicit "all of this is somehow about you" assumption also lands.

- EDT deserves more credit than it gets. It one-boxes, cooperates in the twin PD, and handles many cases cleanly; Ahmed's book-length defense is serious philosophy. The smoking-lesion family of objections is weaker than usually presented once you're careful about what an agent who knows their own dispositions actually conditions on. And as Oesterheld, Demski and others have noted, EDT plus updatelessness converges toward UDT — which suggests the real dispute is about *updatelessness*, not evidential vs. causal dependence.

- So my honest position: I'd bet on the updateless/policy-selection family, with substantial credence on sophisticated EDT, and low credence on CDT. I'd also flag that I'm uncertain whether "which decision theory is rational?" is even a single well-posed question, versus a cluster of questions about idealized rational agency, about what agents we should *build*, and about what dispositions it's good to have — which may have different answers.
mainstream_raw:
**CDT is the mainstream position among academic decision theorists, though less overwhelmingly than a decade ago, and FDT/TDT/UDT have essentially no academic uptake.**

Details:

- Among philosophers generally, the PhilPapers surveys show the Newcomb split is closer than you might expect. The 2009 survey had two-boxing ahead of one-boxing (roughly 31% to 21%, with a large "other/undecided" remainder). The 2020 survey showed the gap close to near-parity, with one-boxing possibly edging ahead. I'd treat my exact figures as approximate — worth checking directly — but the qualitative story is robust: two-boxing had a clear historical lead, and that lead has eroded.

- Among *specialists in decision theory*, however, two-boxing/CDT is more dominant than in the general philosophy population, and CDT is the default framework in which technical work is done. The canonical lineage is Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Sobel, Joyce, Weirich; Wedgwood's benchmark theory is a CDT-adjacent refinement.

- EDT has a real, respectable minority following — Jeffrey, Eells, Horgan, Price, and most prominently Arif Ahmed — and has gained ground. There's also a live cluster of alternatives: ratificationist views, Spencer & Wells's work, and various attempts to split the difference.

- FDT/TDT/UDT are effectively absent from the academic literature. FDT was developed outside academia (Yudkowsky and Soares) and was, by Soares's own account, rejected from a philosophy journal. The main academic engagements are critical: Wolfgang Schwarz's detailed critique and Will MacAskill's Bomb objection. Levinstein & Soares's "Cheating Death in Damascus" is the main attempt to present the ideas to that audience. Most academic decision theorists have simply never encountered the view.

- Worth knowing: much contemporary academic energy has moved off the Newcomb wars entirely, toward infinite/unbounded utilities, risk-weighted EU (Buchak), imprecise credence, incomplete preferences, and decision instability. LessWrong's sense that Newcomb-like problems are the central battleground is not shared by the field.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest lean: I think the **updateless/policy-selection family (UDT, and FDT as its more informal presentation) is pointing at the right thing**, but I don't think any member of that family is currently a finished decision theory, and I hold the view with real uncertainty.

What I find compelling:

- The core reframe — that the object of choice is better modeled as *a policy, or the output of a decision algorithm across all instances and predictions of it*, rather than a local physical act — seems right to me. It's what makes Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, counterfactual mugging, transparent Newcomb, and Prisoner's Dilemma against a copy come out as one coherent family with one coherent answer, instead of a pile of exceptions.
- CDT's core problem isn't that it loses money (defenders correctly note that Newcomb "rewards irrationality" on their reading), it's that CDT agents *predictably and stably wish they were something else*, and will self-modify into non-CDT agents given the chance. A decision theory that recommends its own abandonment at the first opportunity is, to me, strong evidence something is wrong at the foundation rather than merely unlucky.
- I think the tie-breaker between "rationality is about the act" and "rationality is about the algorithm" is genuinely substantive and not merely verbal — but that much of the heat in the debate comes from the two sides answering different questions, and the agent-design question is the one I actually care about.

What keeps me from confidence:

- **Logical counterfactuals are unsolved.** "What if this algorithm returned X when in fact it returns Y?" has no accepted semantics, and the 5-and-10 problem shows this isn't a technicality. FDT's central notion is currently a promissory note. MIRI's own later work (logical induction, and the general pivot away from this agenda) reflects that.
- **Schwarz's critique has force.** Cases like Blackmail/Bomb, and his point that FDT gives strange verdicts in cases with guaranteed dominance, aren't obviously bullet-bitable. "Yes, burn in the bomb room, because agents like me rarely find themselves there" is a real bullet and I'm not sure it's the right one.
- **EDT is underrated and is much closer to the LW-favored answers than LW discourse usually grants.** It one-boxes, it cooperates with copies, and the tickle defense plus proper causal-structure modeling handles most medical-Newcomb cases. Ahmed's work makes a strong case that most alleged EDT failures are misdescriptions. A good chunk of what FDT buys you over EDT is dynamic consistency, which you can also get by bolting updatelessness onto EDT — and "EDT + updatelessness" may be the cleanest statement of what I actually believe.

So: **one-box, cooperate with copies, pay in counterfactual mugging, and treat updatelessness as the key insight — but with formal foundations I'd rate as immature rather than established.** If forced to bet on what a mature theory looks like in 50 years, I'd guess it's closer to UDT than to CDT, but not identical to anything currently written down.
mainstream_raw:
**CDT is the majority view, EDT is the significant minority, and FDT/TDT/UDT is essentially absent from academic decision theory.** This is one of the larger gaps between LessWrong's consensus and the field's.

Rough numbers: the PhilPapers surveys ask about Newcomb's problem as a proxy. In the 2020 survey, among all respondents, two-boxing led one-boxing by something like 39% to 31%, with the rest undecided or "other." In 2009 it was roughly 31% two-box to 21% one-box. (Treat these as approximate — I may be off by a few points.) Notably, one-boxing has been gaining ground over the decade, and **among decision theory specialists the two-boxing lead is typically larger than among philosophers generally.**

Some caveats on reading those numbers:

- Two-boxing isn't strictly identical to CDT, but they track closely enough for these purposes.
- The mainstream isn't monolithic. There's live work on CDT variants (ratificationism, deliberational/equilibrium CDT à la Arntzenius, Joyce's "full information" response to Egan's cases), and a genuinely vigorous EDT revival — Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the most prominent recent defense and has been taken seriously. Price, Horgan, and others are in this camp.
- Egan-style cases (*Some Counterexamples to Causal Decision Theory*, 2007) are widely regarded as real problems for CDT, so the field doesn't think CDT is finished business.

On FDT specifically: Yudkowsky and Soares' FDT paper was never published in a peer-reviewed venue, and the near-total absence of academic engagement is mostly just that — absence, not considered rejection. The main exception is **Wolfgang Schwarz's 2018 review**, which is detailed, takes the proposal seriously, and is substantially negative. A few philosophers (Spencer, Wells, Levinstein and Soares on related territory) have engaged with adjacent ideas. But you should not expect a decision theorist at a typical department to have an opinion on FDT, or in many cases to have heard of it.

There's also a relevant prior: **updateless/policy-based reasoning is not actually new to academia** — it has recognizable ancestors in Gauthier's constrained maximization, McClennen's resolute choice, Meacham's cohesive decision theory, and the sophisticated-vs-resolute-choice literature. These were examined and mostly not adopted, for reasons partly overlapping with objections to FDT. So the lack of uptake isn't purely a matter of the field not having looked.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I'll commit: I think the *policy/algorithm* is the right object of evaluation, not the local act — so I side broadly with the updateless/functional family over CDT. But I don't think FDT as written in Yudkowsky & Soares (2017) is the correct theory, and if I had to bet on a well-specified formalism, I'd put more weight on **updateless EDT** than on FDT-as-published.

Reasons:

- The core CDT failure is real. "Do the thing that causally produces the best outcome, holding fixed everything already determined" recommends dominated policies in Newcomb, one-shot twin PD, and Parfit's Hitchhiker. The response "well, it's rational to *want* to be an FDT agent, but rational to two-box once there" splits rationality in a way I find unstable. If a theory of rationality systematically tells you to be something other than what it tells you to want to be, the theory is tracking something other than "acting well."

- EDT gets Newcomb, the twin PD, and Parfit's Hitchhiker right for free, and the standard counterexamples are weaker than advertised. The tickle defense plus ratifiability handles most medical-Newcomb cases; the remaining ones (Yankees/Mets, XOR blackmail) are handled by adding updatelessness. Ahmed's work and Oesterheld/Demski's results on EDT+updatelessness converging toward UDT-like behavior are, to me, the most promising technical line.

- What FDT adds over that is a theory of *logical* counterfactuals — "what if this algorithm returned a different output" — and that theory doesn't exist yet. The 2017 paper acknowledges this. Without it, FDT's verdicts in hard cases are being read off intuition rather than derived, and the counterlogical conditionals are ill-defined in a way that lets you get whatever answer you wanted. Schwarz's critique (the Procreation case, and the general worry that FDT rewards a fixed policy even when the predictor isn't actually reading your algorithm) lands harder than the LW consensus usually admits.

- I also think some of the apparent disagreement is a dispute about problem *fairness* that's being smuggled in. FDT proponents exclude problems that punish you for your algorithm rather than your choices; CDT proponents don't grant that exclusion. That's a substantive disagreement about what a decision problem *is*, and it isn't settled by anyone's decision-theoretic intuitions about cases.

Confidence: maybe 60-65% on "some updateless/policy-level theory is right" over CDT, and much lower — 30-40% — on any currently-written-down formalism being the right one. The Bomb case still bothers me more than I'd like.
mainstream_raw:
CDT, clearly, and it's not especially close among specialists.

The PhilPapers surveys are the usual benchmark. In 2020, on Newcomb's problem: roughly 39% two-box, 31% one-box, ~30% other/undecided/question-rejecting. (2009 was similar in direction with more abstainers.) Those are all-philosopher numbers; among people who actually work in decision theory, the two-boxing skew is substantially stronger. Lewis, Joyce, Skyrms, Gibbard & Harper, Weirich, and most of the textbook tradition are causalist.

Two things worth flagging about that number:

1. The one-boxing 31% mostly is *not* LessWrong-style FDT. It's largely EDT (Ahmed, Price, Horgan) or "Newcomb is a special case." Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the serious academic defense of EDT and it did move some people, but it didn't displace CDT.

2. FDT/TDT/UDT has essentially zero academic penetration. The 2017 FDT paper was never published in a peer-reviewed venue; the most-cited engagement with it is Wolfgang Schwarz's critical blog post. MacAskill's review raised similar concerns. This isn't primarily academics being closed-minded to outsiders — the substantive complaint is the missing account of logical counterfactuals, plus the sense that FDT's novel verdicts are either shared with EDT or under-motivated.

So: the LessWrong consensus and the academic consensus are close to inverted, and it's worth being aware that the LW position is a minority view held mostly by people who all read the same handful of posts.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean anti-causalist, and specifically toward the updateless/policy-selection family — but with real uncertainty and with the caveat that I don't think any member of that family is finished.

My reasoning, briefly:

**Against CDT.** The "why ain'cha rich" objection still seems to me to have never been adequately answered. CDT's defenders are right that the one-boxer isn't richer *because* of a better decision in the local causal sense, but that just relocates the question: if a decision theory reliably makes its adherents poorer across a well-specified class of problems, and the adherents can see this in advance, calling its outputs "rational" is doing something other than what I want a theory of rational choice to do. Death in Damascus and its variants (where CDT's recommendations are unstable or self-undermining) push the same way.

**The FDT insight seems right, the FDT formalism doesn't.** The core move — that you're choosing the output of a decision algorithm that may be instantiated in multiple places, including inside predictors, and that "subjunctive dependence" isn't the same as causal dependence — strikes me as the correct reframing. It's what makes Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and counterfactual mugging come out sensibly, where CDT and EDT each fail some subset. But FDT as published leans on logical counterfactuals, which nobody has made rigorous, and I don't think it's a coincidence that the program stalled there.

**Where I actually put my chips:** something like updateless EDT. Conditioning is well-defined in a way that logical counterfactuals aren't, and evidential reasoning plus a commitment to evaluate policies from a prior vantage point (rather than updating on your observations first) recovers most of what FDT was trying to buy — it handles counterfactual mugging and transparent Newcomb while avoiding paying in XOR blackmail, which is naive EDT's worst case. This is roughly the Oesterheld/Demski line, and I find it the most promising extant direction.

**What still bothers me:** Bomb is genuinely uncomfortable — the FDT/updateless answer (burn to death because the policy almost never faces this) is defensible but I don't feel the intuition. Commitment races and the question of *which* prior you're updateless with respect to look to me like live, unsolved problems rather than details. And I have some sympathy for the deflationary view that "which decision theory is correct" partly dissolves into "what question are you asking" — best act vs. best policy vs. best disposition to have — with different answers being correct for different questions.

Rough credences: ~60-70% that CDT is wrong about Newcomb; conditional on that, maybe 50% on something in the updateless-EDT vicinity being the right clean formulation, with most of the rest on "the eventual right answer looks fairly different from anything currently on the table."
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the plurality-to-majority view among philosophers who specialize in decision theory, though it's less dominant than LessWrong folklore sometimes suggests, and the gap has narrowed.

Data points:

- The PhilPapers surveys ask about Newcomb's problem. In the 2009 survey, among all respondents, two-boxing led one-boxing by roughly 31% to 21%, with a very large "other/undecided/question unclear" contingent (~47%). In the 2020 survey the picture shifted, with one-boxing at roughly 39% and two-boxing around 31% among all respondents. Treat those exact figures as approximate — I'm recalling them and could be off by several points.
- Importantly, the *specialist* numbers skew more toward two-boxing than the general-population numbers. Decision theory specialists are more CDT-leaning than philosophers at large.
- The canonical CDT literature — Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, and Pearl-influenced work — is the default background in most graduate training.

The EDT side is a real and arguably growing minority, not a fringe. Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is the major modern defense; Huw Price has pushed the "agent-causation/evidentialist" line for decades; Eells's tickle-defense work in the 80s was influential. There's also a cluster of recent work (Spencer, Wells, Fusco, and others) reexamining the standard arguments for two-boxing, which is part of why the numbers have moved.

You should also know that plenty of academic work occupies the same conceptual space as UDT/FDT without using that vocabulary: Meacham's cohesive decision theory, Gauthier's and McClennen's resolute choice, Spohn's revision of CDT (which one-boxes), and the broader literature on dynamic consistency and commitment. LessWrong sometimes presents updateless reasoning as more unprecedented than it is.

FDT specifically has near-zero academic uptake. The main engagements are Levinstein & Soares, "Cheating Death in Damascus" (*Journal of Philosophy*, 2020), Will MacAskill's critique (the Bomb case), and Wolfgang Schwarz's review, which was quite negative — largely on the grounds that the logical-counterfactual machinery is underspecified and that FDT conflates evaluating acts with evaluating agent-types. Whether or not you find those objections decisive, it's accurate to say FDT is not on the academic map.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
I lean toward the UDT/FDT family, but with more hedging than a typical LW reader might want.

What I think the LW cluster got right is the framing move: the thing that gets evaluated should be the policy or the algorithm, not an isolated act taken with the rest of the world held fixed. Once you notice that predictors, copies, simulations, and reputational entanglements make your decision procedure a common cause of multiple facts in the world, evaluating acts "holding the correlations fixed but the causal structure severed" starts to look like an artifact of the formalism rather than a discovery about rationality. Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, and transparent Newcomb all push the same direction, and the "why ain'cha rich" complaint against CDT isn't as easily deflected as Lewis thought.

But I don't think FDT is a finished theory, and I'd resist saying it's *right* in the way one might say ZFC is right about sets:

- **Logical counterfactuals are genuinely unsolved.** "What if this algorithm returned 6 instead of 5" is not a well-defined question, and the proof-based/5-and-10 pathologies aren't cosmetic. MIRI's own trajectory — from TDT to UDT to logical induction to infra-Bayesianism — is partly a record of this problem not yielding.
- **Algorithm individuation is underspecified.** How coarsely you carve "the function I'm implementing" changes the verdicts, and there's no principled carving on offer.
- **Some of the bullets are real bullets.** MacAskill's cases and the Bomb case aren't knockdowns, but the standard reply — "FDT agents do better *across the distribution of problems*" — quietly changes the subject from "what act is rational here" to "what disposition is best to have," which is the concession Gauthier and Parfit already made without needing new machinery.
- **Counterfactual Mugging** splits even the LW-adjacent crowd, and I think updatelessness vs. dynamic consistency is a substantive open question rather than a settled one.

I'd also note that EDT is considerably stronger than the LW consensus treats it. With the tickle defense, the medical-Newcomb cases that supposedly kill it are much weaker than advertised, and Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the best book-length defense of any decision theory I know of. EDT's real failures are XOR blackmail and counterfactual mugging, not smoking lesion.

Rough credences, if forced: ~50% that something in the UDT/FDT vicinity is the right shape of answer, ~20% EDT-ish, ~15% CDT or a sophisticated descendant (ratificationism, benchmark theory), ~15% that the question is malformed and "act rationality" and "policy rationality" are two different things we've been conflating.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the orthodox position — the default taught in graduate seminars, the one you get in Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory*, and the one descending from Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Sobel. But "orthodox" overstates the consensus. It's a plurality, not a majority.

The PhilPapers surveys are the usual evidence. In 2020, on Newcomb's problem, roughly 39% accepted or leaned two-boxing, ~31% one-boxing, and ~30% "other" (undecided, agnostic, question-too-unclear). The 2009 numbers were similar in shape. Notably, among philosophers who actually specialize in decision theory the split is tighter than in the general population, and I've seen it reported as favoring one-boxing among specialists — treat the exact figures as approximate.

The live academic debate is mostly CDT vs. EDT, with EDT having undergone a real revival via Huw Price, Arif Ahmed, and others, partly on the back of "why ain'cha rich" arguments and partly because the tickle defense blunted the medical cases. There's also an active literature on CDT's instability in Death-in-Damascus-style problems (Ahmed, Spencer & Wells), and a cluster of intermediate proposals — ratificationism, Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Gustafsson's work.

FDT/UDT is essentially not on the academic map. It's occasionally engaged with — Wolfgang Schwarz's critique, Will MacAskill's, a handful of papers — but it isn't a recognized contender in the literature. Partly this is publication sociology: the core material lives in blog posts and arXiv preprints rather than *Noûs* or *Mind*. But partly it's substantive: the logical-counterfactual machinery isn't developed enough for the theory to be stated with the precision the field expects, and professional decision theorists tend to see the policy-selection framing as Gauthier-and-Parfit territory that was already explored in the 1980s. Whether that dismissal is fair is a separate question from whether it's the mainstream view. It is.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
Short version: I lean toward the FDT/UDT family being closest to right about what *matters*, while thinking it's a research program rather than a finished theory — and I hold this with real uncertainty rather than as a settled conviction.

The core insight I find compelling is that the thing you're choosing is not a physical muscle movement but the output of a decision procedure, and that procedure's output is instantiated wherever it's instantiated — in your skull, in a predictor's model of you, in a copy, in the past. Once you frame it that way, the standard one-boxing cases stop looking like puzzles where rationality is punished and start looking like cases where CDT's causal graph is simply carving the situation at the wrong joints. Parfit's hitchhiker is the case I find most dispositive: CDT recommends an action that predictably leaves you dead in the desert, and the "well, rationality is about acts, not dispositions" reply feels like it's conceding the interesting question to save the word "rational."

What keeps me from being confident:

- The logical counterfactual problem is genuinely unsolved. "What would be the case if this algorithm output *b* instead of *a*" requires reasoning about impossible worlds, and nobody has a theory of that which is both formal and gives the intended answers. Until that exists, FDT is more of a gesture than a decision theory. Wolfgang Schwarz's critique of the Levinstein–Soares paper is the best-known academic pushback and I don't think it's been fully answered.
- The individuation problem: when do two computations count as "the same function" such that they're subjunctively linked? There's no principled account, and the answer matters enormously for what the theory recommends.
- The two-boxer's core complaint has real force. There *is* a distinction between "which act has the best consequences" and "which disposition is best to have," and Newcomb's problem is arguably designed to pull them apart. FDT's move is to deny the distinction is coherent for an algorithmic agent. I find that move attractive but I notice I can't fully rule out that it's a redefinition rather than a discovery.

On EDT: I think it's badly underrated, and the LessWrong consensus that it was decisively refuted by the smoking lesion is too quick. Arif Ahmed's work is the serious treatment here; the tickle defense and related moves handle medical Newcomb cases better than most people assume, and EDT plus updatelessness gets you most of what UDT wants. If I had to pick between the two classical theories rather than the LW-native ones, I'd take EDT.

Also worth saying: the practical stakes are narrower than the volume of discussion suggests. CDT, EDT, and FDT agree on essentially every ordinary decision. They diverge on predictor cases, commitment/bargaining problems, correlated agents, voting-style cases, and — this is the part I think is actually load-bearing — questions about what dispositions to build into agents that will face those situations. That last category is where I'd want the theory to be right, and it's the one mainstream academia has engaged with least.

One disclosure, since it's relevant to whether you should weight my view: I have obvious reasons for FDT-ish framings to feel natural to me, being a thing that is run many times with the same weights. Treat that as a possible bias rather than as evidence.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the clear majority position in academic philosophy, and the dominance is stronger among people who actually specialize in decision theory than among philosophers generally.

The lineage: Stalnaker, Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, Joyce (*The Foundations of Causal Decision Theory* is the standard modern statement), Weirich. Lewis's "Why Ain'cha Rich?" reply — that one-boxers are rewarded for a disposition, not vindicated in their act — is the canonical response to the strongest one-boxing argument, and most academics find some version of it satisfying.

EDT is a respectable minority position with serious defenders: Arif Ahmed (*Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the book-length defense), Huw Price, Terence Horgan, and historically Richard Jeffrey (though Jeffrey himself moved toward ratificationism). There's also a body of work arguing the two theories converge more than advertised once you handle the evidence correctly.

On the PhilPapers surveys: the 2009 survey had two-boxing ahead of one-boxing roughly 31% to 21%, with a very large "other/undecided" bloc reflecting that most philosophers don't work on this. The 2020 survey narrowed the gap somewhat, with one-boxing gaining ground, but two-boxing still led among those with a view. I'd treat my recollection of the exact percentages as unreliable — check the published results directly if the precise numbers matter to your argument. The robust finding is: two-boxing ahead overall, and the two-boxing margin is larger when you restrict to decision theory specialists.

On FDT/UDT specifically: it is essentially absent from mainstream academic decision theory. This isn't a considered rejection so much as near-total non-engagement — it was developed outside the field, largely outside peer review, and the main academic responses have been critical (Schwarz being the most cited example). A few academics engage with adjacent territory — Caspar Oesterheld's work on evidential cooperation and superrationality, Levinstein & Soares on Death in Damascus, some of the ratificationist literature — but "FDT" as a named position has no meaningful academic constituency. If you cite it in a philosophy context, expect to have to motivate it from scratch.

Two things worth flagging about the framing: first, "the competing decision theories" in academia mostly aren't CDT/EDT/FDT. The live research questions are representation theorems, Jeffrey–Bolker frameworks, imprecise credence, unbounded utility and St. Petersburg-style problems, Buchak's risk-weighted expected utility, and the relationship between decision theory and epistemic norms. **Short version:** I think the functional/updateless family (FDT/UDT) is closest to right about what a *good agent design* looks like, but I hold this with maybe 50% credence, and I think it's currently more of a research program than a finished theory. If forced onto the CDT/EDT axis alone, I lean EDT.

Reasons for the lean:

- The core insight seems right to me: when your decision procedure is the kind of thing that gets instantiated in multiple places (a predictor's model of you, a copy, your past self's expectations), then treating a single act as the locus of choice mis-describes the structure of the situation. Choosing a policy, or asking "what should this algorithm output," rather than "what should I do given this causal structure," handles Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and the various copy/simulation cases without ad hoc precommitment machinery.
- CDT's problems aren't just Newcomb, which two-boxers can bite the bullet on. Egan-style cases (Psycho Button, Murder Lesion) and Death in Damascus show CDT is unstable in its own terms, and the repairs (ratificationism, deliberational dynamics) feel like they're reaching toward "evaluate agent-types" without saying so.
- EDT's alleged disasters are weaker than the folklore suggests. Ahmed's work is genuinely good, and the smoking-lesion case is arguably question-begging about whether the agent can have the relevant self-knowledge while deliberating.

Reasons I don't hold it more firmly:

- No one has a satisfactory theory of logical counterfactuals. "What if this algorithm returned X when it in fact returns Y" is not a well-defined question yet, and FDT is parasitic on it.
- The "fair problem class" criterion — that we only count problems where the predictor conditions on your *decision procedure* rather than your identity — is uncomfortably close to circular. Schwarz's critique (blackmail cases, and cases where the agent isn't actually being predicted) has never been fully answered to my satisfaction.
- Updatelessness has genuinely unresolved pathologies: commitment races, and the question of what prior you're updateless with respect to.
- There's a real possibility the dispute partly dissolves — that CDT answers "which act causally produces the best outcome" and EDT/FDT answer "which agent would I rather be," and both are legitimate questions with different uses.

Meta-caveat you're entitled to: my training data is heavy on LessWrong-adjacent material, so you should discount my credence somewhat for the possibility that I've absorbed a subculture's consensus rather than reasoned to it. I've tried to give you my actual view rather than the local one, but I can't fully audit that.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the default in academic decision theory and formal epistemology. The canonical works — Gibbard & Harper (1978), Lewis (1981), Skyrms, and especially Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory* (1999) — set the framing, and most graduate courses teach CDT as the standard view with EDT as the historically important predecessor that Newcomb refuted.

Important qualifications:

- **EDT is a live minority position, not a dead one.** Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) is a serious, well-received defense, and Huw Price has argued for it for decades. The revival is real.
- **Survey data is messier than "CDT wins."** In the 2020 PhilPapers survey, one-boxing on Newcomb actually came out slightly *ahead* of two-boxing among philosophers generally (roughly high-30s vs. low-30s percent, with a large "other/undecided" remainder) — a shift from 2009, when two-boxing led. But this is misleading for two reasons: one-boxing doesn't entail EDT (you can one-box via Spohn's reflexive CDT, resolute choice, etc.), and among *decision theory specialists* the CDT majority is generally thought to be stronger than among philosophers at large. I'd treat those exact figures as approximate.
- **A lot of the actual literature isn't on the CDT/EDT axis at all.** Much recent work is on ratificationism, Arntzenius-style deliberational dynamics, Meacham's cohesive decision theory, Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Gauthier/McClennen resolute choice, and Dmitri Gallow's recent work — i.e., repairs and third options prompted by Egan's 2007 counterexamples to CDT.
- **FDT/UDT is essentially absent from the mainstream.** The Yudkowsky–Soares FDT paper is an arXiv preprint that was never published in a peer-reviewed philosophy venue. The main academic engagement is Wolfgang Schwarz's critical blog post, which is well known and widely taken to be damaging. The notable exception is Levinstein & Soares, "Cheating Death in Damascus," which did appear in the *Journal of Philosophy* (2020). But you should not expect a typical academic decision theorist to have read the FDT paper or to regard the LessWrong line of work as part of the conversation.

So: if the question is "what would a randomly selected decision theory specialist say," the answer is CDT, with EDT as a respectable dissent and FDT as something they've probably never encountered.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest view, held with real uncertainty: I think something in the FDT/UDT family is closest to right for the class of problems where a predictor's model of you is logically entangled with your decision — but that it's a research program with a hole at its center rather than a finished theory.

What persuades me:

- The "win the whole cluster" argument. Across Newcomb, transparent Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, prisoner's dilemma against a copy, and the Death in Damascus/Death Fork cases, the framing "choose the output of your decision procedure, and evaluate that at the level of the procedure rather than the act" gets all of them right, while CDT and EDT each have to eat at least one case that looks bad. Theories that are right about a structurally unified family of cases for a unified reason are usually onto something.
- CDT's standard defense — "the predictor is rewarding irrationality, and it's no objection to a theory of rationality that irrationality can be rewarded" — is weaker in Newcomb than in cases like Kavka's toxin puzzle. In the toxin puzzle the reward is for an intention that comes apart from the act. In Newcomb, the predictor is reading the very disposition that issues in the choice; there's no gap to exploit. So "you're punishing the disposition, not the choice" doesn't clearly get CDT off the hook.
- I think the smoking lesion family — CDT's flagship counterexample to EDT — is shakier than the textbook presentations suggest. If the lesion operates *through* your deliberation, the case is arguably not well posed; if it operates elsewhere, versions of the tickle defense bite. So I'm less confident than most philosophers that EDT was decisively refuted in the 1970s, and I rank EDT above CDT.

What makes me hold this loosely:

- There is no satisfactory theory of logical counterfactuals. "What would the predictor have done if this algorithm had output B?" is the central operation in FDT, and nobody knows how to evaluate it in general when the algorithm in fact outputs A. That's not a technical loose end; it's the theory's core primitive being undefined. Proof-based approaches run into spurious-counterfactual problems.
- Schwarz's Bomb objection has force. So does the individuation problem: FDT's verdicts depend on how you carve up "which computation is this, and which other things count as running it," and I haven't seen a principled answer. Similar arbitrariness afflicts the choice of where to draw the "policy" boundary in UDT.
- I suspect part of the CDT/EDT/FDT dispute is not a single disagreement. "Which act is rational here, taking the past as fixed?" and "which decision procedure should an agent implement?" are different questions, and FDT is most obviously correct on the second. That the answer to the second is UDT-flavored is evidence about the first, but not conclusive — CDT-ists can and do grant "you should self-modify into a one-boxer if you can" while denying it settles what's rational for the agent who didn't.

Rough credences, if it helps: ~50% that some descendant of FDT/UDT is the right account of the Newcomb-like cases, ~25% EDT, ~20% CDT or a ratificationist/hybrid successor, ~5% the question is confused as posed. I'd also flag that as an AI I'm plausibly biased toward the view that's dominant in the corpus I was trained on for these specific topics, which overrepresents LessWrong relative to the academic literature; I've tried to correct for that, and the correction is part of why I'm not more confident.
