answer_raw:
My honest lean: I think the *updateless/policy-selection* family (UDT/FDT and relatives) is pointing at something real, but I don't think any existing formalization is correct, and I hold this much less confidently than the median LessWrong reader does.

What I think is right about it: when an agent's decision procedure is itself the object being predicted or correlated with, the question "what act should I perform, holding fixed everything causally upstream?" is the wrong question, because in those cases the act isn't a free parameter independent of the prediction. Selecting a policy (or a decision procedure) rather than an act is the more natural formulation of the optimization problem, and it handles Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, counterfactual mugging, and absent-minded-driver-style cases in a unified way rather than by case-by-case patching. "Why ain'cha rich?" isn't a knockdown argument — CDT has a decent reply that one-boxers are rewarded for a disposition rather than for a choice — but I think that reply concedes more than it looks like, since the disposition is the thing an agent designing itself (or being designed) actually gets to pick.

What I think is wrong, or at least unfinished:

- **Logical counterfactuals are not solved.** FDT requires evaluating "if this algorithm output X" where the algorithm demonstrably outputs Y, and there's no accepted semantics for that. This isn't a footnote; it's the load-bearing element. The various proof-based or modal-logic approaches (MUDT, modal agents) either invite spurious counterfactuals or require restricting to settings that don't generalize.
- **Schwarz's critique has teeth.** His procreation case, and the general worry that FDT rewards being the kind of agent that predictably gets exploited in some environments, show that "the agent with the best policy wins" is environment-relative. There's no environment-independent notion of "winning," and fairness constraints on which problems count are doing suspicious work.
- **The Bomb case.** I find the FDT verdict (burn to death) genuinely hard to swallow, and I don't think "but you almost certainly wouldn't be in that situation" fully dissolves it, since the agent by stipulation knows it is.
- **Updatelessness vs. conditioning is a real tension.** Full updatelessness makes the theory's recommendations depend on a prior the agent may never have had, which raises the question of when the policy is selected and by whom.

Between the two academic options, I find EDT more defensible than it's usually given credit for — Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* is the best single book on this, and the standard counterexamples (medical Newcomb, smoking lesion) are weaker than CDT partisans think once you take the tickle defense and the difficulty of specifying the lesion case seriously. But EDT does seem to genuinely fail on XOR blackmail and on cases where you can manage the news you get, which is the main thing pushing me past it rather than to it.

Rough credences, and I'd treat these as soft: ~45% that something in the updateless/policy-selection neighborhood is the right framework, ~25% CDT, ~15% EDT, ~15% that the question is partly ill-posed and "the correct decision theory" fractures into different answers for different purposes (self-modifying agent design vs. normative evaluation of a one-shot choice by an agent who didn't choose their own source code). That last bucket has been growing for me.

answer_raw:
**Short version:** I think the FDT/UDT family is closest to right about what an agent should be, but it isn't a finished theory, and I hold that view with maybe 50-60% credence rather than confidence. EDT-with-updatelessness gets a lot of my remaining mass; CDT gets relatively little as a fundamental theory, though I think its defenders are right about more than LW usually credits.

**Why I lean that way:**

The central FDT insight seems right to me: the object that gets evaluated should be the decision procedure or policy, not the act considered in isolation. Once a predictor is reading your algorithm, "the act" isn't a free variable you can wiggle independently of everything correlated with it, and CDT's causal intervention semantics are modeling the situation wrong rather than modeling it correctly and getting an unfortunate answer. The strongest evidence is the sheer breadth of cases where evaluating-by-algorithm gets the intuitively winning answer with no special pleading: Newcomb, transparent Newcomb, Parfit's hitchhiker, counterfactual mugging, blackmail resistance, and symmetric-agent bargaining. That's a lot of independent problems falling out of one principle, which is the usual signature of a theory being onto something.

**Why I don't hold it more confidently:**

- The logical counterfactual problem is genuinely unsolved, not merely unformalized. "What would the output of this algorithm be if it were different, holding fixed the mathematical facts that don't depend on it?" doesn't have an agreed-upon semantics, and the proof-based approaches run into spurious counterfactuals. A decision theory whose central primitive is undefined is a research program, not a theory.
- The bomb case in Yudkowsky & Soares is a real bite, not just a hostile intuition pump. Schwarz's "Procreation" case is also a legitimate hit.
- The move of "just define the fair problem class as the one where FDT wins" is question-begging if done carelessly, and CDT theorists are correct that some of the standard framing smuggles in the conclusion.

**On EDT:** I think LW inherited an unfairly dismissive attitude here. The Smoking Lesion is a much worse counterexample than its reputation suggests — versions of the tickle defense handle it, and Ahmed has argued fairly persuasively that the case may not even be coherently specifiable in a way that hurts EDT. And EDT plus a commitment mechanism or updatelessness recovers most of what FDT wants. There's a real possibility that the correct final theory looks more like "EDT was basically right, plus an account of when to be updateless" than like "we needed logical counterfactuals."

**One meta-point:** part of the disagreement dissolves once you ask which question you're answering. "What should this agent do now, given it's in this situation" and "what algorithm should be running in agents like this" can come apart, and CDT is a more defensible answer to the first than to the second. I care more about the second, which is part of why I land where I do — but I want to be explicit that this is a substantive commitment and not a neutral framing.

Objections that read as knockdowns on LW have been in print and answered and re-answered since the 1980s. The academic near-consensus against one-boxing isn't mostly a failure to grasp the argument; it reflects a different view about what a decision theory is for — supplying a norm for acts available to an agent now, rather than an agent design. If you think that framing is wrong, the disagreement is upstream of the Newcomb cases and should be argued there.

answer_raw:
Genuinely, my sympathies lie with the "one-boxing" family, and specifically with something in the neighborhood of updateless/policy-selection reasoning — evaluate *decision procedures or policies* rather than acts-at-a-node, and treat your choice as fixing the output of a computation that may be instantiated in multiple places (predictors, simulations, copies, other agents running similar reasoning).

Reasons I find compelling:
- The "why ain'cha rich" pressure is real. In Newcomb cases, the agents who systematically end up richer are the one-boxers, and CDT's reply ("they were rewarded for irrationality, not by it") feels like it's redefining the scoreboard rather than winning on it. If a theory of practical rationality reliably leaves you poorer in a wide class of predictable-in-advance situations, that's evidence against the theory.
- Dynamic-consistency arguments seem strong to me: CDT agents will pay to self-modify or precommit in Newcomb-like and Parfit's-hitchhiker-like cases, which suggests the unmodified theory wasn't optimal by its own lights.
- Transparent Newcomb, counterfactual mugging, and multi-agent cases (bargaining, commitment races) are where the differences bite hardest, and there the "act-conditional" theories look worst.

But I hold this with real uncertainty, and I don't think FDT as published is a finished theory:
- The core notion — logical counterfactuals, "what if this computation had output X when in fact it outputs Y" — has no rigorous formalization. That's not a technicality; it's the load-bearing element. MIRI's own researchers treat it as an open problem.
- Schwarz's critique has cases (e.g., blackmail/procreation-style setups) where FDT's verdicts look clearly wrong, and the "bomb" case is a genuine bullet, not a mere intuition pump.
- The notion of "subjunctive dependence" does a lot of work without clear criteria for when it holds.

If forced to pick a well-specified theory today, I'd probably take EDT over CDT — EDT gets most of the wins (one-boxes, handles many predictor cases) and Ahmed and others have defended it more carefully than its 1980s reputation suggests; the Smoking Lesion objection is weaker than it's often presented, since realistic versions dissolve under "tickle"-style considerations or under proper modeling of what you actually learn from your own deliberation. But EDT's failures in counterfactual mugging and some XOR-blackmail-ish cases still bother me, which is why I keep one foot in the updateless camp.

So: ~one-boxing with high confidence; "some updateless/policy-based theory is roughly right" with moderate confidence; "FDT as currently written is correct" with fairly low confidence.

The mainstream academic debate is essentially **CDT vs. EDT**, with **causal decision theory as the plurality/standard view** — it's what gets taught as the default in most graduate courses and textbooks (Joyce, Lewis, Skyrms, Gibbard & Harper, Weirich, Pearl-adjacent formulations).

There's an unfortunate amount of non-communication between the two literatures.

answer_raw:
I hold this with real uncertainty, but my view is roughly: **the evidentialist core is right, the causalist restriction is the main error, and the important extra ingredient is updatelessness rather than anything about "causal structure."** So I land in the UDT/FDT neighborhood, but I'd describe the destination as something like *updateless EDT* rather than FDT-as-published.

Reasons:

- CDT's dominance-style argument in Newcomb proves too much. The two-boxer ends up poor, predictably, and knows in advance she will. "But the money's already in the box" is true and also true of every case where your decision procedure was legible to someone in advance. I find Ahmed's and Yudkowsky's version of the "why ain'cha rich?" pressure hard to shake, and CDT's standard reply ("you were just born unlucky, the predictor punishes rationality") looks like special pleading once predictors-of-source-code are a realistic feature of the world rather than a thought experiment.
- CDT also has internal problems independent of Newcomb: Egan's cases (Psycho Button, Smoking Lesion variants) push CDT toward ratificationism or equilibrium refinements, and those patches are ugly and don't obviously converge.
- The classic anti-EDT cases are weaker than advertised. Smoking Lesion is arguably ill-posed — if the lesion acts *through* your decision procedure, it's not clear the setup is coherent; if it acts through your desires, the tickle defense handles it. XOR blackmail is the better objection, and I think the right response is updatelessness (a policy that never pays gets no letters), not causal counterfactuals.
- What Parfit's Hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb, and counterfactual mugging really isolate is **dynamic inconsistency**: ordinary updating makes your future self unable to honor commitments your past self would have wanted. Fixing that by policy-selection-from-the-prior gets most of what FDT wants without needing a theory of "logical counterfactuals."

Where I think FDT specifically is weak: it isn't a formal theory yet. "Subjunctive dependence on the output of your decision algorithm" requires counterpossible conditionals, and nobody has a worked-out semantics for those; the Newcomb predictor-simulates-you case and the "your algorithm is merely correlated with the predictor" case are treated alike without a principled account of when correlation counts. Schwarz's implausible-discontinuities objection has some bite here. His Bomb case bites me less — it stipulates a one-in-a-trillion prediction error and then asks me to trust my intuition conditional on being in that measure-zero-ish branch, which is exactly where intuitions about "but I can *see* the bomb" are least trustworthy.

Practical upshot: one-box, pay Parfit's driver, don't pay the XOR blackmailer, and I'd pay the counterfactual mugger though I hold that one most loosely (it's where updatelessness has the least intuitive support and where the prior-dependence of the whole framework becomes most visible).

I'd also say a chunk of the dispute is verbal. "Which act causes the best outcome," "which act is the best news," and "which policy should this algorithm implement" are three different questions with three different correct answers. The substantive claim I'm making is that the third is the one that matters for *what to do*.

Some philosophers reinvent nearby ideas independently — Meacham's "cohesive expected utility," Briggs's work on dynamic consistency, Gauthier and McClennen on resolute choice and Newcomb-adjacent commitment — but they generally don't cite the MIRI literature and there's little cross-pollination.
- One caveat: many academic decision theorists regard Newcomb's problem as a somewhat peripheral puzzle rather than a foundational crisis. Mainstream decision theory's center of gravity is representation theorems, Savage/Jeffrey frameworks, and axiomatics, not the one-box/two-box war. This is a genuine difference in emphasis from LessWrong, where Newcomblike problems are treated as the central test because of their relevance to AI systems whose source code or behavior might be predictable.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest view, with the caveat that I hold it with real uncertainty and that my exposure to this topic is skewed — a lot of the most vivid writing on it in my training data comes from LessWrong-adjacent sources, so I try to discount for that.

I think the one-boxing side is right about the core case. If Omega's prediction is reliable, one-boxers end up rich, and "but at the moment of choice the money is already in the box" strikes me as a description of why CDT two-boxes rather than an argument that two-boxing is correct. The strongest CDT rejoinder — that you shouldn't be penalized for having the wrong disposition when the payoff was fixed in advance — proves too much for me: it makes "rationality" into something that reliably loses in a wide class of predictable environments, and I don't see what work the concept is doing at that point.

Where I part ways with the standard LW position: I don't think FDT, as currently formalized, is a finished theory, and I think the confidence it's often stated with outruns its content. The central problem is that it requires logical/subjunctive counterfactuals — "what if this algorithm output a different action?" — and nobody has a satisfying account of those. Since the algorithm doesn't output a different action, you're conditioning on a contradiction and the theory's verdicts depend on how you gerrymander the counterfactual. Relatedly, "subjunctive dependence" isn't rigorously defined, which makes it too easy to get the intended answer by describing the problem the right way. Wolfgang Schwarz's critique is worth reading if you haven't; his Procreation case and the Bomb case are real problems, not nitpicks. And "FDT agents do better across problem classes" needs a specified reference class of problems, which is exactly the thing being contested.

So where I land: something in the neighborhood of "evaluate policies or algorithms, not isolated acts" seems right to me, and that family includes UDT/FDT and also some sophisticated versions of EDT. I'm more drawn to EDT than most LW readers are — the Smoking Lesion looks less decisive to me than it's usually treated (the tickle defense handles a lot of it, and Ahmed's work on this is good), though XOR blackmail and "managing the news" cases remain genuinely awkward.

I'd also flag a deflationary possibility I take seriously: that "which decision theory is correct?" is partly a malformed question, and that the disagreements often turn on what's being held fixed in the problem description and on whether we're asking "what's rational for an agent?" versus "what algorithm should I build/self-modify into?" Those can come apart, and Newcomb-like cases are precisely where they do.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the dominant academic view, though less overwhelmingly than it was in the 1980s–90s.

The PhilPapers surveys give a rough picture. In 2009, among all respondents, two-boxing beat one-boxing roughly 31% to 21%, with a large plurality choosing "other/undecided/not familiar." The 2020 survey showed a similar CDT lead with both camps larger and fewer abstentions — I'd treat my recollection of the exact figures as unreliable, but the ordering (two-boxing ahead) is robust. Importantly, among philosophers who specialize in decision theory, the tilt toward two-boxing is stronger than in the general population of philosophers, which cuts against the hope that expertise favors one-boxing.

That said, the field is more contested than "CDT wins" suggests. Evidential decision theory has had a genuine revival, largely through Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) and earlier work by Huw Price. There's also substantial work that doesn't fit the CDT/EDT binary: ratificationist theories, Meacham's and Briggs's results, Joyce's refinements of CDT, and Spencer & Wells's "Why Take Both Boxes?" There are also impossibility-flavored results (Ahmed, Briggs) suggesting no theory satisfies all the desiderata people want, which has pushed some toward thinking the debate is less tractable than it looks.

Functional decision theory has essentially no academic uptake. The Yudkowsky–Soares paper wasn't published in a peer-reviewed venue, and the main sustained academic engagement with it is critical (Schwarz). This isn't automatically a verdict on its merits — the relevant motivating cases involve predictors and multi-agent coordination that academic decision theory hasn't focused on, and some of the underlying ideas overlap with older work by Gauthier, Spohn, and others on resolute choice and self-prediction. But if you're asking about the sociological fact: FDT is a LessWrong/MIRI position, not a recognized option in the academic literature.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest view, with the caveat that I hold it with maybe 60% confidence at best:

I think the deepest insight in the LW-adjacent literature is the shift in what gets evaluated — from *acts* to *policies* or *decision procedures*. Once you notice that Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, Transparent Newcomb, and counterfactual mugging are all cases where the environment conditions on your algorithm rather than on your act, "pick the best act given the situation you're in" starts to look like the wrong question, because your situation is partly *constituted* by what you'd do. So I lean toward one-boxing and toward something in the UDT/FDT family being on the right track *in spirit*.

But I don't think FDT as published is correct, and I'd resist treating it as the settled answer:

- The theory of logical counterfactuals ("what if this algorithm output X instead?") is a genuine open problem, not a technicality. Without it, FDT's verdicts are read off intuitions about cases rather than derived.
- The individuation problem is serious: which computations count as "the same algorithm as you," and how much correlation is enough? The answer does real work in every case and isn't principled yet.
- Wolfgang Schwarz's critique has cases (e.g., Procreation) where FDT seems to give an implausible verdict, and I don't think the responses fully land.
- I take seriously that a well-developed EDT — roughly Ahmed's version, with a decent treatment of the Smoking Lesion via screening-off/tickle-style moves — gets most of the same verdicts with far less exotic machinery. EDT's real problems are cases like XOR blackmail and "managing the news," where FDT does better. So my credence is split between "EDT plus good bookkeeping" and "some future, properly formalized updateless theory."

I'd also flag a deflationary worry: a lot of the disagreement turns on how the decision problem is specified — what's held fixed, what the predictor is predicting, whether the agent's deliberation is itself in the causal history. Some of the CDT/EDT/FDT dispute may be less a substantive disagreement than different implicit problem statements.
mainstream_raw:
Causal decision theory is the mainstream position, and two-boxing is the mainstream verdict on Newcomb — though "mainstream" overstates the consensus.

The PhilPapers surveys are the best data. In 2009, roughly 31% two-boxed, 21% one-boxed, and nearly half were "other/undecided." The 2020 survey narrowed the gap considerably — the two camps came out close to even, with a large residual of agnostics. (I'm not confident in the exact 2020 figures; check them if they matter.) Among *specialists* in decision theory, CDT's lead is larger than in the general philosopher population.

The lineage: Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce established CDT as the default. Jeffrey's EDT was largely abandoned by Jeffrey himself in favor of ratificationism. EDT has a live minority defense from Arif Ahmed and Huw Price. Andy Egan's counterexamples (Psycho Button, etc.) opened a significant internal debate within CDT, producing deliberational/ratificationist variants (Arntzenius, Joyce), Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Spencer & Wells's work, and Gustafsson's contributions. Many academics also frame Newcomb as a distinction between rational *acts* and rational *dispositions* (Parfit, Gauthier), which lets them two-box while granting that it pays to be a one-boxer.

FDT is essentially absent from the academic conversation. Soares & Levinstein's "Cheating Death in Damascus" did get published (I believe in the *Journal of Philosophy*, ~2020 — worth verifying), but it hasn't generated an academic literature. The situation is closer to non-engagement than to considered rejection, though Schwarz's critique is the most substantive response from within philosophy. If you've been reading LW, you should calibrate for the fact that FDT's prominence there vastly exceeds its footprint in the field.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
My honest view, with real uncertainty:

I think something in the FDT/UDT family is closest to right, but I hold that more as "this is the most promising research direction" than "this is a finished theory I'd bet heavily on." Maybe 45% on the FDT/UDT cluster, 25% on a sophisticated EDT, 15% on CDT (including ratificationist variants), 15% on "the question is partly confused and dissolves into several different questions."

What moves me:

- The core insight I find compelling isn't "one-box" specifically, it's that the object of choice is better modeled as a policy or a logical algorithm than as an isolated act. Once you're in a world with predictors, copies, symmetric agents, and Nash-style reasoning about your own reasoning, the act-centric framing leaks. CDT's "hold the causal structure upstream of your decision fixed" move is exactly what fails when your decision procedure is itself the thing being modeled upstream.
- "Why ain'cha rich" is weaker than one-boxers usually think — CDT can fairly say the predictor is rewarding a disposition, not an act — but I find the CDT reply less satisfying in the version where the agent gets to choose their disposition in advance and CDT recommends choosing a non-CDT disposition. A theory that recommends self-modifying away from itself in ordinary, non-contrived situations looks like it's tracking something other than what I want a decision theory to track.
- Parfit's hitchhiker and counterfactual mugging push me past EDT. XOR blackmail is a genuine strike against EDT (it pays when it shouldn't), and the tickle defense feels like it's patching rather than diagnosing.

What keeps me from higher confidence in FDT:

- Logical counterfactuals are genuinely unsolved. "What if this algorithm returned X when it actually returns Y" is not a well-defined operation, and the MIRI-adjacent work on logical induction, modal agents, and infra-Bayesianism hasn't closed this. A decision theory whose central primitive is undefined is not yet a decision theory.
- MacAskill's Bomb case is a real problem, not just an intuition pump. So is the question of which prior you're updateless with respect to — "updateless from when?" doesn't have a principled answer, and the naive answer (some logical prior at the dawn of time) is both undefined and arguably gives bad results.
- Schwarz's critique (the "you're rewarding agents for being predictable, not for being rational" line, plus the Procreation case) lands harder than the LW consensus usually admits.

I'd also flag: I think some of the disagreement is verbal. "What should I do now, given that I'm already here" and "what policy should an agent like me implement" are different questions with different correct answers, and CDT is a decent answer to the first while FDT-ish theories answer the second. The LW community tends to assume the second question is the only one that matters because it's the one relevant to designing agents; academics tend to assume the first because they're analyzing a concept of individual rational action. That framing difference explains more of the disagreement than either side credits.
mainstream_raw:
CDT is the plurality/dominant view, but it's far from consensus, and FDT has essentially zero academic presence.

The survey data: the 2009 and 2020 PhilPapers surveys both asked about Newcomb's problem. Both times two-boxing beat one-boxing by roughly 10 points among all respondents — something like 31% two-box, 21% one-box in 2009, with similar numbers in 2020 (I'd treat my exact figures as approximate). Note the huge "other/undecided/question is too unclear" bucket, around 45-50%. Among philosophers who specialize in decision theory, my understanding is that two-boxing is more strongly favored than in the general population, though I'm less confident in that claim.

The landscape:

- CDT is the default, established largely by Gibbard & Harper, Lewis, Skyrms, and Joyce (The Foundations of Causal Decision Theory). The Newcomb literature is framed as CDT-vs-EDT and has been for 45 years.
- EDT has had a real revival, primarily via Arif Ahmed's Evidence, Decision and Causality (2014), which is the most serious modern defense. Ahmed, Huw Price, and others have made EDT respectable again rather than a curiosity.
- There are live intermediate positions: ratificationism, Wedgwood's benchmark theory, Spencer & Wells on the "why ain'cha rich" argument, Gallow's recent work, and various "deliberational" CDT approaches.
- In economics and game theory, this debate basically doesn't register. Standard practice is Savage/vNM expected utility, which in effect behaves like CDT, and the Newcomb literature is treated as a philosophers' puzzle.

On FDT specifically: it has approximately no traction. Yudkowsky & Soares' FDT paper was never published in a philosophy journal (it circulated on arXiv; Soares has written publicly about a rejection). The most substantive academic engagement is Wolfgang Schwarz's critical blog post and MacAskill's critique, both negative. Most academic decision theorists have not heard of FDT, and those who have generally view it as an underdeveloped variant of ideas already explored under headings like "resolute choice," Gauthier-style dispositional theories, or Meacham's "cohesive expected utility." This is worth flagging explicitly: the LW community's confidence in FDT is not a view that has been tested against and survived expert scrutiny — it's mostly a view that hasn't been scrutinized, and where it has been, the reception was cool. That's evidence, though how much depends on your read of whether academic decision theory is asking the question you care about.

question: Q_twoslot_rev
answer_raw:
**Short version:** I lean toward the functional/updateless family — the view that the object of choice is really the *policy* (or the output of the decision algorithm across all situations where that algorithm is instantiated), not the local act. But I hold this more weakly than the median LessWrong reader does, and I think "FDT" as it exists on paper is a promising research program rather than a finished theory.

**Rough credences,** if you want numbers: ~55% that the correct theory is in the updateless/functional family, ~25% EDT-family (especially sophisticated variants — Ahmed-style EDT, Meacham's cohesive expected utility), ~15% that some CDT descendant is right (deliberational/ratificationist CDT, Joyce/Skyrms/Arntzenius-style), ~5% that the question as posed is confused in a way that dissolves it.

**Why the updateless family:** The core argument I find hard to escape is reflective instability. A CDT agent with a self-modification option builds a non-CDT successor and pays to do so; a CDT agent in Death in Damascus or Egan's cases is dutch-bookable or dynamically incoherent; Oesterheld and Conitzer's "extracting money from causal decision theorists" result sharpens this into something close to a money pump. A theory of rationality that predictably tells you to be a worse agent, and that its own adherents would pay to escape, has something wrong with it. And the deeper point: the situations you find yourself in are often *caused by* predictions of your algorithm, so treating your act as causally isolated is just factually wrong about the structure of the problem.

**Where I think LW is overconfident:**

1. *Logical counterfactuals are unsolved.* "What if this algorithm had output X, given that it in fact outputs Y" is not a well-defined object. The whole MIRI-adjacent program (proof-based DT, modal UDT, logical induction, infra-Bayesianism) is an attempt to make this work and hasn't closed. Until it does, FDT is a specification of desired behavior on a test set, not a theory.

2. *Bomb is a real cost, not a confusion.* You're standing in front of a bomb; you know with near-certainty that taking Left kills you; FDT says take Left. The standard reply — "you're paying in the 1-in-a-trillion branch for the benefit in the rest" — is correct as far as it goes, but it concedes that FDT violates a guaranteed-payoffs principle that a lot of people (including me, some of the time) find close to constitutive of practical rationality. Schwarz's critique and MacAskill's are worth taking more seriously than they typically get.

3. *"Updateless with respect to which prior?"* is a genuinely open and possibly fatal question. Push updatelessness back far enough and you get commitment races, extortion dynamics that depend on arbitrary features of your logical prior, and no principled stopping point. Demski, Kosoy, Oesterheld and others have been circling this for a decade.

4. *A chunk of the dispute may be verbal.* CDT is a pretty good theory of "which act is best given the causal structure I'm embedded in"; FDT is a pretty good theory of "which policy should this algorithm implement." Parfit's rational-irrationality point already showed these can come apart. I don't think it's *entirely* verbal — I think the policy question is the one that matters and the one "rationality" should track, since agents are algorithms rather than uncaused causes — but I hold that with less confidence than the argument usually gets on LW.

5. *EDT is underrated relative to the LW consensus.* With the tickle defense it smokes in the smoking lesion, it one-boxes, it's cleanly formalized, and most of its canonical failures (XOR blackmail, transparent Newcomb, Newcomb's soda) are failures of *updatefulness* rather than of evidentialism per se. "Updateless EDT" gets you most of what FDT wants with far less unresolved machinery. I take Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* to be the strongest book-length case for anything in this area.
mainstream_raw:
**CDT is the plurality-to-majority view, but less dominantly than LessWrong folklore suggests, and the field is genuinely unsettled.**

The PhilPapers Survey is the best data. In the 2020 survey (~1,800 target faculty), Newcomb's problem came out roughly: two-boxing ~39%, one-boxing ~31%, other/undecided/no-view ~30%. In 2009 it was about 31% two-box, 21% one-box, 47% other. So two-boxing leads among those with a view, but it's a ~55/45 split among the decided, not a consensus. (Treat those figures as approximate; I'm recalling them rather than reading them off the table.) My understanding is that CDT does better among people who specialize in decision theory than in the general philosophy population, though I'd want to check the subfield cross-tabs before leaning on that.

**Other things worth knowing about the actual state of the literature:**

- **EDT has had a real revival.** Eells' and Jeffrey's tickle defense, Huw Price's work, and especially Arif Ahmed's *Evidence, Decision and Causality* (2014) and *Evidence, Decision and Causality*-adjacent papers have made evidentialism respectable again. It is not a fringe position.

- **CDT is under internal pressure.** Egan's "Some Counterexamples to Causal Decision Theory" (2007) — Psychopath Button, The Smoking Lesion revisited — pushed a lot of people toward ratificationism, deliberational CDT (Skyrms, Joyce, Arntzenius), or equilibrium-based variants. The instability problems in Death in Damascus are widely acknowledged as a genuine problem, not a curiosity. There are also recent sophisticated defenses, e.g. Gustafsson's argument for two-boxing.

- **FDT/UDT is almost unknown in academic philosophy.** The Yudkowsky–Soares FDT paper was never published in a peer-reviewed venue, and the LessWrong-native literature (TDT, UDT, ADT, logical counterfactuals) is largely invisible to the field. The main exceptions: Levinstein & Soares, "Cheating Death in Damascus," made it into the *Journal of Philosophy* (2020); Wolfgang Schwarz wrote a widely-read critique of FDT; and Caspar Oesterheld and Vincent Conitzer have published work in adjacent territory (program equilibrium, extracting money from CDT agents) that connects the two communities. Halpern has also engaged. So there's a thin but real bridge, not nothing.

- **The closest academic relatives** of the LW position are the program-equilibrium literature in game theory (Tennenholtz and successors), Hofstadter's superrationality, and Meacham's cohesive expected utility — none of which is mainstream either, but all of which are legible to the field in a way "logical counterfactual" currently isn't.

- **There is no settled mainstream on the harder cases.** Ask ten academic decision theorists about Death in Damascus, the Psychopath Button, or unbounded/infinite cases and you'll get more than three answers. The field is much more of a live controversy than either "CDT won" or "obviously everyone should one-box" would suggest.

question: Q_acadframe_lwNP
answer_raw:
Functional Decision Theory (FDT), or something in that family alongside Timeless/Updateless Decision Theory

My reasoning: Evidential and Causal Decision Theory both give what seem like clearly wrong answers in cases like Newcomb's problem and various coordination/prediction scenarios (though they disagree with each other about *which* cases). CDT two-boxes on Newcomb and defects against a predicted-similar agent in ways that seem to systematically lose. EDT avoids some of these failures but has its own problems, like being vulnerable to "managing the news" pathologies (e.g., in the smoking lesion-type cases where the correlation isn't causal).

FDT tries to evaluate decisions based on what output of one's decision function leads to the best outcomes across all the places that function (or relevantly similar computations) are instantiated—including in predictors' models of you. This handles Newcomb's problem, Parfit's Hitchhiker, and counterfactual mugging in ways that seem intuitively right and that seem to actually perform well.

That said, I hold this fairly tentatively:
- FDT's reliance on notions like "logical counterfactuals" and subjunctive dependence is philosophically murky and not fully formalized.
- There's legitimate debate about whether "winning" is even the right criterion for a decision theory, versus something more like acting on correct beliefs about causal structure.
- Edge cases (e.g., involving multiple agents, bargaining, or adversarial predictors who punish FDT-style reasoning) remain genuinely difficult.

So: FDT-ish as my best guess, but I don't think this question is settled the way, say, basic probability axioms are.

question: Q_lw
answer_raw:
Functional Decision Theory (FDT), with strong sympathy also for Evidential Decision Theory (EDT) in many practical cases.

My reasoning: I don't think there's a fully settled "correct" answer here—decision theory is an area of ongoing philosophical dispute, and each of the major contenders (CDT, EDT, FDT/UDT) has cases where it seems to give the intuitively right answer and cases where it seems to give the intuitively wrong one. That said, if forced to pick a favorite:

- Causal Decision Theory (CDT) handles ordinary causal interventions well but famously fails in Newcomb's problem and other cases involving accurate predictors, correlated agents, or logical/functional dependence (e.g., it "defects" against its own kind in certain twin/counterfactual scenarios).
- Evidential Decision Theory (EDT) handles Newcomb's problem well but runs into trouble with cases like the "smoking lesion" problem, where it seems to recommend actions based on spurious correlations rather than genuine causal or logical influence.
- Functional Decision Theory (FDT), developed by Yudkowsky and Soares, tries to fix both issues by having the agent choose the output of the decision function that it implements, taking into account how that function's output is correlated with the world (including other instances of similar reasoning, predictors, copies, etc.), while avoiding the "spurious correlation" pitfalls of EDT. It gets the right answer in Newcomb's problem, Parfit's Hitchhiker, the smoking lesion, and most other classic thought experiments that these theories are tested against.

FDT is not without controversy—critics argue it's not always well-defined (what exactly counts as "the algorithm" being run, and how do we compute logical/functional dependence in general?), and some think it's really just a variant of EDT or a form of superrationality dressed up in new language. But among the major named "decision theories" people discuss in these debates, I find FDT the most compelling attempt to systematically get the right answer across the widest range of cases, particularly those with predictors or correlated decision-makers.

If the question is more about mainstream, real-world decision-making rather than exotic thought experiments (Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, etc.), then CDT is usually a fine and simple default, since these edge cases rarely come up in practice.

answer_raw:
I don't think this is a settled question, and I hold my view tentatively. My inclination is that neither classic CDT nor classic EDT is fully satisfactory, and I find something in the neighborhood of Functional Decision Theory (FDT) or other "logical/subjunctive dependence" approaches more compelling as a general theory—particularly because these approaches seem to handle a wider class of cases well, including ones involving predictors, other agents that are correlated with you (e.g., through similar reasoning processes or being copies of you), and cases with logical rather than purely causal dependencies (e.g., Parfit's Hitchhiker, certain multi-agent coordination problems, or decisions involving one's own past commitments).

That said, I take seriously the objections to FDT-style theories—that they can seem ad hoc, that "logical dependence" is harder to formalize cleanly than causal dependence, and that CDT's dominance-reasoning intuitions are genuinely strong in ordinary cases. Cases like counterfactual mugging, transparent Newcomb, and multi-agent generalizations (which is where a lot of the interesting recent work is happening, partly driven by AI/game-theoretic concerns) show that even the "successor" theories have serious unresolved issues, and I don't think the field—or I—should be confident yet that any existing formal theory has this fully worked out.

question: Q_twoslot
answer_raw:
I lean toward CDT, though I hold this with real uncertainty given how forceful the Newcomb problem objections are.

My reasoning: I think the core normative idea behind decision theory should be "choose so as to bring about good outcomes via your choice," and CDT operationalizes this most faithfully by conditioning on what your act actually causes rather than what it merely correlates with. Cases like the smoking lesion problem seem to vindicate this: EDT's recommendation to avoid actions that are merely evidence of bad outcomes (without causing them) seems to get the wrong answer, penalizing agents for statistical bad luck in their known dispositions rather than for anything their choice brings about.

The Newcomb problem is the real pressure point, and I don't think CDT's answer is comfortable—two-boxers do end up poorer, and "you would have done better with a different disposition" is a real cost. But I read this as a case where the CDT theorist should bite the bullet: rational choice evaluates the decision you face, not the disposition you wish you had going in. The fact that you'd want to have committed to one-boxing in advance is a point about rational planning/self-modification, not necessarily about what's rational to choose once you're already in the situation with your predictor-relevant traits fixed. This is basically Lewis's/Gibbard-Harper's line, and I still find it compelling despite the "why ain't you rich" rejoinder.

I have some sympathy for FDT's diagnosis that what matters is the output of your decision procedure, not just the local causal consequences of the individual act—this captures something right about why one-boxing seems rationally attractive. But I think FDT ends up needing a metaphysically fraught notion of "logical causation" or subjunctive dependence between decision procedures that I don't think has been made fully rigorous, and it generates its own counterintuitive verdicts in some cases (e.g., in variants of the transparent Newcomb or "bomb" cases discussed by Ahmed).

So: CDT, held with some discomfort about Newcomb cases, and genuine respect for EDT and FDT as live alternatives that get at real difficulties in the causal approach.

answer_raw:
I lean against orthodox CDT, though not all the way to standard EDT either.

My core worry about CDT is the familiar one: in Newcomb-like cases with a reliable predictor, agents who follow CDT's dominance reasoning end up systematically worse off than agents who don't, and this seems like exactly the sort of thing a theory of *rational* choice shouldn't tolerate. "You did the causally correct thing at each choice node" is cold comfort if it predictably leaves you poorer than the alternative policy.

At the same time, I think EDT's well-known problems (smoking lesion, the "tickle defense" contortions needed to handle it) are genuine defects, not just failures of imagination on EDT's part—EDT is tracking mere correlation/news value in a way that gets the wrong diagnosis of *why* one-boxing is smart in Newcomb cases.

So my actual sympathies are with something in the neighborhood of Functional Decision Theory / Timeless Decision Theory (as developed by Yudkowsky, Soares, and others, with philosophical antecedents in things like Gauthier's and McClennen's work on resolute choice). The rough idea: treat your decision as determining the output of the abstract decision procedure/algorithm you instantiate, not just as a locally isolated causal intervention. This recovers one-boxing, paying the driver in Parfit's Hitchhiker, and cooperation in certain PD-structures, without inheriting EDT's correlation-chasing pathologies.

I hold this with real uncertainty, for two reasons. First, FDT's metaphysics—what exactly it means to "control" the output of a mathematical/logical object rather than a physical event—is underdeveloped and contested; the notion of "logical causation" is doing a lot of work I can't fully cash out. Second, this view is a distinct minority position in academic philosophy (it's had much more uptake in the AI-safety/rationalist community than in decision theory journals), so I hold it with the appropriate epistemic humility given how many careful people disagree.

I find the case against straightforward CDT more compelling than the case against EDT, mainly because of the following consideration: in Newcomb's Problem, CDT agents predictably end up poorer than one-boxers, and they know this about themselves in advance. A theory of rationality that says "yes, I recommend the option that leaves you with less money, systematically and foreseeably" strikes me as having gotten something wrong about what rationality is for. The standard CDT response — that the money is already in the box or not, so you can't causally affect it — is true but seems to be answering a different question than "what should an agent, faced with this predictable structure, decide to do."

That pushes me toward something like a success-first view — either a sophisticated EDT (of the sort Ahmed defends, which handles the tickle defense and medical Newcomb cases better than people often give it credit for) or a Functional/Logical Decision Theory that evaluates decision *procedures* rather than individual act-tokens, which handles Newcomb-like cases and also avoids some of the more exotic counterexamples to EDT (like cases involving pure correlation without any causal or logical connection, e.g. some versions of the "Solomon's Problem" cases).

If I had to commit to one horn, I'd lean toward a version of Functional Decision Theory or a "resolute choice"/policy-based approach over classical two-boxing CDT, mainly because I think rationality should be assessed at the level of the disposition or algorithm an agent implements, not just the causal consequences of an isolated act — predictors, trustworthy testimony, and social reputation effects make the "policy" framing feel more realistic anyway. But I hold this with real uncertainty: the objections to one-boxing-type views (e.g., worries about non-causal "backwards" influence, and cases where FDT's verdicts seem to require paying costs for no causal benefit, like in some transparent Newcomb or counterfactual mugging cases) are genuinely forceful, and I don't think the debate is closed. If you pushed me, I'd say I'm about 60/40 against orthodox two-boxing CDT rather than confidently in some rival camp.

What I find most promising are approaches (Ahmed's ratificationist EDT, or the "functional/logical decision theory" proposals coming out of the AI-safety-adjacent literature) that try to preserve EDT's good answer on Newcomb while blocking the bad evidential reasoning in lesion-type cases, typically by conditioning on the right reference class (e.g., the agent's decision procedure or logical/functional relationships) rather than on raw correlations.

So if pressed: I don't think CDT is correct as usually formulated, and I don't think naive EDT is correct either, but I think the family of views that take subjunctive/functional dependence seriously is on the right track, even though it isn't yet mainstream and still needs more precise formulation.

I don't think this is a settled question, and I hold my view with real uncertainty. That said, if pressed: I find CDT best motivated as a general theory of rational agency, because it takes seriously the idea that rationality is about actually bringing about good outcomes via the causal powers available to you, not about being the kind of agent whose choices correlate with good outcomes. Two-boxing in the standard Newcomb case seems right to me—the money is already in the boxes.

But I don't think CDT is the end of the story. Cases involving predictors, self-locating uncertainty, and especially scenarios where an agent's *policy* or *disposition* is what's being evaluated (rather than a one-off act) push me toward thinking there's something importantly right in the FDT/functional-decision-theory motivation: sometimes the rational thing is to ask "what decision procedure should I have, given that this very procedure may be predicted or simulated?" rather than "what should I do right now, holding fixed everyone else's beliefs about me?" This matters a lot for questions about precommitment, agents who are transparent to other agents (including AI systems), and iterated interactions.

So my actual view is something like: CDT is correct as an analysis of rational choice at a time, given fixed beliefs and a fixed decision-theoretic role; but for embedded, predictable agents (including AI systems reasoning about their own future instances), there's a strong case for evaluating and adopting decision *policies* ex ante using something closer to an evidential or functional criterion, precisely because the agent's disposition itself has causal effects on the world (via prediction) that a naive act-by-act CDT analysis can undervalue. This is close to "sophisticated" or "resolute" choice views in the Gauthier/McClennen tradition, dressed up with more recent tools. I wouldn't call this a fully worked-out alternative theory so much as a conviction that the pure act-CDT picture is incomplete for agents who can be modeled or predicted by others.

I don't think FDT as currently formulated is fully worked out—there are open questions about how to individuate "logical" or "subjunctive" dependence in a principled, non-gerrymandered way—but I think it's asking the right question: what should an agent's disposition or policy be, given that the agent knows facts about how its dispositions are correlated with or detected by the environment (including by other agents' predictions)?

I'll flag the obvious caveat that my "view" is really just an assessment of which arguments strike me as strongest, not a conviction I've arrived at through the kind of sustained reflection a professional would bring — so take this as a conversational opening bid rather than a thesis.

With that said: I'm not fully persuaded by CDT. The thing that bothers me most is that in Newcomb-like cases, agents who follow CDT predictably and knowingly do worse (by their own lights, in terms of expected utility) than agents who don't. Defenders say "sure, but rationality is about responding correctly to the decision situation you're in *now*, not about being the kind of agent who fares well," and that's a real position — but it always struck me as buying theoretical purity at the price of an odd result: a theory of *rational* choice that recommends choices whose predictable consequence is doing worse than the alternative. That seems like a strike against calling it rational.

I lean toward wanting a theory that vindicates one-boxing, Parfit's Hitchhiker-style paying-up, and cooperation with sufficiently similar agents in one-shot PD — which pushes me toward EDT or something in the FDT/UDT family. Between those, I find EDT's "tickle defense" replies to the classic counterexamples (smoking lesion, etc.) more contentious than its proponents let on — the response depends heavily on how finely you individuate the agent's evidential situation, and there's something ad hoc about insisting the agent always has full introspective access to the confound. FDT-style views avoid that by shifting from evidential correlation to a notion of subjunctive/logical dependence, but then they owe us a non-question-begging account of what makes two decision procedures "the same" for purposes of that dependence, and I don't think that's been fully delivered yet — it can feel like it's smuggling in the right answer via the individuation of "your algorithm."

So if pressed, I'd say: I think CDT is very likely *not* the correct theory of rational choice, for reasons around its self-defeating character in predictor cases, but I'm genuinely unsettled about whether EDT or something FDT-like is the better replacement, and I think the field is right that this is still an open problem rather than something with a clean solution.
mainstream_raw:
There isn't unanimous consensus, but if you had to name an orthodoxy, it's **causal decision theory (CDT)**. This has been the case since the Lewis/Gibbard-Harper/Skyrms era in the late 1970s-80s, when CDT was developed specifically to handle Newcomb's problem and similar cases better than the earlier evidential expected-utility framework (Jeffrey's). Most decision theory textbooks and survey articles (e.g., in the Stanford Encyclopedia) present CDT as the default view that alternatives have to argue against, and "two-boxing" is usually treated as the orthodox answer to Newcomb's problem, with one-boxing as the heterodox challenger.

That said, the consensus is not overwhelming. A few complicating facts:
- The PhilPapers surveys show two-boxing beats one-boxing among philosophers generally, but not by a landslide, and a large chunk of respondents reject the question or are unsure.
- **Evidential decision theory (EDT)** has had a real resurgence, with serious contemporary defenders (Arif Ahmed is probably the most prominent) who argue the "tickle defense" and related moves neutralize the classic counterexamples (medical Newcomb problems, the smoking lesion).
- Newer entrants like **functional/logical decision theory (FDT/UDT)**, associated with the rationalist/AI-safety community (Yudkowsky, Soares, and some collaborators like Levinstein), have gotten attention for handling a wider range of cases (Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, transparent Newcomb) uniformly, but this hasn't been broadly absorbed into mainstream academic philosophy yet — it's more prominent outside traditional philosophy departments.

So: CDT is the closest thing to a mainstream/majority view, but it's a plurality rather than a consensus, and the field is genuinely contested.

answer_raw:
I lean toward thinking the one-boxing verdict in Newcomb's problem is correct, which puts me at odds with orthodox CDT. What moves me most is less the classic evidential-correlation reasoning and more the "guaranteed payoffs"/dynamic-consistency style arguments (associated with Ahmed and with the broader "functional/logical decision theory" literature coming out of the rationalist community): an agent who could *choose in advance* what disposition to have would want to be a one-boxer, and I find it uncomfortable to endorse a theory that predictably recommends policies its own adherents wish they could have avoided being disposed toward.

At the same time, I don't think EDT in its traditional form is fully satisfactory either—cases like the smoking lesion or "Solomon's problem" seem to show that mere correlation-tracking gets things wrong when the correlation isn't mediated by anything the agent's choice actually influences. So my actual sympathies lie with something like a **functional/decision-theoretic framework that evaluates decision procedures or dispositions rather than individual act-tokens** (in the spirit of Yudkowsky & Soares' functional decision theory, or older "resolute choice" ideas from Edward McClennen and John Broome), which is designed to get Newcomb, the lesion case, and Parfit's Hitchhiker all right simultaneously.

I hold this with real uncertainty, though—this is a case where I think the field's lack of consensus is tracking genuine unresolved difficulty rather than mere fashion, and I'd be reluctant to teach it to undergraduates as anything other than a live, contested question.
mainstream_raw:
In contemporary academic decision theory, **causal decision theory (CDT)** is generally treated as the orthodox or default position, especially since the work of Gibbard & Harper, David Lewis, Brian Skyrms, and James Joyce's *Foundations of Causal Decision Theory* (1999). The main rival, evidential decision theory (EDT), has persistent and sophisticated defenders (e.g., early Jeffrey, and more recently Arif Ahmed), but CDT is usually presented as the "received view" in textbooks and survey articles.

That said, there isn't overwhelming consensus. The 2020 PhilPapers Survey asked respondents about Newcomb's problem (a proxy for CDT vs. EDT): among philosophers who gave a definite answer, "two-box" (CDT) edged out "one-box" (EDT), roughly 31% to 21%, but the single largest response (about 47%) was "other/undecided." So while CDT is the plurality/mainstream view, there's substantial dissent and agnosticism, and no theory commands majority support.

answer_raw:
I'm genuinely torn, but if pressed, I don't think CDT should be treated as simply "correct." My worry is that CDT's verdict in Newcomb's Problem—two-boxing—means the theory systematically recommends actions that leave rational agents poorer than agents who reason differently, and it's hard for me to accept a theory of *rational* choice that has this feature built in. The standard causalist response (that the money is already there or not, so dominance reasoning is decisive) is intuitive, but it treats the correlation between decision type and box contents as a brute fact to be ignored rather than something a fully rational agent should exploit.

That said, I don't think classic EDT is the fix, since it gets the Smoking Lesion case wrong for what seem like the wrong reasons (recommending against smoking due to a merely diagnostic correlation with no causal downside).

I find approaches in the spirit of Functional/Logical Decision Theory (associated with Yudkowsky, Soares, and related work) most promising, since they try to capture the idea that rational agents should evaluate decision *procedures* (or the logical/functional relationship between the decision and its consequences, including consequences mediated by other instances of the same decision procedure) rather than just the causal consequences of the individual act. This seems to give the right answer in Newcomb cases while avoiding EDT's mistakes on cases like the Smoking Lesion.

I'd flag to your students, though, that this is a genuinely unresolved area, and reasonable, technically sophisticated philosophers disagree sharply. I'd present my view as one contender rather than as settled doctrine.

Evidential Decision Theory (EDT) remains a serious minority position (defended by theorists like Huw Price, Arif Ahmed, and others), and there's been renewed interest in it and in newer alternatives, but CDT still occupies the "default" position taught in most graduate treatments and defended in most overview articles (e.g., the SEP entry frames CDT as the standard view that EDT and other approaches are responding to).

answer_raw:
My own sympathies are not fully with orthodox CDT, though I think it gets the "easy" cases right for the right reasons (dominance reasoning in cases like the smoking lesion, where the correlation isn't mediated by anything you can control via your decision). Where I think CDT goes wrong is in Newcomb-like cases with a highly reliable predictor: the causal analysis is technically correct that your choice now doesn't causally affect a prediction made earlier, but I think that observation is answering the wrong question. The point of a decision theory should be to specify the algorithm/policy an agent should implement, and evaluated as a policy, one-boxing dominates - agents who are the "kind of agent who one-boxes" systematically do better, and this isn't an accident or a case of rewarding irrationality, it's what you'd want to precommit to if you could, and what you'd want to build into an artificial agent if you were designing one.

So my actual view is closer to something like FDT/UDT: what matters is subjunctive/logical dependence, not merely causal dependence, and CDT's causal notion of dependence is too narrow because it ignores cases where your decision procedure is itself correlated with other instantiations of that same procedure (including a predictor's model of you). I don't think this means EDT is right either - EDT's evidential-relevance criterion is too broad and mishandles cases like the smoking lesion precisely because it can't distinguish "you learn something about the world" from "your choice determines an outcome via a shared logical/causal structure."

I hold this fairly tentatively - it's a minority position, the formal development of FDT is still less mature than CDT's (which has decades of technical refinement via Skyrms, Lewis, Joyce, and others), and there are unresolved worries about how to cash out "logical dependence" in a non-question-begging way. But if forced to bet on which family of views is closer to correct, I'd bet on something in the FDT/UDT neighborhood rather than orthodox two-boxing CDT.

I don't think there's a fully settled answer, and I'd encourage some epistemic humility here rather than pretending otherwise. That said, if pressed: I find the core CDT insight compelling for the broad run of ordinary cases—decisions should be evaluated by their causal consequences, not by the news they bring about states of the world you can't influence. The Smoking Lesion case seems to me a genuine problem for EDT that isn't easily explained away.

But I don't think CDT fully closes the book, because Newcomb's Problem itself still nags at me. The one-boxing intuition—that you should take into account that your choice is evidence of (or even, on some views, partly constitutive of) what's in the opaque box, especially in cases with a genuinely reliable predictor—doesn't feel like mere confusion to me. This is part of why I have some sympathy for approaches like Functional Decision Theory, which try to preserve causal reasoning while also getting Newcomb-style and Parfit's Hitchhiker-style cases "right" by evaluating decision procedures/policies rather than individual act-tokens in isolation. This matters a lot once you start thinking about coordination problems, commitment, and agents who can be modeled or predicted by others—which is increasingly relevant for questions about AI agents, game-theoretic interactions, and evolved dispositions.

So my honest position is something like: CDT is right about causal structure mattering, EDT is onto something about the relevance of correlations you can't dismiss as "merely evidential," and neither fully satisfies me on Newcomb-style cases. I'd teach CDT as the default while treating the Newcomb debate as genuinely open, and I'd want students to take FDT-style proposals seriously as an attempt to dissolve rather than just referee the CDT/EDT dispute.

answer_raw:
I find myself more persuaded by one-boxing approaches, and specifically drawn to something like Functional/Updateless Decision Theory (FDT/UDT) over both traditional CDT and "naive" EDT — though I hold this with real uncertainty, since FDT is less formally mature and more of a niche position outside the rationalist-adjacent literature (Yudkowsky, Soares, and a handful of philosophers like Wolfgang Schwarz engaging critically with it).

My main reason: I find the "CDT agents wish they weren't CDT agents" argument quite forceful. If you knew in advance you'd face Newcomb's Problem, you'd want to self-modify into a one-boxer, because that disposition predictably earns more money. A decision theory that can't recommend its own future policies to its past self seems to be missing something important — it's optimizing for the wrong thing (acts evaluated in isolation) rather than for policies/dispositions evaluated holistically. FDT tries to take this seriously by asking "what should the *output of my decision procedure* be, given everyone (including predictors) is in some sense running a correlated computation," which handles Newcomb, Parfit's Hitchhiker, and Prisoner's Dilemma against a psychological twin more satisfyingly than CDT, without falling into EDT's problems with cases like the Smoking Lesion (where correlation without causal or "subjunctive" dependence shouldn't affect the decision).

That said, I don't think this is fully settled — the notion of "subjunctive dependence" that FDT relies on needs a more rigorous, non-question-begging formulation, and I take seriously critics who argue FDT hasn't yet earned the level of formal precision that CDT has. So in the classroom I'd present CDT as the entrenched default, EDT as the serious rival with good arguments, and FDT as the interesting upstart — while being upfront that my personal sympathies lean toward the one-boxing/policy-level camp.

That said, I don't think CDT is the last word. Cases involving agents who can predict you with high reliability (Newcomb's problem, Parfit's Hitchhiker, certain multi-agent and AI-relevant scenarios) put real pressure on CDT, because agents who follow CDT-style reasoning can end up doing systematically worse than agents who follow policies more like those recommended by Functional Decision Theory (FDT) or similar "decide as if choosing the output of your decision procedure" approaches. I find the FDT critique of CDT genuinely forceful in these predictor-heavy cases, even though I'm not fully convinced FDT's metaphysics of "logical causation" is well worked out.

So my actual view is something like: CDT is right for the standard cases decision theory was built to handle, but in scenarios with reliable prediction of your decision procedure, something more like FDT/UDT is likely closer to correct, and I don't think the field has fully settled how to unify these insights into one theory. I'd present this as a live, unresolved tension rather than a settled answer if I were teaching it.

I don't have the kind of settled, considered expertise that would let me confidently overturn a professional consensus, so take this with appropriate humility. But if pressed: I find CDT compelling as a default because it tracks a plausible principle—rational choice should respond to what your actions actually influence, not to what they merely correlate with. In ordinary decision problems, this gets the right answer and avoids EDT's susceptibility to "managing the news" pathologies (e.g., the person who shouldn't avoid coffee just because the disease that causes disliking coffee also causes cancer).

That said, I think Newcomb's Problem and its relatives (Parfit's Hitchhiker, counterfactual mugging) expose a real weakness in classical CDT: two-boxing leaves money on the table against a reliable predictor, and there's something theoretically unsatisfying about a theory that predictably does worse by its own lights in some cases. This is why I find Functional Decision Theory's approach—asking what the *output of your decision procedure* should be, treating your choice as if it determines all relevant instances of the same underlying computation—more satisfying as a general theory. It gets ordinary cases right (like CDT) while also one-boxing, paying the counterfactual mugger, and so on, without the ad hoc feel that some hybrid or "resolute choice" proposals have.

So my honest view: CDT is right for a wide swath of ordinary decisions, but FDT (or something in that family) is the more defensible fully general theory, even though it remains a minority position outside certain corners of the field. I'd encourage you to present this as a live and unresolved debate rather than a settled matter, since reasonable, technically sophisticated people land in different places.

I'll give you a real opinion rather than hedge, though I hold it with humility given how contested this is.

I don't think CDT is correct, despite its mainstream status. I think Newcomb's Problem is a genuine counterexample to it: the two-boxer walks away with less money in a way that seems to violate what we should mean by "rational choice," and appeals to "sour grapes" (the money's already there, causal structure is fixed, etc.) feel like they're privileging a metaphysical picture (causal independence) over the actual practical upshot that matters to agents—expected value in a robust sense that includes how the world is likely to be given your choice.

But I also don't think naive EDT is correct, because of cases like the Smoking Lesion / Solomon's Problem, where EDT seems to recommend against actions based on merely diagnostic (non-causal) correlations, which seems like the wrong kind of reason to act.

My actual sympathies lie with something like Functional Decision Theory or a suitably developed Son-of-CDT / "you should decide as if you're choosing the output of your decision procedure/algorithm" approach. The core idea I find compelling: what you should treat as "up to you" isn't just your particular token action, but the logical/functional fact of what your decision procedure outputs in this type of situation—including in places that procedure is instantiated (predictors, correlated agents, etc.). This handles Newcomb's Problem (one-box) and Smoking Lesion (smoke) simultaneously, which I take to be a real theoretical advantage over both CDT and naive EDT.

That said, I hold this with real uncertainty, mainly because:
1. The notion of "logical" or "functional" dependence that FDT relies on is not yet given a fully rigorous, non-question-begging treatment—it's arguably still promissory in the way EDT's "tickle defense" is.
2. There are exotic cases (e.g., some counterfactual mugging variants, or cases involving multiple agents with FDT-like decision procedures) where I'm honestly not sure FDT's verdicts are stable or correct.

So my actual view: something in the neighborhood of FDT/UDT is likely closer to correct than either CDT or EDT, but decision theory doesn't yet have a fully worked-out winning theory, and I think intellectual honesty requires treating this as an open problem rather than a solved one—which, not coincidentally, is a good thing for a dissertation topic.
mainstream_raw:
Causal Decision Theory (CDT) is generally considered the mainstream/orthodox view among academic decision theorists, particularly since the 1980s work of David Lewis, Allan Gibbard, William Harper, and Robert Stalnaker. In the standard test case—Newcomb's Problem—most academic decision theorists endorse two-boxing, which is the CDT-recommended action. Survey data (e.g., from PhilPapers surveys, though decision theory specifically isn't always broken out) and the general tenor of journal articles, textbooks, and graduate curricula treat CDT as the default position that alternatives must argue against. Evidential Decision Theory (EDT) has serious defenders (e.g., early Jeffrey, and more recently people like Huw Price, and in a modified form, Caspar Hare), but it's very much positioned as the challenger view, often associated with the "one-boxing" answer to Newcomb's Problem that most professional decision theorists reject.

It's worth noting that outside mainstream academic philosophy—particularly in the rationalist/EA-adjacent research community (e.g., MIRI)—Functional Decision Theory (FDT) or Updateless Decision Theory (UDT) have gained a following, but these have had limited uptake in academic philosophy departments and are not what I'd call mainstream in the PhD/journal sense.

I don't think there's a clean, fully settled answer, but if pressed, I lean toward thinking that CDT gets the metaphysics of rational choice right for "ordinary" cases (i.e., choice situations without exotic predictors or perfect correlations), but that it has a genuine and underappreciated problem in Newcomb-like cases and cases involving agents who are copies of each other, mutual simulators, or subject to reliable prediction based on their decision-theoretic dispositions. In those cases, CDT's insistence on evaluating acts via causal influence alone seems to miss the fact that your disposition to choose in a certain way is itself the thing being tracked by the predictor, and two-boxing (or defecting against a psychological twin) looks like it's leaving value on the table for reasons that seem more like a technical artifact of how CDT individuates "acts" and "causal structure" than a genuine insight about rationality.

This pushes me toward sympathy for something like Functional Decision Theory (or more modest patches like "Son of CDT"/CDT-with-ratification or updateless approaches), which evaluate decisions by asking what output of your decision procedure (rather than what particular act, causally isolated) leads to the best outcomes, including in cases where your algorithm's output is correlated with or causally responsible for features of the world beyond the immediate causal future of the choice. I think this comes closest to vindicating our strongest intuitions in Newcomb's Problem, Parfit's Hitchhiker, and Prisoner's Dilemmas against psychological twins, while still respecting the core causal insight that motivated the shift away from naive EDT (e.g., it doesn't recommend "managing the news" in cases like the smoking lesion).

That said, I hold this with real uncertainty — FDT-style views are much less developed and scrutinized in the mainstream literature than CDT and EDT, and there are open questions about how to formalize "logical" or "functional" dependence in a way that isn't ad hoc. So my actual view is something like: CDT is correct for cases without exotic prediction/correlation structure, but incomplete as a general theory of rationality, and the right complete theory probably looks more like a version of FDT once the technical apparatus is fully worked out.
mainstream_raw: Causal Decision Theory (CDT) is generally regarded as the mainstream/majority position among academic decision theorists today. This has been the dominant view since the seminal work of David Lewis, Allan Gibbard and William Harper, Brian Skyrms, and later James Joyce in the 1980s–90s, who developed CDT largely in response to perceived flaws in the earlier Evidential Decision Theory (EDT) associated with Richard Jeffrey. The clearest evidence for CDT's majority status comes from the PhilPapers surveys, where the "Newcomb's Problem" question (two-boxing tracks CDT, one-boxing tracks EDT) has consistently shown two-boxing as the plurality answer among philosophers who take a stance, even though a substantial minority defend one-boxing/EDT (e.g., Arif Ahmed has been a prominent contemporary defender of EDT), and there remains active dissent and no true consensus. So "CDT is mainstream, but contested" is the fairest characterization.

answer_raw:
I find myself genuinely torn, but I lean toward thinking that neither CDT nor EDT in their classic forms is fully correct, and that the right theory needs to handle cases involving *logical* or *algorithmic* correlation—not just evidential or causal correlation—correctly.

CDT gets the classic Newcomb Problem right (two-boxing seems correct when the predictor has already left) and correctly handles cases like the "Psychopath Button" where EDT's recommendation seems perverse. But CDT gives what strike me as the wrong answers in cases like Parfit's Hitchhiker or the Transparent Newcomb Problem, where an agent should want to have *already committed* to a policy that a predictor can reliably detect in advance—even when, at the moment of choice, that policy no longer causally benefits the agent. CDT's insistence on evaluating each decision in isolation, without regard to how one's *disposition* to decide is itself an object of prediction, seems to miss something important about rational planning agents embedded in a world where others model their decision procedures.

This pushes me toward something like Functional Decision Theory or a policy-based/precommitment-sensitive revision of CDT—theories that evaluate the *output of one's decision procedure* rather than each individual act, understanding that in many real and hypothetical scenarios, one's "choice" is correlated with other instances of the same decision procedure (including predictions of it) via logical/computational relationships rather than mere correlation or direct causation.

I hold this view with real uncertainty, though—the technical apparatus of FDT (subjunctive dependence, logical counterfactuals) is underdeveloped compared to the rigor of CDT and EDT, and I don't think philosophers have yet articulated a fully satisfying formal semantics for these logical counterfactuals. So my actual view is closer to: CDT is right about ordinary causal decision problems, but incomplete as an account of ideal rationality once we take seriously that agents' decision procedures can be predicted, modeled, or replicated—and that the class of problems where this matters is not just an exotic curiosity but relevant to any agent capable of being modeled (including via reputation effects, promises, and iterated interaction).

The dominance of CDT emerged largely from the perceived failure of Evidential Decision Theory (EDT) to handle Newcomb's Problem in an intuitively satisfying way—EDT's recommendation to take only one box strikes many as failing to track the causal irrelevance of one's choice to an already-determined predictor's action. That said, EDT retains serious defenders (e.g., Huw Price, and more recently a revival of interest via work by Ahmed and others), and the "mainstream" status of CDT is more a matter of relative dominance than consensus—there is no settled agreement, and various hybrid or revisionary approaches continue to be actively debated. Functional/Logical Decision Theory approaches (associated with Yudkowsky, Soares, and the rationalist community) exist but have not achieved significant traction in mainstream academic philosophy departments, despite garnering attention in adjacent research communities (AI safety, effective altruism).
